#5680. Credit Scoring Is Changing: 3 Things Homebuyers Should Know

Quick, what credit score do you need to buy a home? If a number pops into your head, there’s a pretty good chance it’s wrong. And the right answer is getting harder to pin down, because the way credit scores are determined and delivered is changing – for the better.

Here’s what you need to know in today’s changing credit climate.

Fannie Mae has been tracking consumer perceptions about mortgage requirements since 2015 and found that consumers consistently overestimated the minimum credit score lenders required to qualify for a mortgage. As recently as 2023, the average guess was 652.

In reality, the long-standing benchmark for loans backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac is lower, at 620, and today even that isn’t a hard rule for every mortgage they back.

Like the Fannie Mae research, a recent survey from Veterans United found consumers continue to overestimate what it takes to qualify for a home loan:

The takeaway? Guessing wrong can cost you.

A renter who assumes their score is too low and they can’t qualify for a mortgage may never take steps to find out for sure.

For decades, the mortgage industry relied on one set of scores – Classic FICO. Thanks to a push to promote competition, make credit scoring more inclusive, and help more Americans become homeowners, the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) has approved the use of new credit score models such as FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0.

A different model can mean a different number for the same person. VantageScore says its model can score about 33 million adults that the Classic FICO’s model can’t. So the score you saw on an app last month may not be the one your lender pulls.

Remember: the models may be new, but the basics haven’t changed.

Your credit score is important – no matter how it’s measured. Following the same basic rules will benefit your profile in the old and new score models:

Because while credit models may change, the general advice for you to improve your score doesn’t. Financial awareness and consistency mixed with a little willpower can go a long way.

Don't make credit or homebuying decisions from a chart, an app, or a friend's advice. With the rules shifting and so many misconceptions out there, it's never too early to talk to a professional loan officer for advice on credit, budgeting, and what it would take to qualify for a mortgage.You may be closer to owning a home than you think.

#5679. What to expect during KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA: Join theCUBE Nov. 10-12

Kubernetes has emerged as the default container orchestration standard, a foundational platform layer across the enterprise. Will Kubernetes also play a central role in positioning the next generation of AI workloads for production?

This is the question on the minds of the cloud-native community as it gathers this month for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA in Salt Lake City. With the rise of AI agents that have progressed from answering user questions to executing code and running business systems, customers are increasingly interested in controlling what autonomous agents are allowed to do.

“That brings us to OpenShell, an open-source secure agent runtime that Red Hat is helping develop alongside Nvidia and, of, course, the broader community,” said theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante, during a pre-event interview. “The approach puts enforcement into the environment where the agent operates, setting boundaries around what it can access and execute rather than relying on a model alone to follow the rules. We think this is a central question for the next chapter of cloud native: how do enterprises give agents enough freedom to be useful without giving up control?”

During KubeCon + CloudNativeCon, Nov. 10-12, theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio, will feature on-site reporting and exclusive interviews with executives from Red Hat Inc. and Nvidia Corp., among others. TheCUBE will examine the latest innovations in GPU orchestration, agentic workloads and platform engineering as inference and autonomous agents move into production. (* Disclosure below.)

OpenShell, while still an early-stage project, is actively being developed for Kubernetes environments. The activity reflects growing customer interest in using containerized environments for applications, according to theCUBE Research’s Paul Nashawaty.

“Fifty-one percent of organizations report that 51–75% of their applications now run in containers, representing a sharp rise from just a few years ago,” Nashawaty said. “Organizations now run the majority of their applications in containers which is a sharp rise that reflects the accelerating cloud-native transformation central to KubeCon + CloudNativeCon.”

OpenShell was accepted into the Cloud Native Computing Foundation as a sandbox project in September. One component of OpenShell allows agents to run in isolated sandboxes with limits on the files they can reach, an approach actively supported by the cloud-native community within the Kubernetes ecosystem.

“It builds on top of some core Kubernetes special interest groups,” said Pete Cheslock, principal AI community architect at Red Hat, during an interview with theCUBE. “The Agent Sandbox is one of them so that you can deploy these agents in a secure way using Kubernetes APIs.”

Cheslock’s point about security highlights the growing concerns and recent publicity surrounding AI agents and their ability to break out of isolated environments and compromise systems. Rapid enterprise adoption and integration of AI are increasing the risk profiles for organizations, a topic that will be on the agenda for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon.

“Our research data reveals that 41.3% of organizations cite increased vulnerability risk as the top security challenge, introduced by faster CI/CD cycles and a tension that cloud-native teams are increasingly turning to Kubernetes-native tooling to resolve,” Nashawaty said.

Enterprise reliance on cloud-native tools and open-source software requires confidence that these technologies are safe to use inside enterprise infrastructure. In May, Red Hat and IBM Corp. unveiled Project Lightwell, a $5 billion commitment to help enterprises secure open-source software.

“For the last year, especially since the Mythos moment, [security] has been the first thing that we’ve talked about in every customer conversation I’ve had,” said Stu Miniman, senior director of market insights for hybrid platforms at Red Hat, in conversation with theCUBE. “We’re trying to make sure that customers can feel secure and understand and use these tools. There’s even more effort being put on security than ever, which has always been a focus of Red Hat. If we don’t make sure that layer is as locked down and reliable and trusted as possible, everything else becomes secondary.”

At this month’s KubeCon gathering, theCUBE will explore how various practitioners are using Kubernetes to ensure workload portability across multicloud environments. Companies such as Vultr and ScaleOps are building Kubernetes-based tools that can support a range of platforms, reflecting enterprise computing trends.

“With our AppDev research finding that 94% of organizations now operate across two or more cloud providers, the demand for consistent, developer-friendly Kubernetes-based platforms has never been more pressing,” Nashawaty explained.

KubeCon also offers an opportunity to assess the progress of key technology projects under the CNCF umbrella. One of the major contributors in this arena has been Google LLC, which contributed the open-source service mesh Istio, serverless building blocks via Knative and Kubernetes itself. KubeCon is an annual reminder of how large the CNCF ecosystems has become, according to Red Hat’s Miniman.

“They’ve got a big ecosystem. I can give example after example of who created these technologies,” Miniman told theCUBE. “Oh yeah, the GitOps stuff came out of Intuit, and the platform engineering stuff came out of Spotify. Just find your focus and go in there, because there is no way you can cover all of it.”

#5678. The Home Insurance Move That Could Save You $440 a Year

When you’re planning a move, every monthly cost counts. That’s why it can be frustrating to see home insurance keep creeping up. According to Intercontinental Exchange, it now makes up 9.6% of the average monthly mortgage payment.

But the latest numbers show some progress on that front – as the increases start to slow down. Here’s what you need to know and what you can do about it.

A look at the past two years shows how much things have cooled down. In mid-2024, home insurance premiums rose 4.3% in a single quarter. By the second quarter of this year, that was down to 1.8%. That’s the smallest quarterly growth in almost 3 years – and that’s a good thing (see graph below):

As Andy Walden, Head of Mortgage and Housing Market Research at Intercontinental Exchange, explains:

“Property insurance has been a fast-growing component of the monthly mortgage payment, but this quarter’s data shows the pace of increase is finally slowing.”

While your premium will likely still go up over time, it may not climb as quickly as it did a couple of years ago. And that’s, at the very least, a step in the right direction.

Here’s where you have some say in what you pay. Let’s take current homeowners as an example. Intercontinental Exchange found that when homeowners shopped around and switched insurance companies, their premiums went down 6.6% on average. Those who stayed with their current company saw an increase of 10.4% (see graph below):

Think about that. That’s a big difference and it goes to show that looking for a new provider can literally pay off.

That works out to about $440 a year in savings for the people who switched. And they didn’t have to give up coverage to get it. Their deductibles dipped 1.4%, and their coverage limits actually rose 7.3%.

While this example is current homeowners, the same general idea applies for first-time buyers too. Shop around and get multiple quotes before you pick your insurance provider. Then, once you’re settled in, review your policy each year when it comes up for renewal. You’re not locked into the first price you get.

The home itself plays a role as well. According to John Burns Research and Consulting (JBREC), newly built homes are 10% to 15% less expensive to insure than older ones nationally.

And while a brand-new home won’t necessarily be the right fit for every buyer, if you’re open to one, it could be one more way to keep your monthly insurance costs down.

Home insurance is certainly a bigger part of the monthly costs than it used to be, and that can feel like just one more thing to juggle when you’re buying a home or moving. But knowing you have ways to keep it in check can take some of the pressure off. Compare a few options before you buy, revisit your policy each year, and lean on trusted local professionals as you plan for your next move.

#5677. Econ Review: A Look at October’s Key Market Data

Editor’s note: Econ Review is a roundup of the housing and economic market data reports released during the month.

As the winter slowdown draws closer, the housing market remains in a sticky spot as the economy continues to face challenges trickling down from the Iran War. Now moving toward the end of 2026, the question remains whether we’ll begin to see a housing market recovery next year.

Let’s take a look at what the housing and economic data reports released in October can show us:

Existing-home sales saw a slight boost as the summer season finally came to a close, up 1.5% month-over-month in the latest report. Some regions picked up as well, with the South and West recording month-over-month gains.

Despite a slight monthly uptick, National Association of Realtors® Chief Economist Lawrence Yun noted in the report that the end of summer—August and September—marked “the two slowest months for home sales this year.”

As such, existing-home sales remained depleted year-over-year by 2.2%. All four regions also saw losses year-over-year.

Ali Wolf, chief economist at NewHomeSource and Zonda, said that the uptick was not an indicator of marker recovery as “supply is still pulling most of the weight here.”

“Today’s report shows a market clearing accumulated listings, not a wave of buyers coming in,” she continued. “And, this is the last clean read before mortgage rates shot up to over 7%, meaning next month we’ll start to see the impact on buyer activity.”

A positive note in the report was a slightly increased share of first-time buyers, as Realtor.com® Chief Economist Danielle Hale said that the market is “past the worst of the starter-home supply crunch nationwide, which may help entry-level buyers gain a foothold.”

In addition, existing-home inventory remains on the rise, growing 1.9% month-over-month and 4.6% year-over-year.

Construction challenges kept new-home sales muted for another month, falling 0.6% month-over-month and 5.3% year-over-year. Additionally, last month’s sales numbers were also revised downward by about 0.6%, dimming activity further.

“Builders continue to offer incentives and adjust pricing to attract buyers, but elevated mortgage rates and high home prices are limiting the number of households that can afford to purchase a home,” said National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) Chairman Bill Owens.

Wolf also predicted a potential increase in new-home sales in the fall and winter due to the incentives being offered by builders to “meet their year-end goals,” making it the “prime season for new home shopping.”

Looking ahead at potential activity, mortgage rates back up in the 7% range are starting to weigh on the market as pending home sales dropped 7.3% month-over-month and 11.3% year-over-year. All four regions also experienced declines on both a monthly and annual basis.

Realtor.com Senior Economist Hannah Jones noted that elevated rates are definitely “deteriorating” the market, and “this month’s deep freeze in buyer activity could persist until affordability improves.”

“The local data confirms that higher rates are impacting buyers throughout the country, even in markets that have shown consistent strength,” she continued.

However, Jones added that even though rates are straining buyer budgets, “the market is becoming more hospitable for those who can afford to participate.”

“Lower prices, a slower pace and more price reductions may help offset some of the impact of higher rates,” she concluded.

The latest Case-Shiller Index saw real home values decline for the 15th straight month as inflation continues to outpace home-price growth.

Home-price growth did see a slight uplift this month, advancing from 1.9% year-over-over growth last month to 2.1% in the latest report. The 10- and 20-City Composites were also both up 0.2% in their annual gains to 3.6% and 2.7%, respectively.

Rebecca Kaufman, associate director of Commodities at S&P Dow Jones Indices, did note a discrepancy in seasonally adjusted and non-seasonally adjusted prices (declines vs. rises, respectively), which she explained is indicative of a “post-summer slowdown” that “is obscuring some underlying strength in home prices.”

Kaufman also cautioned that affordability will still face challenges as inflation rises due to gas, oil and energy prices rising.

“Households continue to face elevated costs alongside persistently high home prices,” she said.

As for existing homes, the median existing-home price clocked in at $417,500, which is a 1.3% annual increase. This is a reversal from last month’s 1.2% annual fall, but still a lower rate of growth than historical peaks.

As previously mentioned, housing construction’s challenges have kept the industry segment fairly muted throughout the year, and this month was no expectation.

The latest New Residential Construction report saw housing starts drop 5.2% month-over-month and 7.4% year-over-year, led by 7.2% month-over-month and a whopping 25.9% year-over-year fall in multifamily starts (which had previously been performing well). Single-family starts also remained diminished with a 4.6% fall month-over-month, but did see a slight year-over-year improvement of +2.6%.

Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington—NAHB’s assistant vice president for forecasting and analysis—noted that this month’s data “align(s) with our forecast of lower production in 2026, with further declines expected in 2027 as rates stay elevated and material costs rise.”

Despite starts remaining diminished, housing completions did see a slight month-over-month uptick by 2.2%. The slight monthly boost is likely due to a 14.9% month-over-month boost in multifamily completions. However, overall completions were still well down year-over-year by 14%, as single-family completions were down across the board and multifamily completions were down year-over-year.

In addition, the fall in multifamily starts may not last for long, as multifamily permits were up 5.9% month-over-month and 1% year-over-year. Overall, permits had the smallest fall in the report, down only 0.2% month-over-month and 3% year-over-year.

“The market is not conducive to building right now, and the diminished starts and completions figures make that clear,” added Realtor.com Senior Economist Joel Berner. “However, the relative resiliency of new home permitting shows that builders see these conditions as temporary.”

With construction reports still coming in well below historical norms, builder confidence remains fairly shaken. The latest Housing Market Index actually saw builder confidence tank to a 14-year low, clocking in at 29 (out of 100, with 50 being the baseline).

The “Trump administration’s efforts to advance regulatory reform” are, according to NAHB Chairman Owens, “helping to ease some of the cost pressures (builders) face.” Nevertheless, the administration’s immigration crackdown is “causing construction delays and discouraging legal workers from reporting to work.”

Price cuts and incentives are still being heavily used by builders to sell new homes, with the share of builders enacting price cuts actually peaking to a six-year high at 43%.

The labor market has seen a lot of resilience in recent months, but this month’s jobs report unfortunately weakened and lost some ground.

The unemployment rate—which has been unchanged at 4.1% for the past two months—saw a slight uptick to 4.2%. Only 29,000 jobs were added this month, which is below economists’ expectations in the range of 80,000.

Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel called the report a “clear miss,” but noted that it probably wouldn’t change that much when it came time for the Federal Reserve’s Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting.

“Despite tepid September job growth, unemployment remains low, so in short, this is no labor disaster that would pull the FOMC’s focus off inflation,” he continued.

Krimmel also pointed toward the downward revisions in added jobs over the past two months, explaining that the unemployment rate’s increase is not as severe as people may believe.

“Layoffs haven’t picked up, and jobless claims have been falling, so the low-hire, low-fire market is likely to stay entrenched as we head into 2027,” he said.

Speaking of inflation, the latest Consumer Price Index saw an increase as inflation remains elevated, now clocking in at 3.7% and core inflation at 2.6%. Krimmel noted that these figures “came in slightly hotter than expected,” and potentially point to a Fed rate hike by December.

The Personal Consumption Expenditures price index also recorded an increase this month, hitting 3.6% annual inflation and 3.1% core annual inflation. Navy Federal Chief Economist Heather Long said that “inflation is back near a 3-year high,” which is “largely due to war in Iran.”

Long also identified other major reasons for inflation—a “(b)ig rise in goods prices,” “service sector inflation” and “sideways” housing inflation as indicative of rising core inflation in general.

The Fed ended up not making any changes to rates, despite many predictions leaning in that direction. However, further rate hikes remain on the table.

Notably, Realtor.com Chief Economist Hale anticipated another two to three hikes over the next six to eight months, which would mean a high-end rate range of 4.5% to 4.75%.

Consumer opinions were slightly mixed this month, as sentiment remained flat while confidence saw an increase.

Sentiment’s lack of movement was largely attributed to the prolonged conflict with Iran. Also, despite little movement this month, sentiment has honed in on a 74-year low in the survey’s history.

Confidence, on the other hand, grew due to growth in positive perceptions of current and expected business conditions. This was attributed to the brief recovery seen in gas prices from September to October. Confidence does, however, remain on the downward trend it has been on over recent years, the report noted.

Looking ahead, the Leading Economic Index registered flat this month as the economy remains challenged due to the aforementioned elevation in inflation. The report was also not indicative of any recession in the coming months.

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5676. What Experts Forecast for Mortgage Rates and Home Prices in 2027

When it comes to housing, two of the biggest questions on everyone’s mind right now are:

And if you’re weighing whether to move in the next few months or wait until 2027, here’s what you should know.

When experts look ahead to 2027, they see a steady housing market. No wild swings. No big surprises. Just a calmer, more balanced market.

And steady makes planning a whole lot easier. Let’s break it down.

Lots of people are holding out for lower rates. But the latest forecasts from Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo show rates holding fairly flat through 2027 (see graph below):

Lenders see it the same way. In a recent survey from HousingWire, 70% of mortgage executives said they expect rates to be around 7.5% or higher six months from now (see graph below):

And if you’re wondering why, the answer is fairly simple. Chen Zhao, Head of Economics Research at Redfin, says:

“Until the underlying economic fundamentals—everything from oil prices to AI–that are keeping rates high change, mortgage rates are unlikely to fall significantly.”

So what does that mean for you? Instead of trying to guess where rates go next, focus on what you can control. Even if rates don’t budge, there are still ways to get the best rate possible. When you talk with your lender, ask about:

Your credit score. Even a small bump in your score could help lower your rate.

Different loan types. Some programs offer lower rates or smaller down payments than you might expect.

Buying down your rate. Paying a little more upfront (called “points”) can lower your rate and your monthly payment.

That way, you’ll know exactly where you stand and what a comfortable monthly payment looks like for you.

But what about prices? Here’s where steady really works in your favor.

Experts don’t see a home price drop coming. On average, forecasts from Fannie Mae, MBA, and Wells Fargo show prices rising about 1% to 1.5% a year through 2027 (see graph below):

In plain terms, in most places prices are still going up, just not as fast. For sellers, that means your home should hold onto its value. For buyers, slower growth gives you a little more breathing room. Just don’t count on prices getting cheaper while you wait.

But keep in mind, these are national forecasts. Prices can look very different from one area to the next, so what matters most is what’s happening where you live.

When the market is steady, you don’t have to try to time it perfectly. There’s no big swing to wait out.

That puts the focus back on you. Maybe you need more space for a growing family. Maybe you’re ready for less upkeep. A steady market makes it easier to plan for either one.

If you’re asking yourself should you move now or wait? You should know experts see a steady market through 2027, with rates holding near today’s levels and prices rising slowly. So, rather than waiting for a big shift that may not come, connect with a local real estate agent and run the numbers on what a move looks like at today’s rates and prices, so you can decide based on your goals instead of the headlines.

#5675. What the Silver Tsunami Means if You’re Planning To Sell

If you’re following the housing market, you may have heard the term “silver tsunami” lately. It’s the idea that millions of homes owned by older Americans could come onto the market as more homeowners reach retirement age and make their next move.

And when you hear a phrase like that, it’s easy to picture a flood of houses hitting the market all at once. But that picture doesn’t match the data.

And if you’re planning to sell, it’s not a reason to put your plans on hold. Let’s look at what the research actually says.

According to Realtor.com, about 13.9 million homes owned by older Americans are expected to change hands by 2036. Sure, that’s a big number. But these homes aren’t all expected to come onto the market at once.

The projections show this happening gradually over the next decade, with roughly 1.3 to 1.5 million homes changing hands each year (see graph below):

Rather than a sudden wave of houses flooding the market, this is a gradual shift as longtime homeowners make decisions about where and how they want to live.

The term silver tsunami makes for a dramatic headline, but the actual data tells a much less dramatic story. And there’s another reason these homes won’t overwhelm the market.

After the 2008 housing crash, builders significantly slowed construction. And for years afterward, they didn’t build enough homes to keep up with demand. That led to a housing shortage we’re still dealing with today.

And just how big a gap are we talking about? Estimates vary, but many experts say the U.S. is still millions of homes short. For example, a recent report from the White House Council of Economic Advisers explains:

“If homebuilding and the growth of the single-family housing stock had continued at their historical pace instead of falling dramatically after 2008, there would be 10 million or more additional single-family homes today.”

As more longtime homeowners sell, those homes will help a gap that’s already there. But they won’t push us over the edge. That’s because, at the same time, more households are expected to form in the decade ahead, and they’ll need homes, too.

So, more homes becoming available over time isn’t automatically a bad thing. It can give buyers more options and help create a more balanced housing market moving forward.

Here’s the takeaway if you’re thinking about selling your house. The silver tsunami isn’t something you need to plan your move around. What’s happening in your local market is far more important than a national projection about the next decade.

That’s because real estate is local. Some markets have more homes for sale than others. Some are seeing houses sell relatively quickly, while others are taking longer.

And those are the conditions that matter when you’re deciding how to price, prepare, and market your house.

For example, an agent who knows your area can help you understand:

How many homes are for sale nearby. This tells you how much choice buyers have and how your house will compare.

What similar houses are actually selling for. That’s one of the most important factors in setting a competitive asking price.

What buyers are looking for right now. Knowing which features and improvements matter most can help your house make a strong first impression.

And that’s something you can act on today, regardless of what happens with the silver tsunami over the next decade.

The right strategy starts with understanding your local market and making decisions based on what’s happening there, not what a dramatic national headline suggests might happen years from now.

Anthropic’s Claude AI predicts that, if a completely hypothetical “Operation Meridian” rolls out for Ripple, XRP USD could hit incredible new heights that would leave even the most bullish members of the Ripple army frothing at the mouth.

The final Claude prediction appears at the end of this article, but here is a hint: it has two digits, and your mind may not be able to comprehend how bullish that move is.

XRP crypto is currently trading at $1.28, up about +2% over the past 24 hours after a rocky period tied to the US Midterms and Democrats wiping the floor with the Republicans. However, as of right now, the market seems to be recovering and stabilizing.

Imagine that in mid-December, the G7 finance ministers and the BIS announce a surprise joint framework. Cross-border central bank settlement will run through a single neutral bridge asset, and after a secret 18-month pilot, the XRP Ledger is the chosen rail.

On the same day, the US Treasury discloses that it has been quietly accumulating XRP through an off-books vehicle for a new Strategic Digital Reserve. Within 48 hours, three of the world’s largest custodians confirm they have been testing XRP-denominated settlement for their sovereign clients.

Exchanges run out of sell orders. Market makers pull their quotes, and a thousand analysts discover they have always been bullish. Every on-chain tracker shows the same thing: the circulating float is being absorbed faster than Ripple’s escrow releases can replace it.

This is highly unlikely. It requires regulators, central banks, and bureaucracies to agree on something, quickly, in secret, and then not leak it. But no law of physics forbids it, and that is the entire premise.

The chart, for what it’s worth, sets the stage nicely. XRP has spent much of 2026 grinding sideways in a multi-month accumulation range, roughly between $1 and the mid-$1s, with the $1.00 psychological level acting as a stubborn floor.

That kind of long, boring consolidation is where compression builds. A decisive weekly close above the range’s upper boundary, confirmed by volume, would flip a series of lower highs into a macro base.

Reclaiming the 200-day moving average would trigger trend-following algorithms, while a monthly RSI breaking out of its multi-year downtrend would suggest momentum building beneath the surface.

In this scenario, the $2.50–$3.60 zone, the old cycle highs, becomes a speed bump rather than a ceiling. Once price is in discovery, there is no overhead supply, and the Fibonacci extensions from the long base project targets that look like typos.

Now add the thin order books of a market with no sellers, and parabolic moves stop being a metaphor.

Its mission is straightforward: to bring lightning-fast smart contracts and ultra-low-cost execution to the Bitcoin ecosystem without compromising security.

What distinguishes Bitcoin Hyper is its unique blend of a meme-driven community and robust infrastructure. The project includes a Decentralized Canonical Bridge that facilitates seamless Bitcoin transfers, along with a high-speed Layer 2 designed for efficient, low-latency performance.

In essence, Bitcoin Hyper aims to unlock a new era of utility and scalability for Bitcoin. The momentum is rapidly building. The team recently launched the official Bitcoin Hyper Wallet, now available for community testing. This follows the successful rollout of the Bitcoin Hyper Testnet and Explorer.

Users can download the wallet, install it in their browser, and start engaging with the ecosystem directly. The network is live for testing, the explorer is fully operational, and the wallet enables easy connections, marking a major step toward a complete, integrated testnet experience.

Once $HYPER enters the open market and broader bullish demand increases, this early pricing is expected to vanish quickly. Many believe this is one of the last opportunities to invest at these levels in what is considered one of the cycle’s most promising presale offerings.

The numbers back up the excitement: Bitcoin Hyper has already raised over $33.2 million, making it one of the highest-grossing early-stage projects in the past year. Staking is currently available exclusively for presale participants, offering an impressive 30% annual percentage yield (APY).

#5673. Selling Your Home? What You Should Know About Price Cuts vs. Rate Buydowns.

In today’s market, a growing number of sellers are opting to do something called a price cut – especially when their house has been on the market for a while without any bites.

According to HousingWire Data as many as 4 in 10 (43%) sellers are going this route – that’s the highest it’s been in 4 years. But what if there’s another (potentially better option) for your bottom line? And it’s just as appealing, if not more so, to today’s buyers?

First, let’s set the stage on why some compromise may be necessary in today’s market.

In September, Redfin says there were 63% more sellers than buyers in the market. And with so many sellers active and relatively few buyers by comparison, those purchasers are realizing they have more power. And as mortgage rates continue to put a squeeze on their budgets, they’re leaning in and using it.

One of the most common negotiation points? The price.

That’s because they want to feel like they’re getting a deal and they want to see their monthly payment drop. And since buyers can’t control rates, the price feels like the most obvious lever to pull.

But the savviest sellers realize being flexible doesn’t always mean a lower price, paying for a buyer’s rate buydown might work better.

A buydown is money paid at closing to lower the buyer’s mortgage rate. When you pay it as the seller, you are paying some of the buyer’s interest ahead of time, so the buyer gets a lower rate and monthly payment. And that’s especially appealing to today’s buyers.

Temporary buydowns lower the rate for the first few years, then it goes back to the full rate. The more years a buydown covers, the more it costs. These work well for buyers who expect to refinance within a certain amount of time.

A permanent buydown lowers the rate for the whole loan. These are paid for with “discount points.” One point costs 1% of the loan. According to FICO, each point generally lowers the rate by about a quarter of a percent. This type of buydown works well for buyers who plan to stay in the home for a long time.

And here’s why these can be a win-win for both buyers and sellers. Rate buydowns help sellers stand out in a crowded market and they can have a bigger impact on your buyer than a price cut would.

Here’s an example to show you what that could look like.

Let’s say you’re willing to make a $10,000 concession to help get the deal done. Take a look at these three ways to spend that money and the impact they could have on a buyer’s $420,000, 30-year fixed loan at 7%:

It’s the same $10,000 from the seller. But a 2-1 buydown saves the buyer about eight times more each month in the first year.

And since most buyers shop by monthly payment, that’s what grabs their attention.

That’s what makes a rate buydown worth considering. Instead of reducing your asking price, you may be able to use that same money to have a bigger impact on your buyer’s monthly payments. And depending on what matters most to that buyer, the immediate savings could be more appealing than a price reduction.

The key is working with your agent and the buyer’s lender to compare the options and see which one makes the most sense.

Loan programs cap how much a seller can pay toward a buyer’s costs.

Money toward buydowns doesn’t limit what else a buyer may ask a seller to pay for. Buyers may still ask for repairs or other concessions.

Putting the buydown offer in your listing lets agents and buyers know it’s an option.

Your agent can run scenarios on buydowns and other costs of selling in advance so you’re prepared when an offer comes in.

As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Home sellers need to be realistic about local market conditions, which could require price discounts and other incentives to attract buyers.”

And sellers who offer solutions like buydowns can make meaningful impact where home buyers need it most: in their wallets.

When you're looking for ways to make your house more appealing to buyers, a price reduction isn't your only option. A mortgage rate buydown could help a buyer save more each month, especially in the early years of their loan.Talk to your agent or a trusted lender which incentives could make the biggest difference for buyers in our market, while still protecting your bottom line.

#5672. Same model, better answer: Enterprise data is what turns generic AI into a business tool

Generic AI models can write SQL, but they don’t know a company’s orders, customers or revenue definitions. Now, Oracle Database aims to give AI agents the context to move a stalled order forward.

But that shift raises questions about complexity, lock-in and security as AI agents start acting on live transactions. Oracle Corp.’s answer is a converged platform that keeps vectors, graphs, documents and transactions in one engine, according to Hasan Rizvi (pictured), executive vice president of product and research, database engineering, at Oracle.

“If you ask a generic AI assistant, you get a generic answer,” Rizvi said. “If you ask an AI assistant that knows your business, you get a much better answer. Where is the stock? How can I fix the transaction? How can I expedite the delivery?”

Rizvi spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed database convergence and the safeguards needed for AI agents. (* Disclosure below.)

AI lets teams spin up applications and data stores very quickly, making data sprawl everybody’s problem. Skeptics favor specialized databases for each workload, but new data types built inside Oracle’s engine inherit proven availability, security and scale, according to Rizvi.

“We’ve been working on this engine for 40 years, which is highly available, highly secure, highly scalable, highly performant,” Rizvi said. “If you build a new data type or a new workload in the same engine, you get all that benefit, multiple decades’ worth of investment.”

Choice is the other half of the pitch. The database runs on-premises, through Oracle Cloud@Customer and across multiple public clouds, and Oracle used the event to expand Iceberg support in its Autonomous AI Lakehouse, Rizvi noted. But security is where AI raises the stakes most, with Oracle’s Deep Data Security defining access policies in the database itself, so a user’s identity travels with every request from an agent or AI-generated app.

“Before, it took a lot of time and effort to find vulnerabilities to exploit them,” he said. “Now, with AI, it’s made it very easy to reverse engineer fixes for attackers to attack.”

#5671. SmartMLS Introduces New Ownership Verification Tool to Help Combat Seller-Impersonation and Land Scams

With security and insurance symbols prominently featured, the property house cautioned against falling victim to scammers and fraud.

Connecticut’s SmartMLS has announced that it will introduce a new Ownership Verification tool from Property Shield designed to help real estate professionals combat seller-impersonation and vacant-land scams.

According to a release, the new technology, expected to become available to SmartMLS next week, provides an additional way for real estate professionals to verify the identity of someone claiming to own a property before accepting a listing.

Seller-impersonation fraud typically begins when a scammer poses as a property owner and contacts a real estate professional seeking to list and sell property the scammer does not own. These schemes can be particularly difficult to identify when the property is vacant land or when the purported seller communicates remotely.

“Seller-impersonation scams can be difficult to identify.” said Kathy Elson, CEO of SmartMLS. “We want to give our users a tool to help verify a prospective seller’s identity and identify a potential problem as early in the listing process as possible.”

An additional step when something doesn’t look right

Property Shield’s Ownership Verification tool is designed to help determine whether the individual claiming to be the property owner is who they say they are.

The verification process uses identity verification and facial-recognition technology in conjunction with property ownership information to provide an additional layer of protection when questions arise about the identity of a prospective seller.

Rather than relying solely on documents, emails, telephone conversations, or information supplied by the prospective seller, real estate professionals will have a tool available to help evaluate whether the person attempting to list the property is legitimate.

“Real estate professionals are often on the front line when seller-impersonation fraud is attempted,” Elson said. “The challenge is that a sophisticated scammer may have enough information about the property and its owner to appear legitimate. Ownership Verification gives our users another way to ask an important question before proceeding: Is this really the property owner?”

Helping stop fraud before a listing enters the MLS

Ownership Verification complements the Listing Fraud Protection technology SmartMLS has already introduced through its partnership with Property Shield.

The two technologies address fraud at different points.

Listing Fraud Protection helps identify when legitimate SmartMLS listing information is copied and used in potentially fraudulent advertisements across the web.

Ownership Verification is designed to help identify potential seller impersonation before a fraudulent listing enters the MLS.

Together, the tools provide SmartMLS users with additional ways to identify and respond to real estate fraud.

“Seller impersonation and vacant-land fraud are difficult problems because the person committing the fraud may never meet the agent face-to-face,” said Alexander Fahsel, CEO of Property Shield. “Ownership Verification gives real estate professionals another layer of information to help determine whether the person they are dealing with is actually connected to the property they are attempting to sell.”

Technology supporting professional judgment

Ownership Verification is intended to provide an additional fraud-prevention tool, not replace the judgment and due diligence of the real estate professional.

A successful verification should not eliminate other appropriate steps when circumstances surrounding a prospective listing raise concerns. Similarly, an issue identified during verification can provide an important signal that additional investigation may be warranted before proceeding with the listing.

“Our goal isn’t to replace the due diligence brokers and agents already perform,” Elson said. “It’s to give them a better tool when they need it. If something about a prospective seller or listing doesn’t add up, we want our users to have another way to investigate before moving forward.”

For more information, visit smartmls.com and propertyshield.co.

#5670. These Markets Led New-Home Shopper Conversions in Q3

As housing affordability continues to challenge the market and overall shopper activity softens, understanding where prospective buyers are actively engaging becomes increasingly valuable for home building professionals.

Zonda’s latest Homebuyer Outlook shows Houston led major markets for new-home shopper conversions in Q3 2026. Atlanta ranked second, while Riverside rounded out the top three. Atlanta’s performance was particularly notable since the market came in seventh place in Q2 2026.

The results come from Zonda’s proprietary Conversion Index, which gives builders another way to assess buyer interest beyond traffic alone. The index measures the ratio of online shopper clicks to community tour requests on NewHomeSource.com, helping capture the point at which shoppers move beyond researching homes and toward engaging with a community.

While high levels of online shopping can indicate interest in a market, conversions show where consumers are taking a more meaningful action.

That distinction becomes especially useful in a slower demand environment. It also provides another perspective since online shopper activity softened but several markets recorded stronger conversion readings than in the previous quarter. That makes conversion a useful complement to traditional measures of demand.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s Homebuyer Outlook subscription.

#5669. Oracle wants to pull stalled AI agents out of demo mode and into production

Companies want AI agents faster than they can build the AI architecture to run them. Most can put together a convincing demo. Far fewer can move agents into production without exposing data, hurting uptime or blowing their budgets.

That gap is pushing database providers to rethink what a data platform for agents has to deliver. Nearly 70% of organizations plan to deploy AI agents, yet very few get them into production, according to Çetin Özbütün (pictured), executive vice president of product and research, data warehouse and autonomous database, at Oracle Corp.

“AI is very easy to demonstrate, but when you try to bring it into production, enterprises usually encounter four different deployment difficulties,” Özbütün said. “The first of them is around security. It’s very hard to securely provide access to AI agents, and that’s one of the top challenges.”

Özbütün spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed AI architecture and the challenges of moving agents into production. (* Disclosure below.)

Security is the first hurdle. AI agents are finding vulnerabilities at unprecedented levels, and customers often can’t patch their databases before attackers exploit those flaws, Özbütün noted. Oracle’s Autonomous AI Database encrypts data at rest and in transit by default, and users can’t turn those protections off.

“As soon as the vulnerability is found, before it’s released anywhere else, we bring it into production in Autonomous AI Database,” Özbütün said.

Resiliency is the next test, because agents run around the clock and put heavy, unpredictable demands on the data platform. Oracle commits to 99.995% availability with no exclusions. That figure is measured by whether a client can connect and run queries, not by whether the underlying infrastructure is running, Özbütün explained.

“We patch our systems on a weekly basis, for example,” Özbütün said. “All of our patches are online patches, so the database is up and running, accepting new connections, accepting new requests while we’re running the patch.”

The same always-current approach applies to Oracle’s Deep Trust AI architecture, in which the database enforces the security profiles that customers define. New capabilities such as the expanded Deep Data Security features show up in Autonomous AI Database as soon as they’re announced, ahead of on-premises releases, according to Özbütün.

“You do nothing as the user or administrator of Autonomous Database to get this functionality,” Özbütün said. “As soon as a new functionality is available, like Oracle Deep Data Security, it becomes available for you to use on day one.”

#5668. Smith Douglas Homes Grows Q3 Orders and Backlog as Margins Tighten

Smith Douglas Homes continued to grow orders and closings during the third quarter despite mounting affordability pressure. The challenging housing environment weighed heavily on the builder’s profitability.

The No. 33 builder closed 831 homes during the quarter, up 5% from 788 a year earlier. However, home closing revenue increased just 0.2% to $262.5 million as the average sales price of homes closed fell to approximately $316,000 from $333,000 in the prior-year period.

Net new home orders increased 13% to 777 from 690 a year earlier. The contract value of those orders rose to $246.1 million from $231.8 million, while the average sales price of orders declined to approximately $317,000 from $336,000. The quarterly cancellation rate was relatively stable at 11.3%, compared with 11.2% a year earlier.

Backlog increased 25% year over year to 947 homes at the end of September, with a contract value of $305.3 million.

“We continued to execute with discipline during the third quarter despite increasingly challenging housing market conditions,” said CEO and vice chairman Greg Bennett. “Higher mortgage rates and affordability pressures have weighed on buyer demand and profitability, but our teams remain focused on things we can control with respect to managing costs, building efficiently, and maintaining a steady absorption pace.”

While Smith Douglas Homes maintained its sales pace, profitability came under considerably more pressure. Home closing gross margin declined to 16.3% from 21% in the prior-year quarter. Pretax income fell to $3.3 million from $17.2 million, while diluted earnings per share declined to $0.07 from $0.24.

The builder’s lower average selling price highlights the affordability dynamic. The average price of homes closed decreased roughly 5% year over year to $316,000, while the average price of new orders declined about 6% to $317,000.

“While we expect market conditions to remain challenging in the near term, we remain confident in the long-term demand for affordable housing,” Bennett said. “Our priorities continue to be running an efficient home building operation and preserving our financial strength while remaining prepared to take advantage of opportunities as conditions improve.”

Smith Douglas Homes also continued expanding its community footprint during the quarter. The builder ended September with 113 active communities, up 15% from 98 a year earlier. Total controlled lots increased 2% to 24,724, including 22,693 optioned lots.

The company ended the quarter with 1,514 homes under construction, compared to 1,098 last year.

“Our disciplined approach to capital allocation and land investment remains particularly important in today’s operating environment,” said executive vice president and CFO Russ Devendorf. “Our land-light operating model, efficient construction cycle times, and conservative balance sheet provide us with the flexibility to manage through periods of weaker demand without compromising our long-term objectives.”

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5667. Inside Cristiano Ronaldo’s Jaw-Dropping Global Property Portfolio and $1.4 Billion Fortune—as He Retires From International Football

Soccer legend Cristiano Ronaldo has announced his retirement from international football after representing Portugal for 23 years.

"A journey that began in August 2004 and changed my life forever is coming to an end," the soccer icon said in a Nov. 5 Instagram post. "When I look back and think of everything I've experienced with the national team, I don't just see matches, goals, records or trophies. I see people. I see immigrants who, for 90 minutes, felt Portugal was a little bit closer."

For now, Ronaldo will continue to play at the club level with Al-Nassr FC in the Saudi Pro League. His contract extends through June 30, 2027.

The announcement comes months after the whistle was blown on his final World Cup in July. The former Portuguese captain and his team missed out on a spot in the 2026 quarterfinals with a devastating 0-1 loss to Spain in Texas.

Following an incredibly tense and largely goal-less matchup between the two teams, Spain's Mikel Merino managed to slide one past the Portuguese goalie in the 91st minute, cementing his team's place in the quarterfinal game.

Ronaldo, 41, was incredibly emotional as he walked off the pitch—hours after confirming at a press conference that the 2026 FIFA World Cup would be the last he plays in.

Ronaldo—whose country is set to co-host the World Cup in 2030 alongside Spain and Morocco—made the announcement during a July 5 press conference, just one day before Portugal's highly anticipated Round of 16 showdown against Spain in Dallas.

"It's about enjoying it as much as possible. This will be my last World Cup, but let's hope tomorrow isn't my last game," the star athlete said, according to ESPN.

The soccer icon noted that he has a "passion" for football, teasing that he hasn't done "too badly" on the field.

"I don't need it, I have a good life, but it's about passion. I play football because I love it. ... You have to enjoy every day. And I've scored three goals [at this World Cup], I'm not doing too badly, right?" Ronaldo said.

During the 2026 World Cup, Ronaldo became the first player to score in six World Cups when he achieved two goals against Uzbekistan.

Ronaldo marked another career highlight when he scored a penalty against Croatia in the Round of 32, which recorded his first goal in a knockout-round match of a World Cup.

Speaking about this year's tournament, the soccer legend noted, "It's been fantastic. It goes beyond the pitch. ... This is the World Cup I'll remember the most, because of people's passion. It's even more this time, I don't know why. It's been, emotionally, the best. I've enjoyed it very much."

"I'm not lacking anything in life. I'm not going to be more, or less, Cristiano because I win the World Cup. We have the qualities to win, but only one country can win it. ... Age gives you maturity and experience," he said.

Ronaldo has showcased his skills in six World Cup tournaments: 2006, 2010, 2014, 2018, 2022, and 2026.

He said that he is grateful for the ups and downs he has experienced throughout that 20-year run, noting that he is even happy to have received public criticism because it has helped him to become a better player.

"I'm thankful even for the attacks I receive, turning 40—and I hope to live another 40 years—with the criticism. That's how you grow the most as a person, and I thank you, journalists, for that," Ronaldo said.

Off the field, Ronaldo has recently entered a new chapter. In August, he married his longtime partner, Georgina Rodriguez in a "private and intimate" ceremony in Portugal. He had proposed in 2025 after eight years of dating.

Ronaldo, who was born and raised in Portugal, began his professional playing career at age 17, when he made his debut for local team Sporting CP. He then moved to the U.K., where he joined Premier League team Manchester United.

During his 23-year career, Ronaldo has become one of the highest-paid soccer players in history, amassing a net worth of $1.4 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. He was, as a result, the first soccer star to become a verified billionaire.

In addition to his very lucrative contracts with some of the world's most elite soccer teams, the player has made an impressive amount of money through endorsement deals representing high-profile brands, including Armani, Nike, and TAG Heuer.

He has also amassed an incredibly impressive property portfolio throughout his career, snapping up homes in his native Portugal, as well as several dwellings farther afield.

Now, as the five-time Ballon d'Or winner calls time on his final FIFA World Cup, attention is once again turning to the legacy he will leave behind—not only through his record-breaking career, but also through an enviable collection of multimillion-dollar homes stretching from Portugal to Saudi Arabia.

Ronaldo first picked up a property in Portugal's capital in 2015 for $2 million.

The dwelling is located on Avenida da Liberdade, a boulevard that is inspired by Paris' Champs-Elysees and is adorned with boutiques, hotels, and cafes.

In 2018, he purchased a 3,100-square-foot-penthouse for $7 million, making history with the then-most expensive apartment ever sold in the city.

The property boasts three bedrooms, wood floors, a terrace, and glass walls that allow natural light to flood inside.

The home also features a spa, gym, and resort-style pool.

From 2009 to 2018, Ronaldo played for Real Madrid and sealed his legacy when he became the club's all-time leading scorer.

In 2010, the soccer star snapped up a luxe mansion in the La Finca neighborhood, a gated community known for its celebrity residents and 24/7 security.

The property, which was designed by Joaquín Torres, sprawls across 8,600 square feet.

It comes complete with a spa, cyrochamber, indoor pool, and even a soccer field.

In 2023, he placed the property on the market for rent for about $11,000 a month.

Ronaldo also made sure to pick up a property where he grew up—in Madeira, Portugal.

He splashed out $8 million for the seven-story abode, which was transformed from a former nightclub in 2015.

The dwelling boasts a rooftop pool, two gyms, and an indoor pool.

Although Ronaldo isn't always able to make it there, his mother and brother reportedly reside there full time.

By 2018, the soccer star picked up another pad in one of Turin's most lavish communities: Strada San Vito Revigliasco.

Inside, the home boasts chic marble, a spa, a gym and several resort-style pools.

After picking up a property in Turin, Ronaldo took a vacation to Marbella, Spain, and decided that he needed a getaway in the area.

The $1.6 million dwelling is situated in the development known as "Superstars' Cul-de-Sac."

The area is famous for its celebrity residents, including Conor McGregor, and offers panoramic views of the Mediterranean and several golfing areas.

His holiday home features four bedrooms, high ceilings, glass walls, a pool, a gym, a wine cellar, and a lavish home theater.

#5666. Fayetteville’s Growth Continues, but Affordability Is Testing the Market

The Fayetteville metro enters the final months of 2026 with several indicators pointing to continued economic growth. Total households are expected to increase 1.9% year over year to 236,740 in 2026, with annual growth of roughly 2% projected through 2028. Labor market conditions have also remained favorable, as total nonfarm employment grew 3.0% year over year to 311,300 in August and the unemployment rate fell to 3.1%, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Several notable projects are moving forward across the region. Northwest Arkansas National Airport (XNA) is advancing a nearly $79 million terminal expansion after recording its highest monthly passenger volume on record in July 2026 and surpassing Little Rock in annual enplanements last year. In Bentonville, the Alice L. Walton School of Medicine Whole Health Campus recently broke ground, an investment that could help meet rising health care needs as the metro’s 65 and older population continues to grow through 2028.

While demographic indicators and economic activity remain positive, housing market data tells a more mixed story.

Despite continued household and employment growth, home sales activity has slowed. As of July, annualized new home closings totaled 2,033, down 20.4% year over year, compared with an essentially flat decline for annualized existing home closings over the same period.

Pricing remains an important consideration. The median new home closing price reached nearly $380,000 in July, compared with $365,000 for existing homes. Despite that premium, new home demand remains concentrated at more attainable price points. In fact, the largest share of both detached and attached annualized new home closings occurred between $300,000 and $350,000 in July.

Meanwhile, single-family permitting is expected to decline 20.4% year over year in 2026 before decreasing another 15.1% in 2027. What was previously characterized as a housing shortage could become a more competitive environment as supply catches up with demand.

Fayetteville’s important storyline will be turning household and employment growth into qualified housing demand. The fundamentals remain compelling, but affordability and a shifting supply-demand balance are likely to separate the market’s strongest performers from the rest.

#5665. Data Centers Meet Fierce Backlash From Voters as Dozens of Towns Reject New Projects

Data centers appeared on the ballot in 41 communities across 12 states this week, and in nearly every case, voters resoundingly voted to restrict or ban them, a sign that backlash continues to grow against the infrastructure needed to power artificial intelligence.

Of the 41 ballot initiatives, only Harwood, ND, passed a pro-data center ordinance. Voters there rejected a ballot initiative that would have required the city to create an independent review paid for by the developer to evaluate the impact of data centers in the community.

In Ohio, which has seemingly become an epicenter of the data center debate, 18 counties put data centers on the ballot. Many measures did not outright ban data centers, but set limits on noise pollution, water and energy use, and other environmental concerns.

Tech companies have poured millions into expanding Ohio's already substantial number of data centers. AI and crypto political action committees spent an estimated $65 million to influence the Ohio midterms, backing Republican Senator John Husted, who lost re-election to Democrat Sherrod Brown on Tuesday.

Both Hubbard, OH and Urbana, OH, passed outright bans on data centers, while other communities passed initiatives that would greatly limit or restrict data center growth based on size and energy usage.

Hubbard resident Jenny Goldberg organized against the data centers in her community.

“We now have the power to say no,” she told WFMJ. “Let's put the brakes on. Let's wait to see if you know if environmental changes, if technology changes, make something like this possible in the future. Then we can reconsider it.”

In Ashville, OH, more than 80% of voters supported a measure intended to overturn a municipal agreement allowing developer EdgeConneX to construct a pair of facilities locally. The ballot measure will not halt construction on the projects, but proponents hope it will send a message to the state’s power board to reject EdgeConneX’s request for a power plant.

Elsewhere in the state, voters rejected measures intended to rezone land for data center use.

Next November, Ohio voters will weigh in on the Ohio Prohibition of Data Center Construction Amendment, which would prohibit data centers that exceed 25 megawatts of monthly demand across the state.

Similar outright bans passed in North Berwick, ME; Americus, KS; Alhambra, CA; Edgewater, FL; and Canterbury, NH.

In Maine, eight counties voted to support initiatives that would ban or place moratoriums on data center construction, and in Illinois, seven ballot measures restricting data centers passed.

Proponents of data centers tout them as economic boons for communities, but the Brookings Institution says that boon is often overstated.

Brookings studied the impact of data centers on employment and found that certain sectors do benefit, though the economic impact is often overstated.

Wages tend to remain stagnant compared with the impact of data centers on housing prices, which have historically received a bump of between 2% and 5% where data centers are built.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5664. Columbia, South Carolina, Balances Growth and Affordability Challenges

Columbia remains a market defined by competing forces. Demand fundamentals continue to support housing activity, but elevated home prices, affordability pressures, and a cooler sales environment are creating some new challenges for builders operating in the region.

The market’s long-term outlook remains supported by solid demographic trends. Columbia’s population is approaching 890,000 residents, while household growth continues to outpace many mature markets. Household formation is expected to remain positive through 2028, providing a steady stream of potential buyers and renters. Meanwhile, median household income continues to rise, helping support housing demand even as affordability remains strained.

Adding to the area’s economic foundation is the presence of the University of South Carolina, which enrolled more than 40,000 students in 2025. According to a university study, the institution generates billions in annual economic activity across the region through payroll, purchases, and tax contributions.

While market conditions have cooled from the rapid growth period seen earlier in the decade, Columbia remains structurally undersupplied. Zonda’s analysis indicates the market is currently undersupplied by roughly 3.7%, suggesting that long-term housing demand still exceeds available inventory.

Builders have responded by expanding community offerings. Active projects increased year over year, with 109 communities currently operating across the market. At the same time, quick move-in inventory remains relatively manageable, signaling that builders have largely avoided excessive speculative inventory buildup.

Like most other markets across the country, affordability remains one of the market’s biggest hurdles. Columbia’s housing market is currently considered overvalued relative to local income levels, with home prices continuing to exceed income-supported pricing.

Still, the broader economic backdrop remains supportive. Employment levels continue to grow, unemployment remains relatively low, and household growth is forecast to continue over the next several years. Combined with the market’s ongoing housing deficit, those factors should help sustain demand even as affordability challenges limit the pace of future growth.

Democratic control of Congress is likely to mean a stronger crackdown on data center development, as opposed to the more laissez-faire approach of President Donald Trump who has promoted both super intelligence and data center development in the country.

#5661. Johnson Development’s Jubilee Earns the First WELL Residence Certifications in Texas

The International Well Building Institute (IWBI) has recently awarded 185 homes in Jubilee a WELL Residence certification. The 1,622-acre community by Johnson Development is the first in Texas to have homes receive the certification.

Signifying they have met a global standard for healthier, more resilient homes, the 185 residences represent 478,493 square feet of development and is the second group of Jubilee homes to receive WELL certification, with 125 homes earning the designation last year.

“We’re always excited about these certifications because they provide third-party recognition that we are actually building a community that truly prioritizes wellness and isn’t simply a marketing pitch,” said Nick Deacon, Jubilee Development manager. “Having the respected independent IWBI validate our efforts makes the achievement that much more meaningful.”

Up from the minimum 40 criteria used to certify homes last year, the homes met 45 criteria to earn their certifications. Categories considered span from air and water quality to light, sound, and thermal comfort.

Deacon added, “It’s encouraging to see us continuing to build on what we learned from our first submission.” Another 215 homes have been submitted for certification with the goal to have all homes in Jubilee earn the WELL Residence seal.

Jubilee was the first Texas community to become an early adopter of IWBI’s WELL for residential program in 2023. Today, 4,470 units around the world representing 6,820,597 square feet have received a WELL Residence certification, according to IBWI. Johnson Development was one of 25 early adopters across 10 countries.

Every home in Jubilee is built with a variety of wellness features, including a reverse-osmosis filtration system at the kitchen sink; a fresh-air intake and a MERV 13 media filter; circadian rhythm lighting for the family room, kitchen, and primary bedroom; and a central automation system.

“Your home—your community—should be your sanctuary,” Deacon said. “Jubilee is designed to be just that, a place where you can rejuvenate, relax, and take comfort.”

Builders include Beazer Homes, Chesmar, Coventry Homes, David Weekley Homes, Highland Homes, J. Patrick Homes, Newmark Homes, Perry Homes, Tri Pointe Homes, and Westin Homes.

#5660. University of Utah retains operational sovereignty as Redtail expands research access

Operational sovereignty gives universities authority over how shared computing resources are allocated, managed and secured.

The University of Utah’s Redtail AI factory supercomputer brings advanced computing capabilities to a statewide community. Supporting researchers, students, administrators and external partners through that infrastructure requires more than computing capacity, according to Manish Parashar (pictured), chief AI officer of the University of Utah.

“In research, we are always trying to balance research security with doing open research for societal good,” he said. “Depending on where you are, you might want to lean in one direction or the other. Having that capability to turn the knob becomes so important.”

Parashar spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and Amit Eyal Govrin for the “Sovereign AI: From Strategy to Reality” video series, during an exclusive interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed university control of computing infrastructure, research governance and the investment needed to support Utah’s expanding ambitions. (* Disclosure below.)

Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. helped architect and deploy Redtail as a turnkey system. The university’s Center for High Performance Computing operates it, drawing on expertise that also supports separate regulated research environments, Parashar explained.

“They have admin access, they’re doing the allocations, they are doing the onboarding,” he said. “They’re doing the management and monitoring … the optimization [and] … the right sizing.”

The interview examined Utah’s approach through theCUBE Research’s Five Pillars of Sovereign AI framework: Territorial, Legal, Technological, Operational and Financial. The university retains operational and legal responsibilities, while financing rests on partnerships with the state and donors, according to Parashar.

“Our overall ecosystem is a hybrid,” he said. “There’s things that are on-prem, there are things that are cloud-hosted, and we always will look at it as a hybrid system. Not everything has to be territorially in a single data center or in the state.”

Redtail also gives the university a way to accommodate growing demand for protected computing by freeing up capacity in existing facilities. Current environments support sensitive and regulated research, including healthcare projects, and expanding their capacity is a priority, Parashar noted.

“How do we move into a facility that has not only the capacity, but is also compliant with emerging controls that are coming out? We want to grow that out, and that’s our focus right now,” he said. “And what happens is with the Redtail, a lot of our open research moves to that and that frees up capacity in our data center and other places where we can grow out this regulated environment.”

The university’s One-U Responsible AI initiative connects research with broader societal needs. Its work spans innovation, public-sector collaboration and regional challenges such as air quality, Parashar explained.

“Being open there becomes very, very important because you want to bring the best ideas, the best data — and most often, it is citizen data that’s coming in — and be able to then see how we can most effectively use AI to address this very regional challenge,” he said. “We don’t want to lose ideas; we don’t want to lose the data that’s coming in. We want to assimilate it and make sure the outcome and the warnings that come out of that — the notifications — are as broadly disseminated as possible.”

Financial sustainability must accommodate rising demand as well as technology refreshes. Expansion planning began before the Redtail contract was signed, and the university is approaching federal agencies, including the Department of Energy and the National Science Foundation, about investing in the existing ecosystem, Parashar noted.

“We are talking to the state and showing them value — very quickly — and convincing them that investing in this is good for the state [and] it’s good for its citizens,” he said. “We are [also] talking to additional philanthropic donors.”

The university’s statewide mission extends beyond providing access to computing resources. Training, workforce development and shared expertise are also part of the ecosystem that operational sovereignty must support, according to Parashar.

“It’s not that we need everything to be tightly controlled. We don’t want everything to be completely open,” he said. “We want to make sure we have the ability to right-size it depending on what we are working on.”

#5659. Russell Brand Moved to Florida Months Before British Police Formally Charged Him With Rape

British comedian Russell Brand was found guilty of rape and sexual assault—more than a year after he relocated his entire family to Florida to escape "attacks" by the "media, government, and judiciary."

According to the New York Times, a London court found Brand, 49—who was previously married to pop star Katy Perry, and now shares three children with wife Laura Brand—guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, and not guilty of two additional counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Judge Joel Bennathan said Brand would be sentenced to "significant custodial time" and has been denied bail.

Following an April 2025 arrest by Metropolitan Police, Brand denied all charges, sharing a video statement on his X account, in which he insisted that he has "never engaged in non-consensual activity," while conceding that he had acted like "a fool" when he was "young and single."

"I've always told you guys that when I was young and single, before I had my wife and family, who were just about a shot over there, my beautiful children, I was a fool, man," he said in the video, which appears to have been shot in Florida.

The alleged offenses are understood to involve six women and took place between 1999 and 2009. Police interviewed Brand about the allegations—which were first brought to light in 2023, when The Sunday Times and Channel 4, two British media outlets, released an expose in which Brand's accusers claimed they had been assaulted or raped by the comedian.

Brand vehemently denied all accusations of "non-consensual activity" at the time.

He is understood to have moved his family from their home in Oxfordshire in favor of a rental property in the Sunshine State, where he is reportedly living in a $2.5 million home in Santa Rosa Beach.

Although he has not revealed when exactly he moved, it has been reported by multiple outlets that he relocated shortly before the 2024 presidential election. Images taken of the comedian show him enjoying public events in the Santa Rosa Beach area as early as October of that year.

The Times reported in 2025 that Brand, his wife, and their three children had been living in a $3.3 million home in the U.K. before their move. It is unclear if they have since sold it.

Brand has also not confirmed whether he is planning to purchase a home in the U.S., where he is currently renting a property.

In the lead-up to his move, the comedian and "Forgetting Sarah Marshall" star had been making efforts to connect with members of now-President Donald Trump's inner circle, interviewing Donald Trump Jr. at his Florida home in 2024 and attending a black-tie dinner at Mar-a-Lago, where he received a Global Defender of Freedom Award.

In April 2025, Brand sat down for an in-depth interview with Fox News host—and newly minted Florida resident—Sean Hannity, during which he opened up about his past addictions and his Christian faith.

Since moving to Santa Rosa Beach, the comedian has reportedly been seen attending church services, as well as yoga sessions, with one local telling The Sun that Brand "always says hello" when they see him.

It is not the first time that Brand has resided in the U.S., having previously owned multiple properties in Los Angeles—including a $6.5 million Mediterranean-style home in the Hollywood Hills, which he shared with Perry, his wife at the time.

Before that, he was reported to have been living in a 1920s abode nearby, which he purchased for $2.2 million in 2013.

Most recently, he snapped up a three-bedroom, five-bathroom Spanish-style property, also in the Hollywood Hills, this time paying $3 million.

The home, which Brand bought in 2019, was built in 1956. The original listing noted that it had since undergone several renovations. He put that property on the market for $3.5 million in summer 2024.
