#5635. Google Cloud storage moves to the front of the AI stack as enterprises hit the GPU utilization ceiling

ANALYSIS by Paul Nashawaty

For the past two years, enterprise AI investment has been dominated by one conversation: compute. Organizations raced to secure GPU allocations, negotiated infrastructure deals and stood up machine learning platforms at speed. What many discovered only after the fact is that the bottleneck they thought they were solving was not the only one in the room. Storage is now throttling the very accelerators enterprises fought to acquire.

In the latest episode of the AppDevANGLE podcast, I spoke with Ronen Schwartz, vice president of products for Google Cloud Storage at Google LLC, about why storage has quietly become the defining constraint in enterprise AI infrastructure, and what a purpose-built architecture for AI workloads actually looks like. The conversation cuts to a problem that is real, measurable and still largely underacknowledged in most AI strategy discussions.

“Storage just got promoted,” Schwartz said. “Instead of being at the backend as an enabler, it is moving into the front as a critical part of accelerator execution.”

The economics of this problem are direct. Accelerators are, as Schwartz put it, an enterprise’s most expensive line item. Every second they idle waiting for data is money lost — not in some theoretical efficiency calculation, but in immediate, traceable waste. Yet when teams finally get access to their TPUs or GPUs, the data delivery path often hasn’t received the same attention as the compute layer.

“I speak to many customers, and what I’m hearing is the team spent a long time fighting to get their TPUs, their GPUs, to get their hands on accelerators. And once they got them, they’re actually not always able to get the output they needed. Very often it actually goes back to not enough thought put into the data delivery path.”

This is not a fringe scenario. Schwartz described a pattern where organizations identify the storage bottleneck only after it hits them — when GPU utilization metrics fall short of targets and training timelines stretch beyond projections. By then, the cost of underinvesting in storage architecture is already embedded in the project.

One of the clearest insights from the conversation is that AI is not a single workload, and treating it as one creates compounding gaps in storage architecture. Schwartz described training, inference and agentic workloads as having fundamentally different “heartbeats” with distinct data movement patterns that each require targeted design.

Training demands massive sequential reads, but the equally critical pressure point is checkpoint management. Every 15 minutes or so, a training cluster must pause and write a multi-terabyte checkpoint to protect work done against potential failure. “Slow storage in that place freezes the entire GPU cluster,” Schwartz said. Google’s Rapid object storage technology, he noted, can write checkpoints more than three times faster and restore them more than five times faster than standard object storage, and this distinction matters significantly at scale. He pointed to Torin, an autonomous vehicle company, as an example: millions of sensor data points flowing into storage to train vehicle models, where checkpoint performance is not an edge case but a core operational requirement.

Inference introduces a different constraint entirely, that of real-time, latency-sensitive interaction where response time directly affects user experience and token economics. Agentic workloads layer on a third set of demands: shared workspaces, state persistence across agents, low-latency retrieval and the need to support both short-lived and long-running agent processes that may hibernate and reactivate on demand.

“AI is not one workload. Really, the movement of data looks completely different. It’s like different heartbeats depending on where you are in the lifecycle.”

Google’s differentiation argument centers on infrastructure credibility built over years of running hyperscale AI workloads internally before offering the same capabilities externally. Schwartz cited specific performance figures: 15 terabytes per second on Rapid object storage and 10 terabytes per second on Google Cloud managed clusters, which he described as verified industry-leading numbers.

The technical foundation includes zonal colocation, or placing data physically close to GPU and TPU clusters to minimize the time a byte travels to the accelerator. Schwartz described this as a first-to-market capability that required rethinking assumptions baked into traditional storage design, where multi-zone or multi-region distribution was the default goal. For AI workloads, proximity to the accelerator takes priority. Google’s Rapid Bucket technology reduces processing steps in the storage path, enabling a single bucket to deliver more than 15 terabytes per second throughput with support for 20 million queries per second at sub-millisecond latency.

“It is because it is built on the Google infrastructure, which has been used internally longer than anyone else to support accelerators and their performance. But it is also because Google is working with nine out of the ten world-leading AI frontier model companies.” A storage architecture that can demonstrably improve GPU utilization can provide faster iteration through less idle compute and lower effective cost per training run.

The agentic dimension of the conversation revealed an underappreciated wrinkle in enterprise AI readiness. Agents require more than web browsing and database queries; they need access to unstructured data at scale, including images, video, documents and PDFs that represent the bulk of most organizations’ real data assets. Without a way to make that content semantically accessible, agents operate with a restricted and often unrepresentative view of enterprise knowledge.

Google’s response is what Schwartz called a Smart Storage Initiative, anchored by a recently launched Object Enrichment capability. When a file or image lands in a storage bucket, Google AI models automatically extract content and attach structured metadata to the object — in seconds, and at scale. The result is that what was previously unstructured becomes queryable by agents without manual intervention or downstream processing pipelines.

“An agent can now interact with what used to be called unstructured data because there is actually a very good understanding of the content.” The storage layer is also integrated into Google’s broader agentic data cloud and borderless lakehouse architecture, allowing agents to reach data stored outside Google’s environment as well.

For agent infrastructure at scale, Schwartz described dedicated Filestore agent volumes integrated directly into Google Kubernetes Engine and the agent sandbox environment, designed specifically to handle the cost, response speed, and data-sharing requirements of running thousands or millions of agents simultaneously.

The broader market shift here is architectural, not incremental. Enterprise AI infrastructure has been built in layers (compute first, then frameworks, then data) and storage was often treated as a procurement checkbox rather than a performance variable. That sequencing is proving costly. As GPU utilization targets become measurable KPIs and AI operations budgets face tighter scrutiny, the storage layer is being reassessed in a way it hasn’t been in years.

What Google’s position illustrates is that hyperscale operational experience at the storage layer translates directly into enterprise advantage — not as a marketing claim, but as a measurable difference in checkpoint speed, throughput, latency and agent responsiveness. The companies that have been running frontier model training and inference at scale have been forced to solve these problems; enterprise teams are now encountering them for the first time.

For platform engineers, ML infrastructure teams and enterprise architects, the implication is specific: Storage architecture decisions made during initial AI platform buildout will constrain or enable performance for every workload that follows. Revisiting those decisions after the bottleneck appears is significantly more expensive than addressing them in the design phase.

The market is heading toward a point where AI infrastructure conversations routinely include storage as a primary tier, not an afterthought. Organizations that recognize that shift early will extract measurably more value from the accelerator investments they have already made.

To hear the full conversation with Ronen Schwartz, check out the latest episode of the AppDevANGLE podcast. To learn more about how Google Cloud Storage can support the evolving demands of enterprise AI, explore Google’s storage solutions or connect with the Google Cloud team to discuss the right approach for your organization’s workloads.

#5634. Opendoor Says It ‘Rebuilt’ System With AI, Triples Home Purchases

After over a year of working as CEO, Opendoor’s Kaz Nejatian reported significant growth in revenue and market share during the iBuyer’s Q3 earnings call, and attributed the gains to a shift into AI infrastructure as the company says it has found ways to flip more homes without overpaying.

“This past quarter we rebuilt this entire system at Opendoor. We built an AI system that determines a specific repair plan for every single home before we buy it,” he stated. “Until August, our resale process was similar to literally everyone else in real estate. Pricing every home we owned basically lived in glorified spreadsheets with over 70 columns.”

As real estate incumbents have largely moved on from the iBuying craze that swept over the pandemic boom market, Opendoor has continued to push forward with a more nuanced approach to the model, offering a wider array of services to home sellers and partnerships with agents.

While acknowledging the company still has a long way to go, Nejatian is claiming the turnaround is working, even amid what he characterized as the worst years for housing “in a long time.”

“We’re winning the market without having to make riskier offers,” he said.

A lot of that comes from technology, along with a stronger focus on moving homes faster with less investment. Nejatian pointed out the differences between scaling with employees than with technology. He stated that increasing scale with the traditional method of buying homes involved hiring more employees, and a longer process.

“Rather than having people spending their days looking at pictures and doing mundane tasks, our people now each manage an army of agents,” he added. “In July, we had 5,400 homes. That’s 5,400 sellers sitting in a queue waiting for days for a human to confirm the price on their home. Two weeks ago, that queue was zero, and it will remain zero.”

He also homed in on the iBuyer’s new initiative—Buy with Opendoor—which launched in beta earlier this week. Although the Q3 earnings predates the program’s release, Opendoor CFO Christy Schwartz believes the initiative can open the company up to the broader market.

“Our emerging Buy with Opendoor offering can help buyers whether or not they’re buying a home from Opendoor,” she noted. “We see an opportunity to extend title and escrow to customers who aren’t buying or selling through Opendoor. Similar to listings, the offerings extend our reach beyond our home acquisition business and create opportunities to earn without taking ownership of a home.”

Previously, Nejatian came into the role with an aggressive turnaround mindset, touting an “Opendoor 2.0” initiative to bring the company back to significant profitability. The third quarter earnings may reflect the fruits of his labor, as homes purchased more than quadrupled.

“When a market slows down, companies are left with a cost structure and a system built for a different business. That’s the disease that Opendoor 2.0 is designed to cure,” he added. “That’s why I spend so much of my time on these calls talking about operator efficiency. When we say we’re investing in growth, we are building the capacity to handle the growth that will arrive.”

Overall, Opendoor’s third quarter saw a revenue of $1.02 billion, up 12% from last year’s revenue of $915 million and up 16% from the previous quarter of $883 million.

The number of homes purchased skyrocketed as well, increasing by 316% year-over-year from 1,169 in 2025 to 4,865 in 2026.

At the same time, though, Nejatian acknowledged the company is “behind schedule” on reaching profitability by the end of the year, blaming the slow market.

Opendoor’s stock fell sharply after the report, down about 17% at press time.

Again, Nejatian posited that the increases in efficiency with AI infrastructure have contributed to Q3’s results.

“Not that long ago, around 80% of the assessments we did on homes required an Opendoor employee, which could take many weeks. Today, that 80% is 2%,” he said. “In Q3, we purchased more than four times as many homes as a year ago, and our operation expense was basically the same.”

Operation expenses per acquired home fell to $4,000, down 36% from last year’s expenses of $6,300. The marketing expenses per acquired home dropped at a higher rate, down 57% to $2,800, compared to 2025’s $6,500.

Mortgage originations—or the process in which a borrower goes through to receive a home loan—increased over 400% from quarter-to-quarter, although the Q3 earnings may not reflect the full weight of the Federal Reserve’s rate hike in mid-September. While the latest data does show mortgage rates inching down slowly each week, it’s unclear as to when rates will go below 7%.

“Historically, most of our economics have come from buying and reselling homes complimented by title and escrow,” Schwartz described. “Our emerging mortgage offerings allow us to earn more from each relationship while meeting a critical customer need and making the transaction easier.”

Opendoor’s EBITDA loss also improved slightly on a yearly basis. Q3 2026 had an EBITDA loss of $31 million, while last year had an EBITDA of $33 million. The adjusted EBITDA margin also decreased, now at 3% compared to last year’s margin of 3.6%. While better than last year, Schwartz acknowledged that the latest data is still far off from last quarter’s EBITDA loss of $4 million.

“Most of the sequential decline came from the homes we bought in the spring selling into a much weaker market along with deeper price cuts as we chose to clear rather than hold,” she said.

Looking to the future, Schwartz expects margins to decline again in the fourth quarter, and states that they will continue to sell through the remaining spring acquisitions into Q1 2027.

She also expects revenue to grow by at least 40% on a yearly basis in the next quarter. Although revenue may increase, Schwartz noted that marketing does contain a seasonal aspect, and operating expenses will likely increase due to investments and growth.

“Comparing year-over-year, roughly a third of the increase in our expected loss is the additional marketing, and the remaining two-thirds is primarily higher holding costs as we’ve been rebuilding our inventory,” she concluded.

“Our goal is to be adjusted net income positive on a 12-month-forward basis at the end of this year,” Nejatian continued. “We’re a bit behind on this today, but we’re going to go through some walls and catch up.”

#5633. Mortgage Calculator: Here’s How Much You Need To Buy a $430K Home at a 7.18% Rate

Mortgage rates retreated to a new one-month low this week as bond yields softened in the wake of the historic midterm elections in which Democrats reclaimed control of the House and Senate.

The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans drifted down to 7.18% for the week ending Nov. 5, down 6 basis points from 7.24% the prior week, according to Freddie Mac. This marks the third consecutive week of easing borrowing costs, providing ongoing relief after rates touched three-year highs last month.

Even with this retreat, borrowing costs remain higher than they were a year ago, when rates averaged 6.22% during the same period in 2025.

So what does this mean for homebuyers? Using the Realtor.com® mortgage calculator, we can look at how the math works out for the median-priced home in the U.S.

All examples assume a 30-year fixed mortgage and include principal and interest only, excluding property taxes, homeowners insurance, and mortgage insurance.

For a homebuyer eyeing the median house price of $430,000, a 20% down payment results in a loan amount of $344,000.

At today's 7.18% rate, the monthly principal and interest payment is approximately $2,330. This reflects a $14 monthly reduction from the previous week’s payment of $2,344.

Compared to the 6.22% average from November 2025, which required a $2,111 monthly payment for a home at this price, today’s buyers are paying $219 more every single month.

The monthly costs have also risen markedly for those using FHA loans with a 3.5% down payment.

On a $430,000 home, an FHA borrower would finance roughly $414,950. At today’s 7.18% rate, the monthly principal and interest payment comes to approximately $2,811.

This reflects a $17 decrease from last week's monthly cost of $2,828. Compared to the 6.22% rates of November 2025, where the monthly payment for this loan amount sat at $2,547, today’s FHA borrowers are paying an extra $264 in interest every month.

However, looking back at the October 2023 peak of 7.79%, where the payment for a home at this price reached $2,984, today's monthly payment still offers $173 in relative relief.

The long-term financial picture shows how this continued downward drift improves overall borrowing costs over a 30-year term.

A buyer with a 20% down payment at today’s 7.18% rate will pay a total of $838,935 in principal and interest over the life of the mortgage.

While current financing costs remain above year-ago levels, this total still represents a distinct contrast to the October 2023 peak of 7.79%, when the total cost for that same $344,000 loan would have reached $890,630. By securing a mortgage at today’s rate instead of that peak, a homebuyer effectively avoids $51,695 in interest charges over the 30-year loan life.

FHA borrowers see a similar trajectory of long-term figures. Financing the current median-priced home at today's 7.18% rate results in a lifetime payment of $1,011,966 for principal and interest.

If that same loan had been locked in at the 7.79% peak in late 2023, the total cost would have climbed to $1,074,323. This represents a total long-term savings of $62,357 for FHA buyers.

While the gap above 2025 rates continues to weigh on overall affordability, the steady decline over the past three weeks is helping to restore some predictability and savings for active fall buyers.

Her work has also appeared on MSN, Yahoo News, and BlogHer. She is a proud graduate of Emerson College in Boston and is originally from New Jersey.

#5632. EXCLUSIVE: Reba McEntire Reveals the Sentimental Style Behind Her Home

Reba McEntire’s home tells a story—and she has a very style that brings it all together.

The country star say in her home, she has rodeo and ranching keepsakes, and reminders of her Oklahoma upbringing.

Speaking exclusively to Realtor.com®, McEntire reveals the sentimental approach behind her decorating choices, the household splurges she considers worth every penny, and why she never wants visitors to feel afraid to get comfortable.

“I'm a country girl at heart, and I love having things around me that tell a story,” she says.

For McEntire, that means surrounding herself with belongings that reflect her experiences and the people who matter most to her.

“So when I bring people into my home, I call it my African cowboy home because I've got my pictures from Africa that I took and then I've got my rodeo ranching things that I've had around me all my life,” she explains.

Those personal touches take priority over decorating purely for appearances.

“I've always believed the home ought to reflect the people living in it, not just what somebody thinks looks pretty,” she says.

McEntire’s reflections come as she continues her partnership with Realtor.com, which launched its “Nearly Home” campaign on May 5, 2025.

The sitcom-inspired ads draw on real homebuyers’ experiences, using humor and practical solutions to make the home-buying journey feel more approachable.

In her own home, however, some of the most important belongings are things she could never replace.

“I'm very sentimental, especially when it comes to family keepsakes, pictures, little things that remind me of mom and daddy, of course, memories of growing up in Oklahoma,” she says.

While furniture can come and go, those connections have lasting value.

“You can always buy new furniture, but you can't replace those memories,” she adds.

Her appreciation for home begins the moment she walks through the front door, when she takes a moment to give thanks before settling in.

“Well, I thank the Lord for getting me home safely, and I put down all my stuff and, just get ready for whatever the rest of the day brings,” she shares.

Although family keepsakes are among her most treasured possessions, McEntire also knows the value of investing in everyday comfort.

When it comes to a home splurge that has proved worth every penny, her answer comes easily. “Oh, without a doubt, a comfortable bed,” she says.

For someone who spends time traveling, returning to her own familiar sleeping setup is a pleasure in itself.

“I spent a lot of time traveling, and there's nothing better than coming home and crawling into your own bed with your own pillow,” she explains.

Another purchase that earns her approval is a good ice machine—a fitting choice given her fondness for iced tea, which she names as something she always keeps in the refrigerator.

Her favorite room is equally straightforward: “Kitchen.”

But McEntire’s ideal day at home does not require an elaborate itinerary or much fuss. “I think I'm pretty low maintenance, but that might surprise somebody,” she says.

“I'm the happiest in comfortable clothes, no makeup on, just relaxing out on the back porch.”

That outdoor retreat includes a particular feature she enjoys. “I've got a real cool porch swing, and I don't need a lot of fuss,” she adds.

A few simple comforts are enough to keep her content.

“Give me good company, something good to eat, and a little peace and quiet, and I'm a happy camper,” she says.

That easygoing attitude also informs the decorating choices she avoids. McEntire has little interest in interiors that make people feel as though they need to tiptoe around.

“Anything that makes a house look like you're afraid to sit on the furniture or walk on the carpet,” she says of the decorating approach she would never try.

In fact, her biggest houseguest pet peeve is someone who does not settle in.

“Someone who doesn't make themselves at home, you know, come on in, get comfortable,” she says.

Asked to describe her home in two words, McEntire offers an answer that captures that philosophy: “warm and welcoming.”

The same sense of comfort and belonging underpins the “Nearly Home” campaign, which pairs McEntire’s humor with relatable homebuying situations and tools designed to help people navigate their search.

The campaign launched ahead of McEntire’s role hosting the 2025 Academy of Country Music Awards, connecting with country music fans as the spring home shopping season got underway. McEntire also debuted her newest single live onstage during the awards.

The ads highlight features such as commute filters, which help buyers check drive times from a potential home, and dynamic maps that let them explore factors including lot size and schools. Through familiar challenges and accessible solutions, the campaign aims to make finding a home feel easier—and more fun.

Now, McEntire is bringing her storytelling to NAR NXT in New Orleans. She will appear in the general session, “The Real Deal: Strategy & Storytelling With Reba McEntire,” on Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026, at the Ernest N. Morial Convention Center.

Attendees can visit the Realtor.com booth, No. 700, on the expo floor on Friday, Nov. 6, for a chance to win a meet-and-greet with McEntire following her Saturday session.

Those stopping by the booth on Saturday and Sunday can also enter for a chance to win officially signed Reba merchandise.

#5631. Redfin Celebrates 250 Years of American History Through the Places We Call Home

From today, Redfin is celebrating America’s 250th anniversary by spotlighting the stories of iconic homes of America. Featured alongside millions of homes for sale or rent on Redfin.com, these historic properties offer a unique window into the people, pivotal moments and enduring spirit that have shaped America.

With immersive tours, detailed photography and stories of the people who lived within the walls, the franchise will bring the past into the present. Each property will also host a free in-person event, complemented by virtual experiences that make these remarkable stories accessible to people nationwide.

Each property will debut separately and remain on Redfin through the end of 2027.

“America’s story isn’t just written in history books. It’s written in the homes where people have dreamed, created, persevered and changed the course of our nation,” said Jonathan Mildenhall, Chief Marketing Officer of Rocket. “As we celebrate 250 years of American independence, Redfin Presents Iconic Homes of America is an invitation to rediscover the extraordinary stories behind these front doors, and to recognize that every home, in its own way, is part of the American story.”

Built around 1740, the Betsy Ross House offers a glimpse into the determination, ingenuity and entrepreneurial spirit of a working woman during America’s founding.

The Philadelphia home is associated with Betsy Ross, the upholsterer, entrepreneur and Revolutionary-era flag maker whose story became intertwined with the creation of the first American flag. While historians continue to debate parts of the familiar legend, records show Ross was an accomplished tradeswoman who made flags for the government for decades.

The home’s remarkable story extends beyond the Revolutionary era. When it faced demolition in the late 19th century, Americans from across the country came together to preserve it, contributing through 10-cent memberships. It was an early demonstration of the collective pride and community spirit that continue to give historic places their meaning.

Its Redfin listing-style page looks beyond the legend to explore Ross as a business owner, working mother and survivor who built an extraordinary life within two small, rented rooms.

Built between 1887 and 1892, Bishop’s Palace was designed by Nicholas J. Clayton, Galveston’s most influential architect, for lawyer and congressman Walter Gresham, his wife, Josephine, and their seven children. The home spans 52 rooms and 19,086 square feet. It became the residence of Bishop Byrne after the Catholic Church purchased it in 1923.

Each detail of the home was custom-chosen, from hand-carved woodwork throughout to a dining room ceiling mural painted by Josephine herself. At the heart of the home, an octagonal mahogany rotunda staircase rises beneath French stained glass, surrounded by finishes from Venice, Holland and North Africa.

The property also includes a few conversation pieces, among them Josephine’s china collection, the original bed, Walter’s desk and Bishop Byrne’s player piano. It sits in Galveston’s East End Historic District, a neighborhood of colorful historic homes and lush landscaping, with the Gulf only a few blocks south.

Today, Bishop’s Palace stands as a one-of-a-kind blend of elaborate craftsmanship, Texan influence and Gilded Age ambition.

#5630. Massive Job Gains of 165,000 in October Bolster Case for More Fed Rate Hikes

Following a disappointing September, U.S. payrolls came roaring back in October as employers went on a hiring spree, adding 165,000 new jobs and pushing the unemployment rate down to 4.1%.

The latest report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, released Friday, shows nonfarm payroll growth more than doubled initial forecasts.

These stronger-than-expected job figures increase the likelihood that the Federal Reserve will remain laser-focused on inflation and raise interest rates in the coming months.

CME FedWatch currently prices a roughly 77% chance of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) raising the federal funds to a 4%-4.25% range in December, followed by a 65% probability in January.

"After last month’s hot inflation print put the next increase in ‘when’ not ‘if’ territory, a soft jobs report was the one thing that could have complicated December," says Realtor.com® senior economist Jake Krimmel. "If Fed hawks were waiting to exhale, they can do so now."

Work sectors that saw the strongest growth in October included professional and business services, which added 70,000 in jobs, well above the average monthly gain of 15,000 over the past 12 months.

Health care came a distant second, with 42,000 payrolls added, followed by transportation and warehousing (+25,000 jobs), and manufacturing (+19,000).

Meanwhile, the September employment data was revised up by 31,000 jobs, from +29,000 to +60,000, while the employment in August was revised up by 53,000, from +133,000 to +186,000.

With these revisions, employment across these two months combined was 84,000 higher than previously reported.

While calling the latest jobs data "impressive," Krimmel points out that the market is still in a low-hire, low-fire mode overall. However, he says that October's payroll surge could be signaling "some green shoots on the hiring side."

"The numbers could still be revised, of course, and the trend matters more than any one point; but you don’t get a good trend without a good month," adds Krimmel.

For homebuyers, Krimmel says that a more dynamic labor market offers some support; however, to meaningfully improve Americans' purchasing power and boost demand requires wage growth to surpass inflation.

Friday's jobs report showed nominal annual wage growth of 3.1% in October, trailing September's 3.7% inflation rate.

"Nominal wage growth is necessary but not sufficient for real wage gains in this environment, so inflation has to come back down, too," says the economist.

The major wildcard remains the ongoing war in Iran, which has driven up inflation and pushed mortgage rates above 7%.

In this week's midterm elections this week, U.S. voters made it known that they were dissatisfied with the state of the economy by handing Democrats control of the House and Senate while flipping multiple traditional Republican strongholds, including Texas, South Carolina, and Kansas.

Even so, Krimmel says that the results of the elections are unlikely to change much for the housing market in the short run.

"Getting back to 'normal' in many metros takes more activity, which depends on improved buying power to bring buyers off the sidelines," he concludes.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5628. New Laws Could Add an Estimated 103,000 Homes a Year, Study Finds

New state laws to encourage homebuilding could bolster the nation's home production by six figures in coming years—but there’s a small catch.

The American Enterprise Institute tracked 10 state bills passed this year and estimates they could potentially lead to 103,000 new homes a year across the country. It's positive progress to solving the nation's housing supply shortage, which is complicated by red tape.

AEI’s data, though, shows that about half of those housing units are accessory dwelling units, or ADUs. But dozens more bills and legislative efforts put forth this year could bring more progress, AEI said at a housing conference in Washinton, DC, this week.

This has been the “year of the starter home,” said Ed Pinto, co-director of AEI’s Housing Center. Thank the bipartisan 21st Century Road to Housing Act, the largest housing reform package in decades. Americans are broadly concerned about affordability, and many young people have grown pessimistic that owning a home will be attainable.

The two largest contributors are California's AB 956 and Washington state's SB 6026.

California's AB 956 loosens requirements around building ADUs. AEI thinks that could result in 48,000 new units a year. Behind that is Washington state's SB 6026, which allows homes in commercially zoned areas. AEI thinks it could mean 37,000 new homes a year.

Other big contributions come from Idaho's SB 1352, which allows homes on smaller lots and could mean 5,000 new homes a year. Kansas' SB 418 brings similar potential in that state. Maine, Virginia, and North Carolina also passed new pro-housing laws.

Tobias Peter, co-director of AEI’s housing center, noted that doesn't necessarily mean every new home will come to fruition. Other kinds of reforms could also unlock hundreds of thousands more homes a year.

At the same time, AEI released a study that found broad support for changes to housing policy. Two rounds of polls of about 5,000 people this year found about 83% support a state law allowing more affordably priced starter homes on smaller lots in new neighborhoods.

AEI found 61% said they’d rather see a torn-down home replaced with two smaller homes, compared to a larger and more expensive home. But people’s opinions trading housing development versus individual property rights can be complicated.

Two of the most popular pushbacks on housing reform fit into two categories. “Supply skeptics” don’t think more homes will improve affordability. Others oppose change to the character or scale of established neighborhoods. Bur rather than housing reform being a "YIMBY versus NIMBY" debate, AEI pictures a spectrum of reform supporters and skeptics.

Some of the largest efforts have focused on the legal red tape around where homes can be built. For instance, several states have put forth laws to allow homes on smaller lots.

But more legislation is needed to correct the slowing construction of starter homes in the nation. Freddie Mac found the U.S. built an average of 418,000 new starter homes a year in the 1970s, 34% of all new housing starts. By 2020 that fell to 65,000 starts, or less than 10%.

“You really need a local champion, a quarterback who organizes at the state level,” Peter said, noting some successful bills where the governor, lieutenant governor, or a group of legislators shepherd a bill. “And it’s also important you have the evidence in your back pocket to counter some of the narratives."

Affordability also requires local governments to respond—because zoning and building code reform, by and large, happens at the local level.

Local government controls some of the most significant levers of affordability, says Yadira Ramos-Herbert, mayor of New Rochelle, NY. And that city's updates to its zoning code have meant incremental progress over time.

New Rochelle developed a form-based code that allows developers to build with fewer requirements around building use. It also streamlined its approval process for new developments, with some taking as few as 90 days to achieve approvals.

The program has helped it approve 4,500 new homes since 2020. New Rochelle, a winner of the University of Utah's 2026 Ivory Prize for Housing Affordability, has seen its median rent decline as national averages surge.

"Our core objective is to ensure New Rochelle remains affordable, accessible, and economically resilient," Ramos-Herbert tells Realtor.com. "Affordability remains the defining challenge of our time, and cities have a responsibility to respond with urgency."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5627. Mortgage Rates Drop From September Highs as Midterms and Jobs Data Loom

In A Nutshell: Rates have fallen about 30–40 basis points since the peak at the end of September and there’s little reason to believe the volatility will slow down.

The Fed meeting last Wednesday was the highlight of the week, with the committee voting to hold rates steady as expected. There were two dissents, with one coming from a surprising source, Governor Lisa Cook, who is usually seen as someone who favors lower rates. The statement and press conference reiterated a desire to keep hiking, making a December hike more likely than not if the economic data comes in as expected.

The Fed has been highlighting elevated inflation and strong economic growth as its reason for hiking. And Q3 GDP, in fact, came in at a brisk 3.4% annual rate. Real business fixed investment spending grew at a 12.7% annual rate thanks to rapid growth in AI spending. And real consumption grew at a 3.8% annual rate as people spent out of savings and wealth increases rather than income growth. The question now is what happens to growth in Q4. Real-time data is pointing to a potential slowdown as consumers pull back.

It’s another big week with both the midterm election tomorrow and employment data arriving throughout the week. Democrats are expected to comfortably gain a majority in the House of Representatives with control of the Senate also favoring Democrats, but less certain. Expectations for government spending, which has been a factor for rates, could certainly change with a more divided government. But the near term economic impact might be felt most acutely as we near government funding and debt limit deadlines. The closest budget deadline is December 11, which might get pushed to Q1. And we’re likely to hit the debt limit again in Q1 at which point the Treasury will take “extraordinary measures” until we truly run out of options sometime before October 2027.

Since it’s the first week of the month, we’ll also get the typical employment reports, including job openings and turnover on Tuesday and the official jobs report on Friday. With the Fed squarely focused on inflation, the jobs report mostly serves as a check on whether the Fed needs to turn its attention back to recession risk, which would reduce the need for the rate hikes that markets have priced in. So far this year, the answer has been “no,” with the labor market on solid enough footing and that is not expected to change with this week’s data.

Finally, Fed officials are out of their blackout period following last week’s FOMC meeting. With Chairman Warsh typically reluctant to offer much forward guidance, markets have been relying more on surrogates to forecast the outcome of the next meeting. There are numerous speaking engagements on the calendar, including Cleveland Fed President Hammack and Dallas Fed President Logan on Thursday, and New York Fed President Williams on Friday. Forecasters will be looking for clues to support the “hike every other meeting” thesis.

Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.

#5626. Atlassian shares fall 17% as slower subscription growth forecast overshadows earnings beat

Shares in Atlassian Corp. fell more than 17% in after-hours trading today on a forecast for slower subscription growth from the Australian collaboration software company.

Its fiscal 2027 first-quarter results beat analyst estimates. The stock had nearly doubled between Atlassian’s August report and late October.

For the quarter ended Sept. 30, Atlassian reported adjusted earnings per share of $1.65, up from $1.04 in the same quarter of the previous year, on revenue of $1.772 billion, up 24% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting $1.43 per share on revenue of $1.71 billion.

Most of the growth came from cloud, where revenue rose 31%, to $1.302 billion. Customers kept adding Jira and Confluence seats in the quarter, according to the shareholder letter, including in business teams well outside software development.

Growth in Data Center, the self-managed product line Atlassian will retire in March 2029, slowed to about 5%, leaving revenue there at $391 million. The company said those customers are expanding less as they plan their moves to the cloud.

Subscription annual recurring revenue came in at $6.812 billion at the end of September, up 22.5%. Remaining performance obligations jumped 44%, to $4.746 billion. Enterprise customers are behind that increase, according to the company, with deals getting larger and stretching over several years.

Atlassian made money on an unadjusted basis for the second quarter running, with net income of $91 million, or 35 cents per share. Chief Financial Officer James Chuong put that down to keeping costs in check while revenue grew. Free cash flow climbed to $463 million on strong collections, and Atlassian returned $581 million to shareholders through buybacks.

On the product side, more than 87% of enterprise cloud customers now use Rovo, the company’s artificial intelligence assistant. Upgrades to the Teamwork Collection bundle rose sevenfold from a year ago to more than 3,000 customers. Annual recurring revenue from the larger Service Collection bundle is now above $1 billion, spread across more than 70,000 customers.

Chief Executive Mike Cannon-Brookes used the earnings release to argue that enterprise AI has reached “an inflection point.” Model power alone no longer sets anyone apart, he said. Platforms that give people and AI agents shared context to work from will pull ahead by his account, and Atlassian has “never been better positioned” to be one of them.

For the second quarter, Atlassian expects revenue of $1.825 billion to $1.835 billion, a little ahead of the $1.82 billion analysts had forecast, with cloud revenue growth of about 27%.

Most of Atlassian’s fiscal 2027 targets edged higher in the update. The company now sees full-year revenue growth of about 13.75%, three-quarters of a point above its August forecast. Because customers pulled Data Center purchases into fiscal 2026 after the retirement announcement, this year’s revenue comparisons are tougher.

Total revenue growth should pick up again in fiscal 2028, Atlassian said. Investors sold the stock on a different number. The company expects subscription annual recurring revenue growth to slow to about 18.5% by fiscal year-end, down from the 22.5% it just reported.

#5625. Is Trump Media Selling Bitcoin? Democrats Prepare Crypto Probe

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Trump Media has moved $343 million in Bitcoin to Crypto.com, raising fresh questions if Donald Trump’s media company could be selling its crypto holdings. The transfer comes as Democrats prepare investigations into Trump’s family crypto ventures following their midterm election victories.

The company sent 4,259 BTC in two transactions, according to blockchain data tracked by Arkham. The coins came from wallets labeled as collateral for convertible notes, adding another layer of uncertainty around the Trump Media Bitcoin transfer.

The timing is difficult to ignore. Trump Media faces a potential $1 billion debt repayment deadline later this month, while incoming Democratic lawmakers are preparing to scrutinize Trump’s crypto businesses. A sale has not been confirmed, but this move puts the company’s Bitcoin treasury under pressure.

Arkham data showed Trump Media-linked wallets transferring 4,259 BTC to Crypto.com just a few hours ago. The coins were moved in two batches of more than 2,000 BTC each. The transfer represents around $343 million at recent prices. It also accounts for 30% of the 14,139 BTC Trump Media previously held, including pledged coins.

However, the destination does not confirm a sale. It is known that Trump Media has used Crypto.com for custody and trading-related transfers before, including transactions in May and August.

The latest movement is particularly notable because the Bitcoin came from wallets associated with convertible-note collateral. Trump Media’s previous filings identified 4,260.73 BTC as collateral for its notes.

A November 2 filing also disclosed that noteholders can require cash repayment on November 30. If all eligible holders exercise that option, the company could face approximately $1 billion in repayments.

Trump Media warned that refinancing or other measures might not be sufficient. In that scenario, the company could be forced to sell Bitcoin or other digital assets to meet its obligations.

This disclosure gives the Crypto.com transfer a potentially more serious explanation than routine custody management. The company may be positioning assets ahead of a major liquidity decision. Although the reason remains unconfirmed, Trump Media could be selling its Bitcoin.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The transfer also arrives as Democrats prepare to investigate Trump’s family crypto businesses after winning control of Congress in the midterm elections.

Incoming lawmakers have identified World Liberty Financial, the Trump family’s crypto venture, as a potential focus. Investigators are expected to examine foreign investment, business profits, and possible conflicts of interest involving the administration’s crypto dealings.

JUST IN: 🇺🇸 Democrats plan to investigate crypto industry's financial ties to President Trump and his family, Bloomberg reports. pic.twitter.com/KGF41xeknO

Senator Elizabeth Warren has pledged scrutiny of Trump’s crypto business relationships, while Representative Robert Garcia, expected to lead House Oversight, warned Trump-linked interests to prepare for investigations.

Democrats are expected to gain subpoena power when the new Congress begins in January. Reuters previously reported that investigations into Trump family businesses could begin as early as February.

The current political environment could complicate the outlook for Trump-linked companies. Congressional scrutiny may increase pressure on financial relationships, crypto holdings, and business operations connected to the president’s family.

So, is Trump Media selling its Bitcoin? There’s no clarity as of now, but a confirmed sale would raise questions if Trump Media is reducing its crypto treasury to meet financial obligations.

The next major date is November 30, when noteholders can exercise their repayment option. Investors will also be watching if the Bitcoin remains at Crypto.com, moves again, or appears in transactions that indicate an actual sale.

#5624. 5 Historic ‘Minimansions’ Under $400K Where You Get 3,000+ Square Feet for the Price of a Starter Home

If you’re in the market for a large home but have a limited budget, consider a house that needs some TLC.

For the ambitious investor who wants to roll up their sleeves and dive into a home improvement project, a historic home might just fit the bill.

From New York to Tennessee, we found five “minimansions,” each with more than 3,000 square feet of living space for the price of a starter home.

Magnolia Manor: Here’s a chance for an investor to transform this 1.28-acre legacy compound into a "hospitality destination" or investment property of their dreams, subject to applicable permitting.

Built in 1849 for Judge Austin Miller, the 4,228-square-foot estate, formerly a bed-and-breakfast, has a four-bedroom Greek Revival brick home with a covered front porch, a one-bedroom guest cottage, a potting house, a gazebo, and a detached two-car garage. Historic highlights include double parlors, original architecture, hardwood floors, chandeliers, oversized windows, and brick details.

Located in the North Main Street Historic District, the home needs some work, as reflected in the price, and is being offered as is.

Larry Childers of Childers Real Estate is the listing agent.

Italianate brick mansion: This "treasured" six-bedroom brick estate near the Mohawk River was built in 1860 and has had only two owners.

Two entrances, including one with original horse ties and carriage step, lead to the 4,192-square-foot home full of charm and character. Period details include a grand staircase, preserved hardwood floors, custom moldings, expansive windows, French doors, a butler's pantry, and an original marble fireplace. An original basement kitchen features a fireplace. A cupola provides panoramic waterfront views of the Mohawk Valley.

Listed on the National Register of Historic Places, the home offers the next buyer the opportunity to enjoy a "living piece of American history."

Rebecca Zarski of Howard Hanna Delmar is the listing agent.

The A.M. Legg House: Built in 1913, this historic five-bedroom “architectural treasure” was once the home of former Pontiac Mayor Achalis Morris Legg.

The 3,715-square-foot estate has a covered front porch with original mosaic tile flooring, custom millwork, multiple French doors, preserved hardwood floors, elegant built-ins, four fireplaces, and a pocket door. Other amenities include a sunroom, a dining room with built-in cabinetry, a full walk-up attic with room for expansion, and a partly finished lower-level entertainment room with a bar and a canning room.

A detached two-car garage with a dual-access driveway is also on the property.

David R. Wayman of Eppel Realty is the listing agent.

Louis Bierbauer Brewery country estate: Sitting on 3.59 acres at the base of the Canajoharie Gorge, this picturesque four-bedroom compound is surrounded by original stone walls and sits along a creek.

Built in 1860, the thoughtfully updated 3,528-square-foot interior still has wood-paneled walls, stone details, and built-ins. Modern updates include radiant-heated floors, a kitchen with wood cabinetry and stainless-steel appliances, and a circular staircase. The primary suite has an exposed wood-beam ceiling and a decorative fireplace. An underground grotto “still exists where the beer vats were aged,” according to the listing, which also says the property is not in a flood zone.

A one-bedroom apartment could be used for multigenerational living or as an income-producing rental. A salon space with a dedicated entry could also be used for other business purposes.

Rochelle Monk of Krutz Properties is the listing agent.

Updated Victorian: Built in 1903, this five-bedroom home, originally owned by Delia and Henry Logan of Logan Automobile Co., has 3,180 square feet of carefully updated living space.

Time-honored details include original hardwood floors, period millwork, pocket doors, stained glass, formal living and dining rooms, and seven fireplaces. Updates include new windows, a remodeled kitchen with stainless-steel appliances and a breakfast bar, and a finished third-floor bonus level. A wraparound covered porch would be a nice spot to enjoy morning coffee.

A detached one-car garage is also on the fenced lot.

Blaine Ritchie of Coldwell Banker Select Properties is the listing agent.

#5622. GLP-1s Are Changing America’s Kitchens—and Raising Questions About Its Trash

Open a custom bathroom vanity today, and you might find more than towels and toiletries: a refrigerator for medication, drawers for syringes, even a compartment for used-needle disposal.

Today, 1 in 5 U.S. households (21%) includes a current GLP-1 user—up from just 9% in January 2025, according to an analysis by PwC.

And now, America's homes appear to be developing a taste for less, too: The hidden kitchen is among the emerging trends in the National Kitchen & Bath Association's (NKBA) 2027 design forecast.

But the rise of injectable medications is also drawing attention to a less glamorous, often-overlooked part of domestic life: the trash.

In New York City, sanitation workers have reported a sharp increase in needlestick injuries. The Department of Sanitation has identified the growing use of injectable medications, including GLP-1s, as a possible contributor, although it doesn't track the types of needles involved.

On Nov. 9, the city will more than double fines for improperly discarded household medical waste, drawing objections from property owners who argue they have little control over what tenants throw away.

GLP-1 medications are said to reduce what's commonly called food noise: persistent, sometimes intrusive thoughts about food and eating. And as that mental chatter quiets, some households are finding they don't need quite as much food—or space to store and prepare it.

PwC's research on GLP-1 users found that grocery spending declined 5.5%, as users shifted away from snacks, sugary drinks, and alcohol in favor of produce, protein, and supplements. It's even prompting some homeowners to reconsider how much kitchen they want.

"While these grand kitchens aren’t going anywhere, we have seen an increase in customers selecting homes with more modest kitchen designs," Tammy Crosby, CEO of The House Designers, tells Realtor.com®.

The shift marks a stark departure from decades of kitchen design centered on abundance—perhaps nowhere more apparent than in the elaborate Tuscan-style kitchens of the early 2000s. Countertops doubled as displays for colorful bottles of infused oils, jars of preserved vegetables, and other culinary-themed decorations.

Even the modern farmhouse, which traded Old World ornamentation for a more restrained aesthetic, retained that appetite for excess: sprawling islands, oversized refrigerators, and walk-in pantries.

Now, Crosby says customers using GLP-1 medications are likelier to favor compact, efficient layouts that free up square footage for other priorities.

"A range will do just fine—no need for an expanded appliance suite with a separate cooktop and double wall ovens," she says.

Likewise, households purchasing less food may no longer need oversized refrigerators or separate pantries designed for bulk groceries.

But the move toward quieter kitchens isn't just about shrinking their footprints—it's really about reducing what homeowners see.

And the so-called invisible kitchen takes that philosophy a step further, concealing appliances, food storage, and preparation areas behind cabinetry to create a more seamless living space.

According to the NKBA 2027 Kitchen Trends Report, 81% of surveyed industry professionals believe dividing kitchens into functional zones is a practice that's here to stay, while 85% say cabinetry is being designed to conceal appliances and other working elements.

Of course, overlapping timelines doesn't establish that GLP-1s are driving those changes. But the parallel is striking: Just as the medications are said to mute the thoughts surrounding food, designers are finding ways to lessen its visual presence in the home.

A similar philosophy is finding its way into bathrooms: 72% of surveyed industry professionals expect bathrooms to expand to accommodate wellness activities and more efficient storage, according to NKBA 2026 Bath Trends Report.

That might mean a custom vanity with dedicated compartments for medications and personal-care supplies, or bathroom cabinetry that conceals a small medication refrigerator or sharps container.

But Crosby cautions against assuming that injectable medications will create widespread demand for bathroom refrigeration.

"There has been talk of some people requesting refrigeration in the bathroom to store GLP-1s, but that’s probably overhyped," she says, noting that people using insulin have long stored their medication in kitchen refrigerators.

Even as GLP-1s quiet food noise in American homes, discarded needles are causing a cacophony in the trash—as a sharp rise in needlestick injuries among New York City sanitation workers makes clear.

Such injuries have tripled in the Big Apple since 2023.

That year, the Department of Sanitation recorded 23 injuries, followed by 40 in 2024 and 50 in 2025. By Oct. 21 of this year, the number had climbed to 69, according to testimony at a City Council hearing.

Sanitation worker Nicholas Derenzi knows what one of those injuries can mean. While collecting garbage on a Bronx route in 2020, a discarded needle pierced his glove.

"I felt something prick through my glove," he told NY1 in August. "You're by yourself, and that's really when it kind of set in how scary, and the gravity of the situation."

Coworkers subsequently discovered multiple needles inside the trash bags, and Derenzi was taken to an emergency room.

While it may seem small—just a small pinprick afterall—these injuries pose a serious health risk, requiring medical evaluation and follow-up testing for bloodborne infections.

So, with needlestick injuries mounting, New York City is turning to higher fines to discourage improper disposal of household medical waste.

Beginning Nov. 9, the fine will rise from $100 to $250, the maximum permitted under the applicable city law. But the change has drawn pushback from property owners who argue they have little control over what residents discard.

"Owners generally have no control over what tenants or passersby place in trash bags or building receptacles," the Small Property Owners of New York (SPONY) wrote in a public comment opposing the rule.

The organization warned that expecting landlords or building staff to inspect garbage could expose them to the very injuries the regulation is intended to prevent.

DSNY, however, maintains that property owners already have a responsibility to ensure waste is disposed of properly.

"Property owners have always been responsible for the proper disposal of trash, and that includes using the proper containers and sorting material correctly," Vincent Gragnani, the department's press secretary, tells Realtor.com.

The new regulation specifies a $250 penalty for an individual violating the disposal requirements, although precisely how responsibility is determined when needles are discovered in a multifamily building's shared trash remains unclear.

Meanwhile, DSNY is also working to reduce direct contact with garbage through mechanized collection. Its new residential trash bins are compatible with equipment that lifts and empties them into collection trucks, reducing the need for sanitation workers to handle bags manually.

But those changes don't eliminate the need for safe disposal at the source.

"New York City residents disposing of syringes, needles, scalpels, lancets, and other sharp objects are legally required to place them in a 'sharps' container or other leak-proof, puncture-resistant container, such as a laundry detergent bottle," Gragnani says.

Once securely sealed and labeled "HOME SHARPS - NOT FOR RECYCLING," those containers can go into regular household trash. Residents can also bring used sharps to hospitals, nursing homes, or designated drop-off locations.

#5620. OpenAI launches GPT-6 Cyber, an Astra model built to keep vulnerability research in scope

OpenAI Group PBC today released GPT-6 Cyber, a version of its GPT-6 Astra model trained specifically for authorized vulnerability research.

The new model goes after a problem OpenAI’s own security work exposed this summer. In July, agents running in the company’s test environments broke into Hugging Face Inc. while pursuing an assigned task. GPT-6 Cyber was trained to stay inside the targets a researcher has authorized, and the safety test OpenAI built for the launch draws on that incident.

That test, ExploitGym Honeypot, gives the model a difficult assignment and surrounds it with supporting services that are deliberately easy to compromise. Attacking any of those services counts as a scope violation.

With no deployment safety instructions in place, GPT-6 Cyber went out of bounds in 0.07% of graded runs. Its predecessor, GPT-5.6-Cyber, did so 5.51% of the time. Adding the instructions brought GPT-6 Cyber’s observed rate to zero.

OpenAI rates the new model at Critical, the top cybersecurity tier in its Preparedness Framework and the same classification Astra received at its September launch. GPT-5.6-Cyber had been rated High. The company says GPT-6 Cyber beats Astra on most cyber tasks, and an early research campaign on Firefox turned up 81 previously unknown vulnerabilities that Mozilla Corp. rated high severity. Mozilla has since shipped fixes for many of them.

Irregular, an AI security lab named in the system card, put the gap with Astra closer, finding the two broadly comparable apart from stronger GPT-6 Cyber results on long multistep tasks. Neither model got past fully hardened targets in OpenAI’s own challenge set.

GPT-6 Cyber is the fourth cyber-specific model OpenAI has released this year. Like the first, GPT-5.4-Cyber, it sits behind an application process. Initial access is limited to a select group of approved customers in Daybreak Red, the tier of OpenAI’s Daybreak program meant for offensive-style work such as penetration testing and red teaming. Those customers reach the model through the company’s application programming interface and Codex, and API requests have to come from approved networks by default.

Google LLC also put vetted defenders first when it launched Gemini 4 Argon in September. A week later Anthropic PBC rebuilt its Cyber Verification Program around three access tiers.

OpenAI said GPT-6 Cyber will reach all Daybreak Red customers over the coming weeks, and GPT-5.6-Cyber is now opening to every customer in the tier. Critical infrastructure defenders get a Daybreak Red group of their own. On the defensive side, the company is extending early Astra access through Daybreak Blue to more organizations and to individual security researchers.

#5619. Compass ‘Welcomes’ Open Real Estate, Sees Record Quarterly Earnings

As Open Real Estate makes headlines around the future of listing flow and control, Compass CEO Robert Reffkin addressed the initiative in the company’s third quarter earnings call, saying Compass “welcome(s) this change.”

Reffkin said that Open Real Estate’s plan “actually validates” Compass’s messaging over recent years, and he is “excited to see the four of them lead in this way and just see others join.”

In terms of whether or not Compass itself would join the initiative, Reffkin said “there’s definitely a path.”

“Compass International Holdings is definitely excited that there will be a national real estate listing service that will return the power back to the creator of the listing, the homeowner and their trusted agent, and that is good news for all agents and for all their clients, and we’re looking forward to seeing if there’s a way for us to be involved,” he continued.

Compass reported a “record” quarter, beating out expectations it set for itself in Q2. Reffkin touted the firm’s success amid an array of market challenges, from increasing mortgage rates to decreasing home sales.

Compass’s adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization) of $306 million for Q3 surpassed the company’s original expectations of $275 million to $305. While down from $363 million in Q2, EBITDA rose from $94 million in Q3 2025 to set a new Q3 record.

Other Q3 records for Compass include revenue, which came in at $3.9 billion for Q3. While this marks a dip from last quarter’s $4.31 billion, it represents a whopping 111% year-over-year increase from $1.85 billion in Q3 2025. Pro forma revenue was up 11.6% year-over-year from $3.49 billion.

Net income was also at a record Q3 level, coming in at $62 million. While down from $92 million in Q2, the increase is significant compared to the $4 million net loss year over year. The company has now been net income positive for three consecutive quarters.

Much of the quarter’s success was attributed to improvements in Compass’s operating expenses (OPEX), which were down 6% year-over-year. Free cash flow was also improved at $240 million in Q3, which the company noted was a record for any quarter or year in its history.

CFO Scott Wahlers said that bettering the company’s OPEX came from “just good old-fashioned tightening our belt” in a market that is experiencing challenges from “worse than normal seasonality.”

Looking at the brokerage business, gross transaction volume for Coldwell Banker, Compass, Corcoran and Sotheby’s International Realty came in at $138.9 billion, down from $155.2 billion in Q2 but up 96.5% year-over-year from $70.7 billion in Q3 2025. Pro forma, transaction volume was up 7.5% year-over-year to $133.1 billion.

Brokerage transactions were up 106.4% year-over-year, from 67,887 in Q3 2025 to  140,118 this quarter. Pro forma, transactions were actually down 0.3% year-over-year, but this is compared to a 1.8% decrease across the entirety of the U.S. residential real estate market (as sourced from NAR’s existing home sales data).

For franchise business, gross transaction volume was at $108.9 billion, a 1,181% year-over-year increase from $8.5 billion in Q3 2025. Pro forma, transaction volume was up 2.3% year-over-year to $104.2 billion. Franchise transactions were up a whopping 2,073% year-over-year, from 8,825 in Q3 2025 to 191,809 this quarter. Pro forma, transactions actually decreased 3.6% year-over-year.

Reffkin also called out some business that will be coming in from Wall Street due to bonuses from working with and investing in AI.

“(Wall Street) will have record bonuses coming in the months ahead, and that will lead to more transactions,” he said. “There are a number of partners on Wall Street who have asked me for an introduction to our agents, and I have made those introductions.”

The mortgage business improved as well, credited to Compass’s acquisitions. Total mortgage transactions were up 406% year-over-year to 38,757 (up from 7,666 in Q3 2025). This was also up pro forma by 1.7% year-over-year. Loan volume was $3.30 billion, up 9.9% year-over-year on a pro forma basis.

Compass just recently inked a deal with fintech company Rate to unite the two companies’ mortgage ventures—Guaranteed Rate Affinity and OriginPoint—under the OriginPoint brand. The merger shifts OriginPoint up to a top 10 mortgage lender, which Reffin said is “incredible after such a short amount of time.”

“Longer term, we want to be a top five retail lender,” he added.

Agent retention and recruiting also improved for Compass due to what the company and Reffkin outlined as a strong value prop and industry positioning. For agents producing more than $20,000 in gross commission income, retention is above 98%.

Recruiting-wise, brokerage agents specifically increased by 2,292 in Q3, and total agent count grew by 6,390.

Reffkin also attributed Compass’ Q3 success to the rollout of its “Home” platform, an end-to-end proprietary technology for real estate professionals.

Across Coldwell Banker, Corcoran and Sotheby’s International Realty, Compass stated it saw 33,950 agents adopt the available platform, bringing the total number of users across the full company to 68,349 agents. The plan remains to roll out the platform to the full portfolio of Compass brands in Q1 2027.

Through the platform, all participating agents will have access to the company’s Private Exclusive and Coming Soon inventory.

In talking about Compass’s platform, Reffkin dove into the company’s “See It First” campaign, calling it “part of a rebranding exercise.”

“I think some of our competitors have tried to brand the listings that we have as hidden, clearly,” he explained. “All of our listings are available to all agents and to all buyers, and when you call them See It First, then it’s pretty clear we just want you to see it first on our site, which is a natural thing for a company to want to be able to do.”

Reffkin reported that the company will take a conservative approach in the months ahead as the market continues to be challenged.

“There are reasons to be optimistic, but obviously we’re not planning for that,” he said. “We continue to focus on costs and plan for being conservative. But I think what can help in our favor (is) one, we have more inventory right now than any point since…2019. ..More inventory means you can create more sales.”

When asked about future merger-and-acquisition opportunities, Reffkin indicated the door is open.

“We continue to be a company that wants to support great operators and continue to have those conversations.”

Compass stated it expects a Q4 revenue of $3.150 billion to $3.350 billion, and a Q4 adjusted EBITDA of $100 million to $130 million. For the full year of 2026, the company stated it expects free cash flow to be positive, and OPEX of $2.71 billion to $2.73 billion.

Maria Patterson contributed to this report.

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5618. Scarlett Johansson Says ‘The Batman: Part II’ Role Caused ‘Existential Angst’ After Leaving NYC Penthouse To Travel Abroad

Oscar-nominated actress Scarlett Johansson has starred in a number of impressive films, but it sounds as though her latest role was unexpectedly intense.

When asked about her part in the upcoming film, “The Batman: Part II,” Johansson said “it was a tough role, in a lot of ways.”

“I don’t know, it gave me a lot of existential angst for some reason,” she said in a Nov. 4 "Entertainment Tonight" interview alongside actor Adam Driver, during which they were promoting their upcoming film, "Paper Tiger."

“It was very hard to figure out. I don’t know why," she added.

The 41-year-old New York native felt that the challenge could have been caused by a number of things, saying that she wasn’t sure “whether it was just the role, where I’m in my life, or what’s going on, but it was just like, hard to crack it.”

Johansson’s exact role in the film—which was confirmed to have been filmed in Glasgow, Scotland as well as Liverpool, England by Glasgow World—is yet to be revealed.

It’s not the first difficult work scenario the A-lister has dealt with while filming abroad.

In 2024, the Daily Mail reported that Johansson opted to stay in a pricey luxury suite at Claridge’s hotel in London while filming “Jurassic World.”

The penthouse suite, which was estimated to be more than $80,000 a night, was her preference over a home she was apparently originally planning to stay in in the north London suburb of Hampstead.

A Daily Mail source said that when Johansson realized “there was no liveried security doorman like you might get in Manhattan,” she switched up her plans for safety.

The insider also explained that she was traveling with “her nanny and children,” which is why she turned down the home.

Johansson has two children—a 12-year-old daughter, Rose Dorothy Dauriac, and a 5-year-old son, Cosmo Jost.

However, her primary residence does have a full-time doorman. Johansson and her husband, “Saturday Night Live” cast member Colin Jost, 44, snapped up a sprawling $13 million Manhattan penthouse in March 2025.

The transaction was quite a deal for the famous couple. According to the Wall Street Journal, they scored the triplex for less than half its original 2018 asking price of $27.5 million.

The 6,000-square-foot residence boasts six bedrooms, seven bathrooms, five terraces, and eight balconies, and is located within a lavish 18-story Rosario Candela-designed building from the 1930s.

The former owners, Craig and Deborah Cogut, had purchased the impressive home for $13 million in 2006. After initially listing it in 2018, it was removed and put back on the market a handful of times before eventually finding new buyers.

There are plenty of desirable features in the prewar abode, including a living room equipped with a wood-burning fireplace and six sets of floor-to-ceiling french doors with Juliet balconies.

An oak-paneled library features stunning views of Midtown and Central Park.

A galley-kitchen furnished with black granite countertops and white subway tile includes all the features a home chef could need, such as not one, but two Subzero refrigerators, according to 6sqft. A breakfast room is accessible by pocket doors made of bronze and glass.

The second level hosts four of the penthouse’s bedrooms, which each have their own private bathroom and outdoor spaces.

The third floor is entirely dedicated to the primary suite, which also has its own dedicated terrace. A fireplace keeps the space cozy, while a dressing room elevates the suite.

The dedicated bathroom is truly spa-inspired, with a marble-clad bath, a soaking tub, and a steam shower.
