#5617. Trump Declares the Oval Office a National Monument—1 Year After Backlash Over ‘Home Depot’ Decor

President Donald Trump declared the Oval Office a national monument aiming to stop future presidents from making any changes. Trump signed a proclamation on Thursday in his first official action since Democrats swept the midterms.

"We've had tremendous victory in this office," Trump said. "So we're making it a national monument, and it will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape."

Only a year ago, Trump, 80, found himself defending the "24-karat gold" Oval Office decorations as critics speculated they were actually painted plastic appliqués from Home Depot.

"You know the one thing with gold?" Trump said during a Fox News interview with host Laura Ingraham in 2025. "You can't imitate gold, real gold. There's no paint that imitates gold."

Ingraham, 63, then pushed Trump further, asking him: "So these aren't from Home Depot or something?"

"No, this is not Home Depot stuff," the president responded. "This is not Home Depot."

After filming, the Fox News host posted the short clip on her social media accounts, captioning it: "In the Oval Office with President Trump and can confirm that it is REAL gold!"

Trump's confirmation that the additions to the Oval Office are "real gold" comes after a frenzy of speculation broke out online that the White House upgrades were nothing more than cheap imitations designed to mock the appearance of the precious metal.

Many pointed to one particular motif that very closely resembles a $58.07 polyurethane applique that is available on Home Depot's website.

Those rumors were further fueled when a spokesperson for the design company behind the appliques, Ekena Millwork, told Buzzfeed that they believe their products could well have been used in the White House renovations.

"We work with several design firms in DC that have worked on the White House and believe these could be our onlays," the spokesperson said.

Ironically, the design that many believe is identical to the moldings used in the Oval Office has since sold out the Home Depot website.

It is not the first time that Trump's White House renovations have caused a stir online—with some hitting out at the president for his "out of touch" emphasis on aesthetic upgrades at a time of such economic volatility, particular in light of the 2025 government shutdown, which had denied millions their SNAP benefits.

Other critics have slammed Trump for making such significant changes to such a historic room in the White House, particularly after he also made several dramatic updates to the building's facade and structure.

The backlash began in March 2025, just two months after his inauguration, when Trump announced plans to pave over the historic White House Rose Garden, telling reporters that he wanted to make the events space safer for guests, particularly women in heels.

"You know, we use [the Rose Garden] for press conference and it doesn't work because the people fall," he said during a March interview on Fox News. "The terrain can be wet, and the soft ground can be an issue for some. Women, with the high heels, it just didn't work."

Despite the backlash over the plans, Trump pressed on with his redesign of the outdoor space, with images taken in June 2025 revealing that the grass had been ripped up and replaced with gravel.

The completed paved area was later filled with tables, chairs, and yellow-and-white umbrellas that many noted were almost identical to those used poolside at Trump's Florida resort, Mar-a-Lago.

As part of the redesign, the Rose Garden has been outfitted with new drainage systems to prevent water from pooling at its center.

Work on the historic garden began June 9, 2025, when employees of the National Park Service began removing a limestone border that had been installed by Trump's wife, Melania, 56, during his first term in office.

The renovation quickly progressed, with images taken on June 17 and June 18 of last year revealing that the entire lawn had been ripped up by bulldozers—as well as several poles that were under the ground—before gravel was laid across the entire surface.

Despite Trump's insistence that the garden renovation was entirely necessary, the project has sparked some backlash from critics, who insist that the "removal" of such an important piece of White House history is disrespectful.

"White House Rose Garden gone. Absolutely crazy," one such person wrote in a post shared on X.

"To remove Kennedy's Rose Garden is removing a piece of our White House history. And for a patio," another person chimed in.

"Melania and Donald Trump are ruining the White House Rose Garden once again. They're deporables," one other person posted.

However, a White House spokesperson insisted to People that Trump and his wife have "the deepest respect for the history of the White House and the Rose Garden," adding: "This restoration to the Rose Garden preserves the beauty of the space and builds on the work done in 2020, with a focus on enhancing practical use and guest experience for those attending special events."

Trump prompted further fury from critics when it was revealed that his $300 million plan to outfit the White House with a new ballroom would require the complete demolition of the building's East Wing.

Initially, Trump had insisted that the addition of a 90,000-square-foot ballroom at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue would not interfere with the existing structure, telling reporters in July: "It won’t interfere with the current building. It won’t be. It’ll be near it but not touching it—and pays total respect to the existing building, which I’m the biggest fan of."

However, those plans are understood to have changed after a meeting with architects revealed there would not be enough space for the planned ballroom without the destruction of the East Wing.

During his interview with Ingraham, the president once again defended the project, telling the Fox News host that the East Wing "looked like hell" when it was torn down—noting that the ballroom will be a much grander addition to the White House.

"The East Wing was a beautiful, little, tiny structure that was built many years ago that was renovated and expanded and disbanded and columns ripped out—and it had nothing to do with the original building," he said.

"It was a poor, sad sight, and I could have built the ballroom around it, but it would not have been—we’re building one of the greatest ballrooms in the world."

#5616. What the World Series can teach real estate agents about focus

ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – OCT. 28: William Contreras, No. 24 of the Milwaukee Brewers, poses with the Willie Mays World Series Most Valuable Player award after defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series at Tropicana Field on Oct. 28, 2026, in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Mindfulness for real estate isn’t about calm. It’s about hearing clients under pressure. See what baseball teaches brokers about training attention.

The Milwaukee Brewers just won the World Series, and while I love baseball, I’ve been watching with a question that has very little to do with it: What happens to your attention when the outcome matters more than you can afford to think about?

Nobody at the plate can win a championship with the swing they wish they’d taken last inning. The players can only deal with the pitch (or batter) in front of them.

That sounds obvious until you notice how often we walk into a seller conversation still arguing with the deal that fell apart yesterday.

What’s interesting to me is that baseball has stopped treating this as a personality trait. Both the Rays and the Brewers have extensive mental performance training programs (as do all Major League ball clubs), but most brokerages treat mental health as a wellness issue, not a performance one.

Whatever name your office gives this kind of work, baseball has made it somebody’s job.

What makes this baseball tale useful to brokers and team leaders, though, is how much resistance the work still meets in a sport that has every reason to embrace it.

Andy McCullough’s recent reporting in The Athletic examines meditation in Major League Baseball, and I found the takeaways instructive.

For over two decades, most teams have invested in behavioral science and expanded their mental-performance staffs. It’s a sport that measures everything, with tens of millions of dollars on every roster, and it has decided the mental side is worth paying for.

What I find fascinating is that even as the evidence piles up, many players remain skeptical. Some call it “woo-woo.” One of the game’s best pitchers says he doesn’t need it. Coaches avoid the word “meditation” altogether because, as one put it, it intimidates people, and if you push it, they’ll tune you out.

My favorite part of the Athletic piece was this: The San Francisco Giants brought in a consultant, titled “Breathing Specialist,” and the players made jokes about it. The next season, the same man did the same work but with a new title: “Human Performance Coach,” and the resistance started to fall away.

By the time he left, about 15 players regularly attended his sessions (complete with Tibetan singing bowls). He concluded that the stigma had more to do with the title than the practice.

I don’t call it meditation when I train real estate teams either. But that doesn’t mean you can’t intentionally sharpen the skills involved.

When the market tightens, brokerages usually prescribe more activity: more calls, more door knocks, more open houses. We can count activity, so we reach for it. Ballplayers do the same thing when they skip the mental work and take extra swings.

The trouble is that pressure narrows attention, and narrowed attention is as poor a state for a batter with two on, two outs, behind two, in the bottom of the ninth as it is for a seasoned agent on a listing appointment, a price-reduction conversation or a buyer about to walk.

Don’t get confused. This kind of performance coaching is not about caring less about the result; it’s about letting go of the need to make it happen. A hitter can care enormously about winning the World Series and still recognize that thinking about winning doesn’t help him see the next pitch.

The same is true when a seller is deciding whether to take your advice. You need the listing, but needing it more isn’t any more effective than gripping and swinging the bat harder.

The goal isn’t calm, either. Mental-performance people who work with ballplayers talk about finding a usable level of activation for the task, since too much overwhelms you and too little leaves you flat. I’m not trying to produce agents who feel peaceful about losing business. I’m trying to help them notice when fear has taken over the conversation so that they can let it go and hear the client again.

There’s sports research worth knowing here. One study of Division I basketball players found that higher measured mindfulness predicted better free-throw percentages in games, a 5.75-point delta, to be exact. A separate training study found something more useful: under high stress, the gap between athletes who trained their attention and those who didn’t was larger than under low stress.

I won’t tell you a practice will add a specific number to your agents’ closing rates. Nobody can honestly promise that, and even baseball struggles to quantify the benefit. What I will tell you is that the moments that make or break an agent’s year are high-pressure, and training for them is a performance issue, not a wellness perk.

In each World Series game, every player must let the last pitch go before the next one arrives. Your agents face the same job on a smaller stage every week.

You don’t need agents who identify as meditators. You need agents who can hear what a client is saying while a deal they “need” is coming apart. That capacity deserves practice before the conversation, not a reminder to calm down halfway through it.

Aaron Hendon is the Managing Broker for Christine & Company with eXp and a mindfulness teacher. Connect with Aaron on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5615. Home prices rise in 78% of metros while weekly demand sinks to a low

Prices climbed in 78 percent of metros in the third quarter, according to NAR, as Redfin data shows pending sales at the lowest level in its records.

Home prices rose in 78 percent of U.S. metro areas during the third quarter, while pending sales in the four weeks ending Oct. 25 fell to the lowest level in Redfin’s records.

The national median single-family existing-home price rose 1.7 percent year over year to $432,900, matching the second quarter’s revised annual growth rate, the National Association of Realtors reported Thursday. Prices rose in 78 percent of the some 235 metros NAR tracks, down from 80 percent in the second quarter, and fell in 21 percent, up from 20 percent. Four percent of metros posted double-digit gains, down from 5 percent.

“Even with affordability challenges causing the housing market to stagnate, home prices continue to set record highs in most parts of the country,” NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement. “Homeowners are the beneficiaries of the price gains. Over the past seven years, the average house has appreciated by $146,000.”

Redfin’s data for the four weeks ending Oct. 25 shows prices dipping. The median U.S. home-sale price fell 0.1 percent year over year to $389,601, according to Redfin, following a 0.2 percent decline the prior week. The two drops are the first in more than three years.

NAR and Redfin measure different things. NAR tracks quarterly sales of existing single-family homes, while Redfin’s figures cover homes listed or sold across more than 900 metros on a rolling four-week basis.

The Northeast posted the largest annual gain, and the West was the only region where prices fell, according to NAR.

Prices declined in many Florida markets over the past year, Yun said.

“This quarter, however, homes in nearly all Florida markets are showing price gains,” he said. “In a similar vein, price declines in other markets may also be brief if the local job market and economy are solid.”

Gulfport-Biloxi-Pascagoula, Mississippi, led large markets with an 11 percent price increase, followed by Rochester, New York (10.9 percent) and Jackson, Mississippi (10.1 percent). Grand Rapids-Wyoming, Michigan; Cleveland-Elyria, Ohio; and Fort Wayne, Indiana, were among the Midwest markets in the top 10.

“Many markets in the Midwest offer exceptional value with more affordable homes, making homeownership more attainable,” Yun said. “Meanwhile, the artificial intelligence technology boom continues to push Bay Area home prices higher, keeping the region the most expensive in the country.”

San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara, California, remained the most expensive market at a median of $1.92 million, up 0.3 percent. Anaheim-Santa Ana-Irvine, California ($1.47 million) and San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward, California ($1.35 million) followed. Nine of the 10 most expensive markets are in California or Hawaii.

The monthly mortgage payment on a typical existing single-family home with a 20 percent down payment was $2,251 in the third quarter, up $48 from the second quarter and $69 from a year earlier, according to NAR. Typical families spent an average of 24.1 percent of income on mortgage payments, up from 23.9 percent last quarter and down from 24.5 percent a year ago.

First-time buyers faced a monthly payment of $2,208 on a typical $368,000 starter home with 10 percent down. That payment took up 36.3 percent of income, up from 36 percent last quarter and down from 37 percent a year earlier.

Pending sales fell 1.8 percent from a week earlier and 15.9 percent year over year, declining in all 50 of the most populous U.S. metros for the third straight week, according to Redfin. Seattle (down 31.6 percent) and Atlanta (down 25.9 percent) posted the steepest annual drops.

Redfin’s median monthly mortgage payment, calculated at a 7.32 percent rate, reached $2,786, up 10.7 percent year over year and the second-highest level in its records. The weekly average rate is down from 7.4 percent a week earlier and near a three-year high.

New listings fell 0.6 percent from a week earlier to their lowest level since January. Total inventory rose 0.3 percent because pending sales fell faster than new listings, Redfin reported. The share of listings with price drops rose to 21.5 percent from 20.9 percent a year earlier.

Redfin reported hundreds of thousands more sellers than buyers nationwide, giving buyers more negotiating power than they have had in more than a decade.

A First American analysis found that since 1991, rising mortgage rates have coincided with falling national home prices in some cases. In eight periods of sustained mortgage-rate increases since 1993, national home prices generally continued to appreciate, though the pace varied, First American Chief Economist Mark Fleming found.

During the rate run-up from December 2021 through October 2023, national prices rose an estimated 14 percent, according to the analysis. Affordability worsened at a steeper rate than prices, Fleming found. First American’s Real House Price Index, which adjusts prices for changes in income and mortgage rates, rose more than 70 percent over the same period.

Limited inventory can offset weaker demand when rates rise, Fleming wrote. Homeowners with mortgages below current rates may hold off on selling, and some sellers pull homes from the market rather than accept lower prices.

“Higher mortgage rates can put pressure on home prices, but the economy, household incomes and the number of homes for sale all play a role in what happens next,” Fleming wrote.

#5614. Kim Kardashian Snaps Up Palm Springs Estate During ‘Gummy’-Fueled Trip to Kris Jenner’s Home

It seems as though Kim Kardashian had quite a bit of fun during her latest real estate transaction.

During a recent visit to mom Kris Jenner’s home in Palm Springs, the star walked away with a new property.

It all went down during the Nov. 5 episode of “The Kardashians,” where Kim and Kris traveled with sister Khloé Kardashian and Kim’s costars from the upcoming comedy, “The Fifth Wheel”—Nikki Glaser, Brenda Song, and Fortune Feimster.

"The whole family just loves Palm Springs," Kim said. "My grandparents lived in Palm Springs and we would spend every Easter in Palm Springs, so it's really nostalgic for us."

The group kicked off the getaway with some special "gummies” Kim had presented to the group during the private jet ride to the desert.

“I’m so excited because when Kris Jenner and gummies get involved, it is a recipe for success,” said Khloé.

When they touched down at Kris’ gorgeous La Quinta abode, the family members gave Glaser, Song, and Feimster a tour of the backyard, showcasing the hidden trails that connect the property to Kylie Jenner’s home right next door.

“We made these so we can all get to each other the back way instead of going the front way,” Kim told the group as they made their way through the hedges.

In an interview during the episode, Kim—who just so happens to also own a home in close proximity to her mom and half-sister—explained that the house between hers and Kylie’s was up for grabs.

She toyed with the idea of snapping up the estate so that the hidden pathways could be extended to a third property.

“Can you imagine?” she asked, noting that it “would be so much fun” to continue their “little backyard connections.”

After deciding she needed to find out if her home had a better setup, or if the listed house would be an upgrade, Kim went on to encourage the ladies to climb aboard her golf cart to “sneak in” to the yard of the available property.

Although, she issued a word of caution to viewers: “It’s definitely trespassing,” she admitted. “Don’t try this at home, guys.”

After taking a look at the gorgeous yard of the listed home, Kim determined she “could buy this one and have a closer lot and a better thing”

Feimster encouraged the idea, adding, “I don’t know anything about how much it is, but you should buy it.”

Instead of sitting and stewing on it, Kim stepped away to contact the real estate agent.

“He offered me the same price, so if I just sell one for half, then I’m close to Kylie, and this view is so much better,” she said.

A confessional interview with Khloé confirmed that Kim did, in fact, get the house.

“She bought it,” Khloé said. “She actually bought it, so all of this works out for the best.”

Back in the desert, Kim thanked her costars and family members for their support, to which Song replied that they’d be there “anytime you need to break and enter into an open house.”

Kris’ resortlike home spans more than 11,000 square feet and was purchased for $12 million in 2018. It boasts seven bedrooms and seven bathrooms, and with a sleek, rectangular pool, outdoor fireplaces, and sweeping mountain views, it’s perfectly-primed for entertaining groups of friends and family.

The dwelling was previously owned by “Rocky” star Sylvester Stallone.

At the time of Kris’ purchase, real estate developer Tyler Drew told Realtor.com® that he had concerns about how existing residents in the “dead-silent” neighborhood might feel about the Kardashians moving in.

“With reality TV stars as neighbors comes reality TV drama, and it’s not like the Kardashians have a low-key lifestyle,” he said. “I wouldn’t blame the neighbors for being upset.”

Luckily, it appeared to be a nonissue, as the famous family eventually became their own neighbors in the years to follow.

In 2019, Kylie acquired her neighboring parcel of land and built her home for $3.25 million.

The next year, Kim and then-husband Kanye West snapped up another undeveloped 2-acre plot in the neighborhood for $6.3 million—which would eventually become the home the Skims founder was looking to offload in the most recent episode of “The Kardashians.”

Aside from Kim’s exciting new real estate update, the family has another thing to celebrate—Kris’ 71st birthday.

The family showed her lots of love on Nov. 5, with Kim and Khloé sharing Instagram Stories showing the sweet moments before Kris blew out the candles on her birthday cake.

“I think one of the most beautiful parts of getting older is getting to know you in so many different ways,” Khloé wrote in another heartfelt post, which used footage from nostalgic family videos, showing Kris at home over the years.

“What I adore most about you is that no matter how much life you’ve lived, you still have this childlike excitement for what’s to come. You’re always dreaming, always evolving, always finding a reason to laugh, celebrate, or make an ordinary Tuesday feel like the most fabulous day of the year,” the doting daughter continued.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5613. Cloudflare shares surge as revenue growth accelerates to 39% and outlook rises

Shares of Cloudflare Inc. jumped more than 14% in late trading today after the connectivity cloud company smashed third-quarter expectations and lifted its full-year outlook well above what Wall Street had been modeling.

The gain more than wiped out an 8% fall in the stock during the regular session.

For the quarter ended on Sept. 30, Cloudflare reported adjusted earnings per share of 38 cents, up from 27 cents in the same quarter of 2025, on revenue of $782.5 million, up 39% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting earnings of 34 cents per share on revenue of $736.8 million.

Revenue growth hit its fastest pace in nearly four years as the annualized run rate crossed $3 billion. Current remaining performance obligations rose 37% from a year earlier. The adjusted operating margin also improved, to 17.5% from 15.3%, after shrinking year-over-year in each of the two prior quarters.

Because stock-based compensation ran to $174.1 million, Cloudflare still lost $34.1 million on an unadjusted basis, compared with a $1.3 million loss a year earlier. Another $11 million went to restructuring from the roughly 1,100 job cuts announced in May. Free cash flow slipped to 10% of revenue from 13% a year ago.

On the product side, short-lived blocking rules that write themselves during a live attack are the core of Adaptive Intelligence, which Cloudflare added to its Bot Management product in late August. AI agents got tools of their own earlier in the month through Cloudflare Wallets and cloudflare.pay, which give an agent an identity handle and will let it pay for services from a stablecoin balance. Federal agencies can now put more sensitive workloads on Cloudflare for Government, which reached FedRAMP High status in August.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Matthew Prince called the period “Cloudflare’s best quarter ever” in the earnings release. Cloudflare has built the development platform for the AI-powered internet, and organizations of every size keep turning to it for protection as digital threats escalate, he said. Prince added that the business has “found an even higher gear for this next phase of growth.”

Cloudflare also named Christian Smith president of revenue today, with responsibility for worldwide sales and revenue operations. He replaces Mark Anderson, who had already said he would retire from the full-time role at year-end. Smith previously ran sales at Splunk Inc. as chief revenue officer.

For the fourth quarter, Cloudflare expects adjusted earnings of 43 cents per share on revenue of $845 million to $846 million. Analysts had forecast 38 cents per share on revenue of $798.2 million.

Cloudflare now expects 2026 revenue of $2.963 billion to $2.964 billion, about $97 million above the midpoint of the range it gave in August. Analysts had been looking for $2.87 billion in revenue and $1.26 in adjusted earnings per share for the year, and the company is now guiding to $1.35.

#5612. How Kyle Whissel built eXp’s top real estate team

The San Diego-based CEO recruits up to 15 agents a month, has a dress code and gives his trainer authority to cut newcomers.

Kyle Whissel has a standing instruction for his “60-day” bootcamp trainers: they should be willing to cut people.

His team brings in 10 to 15 new agents a month, puts them through approximately 60 hours of training over two weeks, and gives the trainer a goal of removing two people from each class.

It’s a striking approach from the leader of eXp Realty’s highest-volume U.S. team in San Diego, California. Whissel is CEO of the Whissel Beer Group, formed in 2025 when his Whissel Realty Group merged with Daniel Beer’s Beer Home Team.

According to Whissel, the team made $875 million in sales volume across 1,042 transaction sides last year (it was the first team in San Diego to break 1,000). The median price in San Diego — which is where he likes to focus his attention  (“we love that median price,” he said) — is around $1 million, he told Inman.

They’ve done that by hiring — and retaining — the right people. “We’ll give people an opportunity to prove themselves … but we’ve grown far more by cutting people than simply by hiring more people,” Whissel told Inman‘s Taylor Anderson during an interview at eXpcon in Salt Lake City earlier this month.

The company’s saying: “Expectations without enforcement are simply suggestions.”

Whissel’s recruiting process starts with a conventional, short interview, but he views the company’s two-week training period as a far better measure of whether someone belongs on the team.

Spending 60 hours in training gives leadership a chance to observe how that person behaves, learns and responds to expectations. Role-playing and scripting exercises also reveal whether new agents have the communication skills needed to work with clients.

The process continues after training, too. New agents are assigned mentors, and Whissel said those mentors are empowered to recommend removing someone who fails to meet team standards.

“If you’re going to be disrespectful to our team, I’ll be damned if I’m going to give you a client because you’re probably going to be disrespectful to them too,” he said.

Whissel also has activity and production expectations for agents already on the team. They include participating in role-playing sessions and attending meetings, along with meeting production targets.

Whissel’s hiring philosophy reaches back to his own first job, scooping popcorn at a movie theater, where he would compete with others to see who could serve the most customers. He looks for that same competitiveness in prospective agents, even if their previous accomplishments have little to do with real estate.

An applicant who participated in a college sorority, for example, might be asked whether they held a leadership position. Whissel said he wants to understand whether someone has a history of taking initiative.

In August 2025, Inman reported the merger of Whissel Realty Group and Beer Home Team, two of eXp’s highest-producing organizations. The combined company launched with approximately 160 agents and more than 60 staff members across five offices.

He said the first six months involved understanding the two organizations’ systems and getting them aligned. Whissel now believes it could take 18 months to fully integrate the companies.

“We’re going to be almost flat year-over-year,” he said, referring to the team’s expected 2026 performance, “but we’re setting up for a really, really big 2027,” he said. “You’ve gotta take a step back to take two steps forward.”

He remains optimistic about 2027, when he expects the operational investments to begin contributing to stronger growth.

Agents need to understand assumable mortgages, he said. “If you are working with a seller … and you’re not asking questions to figure out ‘does this seller have an assumable mortgage?’ (If it’s FHA, VA or USDA, those are assumable), I’m gonna beat you, because I am asking those questions.”

To find out whether a mortgage is assumable, agents simply need to get the closing disclosure from the seller. “It’s simple,” he said.

#5611. Massachusetts Plan for More Starter Homes Fails as ‘NIMBY’ Voters Insist on Local Zoning Control

Massachusetts voters rejected Question 7, a ballot initiative aimed at promoting starter homes by reducing the size of the lot required to build a home.

The initiative would have established a new minimum lot size of 5,000 square feet for single-family homes. The lot would need at least 50 feet of land bordering the street or public way, and it would also need access to public sewer and water, but otherwise, it would pave the way for smaller starter homes to be built across Massachusetts.

The measure failed by a slim margin of 50.6% to 49.4%.

"I think that, you know, there unfortunately is still a lot of NIMBYism throughout Massachusetts," says Mike Travaline, the government affairs chair of the Homebuilders and Remodelers Association of Massachusetts. The HBRA supported the measure, arguing that it would help address the state's 220,000-home shortage and allow builders to build more starter homes.

"There's a lot of resistance to any type of legislation or referendum that would take away local control from each individual municipality," he tells Realtor.com®. "Residents and town politicians really want to have the final say in what gets built in their towns."

Massachusetts has a serious lack of smaller, more affordable starter homes, which is preventing young residents from becoming homebuyers and keeping older residents locked into larger homes they can no longer afford to keep up.

The lack of starter homes in the state is part of an overall national trend away from smaller homes. The median home size in the 1960s was 1,500 square feet. By 2024, the median home size had grown to 2,205 square feet.

A Tufts University study found that approving Question 7 could create between 3,500 and 12,000 net new homes in its first decade and ultimately increase Massachusetts' housing supply by up to 320,000 units.

Andrew Mikula, the ballot initiative's organizer and chief housing economist at the Pioneer Institute, spearheaded the effort.

"We're grateful to have the support of more than 1.2 million voters who support bringing more starter homes to families across Massachusetts," he tells Realtor.com.

Currently, lot minimums are determined at the local level. A zoning report from the National Zoning Atlas found that over half the municipalities in the state require lots to be a minimum of 40,000 square feet—or about an acre—to build a home.

Those restrictive zoning laws are part of why Massachusetts received an "F" grade and was ranked almost dead last in the Realtor.com Affordability and Homebuilding Report Card two years in a row. The state was dinged for its complex zoning rules, along with its high prices, and high construction costs.

Massachusetts' median listing price is $699,990, around $250,000 more than the national median listing price of $415,000.

"From a developer perspective, we know that if we if we did build it, they will come," Travaline says.

"There's just gigantic pent up demand for that type of housing in Massachusetts because that housing really just does not exist in any sort of substantive quantity," he continues. "We don't have enough small homes that would appeal to first time homebuyers or young professionals, young families or empty nesters."

Travaline believes the bill was defeated because of pushback from local politicians who "really want to have the final say in what gets built in their towns."

Indeed, that was a major point of contention, according to Adam Chapdelaine of the Massachusetts Municipal Association, which opposed the measure. Chapdelaine wrote in an op-ed that the proposed zoning law would "override local planning" and replace "thoughtful local planning with a one-size-fits-all mandate that ignores the individual needs of all 351 Massachusetts cities and towns."

Travaline says that many towns are concerned about how the passage of Question 7 might impact housing density.

But from his perspective, "it gives developers another alternative when they're buying a lot. Rather than maybe taking the risk that they have to build a really large single-family home on a lot in order to make their return that might have to sell for you know, $1.8 to $2.5 million, they could instead create two or three smaller homes on that lot and still make their return."

"Massachusetts residents, especially young people, are leaving the state to find a more affordable place to live, separating extended families and hurting our economy," Wesley Lima, of Legalize Starter Homes, wrote in an op-ed. "Requiring huge lot sizes to build a single family home makes houses expensive, reduces construction of new single-family housing, and encourages developers to build giant McMansions to recoup land costs. Anyone who needs a low-cost, single-family suburban home is all but locked out of the market."

Mikula says his next step is to "get into all the demographic data and kind of assess you know, where where we think, you know, policies like this can pass and then go from there."

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5610. 12 housing bills that could shape affordability after the midterms

Concerns over housing supply and affordability have reached a fever pitch and become a major issue for voters in this year’s midterms.

With the midterm elections just days away, housing affordability remains a pressing issue for voters — and a growing legislative priority for lawmakers in Washington.

Congress has spent much of the past two years considering proposals aimed at lowering housing costs, helping first-time buyers, unlocking existing inventory and encouraging new construction. But despite growing bipartisan interest in housing policy, many of those proposals remain stalled in committee as voters prepare to decide which party will control Congress.

Lawmakers scored a significant bipartisan victory in July with the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a sweeping package aimed at boosting housing supply and addressing barriers to development. Yet much of the broader housing agenda remains unfinished, including proposals to expand homebuyer assistance, increase affordable housing investment and raise the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Some bills have continued attracting additional congressional support in recent weeks, but none of the proposals highlighted in September has advanced since. With both chambers largely out of session until after Election Day on Nov. 3, further legislative action will likely have to wait until lawmakers return to Washington.

Inman revisited the most consequential housing bills that could help shape the federal government’s approach to supply, affordability and homeownership in the next Congress.

What it does: The bipartisan legislation would double the capital gains exclusion on the sale of a primary residence, from $250,000 to $500,000 for individuals and from $500,000 to $1 million for married couples, and automatically adjust those limits over time to account for inflation. Why it matters: Supporters argue that the limits, which have remained unchanged since 1997, discourage longtime owners with substantial equity from selling and effectively lock inventory off the market. NAR has made the proposal a major 2026 priority and is currently framing it as one of the fastest ways to increase existing-home supply. Status: The House version remains before Ways and Means and the Senate bill before Finance, and neither has advanced beyond referral. Support has continued growing, however, with 159 House cosponsors and 25 Senate cosponsors as of late October, including lawmakers from both parties. With Congress largely out of session until after the election, inclusion in a broader tax package during the lame-duck session or next Congress remains one possible path forward.

What it does: This legislation would establish a refundable federal tax credit equal to 10 percent of a first home’s purchase price, capped at $15,000. Eligibility and the size of the credit would be subject to income and local home-price limits.

Why it matters: Unlike proposals intended to increase supply over time, the bill would directly reduce the cost of purchasing a first home for qualifying households. The tradeoff is that giving buyers more purchasing power does not add more homes to the market, and in a supply-constrained market, it can also put upward pressure on prices.

Status: Both versions were introduced in July 2025 and remain before the House Ways and Means and Senate Finance committees, respectively. Neither chamber has taken action beyond committee referral.

What it does: Introduced by Rep. Maxine Waters, D-Calif., the bill would increase the mandatory share of Federal Home Loan Bank earnings devoted to the system’s Affordable Housing Program. The Consumer Federation of America estimates the change would generate roughly $300 million in additional annual funding for affordable housing development, down payment assistance and home repair programs, without requiring additional taxpayer funding.

Why it matters: The 11 Federal Home Loan Banks provide liquidity to more than 6,500 member institutions, including banks, credit unions and community development financial institutions. Housing advocates have argued that the system should devote more of its earnings to its public mission. In a broader reform proposal, the Coalition for Federal Home Loan Bank Reform has called for doubling the mandatory Affordable Housing Program contribution from 10 percent to 20 percent, which it estimates would add about $600 million annually for affordable housing.

Status: The House Financial Services Committee considered H.R. 10325 on Sept. 16, but a motion to report the amended bill favorably failed 21–28. That leaves the measure facing a significant setback in the House, even as housing and consumer groups continue pushing for broader FHLBank reform.

What it does: Designed to make it easier to pull together a down payment, this bill would raise the amount first-time buyers can withdraw from an IRA without paying the usual 10 percent early-withdrawal penalty from $10,000 to $50,000.

Why it matters: The proposal targets a major barrier for many prospective first-time buyers: saving enough cash for a home’s down payment and covering closing costs. It would expand access to buyers’ existing retirement savings rather than create a new federal subsidy. NAR lists the bill among its current legislative priorities.

Status: The House version remains before Ways and Means, while the Senate companion, introduced by Sens. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., and Todd Young, R-Ind., is before Finance. Neither has advanced beyond committee, though the Senate bill’s bipartisan sponsorship distinguishes it from some other first-time buyer proposals.

What it does: Seeking to make homebuilding and rehabilitation more feasible in distressed neighborhoods, this legislation would create a federal tax credit to support the construction and rehabilitation of owner-occupied homes where development costs exceed what finished properties can command on the market. The credit is designed to help close that gap and make projects financially viable.

Why it matters: The credit is intended to make starter-home projects possible in communities where builders currently cannot make the numbers work, with a particular focus on for-sale housing rather than rental development.

Status: The House bill remains before Ways and Means and the Senate version before Finance. In May, the bipartisan sponsors released planned revisions, including more flexibility for state housing finance agencies and a shorter four-year authorization, that they intend to carry into the next version of the bill, whether in a year-end package or the next Congress.

What it does: This proposal would establish a federal investment tax credit covering 20 percent of qualifying costs to convert nonresidential buildings into housing, increasing to 30 percent in certain areas where development is particularly challenging. At least 20 percent of the resulting units would need to remain affordable to households earning no more than 80 percent of area median income for 30 years.

Why it matters: The bill targets two persistent real estate problems at once — underutilized commercial buildings and the shortage of housing. Office-to-residential conversions have attracted substantial interest, but challenging layouts, financing hurdles and construction costs can make projects difficult to pencil out. A tax credit is intended to help close that feasibility gap. NAR also lists this bill among its 2026 legislative priorities.

Status: Introduced in March 2025, the bipartisan bill has attracted 57 cosponsors, including lawmakers from both parties, but remains before the House Ways and Means Committee without advancing beyond referral.

What it does: Focused on expanding and modernizing the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, the proposal includes a broad series of changes involving tenant eligibility, project financing and credit administration.

Why it matters: LIHTC is a central federal financing tool that helps drive the construction of affordable rental housing across the country. Congress already adopted two pieces of the broader proposal in 2025, permanently increasing annual Housing Credit authority by 12 percent and lowering the bond-financing threshold from 50 percent to 25 percent. According to the National Council of State Housing Agencies, roughly two dozen other provisions remain unenacted.

Status: The House bill remains before Ways and Means and the Senate version before Finance, with both measures drawing broad bipartisan support. Advocates continue pushing the remaining provisions either through the standalone bills or as part of future tax legislation.

What it does: The bill would update federal rules for mortgage revenue bonds and mortgage credit certificates used by state housing finance agencies, including increasing limits on certain home improvement loans and changing refinancing and recapture provisions.

Why it matters: Those programs can help lower- and moderate-income households access lower-cost mortgage financing, giving this technical tax legislation a direct connection to homeownership affordability.

Status: The House version, introduced in February 2026, remains before Ways and Means, while the Senate bill remains before Finance. The Senate measure was discussed during an Oct. 21, 2025, Senate Banking housing subcommittee hearing, but neither version has advanced beyond committee.

What it does: Seeking to open underused land owned by churches and other religious organizations to new housing development, this bill would preempt certain state and local laws that block affordable housing on those properties.

Why it matters: Religious institutions collectively control substantial amounts of land, including parcels in expensive housing markets where zoning can constrain redevelopment. The bill is notable because it tackles supply by asserting federal authority over certain local land-use restrictions, rather than relying primarily on grants or tax incentives.

Status: Introduced by Reps. Scott Peters, D-Calif., and Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., in September 2025, the bipartisan legislation remains before the House Financial Services Committee. Rep. Emilia Strong Sykes, D-Ohio, joined as a cosponsor in October, but the bill has not advanced beyond committee referral.

What it does: This measure would amend the Fair Housing Act to prohibit discrimination based on a person’s source of income, veteran status or military status.

Why it matters: The change would expand federal fair-housing protections for veterans, service members and renters who rely on housing vouchers or other lawful sources of income. It could also create new federal compliance obligations for landlords, property managers and real estate professionals.

Status: Both versions remain in committee, with the House bill before Judiciary and the Senate measure before Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs. The House proposal has continued attracting support, reaching 23 cosponsors following the addition of Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-Texas, on Oct. 22. Neither chamber has advanced the legislation beyond referral.

What it does: Rather than establishing a tax credit or housing-production program, the Saving the American Dream Act would require HUD, Treasury, Agriculture, Veterans Affairs and the Federal Housing Finance Agency to coordinate housing research and market data and submit a joint report to Congress identifying opportunities to improve housing affordability.

Why it matters: Federal housing policy is currently divided among HUD, Treasury and other agencies. Supporters of the effort argue that greater coordination could reduce conflicting policies and give Washington a more coherent strategy for addressing affordability.

Status: Introduced in September 2025, the bipartisan bill remains before the House Financial Services Committee and the Veterans’ Affairs Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity. It has attracted 40 cosponsors, including two who joined on Oct. 1, but has not advanced beyond committee referral.

What it does: Introduced by Rep. Norma Torres, D-Calif., on Oct. 22, the legislation would establish a new HUD grant program to help states streamline financing and administrative processes for affordable housing development. The proposal would authorize $90 million annually from fiscal 2027 through 2029, including funding to consolidate state financing programs, simplify applications for builders and improve access to development assistance.

Why it matters: Affordable housing developers often navigate multiple state agencies, financing programs and administrative requirements to move projects forward. By simplifying those processes, the proposal aims to reduce administrative barriers that can delay projects and increase development costs. States that meet the bill’s initial requirements could also use funding to streamline zoning, permitting and Low-Income Housing Tax Credit administration.

Status: Torres introduced the bill without cosponsors on Oct. 22, and it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee. It has not advanced beyond committee referral.

NAR’s current legislative agenda is centered heavily on housing supply, with the trade group estimating the country is short 4.7 million homes. Following the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July, NAR has continued pressing lawmakers on housing supply, with its latest advocacy materials putting particular emphasis on unlocking existing inventory through the More Homes on the Market Act and proposed changes to the capital gains exclusion for longtime homeowners.

The organization is also pushing lawmakers to fully fund several HUD programs, including fair housing enforcement and housing counseling services, while calling for long-term reauthorization of the National Flood Insurance Program. NAR says the flood program supports roughly 500,000 home sales each year and argues that lapses or uncertainty around coverage can disrupt transactions in flood-prone communities.

The flood insurance program’s current authorization expires Dec. 11, the same day a temporary spending measure funding federal agencies, including HUD, is set to expire. The deadlines leave Congress facing another round of funding and insurance negotiations during its post-election lame-duck session.

Passage of ROAD has not ended NAR’s work on the legislation itself. Many of the law’s new grants and housing programs still depend on future congressional appropriations and HUD rulemaking, including incentives for local housing production, zoning and permitting reforms, commercial-to-residential conversions and home-repair programs. NAR is now encouraging states and local governments to prepare for those programs, while pressing Congress to provide the funding needed to put them into effect.

Implementation of the law is also underway. On Oct. 22, the Treasury Department proposed regulations clarifying restrictions on large institutional investors purchasing single-family homes. Under the law, beginning Jan. 7, 2027, investors controlling at least 350 single-family homes will generally be prohibited from purchasing additional properties, subject to exceptions for activities including build-to-rent and renovate-to-rent programs.

For qualifying programs designed to help renters become homeowners, the proposal also establishes a framework for a 30-day first-look period and a right of first refusal before investors sell the properties to other buyers.

Reporter’s note: This story was originally published on Sept. 24, 2026, and has been updated to reflect the latest available information.

Additional note: AI tools were utilized in reviewing and verifying current federal housing bills, legislative priorities and related reporting for this story. All substantive details were checked against congressional records, primary-source materials and prior reporting before publication.

#5609. Open Real Estate: We’re almost there, but not quite

OPINION: The Open Real Estate options give sellers just two choices: market or participant view. Darryl Davis makes the case for a third door.

Picture a homeowner at the kitchen table. She likes you. She trusts you. And she says something agents hear every week: “I want you to sell my house. Just you. I don’t want a parade of strangers walking through my bedroom with agents I have never met. But I don’t want to hide it either. Advertise it. Get the word out. I want the best price.”

That is not a strange request. Some homeowners would happily give up a few dollars on the sale price for less stress, more convenience, and the peace of working with one agent and one office. And right now, the newest system in real estate has no way to say yes to it.

On October 26, Keller Williams, AGNT (the parent of eXp and NextHome), HomeServices of America and Real REMAX Group launched Open Real Estate (ORE). Four competitors came together to stop listings from disappearing into company silos. They deserve real credit. But read the FAQ, and you will see the system gives a seller only two doors.

Now go back to our homeowner. Door one sends strangers through her bedroom. Door two gives her one agent but forbids anyone to advertise her house, the last thing she asked for. She wants one agent and full marketing. ORE makes her pick one.

That is not seller choice. That is a choice between two things she did not ask for.

Here is the option that is missing, and it is simple.

I can already hear the objection. “Darryl, isn’t this just a pocket listing with a nicer name?”

No. A pocket listing is hidden. A Coming Soon tease builds buzz while keeping other agents out, and nobody, not even the listing agent, can show it. The true exclusive is the opposite of both. The house is actively marketed to the public, and every member company knows it is available. The only thing exclusive is who walks through her front door.

Think of a restaurant that only takes reservations. Everybody sees the menu and knows where it is. You call first, and the owner decides who gets a table. Nobody calls that a secret restaurant.

Let’s say it out loud. In a true exclusive, the listing agent may well sell the house to their own buyer and get paid on both sides. For some sellers, that is exactly why they choose it. They understand that one cook in the kitchen managing the whole process beats two, especially when the second one is an untrained buyer’s agent.

ORE already has what it needs to offer this, and technology can make the fiduciary piece stronger than ever.

CCP had the right intentions. NAR wanted to stop listings from disappearing. But it was the wrong strategy, and it did the opposite. Once a listing is publicly marketed, it must go into the MLS within one business day.

Keep it quiet, though, and it falls under the office exclusive exemption. That does not tell agents to share. It tells them to stop advertising and keep the listing inside their own company. The brokerage itself became the pocket.

A rule meant to bring listings into the open pushed many further underground. As I wrote earlier this year, a Redfin analysis found pocket listings rose 67 percent after CCP passed. NAR leaves enforcement to local MLSs, and in a lot of markets, they have quietly stopped enforcing it or issuing penalties. A rule on the books but not enforced protects no one. It only confuses the agents trying to follow it.

For newer agents: Before CCP, a seller could hire one brokerage to market and show her home exclusively. But those exclusives usually stayed out of the MLS, so other agents often never knew the house existed. The true exclusive keeps what sellers liked about the old way and adds what was always missing: every agent knowing the house is for sale. That is the replacement.

Let’s give our homeowner the third door: one agent, full marketing and a way for the right buyer to find her. That is real seller choice.

Until a model like this is in place, we are still hurting buyers and sellers. Period.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

Darryl Davis is the CEO of Darryl Davis Seminars. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

#5608. California Passes Down Payment Assistance Plan, but Push To Cut Red Tape Remains in Limbo

California voters headed to the polls on Tuesday to decide three new housing-related ballot measures. While two of them handily passed, votes are still being counted on a plan to cut red tape and streamline environmental reviews for new homes.

Voters approved Proposition 1, which authorizes California to issue $11.25 billion in bonds to support housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, permanent supportive housing, and affordable housing. The funding also backs both down payment assistance programs and mortgage programs for veterans.

Gov. Gavin Newsom expressed support for the measure, as did the Democratic Party of California. The ACLU, the California Apartment Association, and the California Housing Consortium also supported the measure, although there was some scattered opposition from Republican state legislators.

"This bond is about building communities, expanding access and affordability in California, where every family has a fair shot at a place to call home," Newsom said in a June statement.

Voters backed a similar measure in 2024 that earmarked $6.38 billion for homelessness and veterans housing programs.

"Higher mortgage rates have squeezed homebuyers and the for-sale market for four years, and they have hurt builders, too, especially in multifamily," Realtor.com senior economist Joel Berner says.

"Apartment projects depend on layers of financing, and assembling it has gotten much harder at today’s borrowing costs, particularly in a state as expensive and complicated to build in as California. When rates jumped in 2022 and 2023, a backlog of [COVID-19] pandemic-era projects that were already financed kept delivering homes. That backlog has been worked through, and the multifamily pipeline behind it is much thinner today," Berner adds.

Berner calls Prop 1 a "modest attempt to plug this gap" but only "one piece of the puzzle," noting that the infusion of cash won't do much to reduce approval times or land acquisition costs.

Californians also approved Proposition 37, which creates a $25 billion loan program for middle-income earners to purchase new homes. The state would issue bonds and use the proceeds to offer fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of the purchase price of newly constructed homes priced below $1.5 million

Borrowers must be California residents who pay at least 3% down and meet some income requirements. This, supporters say, would help lower the amount they'd need to save for a down payment on a new home. They expect the measure to spur the construction of new homes and be paid for when investors and home borrowers repay the loans.

The California Association of Realtors and the California Chamber of Commerce both supported the measure.

"Voters in California have seized the opportunity to help alleviate the burden of current mortgage rates on new-home buyers," says Berner of the initiative's passage. "With current mortgage rates holding above 7%, this presents the opportunity for buyers to save on interest payments for part of their home purchase, which could be a boon to the new-home segment of sales in the Golden State."

But, says Berner, housing is still above $1.5 million in many California metros, signaling that the measure's impact may be circumscribed.

"The median listing price for newly built single-family homes in the San Jose metro is over $2.1 million. In Los Angeles, it’s over $1.7 million. San Francisco has a median of about $1.5 million, and San Diego’s median is about $1.3 million. Among newly built single-family homes for sale in 2026 in the San Jose metro, just 41.7% were priced below $1.5 million. In Los Angeles, the share was 41.7% as well; 49.5% of newly built single-family homes in San Francisco were below the threshold; and in San Diego, 61.4% were. Proposition 37 has the potential to help prospective California homebuyers, but only if they can find new homes to buy."

Proposition 45 limits timelines on environmental reviews for some projects under the California Environmental Quality Act. These new requirements would expedite environmental review and court challenges to projects.

Votes for the measure are still being counted. With 65% of the votes counted on Friday, 54.9% of Californians have voted against it while 45.1% voted in favor.

Affordable housing advocates—including the Associated General Contractors of California, the California Building Industry Association, the California Council for Affordable Housing, and the California Chamber of Commerce—expressed support for the measure.

Environmental groups and labor unions widely opposed it, arguing that it would reduce environmental oversight and community decision making around new development.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5606. AGNT Posts 6% Revenue Growth in Q3, Expects ‘Difficult’ Market Into 2027

AGNT, the parent company for eXp Realty and NextHome, posted revenue growth despite economic headwinds of high rates and sluggish home demand, the company announced during an earnings call Thursday.

Closed real estate sales transactions reached 131,000 in the third quarter of 2026, up 8% year-over-year, alongside a 10% jump in sales volume to $59.3 billion, executives said. That productivity pushed AGNT revenues to $1.4 billion over the quarter, up 6% from $1.3 billion a year ago.

Meanwhile, the company saw a net loss of $4.3 million over the quarter and 7% higher operating expenses from a year ago. AGNT’s adjusted EBITDA closed out the quarter at $17.1 million, down 3% from $17.7 million compared to the previous year.

Newly minted AGNT CEO Leo Pareja acknowledged the market is challenging, with existing-home sales expected to be near 4 million, inventory up about 7% year-over-year but still below pandemic levels and mortgage rates above 7.3%. He said the market was “not broken” but “resetting to normal” after two unusually strong booms.

Overall, the company saw agent count grow to 87,457 by the end of the third quarter, up 5% year-over-year (including NextHome, which was acquired earlier in the year).

Pareja attributed most of its agent attrition mostly to unproductive agents leaving eXp or NextHome, with 49% of those nonproductive agents leaving the real estate industry altogether in Q3. Newer agents to the company tend to join a team, where they get a stronger start, he added.

“With 44% of new agent joiners on teams in Q3, and this is important because agents on teams are 77% more productive than individual agents,” Pareja said.

The company’s Q3 earnings call came on the heels of AGNT, along with Keller Williams, HomeServices of America and Real REMAX Group, forming Open Real Estate, a new shared listing-data company. The new initiative uses standard fields for listings to be entered then distributes the data out to participating members, local MLSs, search portals and other platforms.

“When listings are fragmented or kept out of view, buyers can miss homes, and sellers reach fewer potential buyers,” Pareja said. Pareja noted that Open Real Estate’s startup costs have limited exposure for the rest of the business.

As mortgage rates stay north of 7% and home sales slow heading into the final stretch of the year, AGNT updated its guidance for the remainder of 2026. AGNT Chief Financial Officer Jesse Hill acknowledged the tough market conditions the company—and the entire industry—is facing.

“Rising interest rates continue to weigh significantly on housing demand, and we’ve seen that softening as we’ve headed into Q4 here,” Hill said. He added that market conditions, along with AGNT seeing “higher-than-baseline” legal expenses peaking in 2026, caused it to update its financial outlook for the year.

In late October, eXp reached a settlement with agent Anya Roberts who sued former eXp agents Michael Bjorkman and David Golden in 2023, alleging they drugged and sexually assaulted her at company events. Roberts also named the brokerage and founder Glenn Sanford in her federal lawsuit for allegedly ignoring or covering up a sex trafficking/recruiting scheme tied to its revenue-share model. The company has consistently denied all wrongdoing in connection to the lawsuit.

While the case was settled for an undisclosed amount, a separate, larger civil lawsuit from four other female eXp agents with similar allegations is ongoing. Hill said the company expects legal costs to “normalize” in 2027, but remain higher for the rest of the year.

Overall in 2026, AGNT expects revenue to reach $4.85 billion to $5.05 billion and adjusted EBITDA in the neighborhood of $40 million to $47 million, Hill noted.

#5605. Americans cling to homeownership as affordability gap widens

New ACS data shows incomes up 3.9 percent, but buyers still need $110,700 to comfortably afford a median-priced home.

Americans are clinging to the dream of homeownership — even though their incomes are barely enough to sustain it.

The U.S. Census Bureau released its 2025 American Community Survey 1-Year data on Thursday, which includes statistics on 40-plus topics, including housing. The national homeownership rate held steady at 65.3 percent, only 0.1 percentage points below the 5-year high of 65.4 percent. The majority of homeowners carry a mortgage (59 percent), with the real median mortgage payment increasing 2.4 percent year over year to $1,598.

Total housing costs, which may include expenses like homeowners association (HOA) fees, maintenance and repairs, increased 3.5 percent year over year from $2,090 to $2,163. Households now spend 21.9 percent of income on these costs, up 0.5 percentage points and just 8.1 points below the widely recognized 30 percent affordability threshold.

Median household incomes are edging up (+1.2 percent yoy after inflation), but Realtor.com Senior Economist Hannah Jones said it’s not enough to keep up with median home value growth.

“New 2025 American Community Survey data show median household income rose 3.9 percent to $84,780, with incomes up nominally in 49 of 50 states,” she said in an emailed statement. “But housing remained out of reach for many households. With a median listing price near $424,000 in 2025, mortgage rates averaging 6.6 percent, a 20 percent down payment, and taxes and insurance at roughly 1.7 percent of home value, a buyer needed about $110,700 to afford a median-priced home, roughly $26,000 more than the typical household earned.”

“Closing that gap would have required incomes to be 30.5 percent higher, prices about $99,000 lower or mortgage rates near 3.5 percent,” she added. “That affordability challenge has persisted, even as the year started with a promise.”

Jones said the market was primed in homebuyers’ favor at the beginning of the year, with sub-6 percent mortgage rates. However, macroeconomic and geopolitical conflicts have pushed mortgage rates up — now in the 7.30 percent range — leaving most homebuyers unable to take advantage of better inventory levels and falling list prices.

“Even assuming incomes have grown in line with recent wage gains of 3 percent to 4 percent since 2025, the typical household income would still be roughly $28,000 short,” she said. “Demand has cooled in response to higher rates, and pending sales fell 4.1 percent year over year in September, the steepest annual drop since March 2025, even as inventory approached pre-pandemic levels and prices softened.”

Realtor.com has released several reports on how homebuyers can attempt to make the math work, even as rates fluctuate. They can improve their credit scores, increase their down payments, shop lenders and build a budget buffer to help them absorb a 0.50 percent rate increase or decrease.

As for what lies ahead this year, homebuyers aren’t expected to receive mortgage rate relief.

The Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate steady (at 3.75 to 4 percent) at its Oct. 28 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting. The federal funds rate affects how banks and financial institutions set rates, including mortgage rates, but a change doesn’t guarantee mortgage rates will move in tandem.

The 10-Year Treasury Yield has the greatest impact on mortgage rates as lenders add a spread — or percentage markup — on top of it. The spread reflects the effects of monetary and fiscal policies, economic growth, inflation, higher origination costs and the gap between mortgage-backed securities (MBS) and Treasury yields.

“Whether the Fed hikes or holds this month, homebuyers shouldn’t expect a big change in mortgage rates,” First American Senior Economist Sam Williamson told Inman on Wednesday after the Fed’s FOMC meeting. “With another hike widely expected in December and further increases possible next year, borrowing costs are likely to remain elevated, keeping many buyers and sellers on the sidelines. But not everyone has the luxury of waiting. New jobs, growing families and other life events will keep some buyers moving forward, even as higher rates delay moves that can wait.”

Jones said mortgage rates will remain “the swing factor” and will shape next year’s American Community Survey results.

“For rates to trend lower, inflation has to cool, and the latest data shows it is moving the wrong way,” she said. “Annual inflation rose to 3.7 percent in September as energy prices surged amid the conflict in the Middle East, and core inflation edged up to 2.6 percent.”

“With the Fed focused on bringing inflation back under control while protecting the labor market, a significant drop in mortgage rates is unlikely in the near term,” she added. “For buyers on the fence, though, today’s mix of more inventory, more price cuts and more room to negotiate is the best they’ve had in years.”

#5604. Bear Grylls Bought a ‘Derelict’ Island With ‘No Power’ and ‘Rats’ at 25 Instead of a London Apartment—Here’s How It Looks Decades Later

Bear Grylls made an unusual decision decades ago, when he acquired a marital starter home with his wife, Shara Grylls.

“At 25, just married, we bought a small, abandoned, off-grid island from an ad in the back of a magazine,” the British adventurer, 52, wrote in a Nov. 3 Instagram caption.

Grylls revealed that the purchase of St. Tudwal’s Island West cost them around $120,000.

“There were many who thought us crazy,” he continued. “The best adventures start with nay-sayers. Thank you Shara for being brave and saying yes!”

While the comment section had users divided over the relatability of purchasing an entire island—with one commenter wondering how “celebrities get so far out of touch from reality and regular people”—there were also a handful of people who stepped in to point out that even when adjusted for inflation, the island was less costly than the average U.S. home.

The “Running Wild With Bear Grylls” star explained the decision to the Sunday Times in 2021, noting that snapping up a Welsh island seemed like a more exciting use of the couple’s money.

“In 2001, we were going to buy a London flat for $288,000, but we bought a houseboat on the Thames [now sold] and the island together, and it cost less than the apartment. So we decided on the path less trodden and an amazing adventure,” he said.

Grylls shed some light on just how dilapidated the property was 25 years ago.

“The island had a 200-year-old lighthouse and two lightkeeper’s cottages, but [the houses] were derelict with no power, no water, no roof, and rats,” he said. “I remember my first bath sitting in 3 inches of water pumped from the old tanks we’d cleaned out. There was rubble everywhere and rain coming through, but it was a great moment.”

Considering Grylls has made a career out of his ability to survive in extremely harsh conditions, it’s not entirely surprising that he was able to get through a few rough years before the island would become a more suitable dwelling.

It took a decade to get permission to build a slipway, which Grylls said they finished just a few years ago.

“It has been life-changing for us,” he said of the addition. “Previously we had to keep a boat on a mooring, row ashore, and walk a mile up the beach with all the shopping.”

Eventually, the two lightkeeper’s cottages were combined into a single home with four bedrooms. But the island is still off-grid.

“It’s 20 acres and 5 miles offshore with no mains, electricity, or running water,” Grylls told Vanity Fair in 2012. “It has a little lighthouse beside our house and is surrounded by amazing sea cliffs, seals, and dolphins. It is my favorite place on the planet!”

To travel to the destination, Grylls and his family take a “30-foot, high-speed ex-lifeboat,” which he described as a “rigid inflatable boat with twin 300-horsepower engines behind it that can tackle any sea it needs to.”

He said the house is “as tough as you get.” Thanks to “2-foot-thick old limestone walls,” it retains heat in the winter and stays cool in the summer.

“But when those gales come in, you can still feel it almost shake,” Grylls admitted. “Sea spray reaches the windows despite the 150-foot elevation.”

While St. Tudwal’s may lack some of the modern amenities guests might typically expect, the Grylls family does “sometimes have friends” visit.

“They need to be up for an adventure and prepared to get stuck there if the weather turns,” he said.

Grylls has recently made headlines for his connection to disgraced former comic Russell Brand, who was recently found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Grylls helped baptize Brand in a ceremony in the River Thames in 2024, after the allegations against the actor had come to light. Prior to the baptism, Brand appeared in a 2023 episode of Grylls’ show, in which the pair traveled across the Hebrides Islands.

“Brand’s faith seemed genuine to me at the time when I was a guest at his private baptism,” Grylls wrote in a Nov. 6 X post. “I have attended a few now. Even visiting in prisons with people who have committed terrible crimes. It’s part of our calling as men and women of faith, to love and serve anyone. It is the sick that need healing.”

Noting that “judgment is for the courts and God,” Grylls added that “it is right that justice has now been served.

“I can’t imagine how hard this time has been for the victims, the heroes of the day,” he said.

#5603. OpenAI makes new data center commitments, AI policy recommendations

OpenAI Group PBC today made a set of commitments designed to ensure that its data centers benefit the communities where they’re built.

It also proposed that lawmakers make some of the commitments mandatory for artificial intelligence companies.

The move comes two days after Democrats won both the House and the Senate on a campaign backing data center construction curbs. Additionally, voters approved dozens of ballot measures designed to scale back or limit AI infrastructure projects.

OpenAI today reiterated a commitment it made in January to fully pay for the electricity and grid upgrades that its data centers require. That covers items such as the construction of new overhead power lines. Additionally, the company pledged to provide “financial assurances” that will protect other grid users from potential project cancellations and delays.

It will also take steps to reduce grid strain. In particular, it will scale back its data centers’ power draw at times when energy demand is particularly high. That approach, which is known as a flexible data center model, has also drawn the interest of other industry players as Nvidia Corp. and Google LLC.

Some data center builders sign non-disclosure agreements with local officials to keep construction details under wraps. OpenAI today pledged not to use NDAs. It will instead only seek “narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.”

OpenAI will publicly share construction plans and noise projections before construction of a new facility begins. Additionally, it will provide information about the jobs that each data center is expected to create. The goal is to help local unions and training providers prepare residents for the positions.

The company plans to tailor its commitments to each data center. It will publish the customized project terms in a document it calls a local compact. Once construction is underway, the company will provide annual updates and designate a local contact to field residents’ questions.

OpenAI hopes to codify some of the best practices that it published today into law. It released a policy paper that calls on lawmakers to limit data center developers’ use of NDAs and require them to cover their electricity costs. Furthermore, it argues that AI companies should be offered incentives to lower their power usage at times of peak grid stress.

Some of the best practices that the ChatGPT developer is prompting are already being adopted by other industry players. Google, for example, today pledged to fully cover the electricity costs of a new $17 billion data center that it plans to build in Wyoming. It will also finance related grid upgrades. Anthropic PBC made a similar commitment in February.
