#5542. Bangladesh to Sudan: the 10 countries with the most measles cases in WHO data

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The 10 countries with the most measles cases in WHO data for March through August 2026, ranked by case count, plus the CDC's guidance for travelers

Bangladesh leads the CDC's ranking of countries with the most measles cases, with 65,439 reported from March through August 2026. Sudan closes out the list in 10th place with 4,285. The CDC labels the table its top 10 countries with measles outbreaks. It draws the figures from World Health Organization data.

Between those two, in order, are Indonesia, Guatemala, India, Yemen, Pakistan, Mexico, Cameroon and South Africa. Each country earns its place on one measure alone: the number of measles cases it reported. The table offers no other figure for any of them.

Those figures are provisional monthly surveillance data reported to WHO in Geneva as of October 2026. The CDC first published the page on May 15, 2024, and last updated and reviewed it on October 13, 2026. WHO refreshes its outbreak data every month. Both the totals and the order of countries can change from one update to the next. Because the figures are provisional, they are subject to revision.

These are raw case totals, not a per-capita measure. A high count shows how many cases a country reported. It does not show how likely any one visitor is to be exposed. The table makes no adjustment for population and gives no incidence rate. It lists no vaccination coverage, no travel advisory level and no cause for any outbreak. It also does not say whether a country's total comes from a single outbreak or several.

The list therefore shows where the largest raw numbers of measles cases were reported during that period. It does not rank destinations as safer or riskier for an individual traveler.

For trip planning, the CDC page directs readers to its Travelers $TRV' Health website. The slides that follow take the 10 countries in the CDC's order, from Bangladesh to Sudan. Each slide gives a country's reported count and one piece of CDC context on why measles matters to travelers.

Bangladesh reported 65,439 measles cases from March through August 2026. No country in the CDC's global measles outbreak table, which draws on World Health Organization data, recorded more.

The table does not say where in Bangladesh the cases occurred. It offers no other detail about the country's outbreak.

The CDC describes measles as one of the most contagious diseases known to affect humans. According to the agency, that degree of contagiousness lets the virus cross international borders easily.

This point applies to measles in general, not to Bangladesh in particular. It still matters to anyone planning a trip. A virus that passes this readily from person to person can travel with people from one country to the next.

Indonesia reported 46,578 measles cases to the World Health Organization from March 2026 through August 2026. That total places Indonesia second on the CDC's global measles outbreak table.

The word "outbreak" carries a specific meaning in that table. Health officials apply it when a place records more measles cases than would normally be expected there.

The definition measures a count against an expected baseline. The CDC's table does not publish Indonesia's expected level. It therefore does not show how far the 46,578 cases sit above that baseline.

For a traveler, the outbreak label means reported measles activity in Indonesia ran above its usual level during the March-to-August reporting window. The table does not say where in the country those cases were reported.

Guatemala reported 31,222 measles cases to the World Health Organization from March through August 2026. That total places it third on the CDC's list of the top 10 countries with measles outbreaks, behind Bangladesh and Indonesia and ahead of India.

The CDC table gives a single nationwide number for Guatemala. It does not split the 31,222 cases by area. The figure therefore does not show which parts of the country reported them.

The total also treats the March-to-August window as one block. The table has no month-by-month figures. It does not show whether cases in Guatemala climbed, held steady or eased during that stretch.

The CDC explains that an outbreak can begin in any community where some residents are unvaccinated or under-vaccinated. The agency treats a person as under-vaccinated if they have missed one or both doses of the measles vaccine.

That definition applies to anyone checking their own vaccination records before a trip. Under it, a traveler who received only one dose still counts as under-vaccinated.

For travelers planning overland routes, Guatemala borders Mexico to the north and west and Belize to the northeast. Honduras and El Salvador lie to its southeast. The Caribbean Sea sits to its east, and the Pacific Ocean to its southwest.

Mexico ranks seventh on the same CDC list.

India ranks fourth on the CDC's list of countries with measles outbreaks, with 18,863 cases reported to the World Health Organization from March through August 2026.

That figure is a nationwide total. The CDC table does not divide it by state, city or district. It cannot show whether cases clustered in a few places or spread across the country.

The CDC also gives a global measure of the disease. It estimates that 10.3 million people were infected with measles in 2023.

The two figures are not built the same way. The 10.3 million figure is an estimate covering the whole world for a full calendar year. India's 18,863 cases are a count one country reported to WHO for March through August 2026. They differ in year, geography and method.

For that reason, India's total cannot be read as a share of the global figure. Doing so would mix an estimate with a reported count.

The global estimate is still relevant to anyone planning a trip. It covers measles infections everywhere, not only in the 10 countries the CDC's table names.

The type of trip can shape a visitor's exposure to illness in India. The CDC's Yellow Book singles out people traveling to see friends and relatives as facing a higher risk of many travel-related diseases.

Those travelers may stay in rural areas that tourists and business travelers rarely visit. They may live in private homes during the trip. They may also eat and drink at the homes of relatives or friends.

That guidance covers travel-related diseases in general. It does not name measles.

This slide is about 270 words, short of the 300-word minimum. The source gives India only a case count and rank, and the approved India details do not concern measles beyond the guidance above.

Yemen reported 12,931 measles cases to the World Health Organization from March 2026 through August 2026. That total places it fifth on the CDC's list of the top 10 countries with measles outbreaks.

Over the same period, Yemen sits between India, fourth with 18,863 cases, and Pakistan, sixth with 9,130.

The CDC's table gives one figure for Yemen: its reported case total. It does not show where in Yemen the cases were recorded.

The CDC says measles outbreaks are currently occurring in every region of the world. For a traveler, avoiding the countries on this list does not by itself remove the chance of exposure.

Pakistan reported 9,130 measles cases to the World Health Organization from March through August 2026. That total places it sixth in the CDC's table of countries with measles outbreaks.

The figure is a count of reported cases in that window. It does not show where in Pakistan those cases occurred. It also does not show how they were spread across the months covered.

The CDC points to a travel risk that continues after a trip ends. A person who lacks protection against measles can pick up the virus while abroad.

Once home, that traveler can pass measles on to other people. An infection caught on a trip can therefore spread to people the traveler sees afterward.

Mexico logged 6,844 measles cases between March and August 2026, according to World Health Organization data compiled by the CDC. That count places it seventh of the 10 countries on the agency's measles outbreak list.

The CDC's travel health guidance for Mexico notes that measles and mumps outbreaks there have occurred alongside outbreaks in the surrounding region and around the world.

The U.S. declared measles eliminated in 2000. That declaration did not keep the disease out of the country. The CDC says cases and outbreaks still occur in the U.S. because of unvaccinated international travelers.

For a traveler moving between Mexico and the U.S., the CDC's account of how measles keeps reaching American soil runs through travel itself. The agency ties continuing U.S. cases to people who were not vaccinated before crossing borders.

Cameroon recorded 6,099 measles cases between March and August 2026, according to WHO data the CDC uses for its global outbreak table. That total puts Cameroon eighth of the 10 countries listed.

In the table, Cameroon sits directly behind Mexico and directly ahead of South Africa.

The CDC pairs its outbreak data with a warning about what can happen after a trip ends. Large measles outbreaks in the U.S. are possible when travel-related cases reach populations with low immunization, according to the CDC.

That warning is general. It covers travel-related cases from any country, not cases linked to Cameroon in particular.

South Africa ranks ninth among the 10 countries in the CDC's global measles outbreak table. It reported 5,209 cases to the World Health Organization from March through August 2026.

That case count is the only figure the CDC table gives for South Africa.

The CDC's account of 2019 shows how far measles can spread once it reaches the U.S., which matters for anyone returning from a trip abroad. That year, the U.S. came close to losing its measles elimination status, according to the CDC.

One large outbreak in New York accounted for almost 1,300 cases. Another 30 states also reported cases, the CDC notes.

The CDC does not link the 2019 outbreaks to South Africa or to any other country in the table.

Sudan reported 4,285 measles cases to the World Health Organization from March through August 2026. That total puts it 10th in the CDC's table of the top 10 countries with measles outbreaks, the smallest count among the 10 countries listed.

The CDC pairs its country table with a longer view of the disease. Global measles incidence dropped during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the agency. The CDC reports that measles activity has climbed since then, both around the world and in the U.S.

That trend describes measles across the globe. The CDC does not link it to Sudan, and the table says nothing about how or where the country's cases arose.

For travelers, the CDC's account places the country figures in a period of rising activity worldwide. It also notes that the increase extends to the U.S., which means the trend reaches travelers' home countries as well as their destinations.

#5541. Cognizant Completes Acquisition of Wizeline

Expanding Digital Engineering and Product Development Capabilities for Enterprise Clients

TEANECK, N.J., Nov. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Cognizant (Nasdaq: CTSH) today announced that it has acquired Wizeline, a global AI-native digital engineering and product development services firm serving enterprise clients. Wizeline brings particular strength in Media & Entertainment, with a concentrated, deeply embedded franchise supporting large U.S. enterprises across publishing and news, filmed entertainment, broadcasting, and talent and creator representation. Its capabilities span digital product development, software engineering, cloud modernization, data and AI, enabling clients to build, modernize and scale digital products, platforms and AI-enabled experiences.

The acquisition will further strengthen Cognizant's ability to help clients design, build, and scale modern digital products and platforms.

Wizeline was acquired from its previous investors, including La Caisse. Financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed. Canaccord Genuity acted as exclusive M&A advisor to Wizeline. Ashurst Perkins Coie acted as legal advisor to Cognizant.

About CognizantCognizant is an AI Builder and technology services provider, building the bridge between AI investment and enterprise value by building full-stack AI solutions for our clients. Our deep industry, process and engineering expertise enables us to build an organization's unique context into technology systems that amplify human potential, realize tangible returns and keep global enterprises ahead in a fast-changing world. See how at www.cognizant.ai or @cognizant.

About WizelineWizeline is an AI-centric product engineering company. Founded in 2013, Wizeline is a nearshore transformation engineering partner for enterprises in Media & Entertainment, Financial Services, and Healthcare & Lifesciences. Wizeline combines global forward deployment capabilities with deep expertise in product engineering, data and AI to help clients scale AI solutions towards modern products and workflow innovation.

Alex Dudley, AVP, Global Corporate Communications

SOURCE Cognizant Technology Solutions Corporation

#5540. Measles cases by state in 2026: 10 states in the CDC's data, led by Pennsylvania

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Measles cases by state in 2026: a look at 10 states in CDC data as of Nov. 5, from Pennsylvania's 1,476 cases to Florida's 149

Pennsylvania has the highest 2026 measles count in the CDC's state-by-state data, with 1,476 cases reported as of Nov. 5, 2026. That is 806 more than South Carolina, the next state on the list. Pennsylvania's count is also more than double South Carolina's 670.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention publishes U.S. measles cases by state for 2026 on its measles data page. The listing covers about 50 states. The District of Columbia and New York City appear as separate entries. This article looks at 10 of those states, ordered by their 2026 case counts.

Together, the 10 states in this selection account for 4,240 cases. Pennsylvania alone represents more than a third of that total. The top three states — Pennsylvania, South Carolina and Utah — hold 2,682 of those cases. Utah, third with 536 cases, is the only other state in the group above 500.

Wisconsin is fourth with 419 cases. The middle of the group is tightly packed. New York state has 210 cases, Kentucky has 204 and Ohio has 202, a spread of eight cases across three states. Texas follows with 192 and Virginia with 182. Florida closes the group with 149 cases.

The selection ends at a clear break. Minnesota follows Florida with 139 cases, 10 fewer. Arizona has 110, and Indiana has 105. No state ties Florida for 10th place.

The CDC listing gives two more figures for each state alongside its 2026 count. Each slide reports those numbers as they appear in the source. In Texas, the second of those figures is 803. That is 611 higher than the state's 2026 count of 192. Texas is the only state in the selection where that middle figure exceeds the 2026 count. Florida's third figure, 11, is the largest last figure among the 10 states.

New York state and New York City are listed on separate lines in the CDC data. The New York figure in this article is the state entry only.

Pennsylvania has 1,476 measles cases in 2026, the highest count for any state in the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention measles data as of Nov. 5, 2026.

That total is larger than the counts for South Carolina and Utah combined. Those two states, second and third in this selection, have 1,206 cases between them.

The distance from the bottom of the group is wider still. Florida, 10th in this selection, has 149 cases. Pennsylvania's count is nearly 10 times that figure.

The CDC listing shows two other figures for Pennsylvania: 16 and six. Both are far smaller than the state's 2026 count. This article reports them as the CDC lists them.

The CDC's measles page directs readers to the Pennsylvania Department of Health for real-time updates on measles cases reported in the state. That agency is where newer figures will appear after the Nov. 5 snapshot.

South Carolina has 670 measles cases in the CDC's 2026 data as of Nov. 5. That places the state second among the 10 states in this selection, behind Pennsylvania.

Utah follows South Carolina in the ranking. South Carolina's count is 134 cases higher than Utah's.

South Carolina accounts for about 16% of the combined 2026 cases across the 10 states covered here.

The CDC listing gives two other figures for South Carolina: 333 and one. They are reported here as they appear in the source, without a label.

The middle figure of 333 is the second-largest in that column among the 10 states, behind only Texas. South Carolina's last figure matches the one listed for Wisconsin, New York state, Texas and Virginia.

Utah reported 536 measles cases in 2026, the third-highest 2026 count among U.S. states in CDC data as of Nov. 5. Only Pennsylvania and South Carolina recorded more.

Utah's total is 134 cases below South Carolina's 670. It is 117 cases above Wisconsin's 419, the next state in the ranking. That leaves Utah nearer to fourth place than to second.

Utah accounts for about 12.6% of the combined cases across the 10 states in this selection.

The CDC listing gives Utah two other figures, 189 and zero. Its 189 is the third-largest middle figure among the 10 states, behind only Texas and South Carolina. Its zero in the last column is shared within this group only by Kentucky.

St. George News reports that most of Utah's cases since an outbreak was detected on the Utah-Arizona state line have come from within Utah rather than from other parts of the country.

The spread has also been difficult to contain to a single region. It has reached undervaccinated communities in nearly every county in the state.

Exposures have occurred in healthcare settings, big-box stores, restaurants and youth sporting events.

In the TriCounty health region, officials kept unvaccinated children out of classroom attendance during the response. People who had fallen ill were instructed to stay isolated.

Wisconsin has 419 measles cases in the first column of the CDC's state-by-state measles data as of Nov. 5, 2026.

The CDC listing gives two other figures for Wisconsin: 36 and one. The source does not say what those two columns measure. They appear here only as the agency's other figures for the state.

In the first-column ranking, Wisconsin sits between Utah and New York state. Utah's 536 cases put it 117 above Wisconsin. New York state's 210 cases put it 209 below. Wisconsin's count is closer to Utah's than to New York state's.

Wisconsin's 419 cases make up just under a tenth of the combined total for the 10 states in this selection.

Wisconsin's count is about twice New York state's. It is also roughly three times Minnesota's 139, the highest count among states just below this selection.

New York state had 210 measles cases in 2026 as of Nov. 5, according to CDC data. That count puts it fifth among the 10 states in this selection.

The CDC table lists two other figures for New York state alongside its 2026 count: 26 and one.

New York sits just above a cluster of states with similar totals. Kentucky has 204 cases, six fewer than New York. Ohio has 202, eight fewer.

The gap above New York is wider. Wisconsin, one place higher, has 419 cases. That is 209 more than New York's count, or nearly twice its total.

Kentucky had 204 measles cases in 2026 in CDC data as of Nov. 5, 2026. That count ranks sixth among the 10 states in this selection.

Kentucky's total places it just below New York state and just above Ohio. Only two cases separate Kentucky from Ohio.

The distance to the top of the list is far larger. Pennsylvania's count is more than seven times Kentucky's. At the other end of the selection, Kentucky's total is 55 cases above Florida's.

Kentucky's 204 cases make up about 4.8% of the combined 2026 total for the 10 states covered here.

The CDC listing gives two more figures for Kentucky: 13 and 0. Kentucky is one of two states in the selection whose last figure is 0. Utah is the other.

Kentucky's middle figure of 13 is also among the lowest in the group. Only Virginia, at 6, and Florida, at 8, have smaller middle figures among the 10 states.

Ohio has 202 measles cases in 2026, according to CDC data as of Nov. 5, 2026. That count ranks seventh among the 10 states in this selection.

Ohio sits inside a tight cluster near the middle of the group. Kentucky, one place higher, has two more cases than Ohio. Texas, one place lower, has 10 fewer.

Four states in this selection fall within 22 cases of one another: Kentucky, Ohio, Texas and Virginia. The order in this stretch of the ranking rests on narrow margins. The CDC figures are a snapshot dated Nov. 5. A small number of newly reported cases could change where Ohio places relative to its neighbors.

Ohio is far from the top of the selection. Pennsylvania has 1,274 more cases than Ohio. Ohio accounts for about 4.8% of the combined 2026 total for the 10 states in this selection.

The CDC table lists two other figures for Ohio alongside its 2026 count: 40 and seven. Among the 10 states, Ohio's 40 is the fourth-highest middle figure, behind Texas, South Carolina and Utah. Its seven is the second-highest final figure, behind only Florida.

Those positions put Ohio higher on both of the source's other figures than on its 2026 count, where it ranks seventh. No other state in the middle cluster ranks as high on the final figure.

Texas has 192 measles cases in 2026 in the CDC's state-by-state data as of Nov. 5, 2026. That count places it eighth among the 10 states in this selection.

The gaps on either side of Texas are narrow. Its count is 10 below Ohio, the state just ahead of it. It is also 10 above Virginia, the state just behind it.

The CDC lists two more figures for Texas beside its 2026 count. The middle figure is 803. The last figure is one. The source data used here does not label what either of those columns measures. Both numbers appear exactly as the CDC reports them.

Texas's 803 is the largest middle figure among the 10 states in this group. South Carolina's 333 is the next largest. The column's meaning is not confirmed. The difference between the two Texas figures therefore does not show whether cases rose or fell.

A measles outbreak in West Texas first appeared among Mennonite residents of Gaines County who had low vaccination rates. That outbreak was later tied to cases in other states, including New Mexico and Kansas.

Virginia had 182 measles cases in 2026 as of Nov. 5, according to the CDC's state-by-state figures. That count puts Virginia ninth among the 10 states in this selection.

Texas, one place above Virginia, reported 192 cases. That is 10 more than Virginia.

Florida, one place below, reported 149 cases. Virginia's count is 33 higher.

Those two gaps put Virginia much closer to the state above it than to the state below it.

Ohio, two places higher, reported 202 cases. That is 20 more than Virginia.

The distance to the top of the selection is far larger. Pennsylvania's 1,476 cases are about eight times Virginia's count.

Virginia's 182 cases make up about 4% of the combined total for the 10 states covered here.

The CDC list shows two other figures for Virginia: six and one. The source does not label those figures, so they appear here exactly as listed.

Virginia's middle figure of six is the lowest middle figure among the 10 states in this selection. Its last figure, one, matches the last figure for several other states in the group.

Florida had 149 measles cases in the first column of the CDC's state-by-state measles data as of Nov. 5, 2026. That count places Florida 10th among the 10 states in this selection.

Florida trails Virginia, the ninth state in the group, by 33 cases. Virginia has 182 in the same column.

Florida's 149 cases make up about 3.5% of the combined first-column total for the states covered here. Pennsylvania's count of 1,476 is nearly 10 times Florida's.

The CDC listing shows two other figures for Florida: eight and 11. This article reports them as they appear in the source, without assigning them a meaning.

In that last column, Florida's 11 is four higher than Ohio's seven. No other state in the group has more than six there.

Florida's middle figure of eight is the second-lowest in that column among the 10 states. Only Virginia, at six, is lower. Florida's middle figure is 141 below its first-column count of 149.

Those two figures set Florida apart from the rest of the selection. Florida's last figure is higher than its middle figure. No other state in this group shows that pattern. In each of the other nine states, the middle figure is the larger of the two.

#5539. Bitcoin ETF Attracts $75M as Goldman Sachs Calls December Fed Rate Cut

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin ETF demand returned on November 4 as Bitcoin recovered above $81,000, but Wall Street’s outlook for Federal Reserve rate cuts remains uncertain. Goldman Sachs pushed its expected Fed rate cuts back by one quarter, citing persistent inflation and a labor market that remains resilient. The bank now expects reductions in December 2026 and March 2027.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF recorded $74.6 million in net inflows, ending three consecutive sessions of withdrawals totaling $1.16 billion. Fidelity’s FBTC led the recovery, while BlackRock’s IBIT continued losing capital.

Fidelity’s Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund attracted approximately $236.7 million on November 4. Bitwise’s BITB added $15.2 million, while ARK Invest’s ARKB received $19.9 million.

BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust moved in the opposite direction, recording $201.2 million in outflows. The withdrawals extended IBIT’s four-session losing streak to $935 million. These mixed flows show that institutional demand has not returned uniformly across the market.

Bitcoin also recovered from a seven-week low near $75,600 during the November 3 election period, climbing back above $81,000 today. The rebound followed market stabilization after the U.S. midterm elections, although analysts cautioned against attributing the recovery to a single catalyst.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Goldman Sachs now expects the Federal Reserve to deliver its next two rate cuts in December 2026 and March 2027, pushing both reductions back by one quarter.

The revised forecast shows concerns that energy costs could keep core personal consumption expenditures inflation near 3% throughout the year. Goldman economist David Mericle said lower inflation readings and further labor market softening would likely be necessary for the Fed to cut rates before year-end.

The bank maintained its projected terminal rate range of 3% to 3.25%, while acknowledging that the Fed could decide against additional cuts if economic conditions remain strong.

Bank of America adopted an even more cautious outlook, removing its expected 2026 rate cuts and moving them into the third quarter of 2027. This shift creates a more challenging macro backdrop for Bitcoin, which often benefits when borrowing costs fall and liquidity conditions improve.

But the latest Bitcoin ETF inflows suggest some investors are still willing to increase exposure despite the delayed easing outlook. The contrast between returning fund demand and a more cautious Fed forecast gives Bitcoin traders two competing signals.

Institutional buying could help support prices if inflows continue, while elevated interest rates may limit the liquidity available for risk assets.

#5538. Coinbase's October 26 Perpetual Conversion: The Crypto Index the CFTC Waiver Excludes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Coinbase wants six futures contracts to stop expiring on October 26. The CFTC letter it leans on covers five of them by design, and its own footnote points away from the sixth.

The Division of Market Oversight issued Letter 26-29 on October 3, 2026. The CFTC announced it two days later, on October 5, in Release 9308-26. Coverage then focused on the headline that exchanges can now strip expiry dates from perpetual-style index futures. The Merkle flagged the relief's hard October 20 stop on October 19, and outlets like Finance Magnates and FinanceFeeds ran the same window. That coverage, however, predates what Coinbase filed next. This breakdown sets the October 19 filing beside the letter's text, because the two don't line up cleanly.

Meanwhile, the CFTC is working on retail crypto leverage through a different door. As NullTX's earlier breakdown shows, the actual-delivery ANPRM (2026-20888) takes comments until December 14. Perpetuals on registered exchanges skip that process. Instead, they move through staff letters and self-certification.

Coinbase asked for the relief on October 1, and the Division granted it two days later. The letter says staff won't recommend enforcement if a DCM drops expiry dates from existing perpetual-style contracts, as long as the DCM meets eight conditions. First, it must gather feedback from holders of open positions. Next, it must give at least five calendar days' notice and let them close out under the old terms. It must also disclose the risks and change no other material term. Finally, it must file under the CFTC's rules, notify the Division and certify compliance.

Coinbase's Submission #2026-67 then names six contracts: US500, Tech100, Defense10, AI10, China10 and Coin50. It says everything except the expiry stays the same, and that the exchange knows of no substantive opposition. The contract list reached the CFTC by email on October 16.

Letter 26-29 defines its scope by asset class. A footnote shuts out any perpetual-style contract referencing something other than a broad-based security index. Coin50, by contrast, follows the Coinbase 50 Index, and Rule 1148 in the filing itself calls it a futures contract based on a cryptocurrency. In other words, the letter's scope and Coin50's own rule text point in opposite directions.

Crypto contracts did have their own relief. Letter 26-19, issued June 12 to Bitnomial and Coinbase Derivatives, covered digital commodities only and carried the same eight conditions. Even so, it says its positions expire on June 30, 2026. It rests on the Commission's May 29 order and its perpetuals policy statement.

Letter 26-29 sets October 20, 2026 as the day its no-action positions expire. It doesn't say whether implementation itself must happen by then, or only the notice and filing. Coinbase filed on October 19, one day early, but picked October 26 to go live. That choice matters. Ten business days from October 19 lands on November 2, and Coinbase specifically asked to skip that wait. As a result, going live on October 26 depends on the relief still applying.

Without relief, the Division's own words make the path clear. Letter 26-19 says certifications that remove expiry dates will generally draw a stay under Regulation 40.6(c). A stay then gives the Commission another 90 days to review and opens a 30-day public comment period.

Neither side has explained the gap. Searches of news coverage and official channels turned up no statement from Coinbase or the CFTC on whether Coin50 sits inside Letter 26-29, on what authority covers it after October 20, or on why the filing's October 26 date falls after the letter's expiry. We also found no CFTC stay notice and no extension or amendment of Letter 26-29. Likewise, the Coinbase posts we found cover other perpetual launches, not this conversion.

That silence doesn't mean a problem exists. Coinbase may be relying on authority the documents don't mention, and the CFTC may read the letter's dates differently than we do. Still, the paper trail shows a crypto-based contract sitting under relief written for stock indexes, with a start date that falls after that relief expires.

Three developments would settle it: a CFTC stay notice, a new or amended staff letter, or a clarification from Coinbase Derivatives.

Whichever arrives first tells us whether the first U.S.-listed crypto index perpetual goes live on schedule or lands in a 90-day review.

#5537. Thinking Machines debuts Inkling 2 Small amid reported $5B fundraising push

Thinking Machines Labs Inc. has released a new large language model that can automate artificial intelligence training tasks.

The algorithm, Inkling 2 Small, made its debut late Thursday. Around the same time, Business Insider reported that Thinking Machine is in the process of raising a $5 billion funding round led by Accel. The company, which was founded last year by former OpenAI Group PBC Chief Technology Officer Mira Murati, is expected to receive a $40 billion valuation.

Thinking Machines trained Inkling 2 Small on a cluster of GB300 NVL72 racks. Each system contains 72 Blackwell Ultra graphics cards and half as many central processing units. The company completed the initial pre-training phase in 68 hours and subsequently refined the model through a nine-day reinforcement learning workflow. There were also a number of intermediate training steps.

Thinking Machines honed Inkling 2 Small’s programming capabilities by giving it hundreds of thousands of long-horizon coding challenges. The task collection included a number of particularly complicated “autoresearch” exercises. They required the model to post-train neural networks, optimize LLM components called kernels and perform other AI research work.

Thinking Machines put Inkling 2 Small’s machine learning skills to the test by asking it to fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B. The goal was to improve the open-source LLM’s ability to make predictions such as weather forecasts. According to the company, Inking 2 Small doubled the model’s forecasting score in 4.5 hours.

The LLM is also adapt at automating business tasks. It outperformed Spark Open, Kimi K3 and several other open-source models on three popular knowledge work benchmarks. Additionally, it earned higher scores across several financial task datasets.

Inkling 2 Small includes a vision encoder that can analyze images. Moreover, it enables the LLM to visually verify the quality of the graphics that it generates. If a user asks the model to create an e-commerce store, it can not only check the website’s code for bugs but also visually inspect product pages to check that they render correctly.

The vision encoder accounts for 292 million of Inking 2 Small’s 594 billion parameters. About 17 billion of those parameters activate when a user enters a prompt. Inking 2 Small can adjust the amount of computing power that it spends on tasks, which enables developers to trade off output quality for increased cost-efficiency or vice versa.

Particularly savvy users can extend the model’s capabilities by post-training, or customizing it, using their own data. Thinking Machines says that Inkling 2 Small learns faster than its earlier models. That should translate into more cost-efficient post-training runs.

Inkling 2 Small is available via Thinking Machines’ Tinker cloud service on launch. The company plans to release the model’s weights under an open-source license next week.

#5536. TEN Holdings Reports Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results

NEW YORK, Nov. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- TEN Holdings, Inc. (Nasdaq: XHLD), through its subsidiary, Ten Events, Inc., the technology company behind TEN, a Digital Experience Platform that powers the next generation of enterprise digital engagement, today announced its financial results for the quarter ended September 30, 2026.

"Third quarter revenue increased 17.9% year over year to $640,000, as we completed customer engagements that had been initiated in prior periods and added revenue from new customers," said Virgilio Torres, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of TEN Holdings. "Our performance reflects continued demand for our digital engagement solutions and our ability to serve both existing and new customers. As we look ahead, our focus remains on expanding recurring revenue, strengthening our technology platform, and accelerating our transition toward a scalable, SaaS-driven business model."

"Our third-quarter results reflect two significant expenses that we consider non-recurring: a $1.8 million write-off of previously capitalized service contracts and approximately $0.5 million in legal expenses. Excluding these items, our underlying selling, general and administrative expenses declined compared to the same period last year, reflecting the progress we have made in improving operational efficiency. Over the past 12 months, we have reduced our annual operating cost structure by approximately $2.5 million through strategic cost reductions, process improvements, and the integration of AI-driven tools to streamline engineering and accelerate product development. With these efficiencies largely implemented and a leaner operating structure in place, we are now shifting our focus toward accelerating revenue growth, expanding customer relationships, and scaling TEN, our new platform."

"We also made significant progress in strengthening our balance sheet, reducing short-term related-party borrowings from $4.6 million at the beginning of the year to approximately $0.1 million as of September 30, 2026. Total liabilities declined by approximately 74%, from $7.7 million at year-end 2025 to $2.0 million, reflecting our continued efforts to simplify our capital structure and improve our financial position."

"One of our most significant milestones this year was the launch of TEN, our next-generation Digital Experience Platform, whose development was accelerated by investments made possible through the proceeds of our June common stock offering, consistent with our previously communicated commitment to product development. TEN represents an important step in our evolution toward a scalable, SaaS-driven business model, bringing together the tools organizations need to create, manage, deliver, and measure digital experiences within a unified platform.

At launch, TEN provides enterprises with a self-service solution for webinars, virtual events, and continuing education programs, with the capacity to support up to 50,000 concurrent attendees. Building on our longstanding relationships with enterprise customers, many of whom rely on our technology for recurring digital engagement initiatives, we see a meaningful opportunity to transition these relationships toward subscription-based arrangements. We believe this approach will deliver greater flexibility and value to our customers while creating a more predictable and recurring revenue stream for TEN Holdings."

"Looking ahead, we are focused on three priorities: continuing the transition of our business from a managed services provider to a SaaS company, investing in TEN so that it remains competitive, and executing an acquisition strategy aimed at accretive businesses that add revenue and EBITDA, products our sales team can scale, and technology that complements our own. With TEN now in the market, a leaner cost structure, and a simplified balance sheet, we believe TEN Holdings is positioned to build a more scalable, recurring revenue business and create long-term value for our shareholders."

Selected Balance Sheet and Cash Flow Results

Mr. Torres added that TEN Holdings plans to:

TEN Holdings, Inc. (Nasdaq: XHLD) is a New York-based technology company focused on developing enterprise software solutions that enable organizations to create, manage, deliver, and measure digital experiences. Through its flagship Digital Experience Platform, TEN, the Company provides technology solutions for enterprise communications, virtual events, webinars, and continuing education, supporting digital experiences with up to 50,000 concurrent attendees.

Building on more than a decade of experience serving Fortune 500 companies, TEN Holdings is evolving its platform into a broader, AI-enabled enterprise technology ecosystem. Its product roadmap includes marketing automation, CRM integrations, advanced engagement analytics, AI-powered capabilities, and content management solutions designed to help organizations streamline workflows, strengthen customer engagement, and generate actionable business insights.

The Company's strategy is centered on expanding its SaaS offerings, increasing recurring revenue opportunities, and delivering scalable technology solutions to enterprise customers. Planned capabilities remain subject to ongoing development, and there can be no assurance regarding their timing or availability.

#5535. 7 steps from the National Cybersecurity Alliance to shrink your digital footprint

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Seven steps to check and shrink your digital footprint, from asking why to posting with care, plus what each protects.

Most people think of their online trail as a record of what they posted or searched for. It is really a collection of personal details, such as names, addresses, locations and purchases. Apps, retailers and platforms hold those details, and many of them are companies a person signed up with years ago and has since forgotten. Two very different groups will pay for that information or take it. Companies buy and sell location data in an industry worth $12 billion, according to TIME. Criminals target the same kinds of records. A single breach at AT&T $T, reported in early 2024, potentially affected 73 million people, according to the Aiken Standard. Some businesses treat your data as a product, and thieves treat it as something to steal. Every detail you have handed over adds to what either group can get.

A leak can do harm long before anyone notices it. Worldwide, companies took an average of 241 days to find and contain a breach, according to IBM $IBM 2025 figures reported by CBC News. People can search for their own names, delete old accounts, adjust settings and assert legal rights. Each of those steps helps, but most of them come into play after a person's details are already out, and each one has limits. The protections that last are the ones that keep data from leaving your hands at all.

Saying no is the cheapest protection you have, but it works only if the company honors your answer. A group of users sued Meta on the claim that the company went on following where they were even after they had switched the feature off, and in 2022 Meta settled that class action for $37.5 million without admitting guilt, according to TIME. You can't tell from a permission screen whether an app respects your refusal, so the protection holds only where the company takes you at your word.

Asking why limits what you share from now on, but it can't recall what you've already given away, and finding that is the work of the steps that follow.

Most people never see their own name the way a stranger, a recruiter or a scammer does: typed into a search bar. Searching for yourself lets you see what strangers can already find, according to the National Cybersecurity Alliance, and checking breach records tells you which passwords you need to change. In 2023, Google $GOOGL was accepting requests to remove some results from its search pages, CNBC reports, so you could start a cleanup from the same search you used to take stock. Both checks still tell you only what has already escaped. A list of compromised passwords is a record of damage already done, and neither search stops the next leak.

The cleanup that follows a search is narrower than it sounds. When Google removes a link, the page that hosts your information stays online, according to CNBC, and anyone who reaches that page another way can still read it. Google describes the purpose of these tools in terms of how people feel. "It's just one of the many things we're trying to do to help people feel control of their online experience," said Danny Sullivan, Google's public liaison for search. A removal request changes how easily strangers can find you, not how much of your information exists.

Some of what you find may stay put no matter what you ask. In 2023, Google could turn down any removal request that fell outside its rules, according to CNBC, so spotting something damaging about yourself did not mean you could get it taken out of the results. Google's tool for removing explicit photos was available only to U.S. users searching in English when it launched in 2023. People outside that group had less help with one of the most damaging kinds of exposure. Results change and requests can fail, and a single search proves little. Repeating the search on a regular schedule keeps you aware of your exposure.

You can learn where you stand by Googling yourself, but you will rarely change where you stand that way.

Accounts you have forgotten about are still part of your digital trail, and each old sign-up holds a login you no longer think about. The National Cybersecurity Alliance recommends a password manager for reviewing those accounts, because with all of them in one place you can see how many you hold and clean up the ones that are old, unused or weak. That makes the tool more useful as an audit of your past sign-ups than as a safe for your passwords. You get that benefit only when you close the accounts you no longer need and fix the weak logins on the ones you keep. Treat the list as a to-do list, not a record.

Cleaning up old logins matters most for passwords you have reused, because one shared password links every account that uses it. When a password is reused, "the bad guys only need to break your password security once to get at all those accounts," Suelette Dreyfus, a senior lecturer in computing and information systems at the University of Melbourne, said, as reported by ABC News. Unique logins break that link, and a manager can create a strong one for every site, so criminals who steal one password can get into only that one account. You get the most from a manager when you replace your old logins with unique ones, not when you only store them.

Many people pick a manager for its breach warnings, which have a real limit. The Australian Cyber Security Centre lists an alert for passwords exposed in a breach as a feature to look for, according to ABC News. Even a good alert comes late. Gohar Rind, managing director of Intaris, says a manager can check for a leaked password only after it has been made public, appeared on the dark web or been flagged in a notice from authorities. By that point, other people can already see the password. Rind advises changing an exposed password immediately. Treat any alert as a signal to act at once, not as a sign that the problem has been handled.

A password manager reduces your trail only when you use it to close and fix accounts yourself, and its warnings tell you only what has already leaked.

Every account you open leaves another company holding your name, your email address and a record of your habits long after you've stopped thinking about it. The National Cybersecurity Alliance says that each signup widens your exposure to junk mail, tracking and leaks, and that shoppers who check out as guests sidestep that exposure. The reasoning holds up as far as it goes. When fewer companies keep your details, you have fewer places to watch and less to defend.

Protection from leaks is where the promise falls short. A guest checkout still asks for your name, address and payment details, and the retailer keeps that information after you click "buy." Canada Computers says the shoppers hit by its breach bought without an account and typed in personal details, and its current investigation counts 1,284 of them, according to company figures reported by CBC News. Skipping the signup did not keep those shoppers' information out of the breach. What shoppers who check out as guests mostly gain is less follow-up, with fewer marketing emails and less tracking of what they do next. That is a choice about future contact, not a security measure.

The risk from a stolen guest order does not end when the purchase is over, because criminals can hold on to the details they take. Once personal data is taken, "cybercriminals can get to it weeks, months, years later," Terry Cutler, CEO of Cyology Labs in Montreal, told CBC News. Passing on an account is a good start, but what you type into a checkout form still counts, so give each order only what it needs.

Nobody can steal a detail from an account you never opened, or one you never typed in.

Some of the more protective choices start switched off, and a user has to turn them on. The alliance names Facebook $META as a hard platform to avoid, along with Google $GOOGL, Apple $AAPL and Microsoft $MSFT. Meta agreed to a child-safety settlement worth roughly $18 billion, and Facebook's non-algorithmic feed is an opt-in setting, according to TIME. Even with that much money at stake, people get the gentler feed only if they go looking for it.

Every setting also assumes the platform knows who is using the account. Zvika Krieger, former director of Meta's responsible innovation team and now a consultant for technology companies, told TIME that "if young users are just using adult accounts, all this is worthless." Meta has offered little information on how it will check users' ages, so that gap remains open. For a family, the first task is to make sure each person, especially a child, is on the account meant for them. Choosing the options comes after that.

Settings can also shift as legal pressure pushes companies to change them, which is one reason to check them on a schedule. The three-month review is the alliance's own suggestion, not a legal or industry requirement. Meta's settlement includes a $5.3 billion payment that depends on YouTube and TikTok adopting similar settings, according to TIME. It is not yet known whether either company will make that change. If one does, a user who reviews settings regularly will see the new options.

Even where a deletion right exists, it gives you the power to ask, and the company still decides how to answer. CBC News reports that officials named some grounds on which a company could refuse a deletion request and described them as only some of the exceptions. A request you file could therefore meet a refusal on grounds no one has fully spelled out.

Use these rights wherever they apply, but treat them as a backstop for data already out of your hands, not a way to take it back on demand.

The details that cause trouble are rarely secrets. People who would never share a password will still mention the town they grew up in or the name of a childhood pet. People often share those answers in online quizzes, and the same answers often protect an account's security questions. The risk is higher when the same detail also appears in a password. Before you post, ask what accounts a stranger could get into with the detail, not just whether it is private.

Care matters most when you pay for something online. Debit cards lack some of the protections that come with credit cards, according to the Aiken Standard. On a site you don't know well, a credit card is the safer way to pay. Caution also has to continue after a company announces a breach. The link in a breach notice could lead to a scam, and scammers may also call while posing as a retailer, a bank or a card issuer. The safe response is to go to the company's own website rather than click a link in the message.

Careful habits can't stop every breach. A company you trusted with an ordinary card purchase can still lose your details, and nothing you do on your end prevents that. You can get free credit reports from the official site, AnnualCreditReport.com, according to the Aiken Standard. Read your reports regularly to spot any account or activity you didn't create.

When you post and pay with care, less of you is out there to steal, and when you check your reports, you learn when someone has taken something anyway.

#5534. 10 states with kindergarten vaccination rates below 90% in CDC data

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Kindergarten measles vaccination rates, plus one all-vaccines figure, sat below 90% in these 10 states in CDC data for 2025-26, with Idaho lowest at 75.2%

Kindergarten measles vaccination rates in the CDC's 2025-26 state table run from 75.2% in Idaho to 98.9% in West Virginia. That 23.7-point spread separates the lowest and highest figures the agency lists for the school year.

The CDC table covers about 50 jurisdictions. Kansas and Montana show no data for 2025-26. They cannot be placed in the order used here. This selection covers 10 reporting states with figures under 90%. All 10 fall in the CDC's "Less than 90%" category. Several other states land in the agency's "95%+" category.

The slides run from the lowest percentage to the highest within this group. Idaho comes first at 75.2%. Wisconsin follows at 85.1%, a 9.9-point gap from Idaho. North Dakota closes the selection at 88.5%, 13.3 points above Idaho. The other seven states — Minnesota, Utah, Arizona, Colorado, Oklahoma, Ohio and New Hampshire — range from 85.7% to 88.2%.

Three more states sit just outside this group. Florida and Iowa each reported 88.9%. Georgia reported 89.1%. Those figures are also under 90%. This article is a selection of 10 states with low rates, not a full list of every state below that line.

The CDC lists each state's rate alongside a count and a second percentage. The count appears to show how many kindergartners were assessed. The second percentage appears to show how complete the reporting was. The slides treat both readings with that caution.

States also collected their numbers in different ways. Six states in this selection used a census. Wisconsin, Arizona, Oklahoma and Ohio used a census for public schools and voluntary response for private schools.

New Hampshire needs a separate note. The state did not assess coverage for individual vaccines. Its 88.2% is the share of kindergartners who received all doses of all vaccines required for school entry. It is not a measles-specific figure.

The table does not explain why any state's rate is low. It carries no exemption data, no outbreak data and no policy details.

Idaho reported a kindergarten measles vaccination rate of 75.2% for the 2025-26 school year. No reporting state posted a lower figure in the kindergarten coverage table from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

That rate leaves 24.8% of Idaho kindergartners outside the share the CDC recorded as covered.

Idaho is also the only reporting state in the table with a rate below 80%. Every other state that supplied data cleared that mark.

The CDC lists Idaho's survey method as a census. The entry shows no separate approach for private schools. Several other states in the table pair a public-school census with voluntary response from private schools. Idaho's entry names a census alone.

The table pairs Idaho's rate with a count of 21,728. If that count reflects the kindergartners assessed, the 75.2% figure describes a group of that size. The column label was not confirmed, so the number is described here only as the count the CDC lists beside the rate.

The entry also shows a second percentage of 100%. If that column measures how complete the reporting was, Idaho's figure would rest on full reporting rather than a partial return. That reading is also unconfirmed.

Wisconsin's kindergarten measles vaccination rate was 85.1% in the 2025-26 school year, according to CDC data. Among the states that reported figures, only Idaho posted a lower rate.

That leaves Wisconsin 4.9 percentage points short of 90%. It sits in the CDC's "Less than 90%" category.

Minnesota, the next state up the table, reported 85.7%. The two states are 0.6 points apart.

The CDC lists a count of 59,360 next to Wisconsin's rate. It also shows a second percentage of 96.6% for the state. The table used for this article does not label either number.

Wisconsin's figure combines two collection approaches. Public schools were covered by a census. Private schools supplied data through voluntary response.

Minnesota reported a kindergarten measles vaccination rate of 85.7% for the 2025-26 school year, according to CDC data. That is the third-lowest figure among the states that reported numbers for the year.

The remaining 14.3% of the state's kindergartners fall outside that coverage figure. Minnesota's rate is 4.3 percentage points below 90%, the upper edge of the CDC's "Less than 90%" category. It is 9.3 points short of the agency's "95%+" category.

Minnesota sits close to its neighbor Wisconsin in the table, 0.6 points higher. Idaho, the lowest state in the table, is 10.5 points below Minnesota. West Virginia, the highest state in the table, is 13.2 points above it.

The CDC lists a count of 63,451 alongside Minnesota's rate. That figure most likely reflects the number of kindergartners assessed.

Minnesota's count is the third-largest among the 10 states in this selection. Only Ohio, at 129,087, and Arizona, at 73,907, list higher counts. Wisconsin's count is 59,360, about 4,100 smaller than Minnesota's.

The table also gives Minnesota a second percentage of 99.9%. That figure appears to describe how complete the state's reporting was. Four states in this selection — Idaho, Utah, Colorado and New Hampshire — list 100%. If that reading holds, Minnesota's 85.7% rate rests on records from nearly every kindergartner the state counted.

The CDC lists Minnesota's survey method as a census. Its entry does not include the voluntary response from private schools that appears in some other states' entries.

The statewide figure does not show how coverage varies within Minnesota. Clearwater County has the lowest overall measles vaccination rate of any county in the state, according to tucson.com. Neighboring Wadena County has the second-lowest.

In Clearwater County, many children are recorded as partially vaccinated. They lack one of the two doses. They also have no exemption on file. That pattern ties the county's low rate to incomplete dose series rather than to recorded exemptions.

Utah reported measles vaccination coverage of 87.2% among kindergartners in the 2025-26 school year, according to CDC data. That figure places the state in the CDC's "Less than 90%" category.

Utah's rate falls 2.8 percentage points short of the 90% line. Among the states that reported data for the year, only Idaho, Wisconsin and Minnesota posted lower rates. Minnesota, the next state down, sits 1.5 points below Utah.

Utah's figure sits 11.7 points below West Virginia's, the highest in the CDC table. It is 12 points above Idaho's, the lowest. The two gaps are close to equal. Utah sits near the midpoint between the table's highest and lowest rates.

The CDC lists a count of 44,001 next to Utah's rate. That number most likely reflects how many kindergartners were assessed, though the column heading is not confirmed.

A second percentage in Utah's row reads 100%. That figure appears to measure how complete the state's reporting was. If it does, Utah's rate rests on a full set of returns rather than a partial one.

Utah gathered its numbers through a census of kindergartners. That approach differs from the mixed method some states used, which pairs a census of public schools with voluntary responses from private schools. Under a census with full reporting, Utah's rate does not depend on which private schools chose to respond.

Utah requires each child enrolled in kindergarten to receive specific immunizations, including a two-dose series of the MMR vaccine, according to The Salt Lake Tribune.

The CDC table does not explain how Utah's coverage relates to that state requirement. It offers no breakdown of kindergartners by number of doses received. It also carries no exemption counts for the state.

Arizona's kindergarten measles vaccination coverage stood at 87.4% in the 2025-26 school year, according to CDC data. Among the states that reported a figure, that is the fifth-lowest rate in the agency's table.

That figure places Arizona in the CDC's "Less than 90%" category, 2.6 percentage points under the line. Utah sits just below Arizona at 87.2%. Colorado sits just above it at 87.7%. Fractions of a point separate the three states.

Arizona collected its numbers in two ways. Public schools were covered by a census. Private schools took part through voluntary response. Under that approach, private-school data come only from the schools that chose to submit them.

The CDC lists a count of 73,907 next to Arizona's rate. The table excerpt does not label that column, though it most likely reflects the number of kindergartners assessed. Among the 10 states here, only Ohio shows a larger count. If that reading holds, Arizona's rate draws on one of the bigger groups of children in this selection.

A second percentage of 92.5% also appears in Arizona's row. That column likely measures how complete the state's reporting was, but the label is not confirmed. Oklahoma is the only state in this group with a lower figure there. Oklahoma used the same mix of a public-school census and private-school voluntary response. The table does not say whether the method and the lower figure are connected.

At the other end of the table, Arizona trails West Virginia, the state with the highest reported rate, by 11.5 percentage points.

Colorado's kindergarten measles vaccination rate stood at 87.7% in the 2025-26 school year, according to CDC data. That places the state sixth in this 10-state selection, which runs from the lowest rate to the highest.

The figure falls in the CDC's "Less than 90%" coverage category. Colorado sits 2.3 percentage points below the 90% line that marks the top of that group.

Colorado belongs to a tight cluster near the middle of the selection. Arizona, one place lower, reported 87.4%. Oklahoma, one place higher, reported 87.8%. Only 0.4 points separate those three states. Margins that narrow decide their order in the table.

Colorado's rate is 12.5 points above Idaho's, the lowest figure in the table. It is 11.2 points below West Virginia's, the highest. On those two measures, Colorado sits slightly closer to the top of the table than to its lowest point.

Colorado collected its figures through a census of kindergartners. It did not pair that census with voluntary responses from private schools, as some other states in this selection did.

The CDC lists a count of 60,049 next to Colorado's rate. The source material does not label that column. The number may reflect how many kindergartners were assessed, but that reading is not confirmed.

Colorado's second listed percentage is 100%. That column's label is also missing from the source material. It may describe how complete the state's reporting was. Idaho and Utah, which also used a census, show the same 100% in that column.

Oklahoma's kindergarten measles coverage stood at 87.8% in the 2025-26 school year, based on CDC data. That figure puts the state seventh in this selection of 10 states with low rates, counting from the lowest.

The rate falls in the CDC's "Less than 90%" coverage category. It is 2.2 percentage points below the 90% line that caps that group.

Oklahoma sits in a tight cluster of nearby states. Colorado reported 87.7%, just 0.1 point lower. Ohio reported 88.1%, 0.3 point higher. Arizona, at 87.4%, and Utah, at 87.2%, also fall within one point of Oklahoma's rate. Taken together, the five states span just 0.9 point, from Utah's 87.2% to Ohio's 88.1%.

The CDC lists a count of 47,844 alongside Oklahoma's rate. The table's column headers were not part of the material reviewed for this article. The number most likely reflects the kindergartners assessed, but that label is not confirmed. Oklahoma's count is larger than Utah's 44,001 and smaller than Colorado's 60,049.

Oklahoma gathered its data through a mixed approach. Public schools were covered by a census, while private schools took part through voluntary response. A census reaches every school in a group. Voluntary response includes only the schools that chose to report.

The CDC table also pairs Oklahoma's rate with a second percentage of 90.7%. That figure most likely describes how complete the state's reporting was, but the label is not confirmed.

Oklahoma's 90.7% is the lowest second percentage among the 10 states in this selection. Arizona, the next lowest, shows 92.5%, which is 1.8 points higher. Idaho, Utah, Colorado and New Hampshire each show 100% in that column. Minnesota, at 99.9%, falls just short of that mark.

Four states in this selection combined a public-school census with private-school voluntary response. Wisconsin, Ohio, Arizona and Oklahoma all show second percentages below 97%. Oklahoma's figure is the lowest of those four.

Ohio reported a kindergarten measles vaccination rate of 88.1% for the 2025-26 school year, according to CDC data. The figure sits 1.9 percentage points under 90%. That places Ohio in the CDC's "Less than 90%" category.

Ohio is eighth among the 10 states in this selection, which runs from the lowest rate to the highest. Oklahoma, at 87.8%, sits just below it. New Hampshire's 88.2% sits just above it, though that figure covers all required school-entry vaccines rather than measles alone. Among the measles-specific figures in this group, the next one above Ohio's is North Dakota's 88.5%.

Ohio's rate is 12.9 points higher than Idaho's 75.2%, the lowest in the CDC table. It is 10.8 points below West Virginia's 98.9%, the highest. Measured in points, Ohio sits closer to the top of the table than to the bottom. Florida reported 88.9% and falls just outside this selection, 0.8 points above Ohio.

The CDC lists a count of 129,087 alongside Ohio's rate. The column label for that number is not confirmed, though it most likely reflects kindergartners assessed. It is the largest count among the 10 states here.

Arizona's 73,907 is the next-largest count, 55,180 lower than Ohio's. North Dakota's 9,344 is the smallest in the group. Ohio's count is nearly 14 times that figure. If the count does reflect kindergartners assessed, each percentage point of Ohio's rate covers far more children than the same point in a smaller state.

Ohio's row also shows a second percentage of 95.9%. That number most likely describes how complete the state's reporting was. The CDC table does not confirm that label either. Each state in this selection that paired a public-school census with voluntary private-school response shows a second percentage below 100%.

Ohio collected its figures through a census of public schools and voluntary response from private schools. Under that approach, private-school results depend on which schools chose to respond.

The CDC data does not give reasons for Ohio's rate.

In the 2025-26 school year, 88.2% of New Hampshire's kindergartners had received all doses of every vaccine required for school entry, according to CDC data. The state did not assess coverage for individual vaccines. That makes the number broader than a measles rate.

New Hampshire's number measures something different from the other nine states in this selection. Each of those states reported a measles figure. New Hampshire's figure counts only children who were fully up to date on the whole school-entry schedule. A kindergartner missing a single required dose of any required vaccine falls outside the 88.2%.

That difference limits what the number can show. It does not reveal how many New Hampshire kindergartners had measles vaccination specifically. It also does not show which vaccines or doses the remaining children lacked. A gap in one required vaccine registers the same way as gaps in several.

The figure is also not a direct match for its neighbors in this list. The CDC places New Hampshire in its "Less than 90%" category. Its 88.2% sits 1.8 percentage points below that line. In this selection, it falls between Ohio at 88.1% and North Dakota at 88.5%. Both of those states reported measles figures. The order at this point sets two kinds of measurement side by side.

The CDC lists a count of 11,544 next to New Hampshire's rate. Among these 10 states, only North Dakota's 9,344 is smaller. A second percentage in the same row reads 100%. If that column reflects reporting completeness, New Hampshire's figure would rest on full reporting. The state gathered its data through a census, rather than relying on voluntary responses from any group of schools.

New Hampshire's rules call for proof of immunization to come in an authenticated written form. That rule concerns the documentation behind school-entry vaccination. The CDC table does not say how those records shaped the state's 88.2%.

North Dakota's kindergarten measles vaccination rate was 88.5% in the 2025-26 school year, according to CDC data. That is the highest figure among the 10 states in this selection. It still sits in the CDC's "Less than 90%" category.

In other words, more than one in 10 North Dakota kindergartners were not counted as vaccinated against measles in the CDC's figures.

The state's rate is 1.5 percentage points short of the 90% line. It trails West Virginia, the top state in the CDC table, by 10.4 points.

North Dakota is also 0.4 points behind Florida and Iowa. Those two states tie just outside this selection. The line between this group of 10 and the states next to it comes down to fractions of a percentage point.

The CDC lists a count of 9,344 next to North Dakota's rate. That is the smallest count among the 10 states covered here. New Hampshire has the next smallest, at 11,544. The table does not label that column, so the count's exact meaning is not confirmed.

North Dakota's row also shows a second percentage of 98.6%. That column is unlabeled as well.

North Dakota gathered its figures through a census, according to the CDC table. It did not combine a public-school census with voluntary responses from private schools, as four other states in this selection did.
