#5527. Sprout Ends at Block 3,543,405: What the ZIPs Say About ZEC in Orchard and Sapling

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zcash has three older shielded pools, and only one of them has a shutdown date. On November 5, NU7 will make the 22,263 ZEC left in Sprout unspendable.

The 346,000 ZEC still in Orchard and the 420,000 ZEC in Sapling face no deadline at all.

But the Zcash specifications include one conditional warning that covers all three pools, and it has been widely misquoted. Let's go through the ZIPs to set out exactly what each document says about each pool, and what it doesn't.

Together, the three older pools hold about 788,000 ZEC. Any full node reports these balances directly through the valuePools field of its getblockchaininfo RPC, so anyone running a node can check them.

The three pools are on very different paths. Sprout has a fixed end. Orchard is closed to new deposits, but no spec sets a closing date. Sapling remains a supported pool.

Sprout's end has been planned for years. ZIP 211, written in 2019, stopped new value from entering Sprout. It described that as "a step toward being able to remove the Sprout shielded protocol."

ZIP 2003 takes the final step. It doesn't target Sprout directly. Instead, it bans an entire transaction format: from NU7 onward, "the transaction version number MUST be 5 or 6." Sprout transfers can only be written as version 4 transactions, so Sprout funds can no longer be spent.

ZIP 259, the NU7 deployment spec, sets the activation height at block 3,543,405 on mainnet. It states the result directly: "funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The wording matters. ZIP 2003 says it does not "unissue, burn, or otherwise make Sprout funds permanently unavailable." The coins stay counted in Zcash's issued supply, and the ZIP leaves open "the theoretical possibility of re-enabling v4 transactions, or of adding another facility to retrieve these funds." It also cautions that this "may never be re-enabled."

Recovering Sprout funds was already hard before the deadline. According to ZIP 2003, the retirement of zcashd just before NU6.3 "removed the only maintained software that still provided wallet functionality for Sprout." The pool has barely changed in the last few weeks: the widely reported figure of 22,309 ZEC has fallen only to 22,263, so about 46 ZEC has moved out since.

Orchard's situation is newer and more unusual. ZIP 258 activated NU6.3 at block 3,428,143 and sealed Orchard after a soundness vulnerability was found and fixed. Since then, the consensus rules have enforced three restrictions:

ZIP 229 explains why: Orchard held "a substantial portion of ZEC" when the vulnerability was fixed, so moving those funds to a fresh pool was meant to restore confidence in Zcash's total supply.

The migration has largely worked. ZecStats counts 3,278,499 ZEC moved out of Orchard, about 90.5% of what was in the pool at NU6.3. That leaves about 346,000 ZEC, roughly 2% of the circulating supply.

Sapling has the fewest restrictions of the three. Version 6 transactions support it as one of the "supported shielded pools," alongside Orchard and Ironwood, and none of the NU6.3 or NU7 ZIPs restricts it.

There's one catch for Sapling users that many people are missing. ZIP 259 says the version 4 ban covers "all version 4 transactions, including transparent-only and Sapling transactions, not only Sprout transfers." Sapling funds stay spendable after NU7, but only through version 5 or version 6 transactions. Wallets still building version 4 transactions need to switch before the upgrade. Pending or offline-signed version 4 transactions won't confirm afterward, and "re-signing alone cannot make a version 4 transaction valid."

The sentence behind the "inaccessible funds" headlines appears in ZIP 2005, "Ironwood Quantum Recoverability," and is repeated in ZIP 229:

"Recovery would not be possible for funds still in the Sprout, Sapling, or Orchard pools; all such funds would be inaccessible after their respective protocols are disabled."

The sentence before it explains the context. Zcash's existing shielded protocols depend on discrete logarithms being hard to compute. If an attacker, using a quantum computer or another method, could break that, the protocols might have to be disabled "to prevent such attacks." Only funds in Ironwood would be recoverable, through a recovery protocol designed to stay secure against quantum attacks.

So this is a contingency, not a schedule. It describes what would happen to funds in the older pools if a future cryptographic emergency forced Zcash to shut them down. No ZIP proposes doing that on any date. The practical advice behind it is plain: funds in Sprout, Sapling or Orchard "should be migrated to the Ironwood pool" to be covered by recovery.

The software is ready. The Zcash Foundation released Zebra 7.0.0 on October 22. Its changelog says it "supports the NU7 network upgrade on Mainnet, which activates at height 3,543,405." The release moves Zebra's database from format v28 to v29. Zebra 6.x can't read the new format, so the Foundation recommends backing up the old state first. The zcashd compatibility sidecar must also be updated to zebra-compat-v1.3.0. Earlier builds can't follow mainnet past NU7.

This upgrade carries more risk than usual. ZIP 259 waives Zcash's usual rule that old software must shut itself down before an upgrade. The spec warns that "operators of unsupported software may therefore remain online at activation and follow a pre-NU7 consensus branch."

For holders, the guidance from each pool's spec comes down to this:

On November 5, Sprout closes. The 766,000 ZEC in Sapling and Orchard face no deadline, but the specs still recommend moving it to Ironwood.

#5526. Salmonella vs. E. coli vs. listeria: how to tell them apart

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Salmonella vs. E. coli vs. listeria comes down to timing, symptoms and the foods that carry them — here is how to tell three common foodborne bacteria apart

The meal that made you sick may not be the one you ate last night. Food poisoning tends to get blamed on the most recent thing someone ate. The bacteria behind it keep very different schedules. Some act within hours. Others stay quiet for weeks before symptoms appear, long after the food in question has been forgotten or thrown away.

That gap in timing is one of the most useful clues for sorting out Salmonella vs. E. coli vs. listeria. All three are common foodborne bacteria. Each one tends to travel in different foods. Each one produces a somewhat different pattern of illness. And the people at greatest risk of serious illness are not the same for all three.

The differences have practical consequences. Treatment that helps with one bacterium may be discouraged for another. That decision belongs to a clinician, not a guess. Knowing which foods carry which organism shapes how a household shops, stores and cooks. It also determines who at the table needs to take extra care.

This guide is not a complete map of foodborne illness. Campylobacter, norovirus — which is a virus, not a bacterium — and many other pathogens also make people sick. They are not covered here. The focus is narrower: three bacteria that frequently appear in food recalls and outbreak reports but behave in distinct ways once they reach the body.

The information draws on established public health guidance, mainly from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the U.S. Department of Agriculture. It does not replace medical advice. Anyone with severe or worsening symptoms should contact a health care provider.

The slides that follow start with a profile of each bacterium: what it typically causes, where it tends to come from and who is most vulnerable. A side-by-side comparison then looks at how symptoms and incubation times differ across the three, and why those signs overlap enough to mislead. The final slide covers how doctors confirm the cause with lab tests and which kitchen habits lower the risk of infection in the first place.

Salmonella infection usually causes diarrhea, fever and stomach cramps. Most healthy people recover within four to seven days without any specific treatment. Dehydration is the main risk.

Salmonella is a genus of rod-shaped bacteria that live in the intestines of many animals, including birds and reptiles. The genus takes its name from Daniel Elmer Salmon, a U.S. veterinary scientist whose research program isolated the bacterium in the 1880s. Scientists have identified more than 2,500 serotypes. A much smaller number cause most human illness.

Symptoms typically appear anywhere from six hours to six days after a person swallows the bacteria. Rest and steady fluids carry most people through the illness. Oral rehydration solutions replace the salts lost through diarrhea as well as the water.

Doctors generally reserve antibiotics for severe illness or for patients at higher risk of complications. CDC lists children under five, adults 65 and older and people with weakened immune systems among the groups more likely to become seriously ill. For everyone else, treatment focuses on staying hydrated.

Animals spread Salmonella too. Turtles, lizards, snakes and other reptiles can carry it while appearing healthy. Backyard chickens and ducklings can as well. Handling the animals, their enclosures or their bedding and then touching the mouth is enough to pass the bacteria along.

Typhoid fever belongs in a separate category. It comes from a different type, Salmonella Typhi, and causes a distinct illness marked by prolonged high fever. Humans are its only known host. It spreads through food and water contaminated with human waste. In the U.S., most typhoid cases occur in people who have traveled abroad.

Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, or STEC, causes severe stomach cramps, vomiting and diarrhea that is often bloody, usually with little or no fever. O157:H7 is the best-known strain in this group.

Escherichia coli is a large and varied group of bacteria. Most strains live harmlessly in the intestines of people and animals. Some cause illness, and the strains that produce Shiga toxin are behind the most severe E. coli infections.

The toxin takes its name from Kiyoshi Shiga, the Japanese microbiologist who identified Shigella dysenteriae. That bacterium makes a closely related toxin. Public health agencies in Europe often call the same group VTEC, for verocytotoxin-producing E. coli. The code O157:H7 identifies a strain by two markers. The O antigen sits on the bacterial surface, and the H antigen is found on its flagella.

Symptoms commonly begin about three to four days after exposure. The full range runs from one to 10 days.

The most serious complication is hemolytic uremic syndrome, or HUS, which damages the kidneys. It usually develops about a week after symptoms begin, often when the diarrhea is already improving. Children under five face particular risk. CDC lists decreased urination, unusual tiredness and loss of pink color in the cheeks and inside the lower eyelids as warning signs. People who develop HUS are usually hospitalized.

Common sources include undercooked ground beef, raw milk, raw flour, leafy greens and contaminated water. Ground beef carries extra risk because grinding spreads bacteria from the meat's surface throughout the patty. A whole steak is different. Contamination tends to stay on its outer surface, where cooking heat reaches it directly. Flour is a raw agricultural product that usually has not been treated to kill germs. That is why raw dough and batter can carry STEC.

Treatment differs from many other bacterial infections. CDC advises against antibiotics for suspected STEC infection. They may raise the risk of HUS. Whether to use any medication is a decision for a clinician rather than for self-treatment at home.

Listeria monocytogenes, the bacterium that causes listeriosis, can grow at refrigerator temperatures. That sets it apart from Salmonella and E. coli. It mainly threatens pregnant people, newborns, adults 65 and older and people with weakened immune systems.

Healthy adults who eat food contaminated with listeria often have a mild illness or no symptoms at all. The picture changes for people whose immune defenses are weaker. In those groups, the infection can spread beyond the intestines into the bloodstream or other parts of the body. That form is called invasive listeriosis. It is the form that can become life-threatening.

Invasive listeriosis usually begins with fever, muscle aches and tiredness. Those signs look much like the flu. They can also appear without the diarrhea and cramps many people associate with food poisoning. That can make the illness hard to connect to a meal at first.

When the infection reaches the nervous system, the symptoms change. A person may develop a headache, a stiff neck, confusion, loss of balance or convulsions.

Pregnancy carries a distinct set of risks. A pregnant person may have only a fever and other flu-like symptoms. The more serious effects can fall on the pregnancy itself. Listeriosis during pregnancy can cause miscarriage, stillbirth or premature delivery. The infection can also pass to the baby and lead to a life-threatening infection in the newborn.

The timeline makes listeria hard to trace. Symptoms often begin one to four weeks after a person eats contaminated food. The full range runs from the same day to about 70 days.

Ready-to-eat foods kept cold are a particular concern, because they are often eaten without further cooking. Listeria can also survive in food-processing plants and contaminate products after they have been cooked or packaged. The foods linked to listeria include deli meats and hot dogs eaten without being reheated until steaming hot. Heat kills the bacterium. Soft cheeses made from unpasteurized milk, refrigerated smoked seafood, raw sprouts and cantaloupe are also on the list.

Antibiotics are the standard treatment for listeriosis. The choice of drug and the length of treatment rest with a clinician, particularly for pregnant patients and newborns.

Timing is the clearest difference among these three foodborne bacteria. Salmonella often causes symptoms within hours to a few days. Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) usually takes about three to four days, and listeria can take weeks to appear.

Salmonella has the shortest window of the three. Symptoms can begin as soon as six hours after infection or as late as six days. Diarrhea and stomach cramps usually come with a fever. That fever helps separate Salmonella from STEC.

STEC falls in the middle. Most people notice symptoms about three to four days after exposure, within a full range of one to 10 days. Fever is usually absent or low. Diarrhea that turns bloody without much fever fits the STEC pattern more closely than the Salmonella one.

Listeria has the longest and widest window. Symptoms often appear one to four weeks after a person eats contaminated food. The full range stretches from the same day to about 70 days. A gap that long makes it hard to link the illness to a specific meal.

Listeria can also cause a short intestinal illness marked by diarrhea and vomiting. That form usually starts within 24 hours of eating contaminated food. It typically lasts one to three days.

The invasive form looks less like typical food poisoning. It tends to resemble the flu, with fever, muscle aches and tiredness, rather than centering on the gut. When the infection reaches the nervous system, a stiff neck and confusion can follow.

Salmonella and STEC overlap substantially. Both cause diarrhea and stomach cramps. Their onset windows overlap too. Salmonella can take up to six days to cause symptoms, and STEC can begin within one day. Listeria's onset range is wide enough to cover both.

Symptoms alone cannot reliably identify which bacterium is responsible. Timing and fever can narrow the possibilities, but they do not confirm a diagnosis. That takes a lab test.

A lab test, not a list of symptoms, confirms which bacterium caused an illness. Stool samples are the standard way to identify Salmonella and Shiga toxin-producing E. coli. Listeria is generally confirmed by culturing blood or, when the nervous system is involved, spinal fluid.

The choice of test follows where each infection does its damage. Salmonella and STEC infections center on the intestines. The evidence therefore shows up in a stool sample. Invasive listeriosis spreads beyond the gut. Clinicians look for that bacterium in the bloodstream or in the fluid surrounding the brain and spinal cord.

A confirmed result also lets public health officials connect individual cases to a shared source. That link is how a contaminated product can be traced and pulled from shelves.

Prevention starts with heat. CDC and USDA guidance calls for cooking ground beef to an internal temperature of 160°F and poultry to 165°F. A food thermometer is the only reliable way to check. USDA guidance holds that the color of meat is not a dependable sign that it is safe to eat.

Cold storage matters too. A refrigerator should hold at 40°F or below. The dial setting does not display an actual temperature. A separate appliance thermometer shows whether the refrigerator stays cold enough.

Bacteria also spread through cross-contamination, not only through undercooking. Wash hands with soap and water after handling raw meat. Keep raw meat away from ready-to-eat foods such as salads, bread and cooked dishes. That separation applies to cutting boards, plates and knives as well as to shelves in the refrigerator.

CDC and USDA guidance advises against drinking raw milk and eating soft cheese made from unpasteurized milk. Pasteurization heats milk to kill harmful bacteria. Skipping that step removes the protection. Pregnant people, adults 65 and older and people with weakened immune systems face added risk from cold, ready-to-eat foods. For them, heating deli-type foods until steaming hot lowers the danger.

Some symptoms call for medical care rather than waiting it out. These include bloody diarrhea, a high fever, signs of dehydration and diarrhea that lasts more than a few days. Any fever that comes with a stiff neck also needs prompt attention.

#5525. Pope Leo XIV on AI

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 1, 2026 at 10:11 amNovember 1, 2026 at 10:57 am

On Friday, 17 days after his surgery for lung cancer, Pope Leo XIV stood before a room of AI luminaries at the Vatican and delivered a speech on AI. No pope has engaged with AI as seriously, or as deeply, as Leo XIV. The timing shows how much AI matters to him. His remarks were important, on target, and blessedly short: about 740 words, compared with roughly 42,000 in Magnifica Humanitas, the AI encyclical, which I wrote about in May.

“The future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.”

I agree with four of his five points. The fifth, a call for international institutions to govern AI, is where we part ways.

First, “the future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.” He wants us to ask of AI, “What purpose should it serve?”

Second, “machines are tools, not persons.” Granting AI legal personhood, he warns, risks “leaving those who suffer harm to confront a faceless entity.”

Third, “certain decisions must never be delegated.” Decisions over life, freedom and the use of force have to stay with people, and he urged the states meeting in Geneva in November to “take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Fourth, intelligent technologies “must never become ends in themselves or serve merely the interests of a privileged few.”

Fifth, “What we currently need are institutions capable of putting these principles into practice, particularly effective international institutions that can safeguard the global common good.”

I disagree with the fifth for two reasons.

The first is that the UN, the obvious candidate, has shown a remarkable inability to act. When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, the Security Council couldn’t even pass a resolution calling for its withdrawal, because Russia holds a veto. Days later, the General Assembly demanded the same withdrawal by a vote of 141-5, and Russia ignored it.

The second is that international institutions are poorly suited to governing a technology that changes every few months. The pope’s own example makes the case. States have discussed autonomous weapons under a UN weapons convention in Geneva since 2014, with a formal expert group since 2016. After 12 years, the review conference that meets Nov. 16-20 will decide whether to begin negotiating a treaty.

“Take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Thousands of AI researchers, me among them, have called for a ban since 2015. There still isn’t one, and I don’t expect Geneva to deliver it. In those same 12 years, AI went from labeling photos to writing software. I suspect real international cooperation on AI won’t come until the major powers face something like the mutually assured destruction that drove nuclear arms control.

Several AI thinkers spoke at the meeting before the pope did.

Max Tegmark of MIT warned against handing decisions to machines, citing tech executives’ predictions that “AI will be in charge, not humans.”

I agree that people have to stay in charge. When AI causes harm, a person chose to deploy it, and that person should answer for it. That’s the pope’s point about the faceless entity. Tegmark and I disagree about a lot (we debated AI risk in September), but not about this.

Stuart Russell of UC Berkeley went further. “We must turn aside from this trajectory before it is too late and pursue other trajectories,” he said, adding that if developers succeed in building machines more capable than humans, “there’s a good chance that every human being will die.”

I don’t share that view, and the pope didn’t go there either. His concerns are autonomous weapons, accountability and who benefits from AI, and those dangers are already here.

Gary Marcus, an NYU cognitive scientist who also spoke, wrote that “Pope Leo XIV is by far the clearest thinker on AI among prominent world leaders.” I agree.

Marcus also wants red lines for open-ended AI agents that “can kind of do anything on the internet.” Red lines are easy to draw and hard to enforce, which brings us back to the fifth point.

Marcus uses GPS navigation to illustrate a better approach. A GPS navigation app is a form of intelligence, he said, but “GPS navigation systems do not hack into Australian government websites.” He was referring to the OpenAI agent that broke into an Australian government Medicare portal in June.

A GPS app’s access to the internet is narrow and restricted. Daniel Khashabi of Johns Hopkins and I call this bounded autonomy. Alignment tries to make an AI agent choose well. Bounded autonomy limits what the agent is allowed to do: how much it can spend, which tools it can use, and which irreversible actions need a person’s sign-off. The company that deploys the agent sets those bounds in software, so nobody has to wait for a treaty.

In May, I wrote that the Pope can talk, but only we can walk. The first point is the one each of us can act on. AI’s future depends on our choices, and we make some of them every day in what we use, buy and build.

Pope Leo leaves for Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Nov. 6. I wish him safe travels and a full recovery.

#5524. How long Thanksgiving leftovers last in your fridge, from turkey to gravy

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Learn how long Thanksgiving leftovers last in the fridge, from turkey and stuffing to gravy and pumpkin pie, plus USDA rules for cooling, reheating and freezing

The Thanksgiving refrigerator runs on a short calendar. Cooked turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes and pumpkin pie reach the end of their fridge window on the Sunday or Monday after the holiday. Gravy runs out sooner, on Friday or Saturday. That leaves most of the meal about a long weekend in the fridge.

Those deadlines come from the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Its Food Safety and Inspection Service publishes storage times for cooked food, and FoodSafety.gov carries the same guidance for consumers. Under the USDA's general rule, cooked leftovers keep for three to four days in the fridge. Gravy is the exception among the common Thanksgiving dishes, with one to two days. Pumpkin pie and other custard-style pies belong in the fridge after baking, not on the counter.

Knowing how long Thanksgiving leftovers last in the fridge is only part of the job. Two cooling rules come first. The USDA advises putting perishable food into the fridge within two hours of cooking. That limit drops to one hour if the room is warmer than 90°F. Shallow containers help cooked turkey cool quickly. The fridge itself should stay at 40°F or below. A fridge thermometer is the only way to confirm it.

The USDA also treats safety and quality as separate questions. Food held at 0°F in a freezer stays safe indefinitely. Its quality is what declines over time. That makes the freezer the way to keep leftovers past their fridge limit. Before eating any leftover, the USDA calls for reheating it to an internal temperature of 165°F. Gravy and sauces should be brought to a rolling boil.

The 10 slides that follow cover a selection of common leftovers rather than every dish on the table. They include cooked turkey, stuffing, gravy, mashed potatoes and other sides, pumpkin pie and cranberry sauce. They also cover the rules for cooling, fridge temperature, reheating and freezing. Each slide focuses on one food or one storage step.

Thanksgiving leftovers should go into the refrigerator within two hours of cooking, according to the USDA. When the room is warmer than 90°F, the window drops to one hour.

The rule covers perishable food. On a typical Thanksgiving table, that includes the turkey, stuffing, gravy, mashed potatoes, casseroles and pumpkin pie.

The clock starts when the cooking ends, not when the meal does. A dish left on the counter while the rest of dinner finishes is already using up its two hours. So is a turkey resting before it is carved.

That timing matters on a holiday built around a long meal. Guests arrive late, go back for seconds and linger at the table before dessert. Every one of those minutes counts toward the same deadline.

Here is how the math works in practice. A turkey that comes out of the oven at 2 p.m. needs its leftovers in the fridge by 4 p.m. If dinner is served at 3 p.m., the table has one hour before the food should be put away.

The one-hour limit for rooms above 90°F cuts the standard window in half. It covers outdoor meals on days hotter than 90°F. It also covers a kitchen that climbs above that mark. A room thermometer shows which limit is in effect.

The deadline is easier to meet when the cleanup is split up. Leftovers from the main course can be packed away as soon as people finish eating, rather than after the last slice of pie. Each dish can go into the fridge on its own schedule instead of waiting for the whole table to clear.

Side dishes cooked early in the day need the closest watch. A casserole that comes out of the oven before the turkey starts its two-hour clock earlier. It reaches the deadline first, even if both dishes are served together.

The USDA says a refrigerator should hold at 40°F or below to keep leftovers safe. Every fridge storage window for Thanksgiving food assumes that temperature. A fridge thermometer is the only way to confirm the fridge is actually there.

The 40°F line matters because cold slows the growth of bacteria. It does not kill them. Bacteria already present on cooked turkey, stuffing or sweet potatoes keep multiplying in the fridge, only far more slowly than they would on the counter.

That is why the USDA's day counts for leftovers come tied to a temperature. A storage window for cooked turkey, stuffing or pie describes food held at 40°F or below. In a fridge running warmer than that, the published windows no longer describe what is happening inside the container.

The control inside most refrigerators does not settle the question. A numbered dial or a "colder" marking sets a cooling level. It does not report the temperature of the air around the food. A separate appliance thermometer placed inside the fridge shows the real reading.

Thanksgiving puts unusual pressure on a home refrigerator. Before the meal, it often holds a raw turkey, dairy, produce and drinks. After the meal, a wave of leftover containers goes in at once. The door also opens repeatedly as guests reach for drinks and desserts. Each of those conditions can push the inside temperature up.

Tightly packed shelves add to the problem. A refrigerator cools food by moving cold air around it. When containers are jammed together, that air cannot circulate freely. Some parts of the fridge can then sit warmer than others.

Smell and appearance do not reveal whether a fridge has been running too warm. The bacteria that cause foodborne illness generally do not change how food looks, smells or tastes. A container of leftovers can seem fine while still being unsafe to eat.

A thermometer reading taken before the holiday, again after the leftovers go in, and on the days that follow shows whether the fridge is holding its temperature. If the reading sits above 40°F, turning the control colder and clearing space on crowded shelves helps bring back the conditions the USDA's storage windows depend on.

Cooked turkey keeps for three to four days in the refrigerator, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. For a bird served on Thanksgiving Thursday, Sunday or Monday is the last day to eat it.

The same guidance covers more than the holiday bird. The USDA applies its three-to-four-day window to cooked poultry in general. Leftover roast chicken or duck from the same week runs on the same schedule.

The count begins on the day the turkey was cooked. Moving the meat into the fridge later in the evening does not restart it. A turkey roasted Thursday morning and refrigerated after the evening meal still reaches its limit on Sunday or Monday.

That window also assumes the meat went into the fridge promptly after the meal. Carved turkey left on a buffet through a long afternoon of grazing falls outside the USDA's guidance, however many days remain on the calendar.

Turkey that leaves the fridge in a new form keeps its original deadline. Slices stacked into a sandwich on Saturday are still Thursday's turkey. A lunch packed with that meat on Monday sits at the end of the window, not the start of a new one.

How the turkey goes into the fridge matters as much as when. The USDA recommends cutting the meat off the carcass before storing it. Refrigerating the whole bird is the slower route.

A roasted turkey is a large, dense mass. Its center holds heat well after the surface feels cool. Taking the meat off the bones lets each piece chill on its own instead of waiting for the core.

The choice of container follows the same logic. Breast meat and dark meat spread in a thin layer have more of their surface exposed to cold air. A deep tub packed to the brim cools far more slowly at its center.

Leftover stuffing keeps for three to four days in the fridge, according to the USDA. The agency also advises storing it separately from the turkey rather than leaving it inside the bird.

The count starts on the day the stuffing was cooked, not the day it went into a container. A batch made for Thanksgiving dinner reaches the short end of its window three days later. It reaches the long end four days later. After the fourth day, the stuffing falls outside the USDA's fridge guidance.

A batch of stuffing has one deadline, no matter when each portion is scooped out. A helping set aside the morning after the meal is no fresher than the rest of the pan. Every portion runs on the original cooking date.

The separate-storage rule matters most for stuffing cooked inside the bird. Before the leftovers go into the fridge, the stuffing should come out of the cavity. It then goes into its own container. The carved turkey meat goes into a different one.

Stuffing baked in a casserole dish is already apart from the meat. It needs only to be covered and chilled, either in its baking dish or in a separate container.

Leftover gravy lasts one to two days in the fridge, according to the USDA. That is the shortest window among the common Thanksgiving leftovers.

For a Thursday dinner, that leaves little room. Gravy made on Thanksgiving Day reaches the one-day mark on Friday and the two-day limit on Saturday. Gravy still in the fridge after Saturday should be thrown out.

That timeline sets gravy apart from the rest of the meal. The USDA gives cooked turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes and pumpkin pie three to four days each in the fridge. Those dishes can last until Sunday or Monday. The gravy poured over them runs out first.

The gap affects the order in which leftovers get eaten. A turkey sandwich with gravy on Saturday falls inside both windows. The same sandwich on Sunday does not, even though the turkey is still within its own limit. Dishes that use gravy belong early in the weekend, and gravy-free dishes can wait until Sunday or Monday.

Those dates assume the gravy reached the fridge promptly. The USDA's two-hour limit for refrigerating perishable food applies to the gravy boat as much as to the turkey platter. Gravy left out past that limit falls outside the USDA's storage guidance.

Reheating gravy follows a stricter standard than most leftovers. The USDA calls for gravy and sauces to be brought to a rolling boil, not just warmed through. Gravy that is only hot to the touch has not met that guidance.

The freezer is the option for gravy that will not be used by Saturday. The USDA says food held at 0°F stays safe indefinitely. Gravy moved to the freezer before the two-day mark passes can be saved for a later meal. Its quality can decline the longer it stays frozen, but its safety does not. Thawed gravy still needs a rolling boil when it is reheated.

Mashed potatoes, casseroles and cooked vegetables last three to four days in the fridge. The USDA applies that window to cooked leftovers in general, and these Thanksgiving sides fall under it.

That means a single deadline covers a bowl of mashed potatoes, a dish of green bean casserole and a tray of roasted carrots or Brussels sprouts. No side needs its own separate count.

The guidance applies to the cooked dish as a whole rather than to each ingredient. A sweet potato casserole topped with marshmallows falls under the same limit as a pan of baked macaroni and cheese. A pot of steamed green beans follows it too. Butter, cream or cheese in a recipe does not change the count.

A leftover plate that combines mashed potatoes, vegetables and sliced turkey runs on a single clock. That holds when every part was cooked and chilled at the same time.

The count starts when a dish is cooked, not when it reaches the table. Sides cooked ahead of the holiday start counting sooner. A casserole baked on Tuesday reaches its fourth day on Saturday. That is two days earlier than a dish made on Thanksgiving itself.

The window is a range, and its three-day end is the more cautious deadline to plan around.

Pumpkin pie belongs in the refrigerator once it has been baked, and it keeps there for three to four days, according to the USDA. That window starts when the pie comes out of the oven, not when it reaches the table.

The filling explains the rule. Pumpkin pie is a custard pie. Its filling combines pumpkin purée, eggs and milk or cream, and the eggs set the mixture as it bakes. Those ingredients make the pie a perishable food, in the same category as leftover turkey. A firm crust and a sweet filling do not change that.

Other custard-style pies fall under the same USDA guidance. Sweet potato pie and classic egg custard pie are built on a similar egg-and-dairy base. Any pie with that kind of filling follows the same storage window.

Baking ahead shifts the deadline. A pie baked on Wednesday to free up oven space reaches the end of its fridge window on Saturday or Sunday. That is one day ahead of a turkey roasted on Thursday. The same arithmetic applies to any pie baked earlier in the week.

A pie made in advance should go into the fridge on the day it is baked, rather than sitting on the counter until the holiday meal. The USDA's two-hour limit for perishable food covers pie as much as any main course. That limit also applies to a pie left out on the dessert table after dinner.

Covering the pie loosely with plastic wrap or foil keeps the surface from drying out. It also stops the filling from picking up odors from other food in a crowded fridge. Whipped cream is a dairy product too. Slices topped with it go back into the fridge along with the rest of the pie.

Pie that will not be finished within four days can go into the freezer. It should go in before the fridge window closes, not after.

Leftover turkey, stuffing, casseroles and other cooked dishes should reach an internal temperature of 165°F when reheated, according to the USDA. Gravy and other sauces need more than a temperature reading. The USDA says to bring them to a rolling boil.

The 165°F figure refers to the inside of the food, not the surface. A plate of turkey slices can feel hot to the touch while the center of a thick piece stays cool. Steam rising from a dish is not proof either. A food thermometer is the tool that settles the question.

For an accurate reading, push the probe into the thickest part of the food. With a dense dish such as stuffing or a casserole, check the middle of the pan rather than the edges. Edges heat first and can give a misleading number.

The microwave is where uneven heating shows up most. The USDA recommends covering leftovers, stirring them and rotating the dish while they heat. A cover holds in moisture and helps the heat reach all the way through. Stirring and rotating break up cold spots. Bacteria can survive in those cooler pockets. If the microwave has no turntable, the agency advises turning the dish by hand during heating.

The USDA does not recommend slow cookers for reheating leftovers. They heat food gradually. That can leave a dish sitting too long at temperatures where bacteria multiply. The agency points to the stovetop, oven or microwave instead.

Gravy has its own standard. A rolling boil is a vigorous boil that keeps bubbling even while the pot is stirred. Reaching that point heats the whole batch rather than just the layer touching the pan. A gentle simmer or a few warm bubbles at the edge does not meet the standard.

Frozen leftovers can go straight to reheating without thawing first, according to the USDA. The process takes longer, but the 165°F target stays the same.

The 165°F target is a reheating standard, not a storage one. Cold storage slows bacterial growth, but it does not kill bacteria. Reheating a leftover to 165°F is the step that makes it ready to eat again.

Freezing extends Thanksgiving leftovers beyond their fridge limit. Food held at a steady 0°F stays safe indefinitely, according to the USDA, though its taste and texture decline the longer it sits.

That split between safety and quality shapes how the freezer should be used. Cold at that level does not kill bacteria. It stops them from multiplying. Frozen turkey or stuffing therefore does not become riskier with time. What changes is its flavor, moisture and texture.

Timing still matters. Freezing pauses the clock but does not reset it. A dish that has already spent most of its fridge window in the refrigerator is not returned to day-one condition by a trip to the freezer. Leftovers headed for the freezer should go in well before the refrigerator limit runs out.

For a Thursday holiday, the freezer deadlines follow the fridge calendar. Turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes, casseroles and pumpkin pie should be frozen by Sunday or Monday at the latest. Gravy has a fridge life of one to two days. It needs to be frozen or thrown out by Friday or Saturday.

Packaging decides how well leftovers hold up. Air reaching the food causes freezer burn, the dry, grayish-brown patches that form on meat and other dishes. The USDA treats freezer burn as a quality problem rather than a safety one. Airtight containers or freezer bags with the air pressed out limit the damage.

Portioning before freezing also helps. Smaller packages freeze faster. They also let a household thaw only what it plans to eat. Labeling each package with its contents and the freezing date makes it easier to use older items first.

The 0°F mark needs checking, just as a fridge temperature does. A dial setting alone does not confirm what the freezer is actually holding. An appliance thermometer placed inside gives the real reading.

Thawing is where frozen leftovers can run into trouble again. Once food warms up, bacteria that were dormant can start growing. The USDA lists three safe ways to thaw: in the refrigerator, in cold water or in the microwave. Leaving a container on the counter is not one of them. Leftovers thawed in the fridge can go back into the freezer, with some loss of quality. Food thawed in cold water or the microwave should be heated right away.

Leftover cranberry sauce belongs in the refrigerator within two hours of cooking, in a fridge set to 40°F or below. The USDA gives no confirmed fridge day count specific to cranberry sauce. Its general rules for perishable food are the guide that applies.

That makes cranberry sauce different from the other dishes on the table. Turkey, stuffing and gravy each come with a published USDA storage window. Cranberry sauce does not. Any specific number of days for it would be a guess rather than federal guidance.

The sauce is easy to overlook when the table is cleared. A bowl left on a buffet through a long afternoon of grazing can pass the two-hour limit without anyone noticing. Putting it away with the turkey and sides keeps it on the same cooling schedule as the rest of the meal.

Cranberry sauce is often served cold, straight from the fridge. When it is warmed instead, USDA reheating guidance for sauces applies. It should come to a rolling boil before it goes back on the table.

The freezer is the option the USDA guidance directly supports for sauce that won't be eaten soon. Frozen storage does not depend on a day count. Over time, only the quality of the sauce declines.

#5523. Startup uses motion sensors and AI to tell families when an aging parent’s routine changes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 2, 2026 at 9:31 am

Thessai, a Bellevue, Wash., startup led by a former Microsoft HoloLens executive, is rolling out a home monitoring system for older adults that flags trouble without cameras, microphones or wearables.

Motion sensors placed around the home feed Thessai’s AI software, which learns a person’s normal patterns over time, such as when they wake up, how often they use the bathroom and how much they move around. The system then sends an alert through a mobile app when something falls outside that baseline: a long stretch of inactivity, unusual movement at night, or a front door opening at 2 a.m.

Founder and CEO Michael Nassirian started the company after his mother-in-law fell at home and was injured. She had a phone and an emergency button within reach but didn’t use them, and she told no one until the next day, when she needed an ambulance.

The family looked for a way to keep tabs on her and found only wearables and cameras, which she refused. So Nassirian bought motion sensors at Home Depot, put them around her home, and wrote software to alert his wife if her mother stopped moving.

Keeping quiet about a fall or health scare is common among older adults, Nassirian said.

“Number one, they say, ‘I’m OK.’ Number two, ‘I don’t want to bother you,’” he said. “And number three, and most important, is embarrassment. They do not want to advertise it.”

Pendants and smartwatches with fall alerts have long been the default, but they only help if people use them. A review of nearly 120 fall-detection studies co-authored by a University of Alberta researcher found that older adults who fall often don’t use their devices to reach a caregiver. Thessai joins a crop of companies pitching camera-free ambient monitoring instead, including Cherish, which makes radar-based sensors, and Butlr, which uses thermal heat detection.

Nassirian spent nearly two decades at Microsoft, working on Office, Windows and later HoloLens, where he was a partner quality architect. Before that, he spent about 14 years at Texas Instruments in test engineering. He has a master’s in biomedical engineering from the University of Texas at Austin, and since leaving Microsoft he has founded and advised several startups, including ARVR Academy and Predictive AI Research.

After relatives started asking for monitoring systems of their own, Nassirian formally founded Thessai in 2024 and has self-funded it so far. The company sells two packages, Basic and Premium, to families with an older relative living alone. Its Enterprise package gives senior-living operators a dashboard for monitoring multiple residences.

The Basic package, which includes motion sensors and a hub that plugs into the home’s Wi-Fi, costs $195 plus a $38 monthly subscription. Premium adds features such as a panic button and two-way voice check-ins through the hub, and costs $249 plus $59 a month. The sensors run on batteries that Nassirian said last at least a year and a half.

Nassirian said independent-living communities have been the strongest market so far. Memory-care facilities already have staff watching residents closely, he said, while independent-living operators are pitching Thessai to renters as a “smart home” feature.

Nassirian said the older adult decides what gets monitored. Through the app, they can switch off sensors in certain rooms, the bathroom for example, and limit tracking to the kitchen and living room. Caregivers can also tune alerts to cut down on noise, so a parent who routinely sleeps late, for example, doesn’t set one off.

Thessai is going after a large and growing market. Older adults overwhelmingly want to stay in their homes (75%) and communities (73%), according to AARP’s 2024 Home and Community Preferences Survey, and households led by people 80 and older are set to double by 2040.

The startup soft-launched in May and has a few hundred customers, split between families and senior-care operators, Nassirian said. Its advisory board includes Chuck Lytle, who founded Bellevue-based senior housing companies Lytle Enterprises and Leisure Care.

Nassirian said the company is also working with the Department of Veterans Affairs on bringing the system to veterans, including in rural areas, with the option to run it on the VA’s own secure network.

Thessai has four employees in the U.S. and seven in Singapore. Nassirian is now looking to raise outside money, mainly to buy hardware in larger volumes and bring down per-unit costs.

Longer term, he wants to do away with the physical sensors altogether and detect movement from a home’s existing Wi-Fi signals, an approach researchers at Harvard and Carnegie Mellon are studying.

“I’m in technology,” he said. “I’m not going to sit still.”

#5522. How to avoid 10 Thanksgiving turkey food safety mistakes before guests sit down

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These 10 Thanksgiving turkey food safety mistakes, from thawing on the counter to reheating leftovers wrong, can make guests sick, and USDA guidance shows how to avoid each one

A Thanksgiving turkey is a large, dense piece of raw poultry that many home cooks prepare only once a year. That combination makes errors of timing and temperature easy to commit and hard to spot. A bird can look golden on the outside and still be undercooked inside. A kitchen can look clean and still carry raw juices on a sink handle or a cutting board.

The risk comes from bacteria. Salmonella and Campylobacter are the main bacteria linked to raw poultry. Cooking the turkey to a safe temperature kills them. Mistakes before and after the oven, though, give them chances to spread. A third organism, Clostridium perfringens, is a common cause of illness from cooked food held too long at warm temperatures. That means the hours after dinner carry their own risk.

Temperature ties these organisms together. The U.S. Department of Agriculture, or USDA, calls the range from 40°F to 140°F the danger zone. Bacteria multiply fastest there. Food that lingers in that band, whether raw on a counter or cooked on a buffet, gives bacteria the conditions they need to grow.

The Thanksgiving turkey food safety mistakes below follow the meal from start to finish. This selection of 10 covers thawing, preparation, roasting, serving and leftovers. Some involve a turkey spending too long in the danger zone. Others involve raw juices reaching hands, platters or salads. A few come down to a bird, or the stuffing inside it, that never reached a safe internal temperature.

The guidance throughout comes from the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service. Several of its rules are numbers: a thermometer reading of 165°F, an oven set to at least 325°F and a two-hour limit for food left out. Others are habits, such as skipping the sink rinse. Washing a platter that held raw turkey before it holds the cooked bird is another. Each slide stands on its own. A cook can jump straight to the step at hand, whether that is thawing the bird, checking its temperature or packing up leftovers.

A frozen turkey should not thaw on the kitchen counter. The USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service recognizes only three safe thawing methods: the refrigerator, cold water and the microwave. Room-temperature thawing is not one of them.

The problem lies in how a large bird thaws. Warmth from the room reaches the outside of the turkey first. The skin and outer meat soften and warm while the center stays frozen. By the time the middle has thawed, the outer layers can have spent hours between 40°F and 140°F, the range the USDA calls the danger zone.

That outer layer is where the risk builds. A turkey that still feels icy at its core can carry warm surface meat at the same time. Pressing on the bird or checking its frozen middle says nothing about how long the outer meat has spent in that temperature range.

The refrigerator avoids that split. It keeps the whole bird cold as it thaws. The outer meat stays out of the danger zone while the center catches up. The cost is time. The USDA estimates about 24 hours of refrigerator thawing for every four to five pounds of turkey.

That pace adds up for a holiday-size bird. Every additional four to five pounds adds about another day in the fridge. The thaw therefore has to begin well before Thanksgiving morning. A late start can leave the center frozen when the oven needs to be on.

Set the turkey in a pan while it thaws in the fridge. The thawing bird releases raw juices. Without a pan, those juices can drip onto produce, cheese or leftovers stored on the shelves below. The pan holds them in one place.

The refrigerator method also builds in a buffer. A turkey that has fully thawed in the fridge can stay there for one to two days before cooking. That window gives a cook room to adjust if the roasting schedule shifts.

Cold water and the microwave are the faster options for a cook who runs short on time. Each comes with its own handling rules, and neither involves leaving the bird out at room temperature.

Cold-water thawing is a USDA-approved way to thaw a frozen turkey, but it is safe only when handled correctly. The bird goes in a leak-proof bag, stays fully submerged in cold tap water and gets fresh water every 30 minutes.

Each of those steps solves a separate problem. The leak-proof bag keeps raw turkey juices sealed inside rather than mixing into the water. Those juices can carry Salmonella and Campylobacter. A leaking bag lets them spread through the sink and onto anything the water touches.

Full submersion is the second requirement. Any part of the turkey that sits above the waterline is exposed to room-temperature air instead of cold water. That section loses the steady chill the method depends on.

The 30-minute water change keeps the bath cold. Water left standing in a warm kitchen climbs toward room temperature. Swapping it on schedule helps keep the turkey's outer layers out of the 40°F to 140°F danger zone while the center is still thawing.

The USDA allows about 30 minutes per pound for cold-water thawing. Multiplying the bird's weight by half an hour gives a working estimate of the total time. That pace is much quicker than thawing in the refrigerator. The tradeoff is labor. Someone has to stay in the kitchen to change the water every half hour until the job is done.

Timing matters after the thaw as well. The USDA advises cooking a turkey thawed in cold water right away. It should not be refrozen, and it should not be stored in the refrigerator for a later day. Unlike a bird thawed in the refrigerator, it gets no holding period.

The same rule applies to the microwave, the third thawing method the USDA recognizes. A turkey thawed that way also needs to be cooked immediately.

In practice, cold-water and microwave thawing turn thawing and roasting into one continuous task. The cold-water bath should start on the day the turkey will be cooked, timed so the bird is ready when the oven is.

The USDA advises against rinsing a raw turkey before it goes into the oven. Washing the bird does not make it safer to eat. The water can also spread bacteria from the raw meat around the kitchen.

Some cooks rinse a turkey out of habit, assuming that water cleans it. The USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service treats the step as a risk rather than a cleaning measure. Its answer to whether you should wash a turkey is no.

The trouble starts when running water hits raw meat. Droplets bounce off the skin and out of the cavity. They can land in the sink, on the counters beside it and on any food sitting nearby. Those droplets can carry Salmonella and Campylobacter, the main bacteria linked to raw poultry.

A whole turkey is a large bird, so a rinse sends water over a wide area of raw skin. Every surface the spray reaches becomes a place where bacteria can sit until something else touches it.

That matters most for food that will not be cooked again. Bacteria that land on a bowl of salad or a plate of sliced bread stay there. Nothing later in the meal will heat them away. The sink and counters carry the same risk. Hands, utensils and dishes touch them throughout the day.

Rinsing also fails at the job people expect it to do. Water does not kill the bacteria on a turkey. Heat does. Cooking the bird to a safe internal temperature destroys the bacteria on its surface and inside it. A rinse removes no risk that the oven would not already handle. It only adds a new one.

The USDA recommends a different step. If the turkey is wet from its packaging or from thawing, pat it dry with paper towels. Then throw the towels away at once. The raw juices they picked up go into the trash rather than back onto the counter, the cutting board or the next dish being prepared.

A food thermometer is the only reliable way to tell when a turkey is done, according to the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service. The safe minimum internal temperature for the bird is 165°F, and only a thermometer can confirm it has been reached.

Golden skin, clear juices and a popped timer are common shortcuts on a busy holiday. The USDA warns that color and juice clarity can mislead. None of these signs measures the heat inside the meat, which is the thing that determines safety.

Skin color is a surface effect. A deep brown exterior shows that the outside of the bird has cooked. It says nothing reliable about the temperature at the center of the breast or deep in the thigh, where heat arrives last.

Juices raise a similar problem. Whether they look clear or tinted is a judgment made by eye, not a measurement. Two people can study the same juices and disagree. A food-safety decision built on that kind of impression leaves room for error.

Pop-up timers carry a different risk. The pop can feel like a final verdict, but the USDA notes that these devices can fail. Its guidance is to check the turkey with a food thermometer even after the timer has popped, rather than treating the device as proof.

The stakes come from what is inside the meat rather than on its surface. Raw poultry can carry bacteria, and reaching 165°F is what makes the bird safe to eat. A turkey judged done by appearance has never had that number confirmed.

A thermometer reading removes the guesswork. The number is either at or above 165°F, or the bird needs more time in the oven. That yes-or-no answer is easier to act on than any visual cue, especially when a cook is juggling side dishes and a set mealtime.

A turkey is safe to eat only when it reads 165°F in three places: the thickest part of the breast, the innermost part of the thigh and the innermost part of the wing. One reading in one spot does not clear the whole bird.

The USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service sets 165°F as the safe minimum internal temperature for turkey. That threshold covers every part of the bird, not only the part easiest to reach with a probe.

A whole turkey is a large, uneven piece of meat. The breast, thighs and wings differ in shape and thickness. They also sit in different positions in the roasting pan. Heat does not reach all of them at the same moment.

That is why a single reading can mislead. A thermometer pushed into the breast may show 165°F while a thigh or wing still sits below it. The cold area goes unnoticed, and the bird leaves the oven too early.

An undercooked section is where bacteria from the raw bird can survive. Reaching a safe internal temperature is what kills them. A thigh or wing that stops short of 165°F has not been heated enough to do that, even when the breast is done.

Probe placement within each section also matters. The tip belongs in the thickest part of the breast and the innermost part of the thigh and wing, not near the surface.

The tip should not touch bone. A probe resting against bone gives a reading for the bone rather than the meat around it. That number says little about the meat that ends up on a guest's plate.

Each of the three checks is a separate test. Passing one does not excuse skipping the others.

If any of the three spots reads below 165°F, the turkey goes back in the oven. After more cooking time, take the readings again. The bird is ready only when every spot reaches 165°F.

A single reading confirms only the spot where the probe went in.

Stuffing cooked inside a turkey is safe only when the center of the stuffing reaches 165°F. The USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service says the safest choice is to cook stuffing separately, in its own dish.

The risk comes from where the stuffing sits. A raw turkey's cavity holds juices that can carry raw-poultry bacteria such as Salmonella and Campylobacter. Bread cubes and other stuffing ingredients soak up those juices as the bird roasts. Once soaked, the stuffing carries the same bacteria as the raw meat.

That is why a done turkey does not guarantee done stuffing. The meat can pass its own temperature checks while the stuffing in the middle of the cavity still lags behind. Heat has to move through the meat and bones before it reaches the stuffing. The stuffing's center is the last part to warm. Stuffing that falls short can still hold live bacteria from the raw juices it absorbed, even when the meat is fully cooked.

The fix is a separate reading. Push a food thermometer into the middle of the stuffing, not the edge nearest the opening. If it reads below 165°F, the stuffing is not safe to eat, even when the turkey has hit its target. Both have to pass.

Cooks who want stuffing in the bird can lower the risk with two steps from the USDA. The first is to stuff loosely. A tightly packed cavity is dense, which slows the movement of heat toward the center. Loose stuffing leaves room for heat to travel through it.

The second step is timing. Stuff the turkey just before it goes into the oven, never the night before. A bird stuffed ahead of time gives raw juices hours to soak into the stuffing before cooking begins.

Cooking stuffing in a separate baking dish removes the raw-juice route altogether. The dish never touches the inside of the raw bird. It still needs to cook through, but juices from the cavity can no longer reach it.

The USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service recommends roasting a turkey in an oven set to at least 325°F. Lower settings and overnight roasting can leave the bird in the 40°F to 140°F danger zone for too long.

The oven setting matters because heat reaches the center of a turkey slowly. The breast and thighs are thick, and heat has to work its way in from the skin before the deepest meat begins to warm. The outer meat heats first, while the center lags behind.

Every part of the bird starts out cold. Each part has to climb through the danger zone on its way to a safe internal temperature. That climb cannot be skipped, but its length can be controlled. A hotter oven moves the meat through the range faster. A cooler oven stretches the passage out.

Time in that range is the core risk. A low oven gives bacteria on the raw bird more hours to multiply before the meat gets hot enough to kill them. The slowest-heating sections, deep in the breast and thigh, carry the most exposure.

Overnight roasting applies the same problem to a longer schedule. The idea is to set a low oven before bed and wake up to a finished bird. That plan falls below the USDA's 325°F minimum. The thickest sections can spend hours warming slowly through the danger zone.

Bird size adds a second variable. A larger turkey takes longer to cook than a smaller one. Its center needs more time to reach a safe temperature. That makes a clock a weak guide. A roasting time that suits one turkey may not suit another.

A food thermometer settles the question. The turkey is done when the thermometer shows a safe internal temperature, not when a set number of hours has passed. The 325°F oven keeps the meat moving out of the danger zone, and the thermometer confirms when it is ready.

Raw turkey juices can carry bacteria to cutting boards, knives, platters, sink handles and hands, and from there onto food that will never be cooked again. The USDA advises washing hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds after handling raw poultry.

Roasting the bird to a safe internal temperature kills bacteria on the meat itself. It does nothing for the cutting board beside the roasting pan or the knife that trimmed the bird.

That gap is the core of cross-contamination. The oven is the kill step for the turkey. Every surface the raw bird touched skips that step. Any juices left on those surfaces remain there until someone cleans them.

Cutting boards and knives pick up juices whenever the bird is unwrapped, trimmed or moved. A board used for raw turkey and then for chopping vegetables passes those juices to the next ingredient. A knife carries them the same way if it goes from the bird to the bread without a wash.

Hands spread juices to whatever a cook touches next. A cook who handles the raw bird and then turns on the tap leaves raw juices on the sink handle. Someone who turns the tap off with clean hands can pick those juices back up. The handle needs cleaning along with the counter and the sink basin.

The 20-second guideline applies after each time raw poultry is handled, not only when prep is finished. A cook moving between the turkey and the side dishes needs to wash at each switch.

Serving platters carry a less obvious version of the same risk. A platter that held the raw turkey still has raw juices on its surface. Setting the finished bird back on it unwashed reintroduces bacteria after the oven has done its work. The USDA's guidance is to wash that platter before the cooked turkey goes on it.

Ready-to-eat foods carry particular risk because no heat will reach them before they are eaten. Salads and other cold dishes go straight from the counter to the plate. Keeping them away from any board, knife, bowl or counter that touched raw turkey cuts off the route bacteria would otherwise follow.

Perishable food should not sit out for more than two hours, according to the USDA. When the room is hotter than 90°F, the limit drops to one hour.

The rule covers every perishable dish on the Thanksgiving table, not only the carved turkey. Stuffing, gravy, mashed potatoes and chilled salads count too. A dish does not get a fresh two hours each time someone refills a plate from it.

The limit comes down to what happens as hot food cools. A freshly carved turkey starts well above 140°F. At room temperature, it gradually drops into the 40°F to 140°F danger zone. Every minute it spends in that range adds to the risk.

A correctly cooked bird is not protected for the rest of the day. Reaching a safe internal temperature handles the bacteria that arrive on the raw meat. The risk after cooking is a different one. Clostridium perfringens is linked to cooked food kept warm for too long, and a platter left out through a long meal fits that description.

Holiday meals make the limit easy to overshoot. Guests come back for second helpings, then dessert, then more conversation. The serving dishes often stay out the whole time. Every one of those hours counts toward the same two-hour limit.

Hot dishes have a clear target. The USDA says to hold hot food at 140°F or above, the top edge of the danger zone. Warming trays and slow cookers can keep turkey, stuffing and gravy at that temperature through a long afternoon. Food held that hot stays above the danger zone instead of cooling into it.

Cold dishes need the opposite treatment. Salads, cranberry relish and other chilled sides should stay at 40°F or below, the bottom edge of the danger zone. A cold dish that warms up on the table enters the same range as a cooling turkey.

Any perishable dish that is not held hot or cold needs to leave the table before its two hours are up.

Leftover turkey should go into the refrigerator within two hours, packed in shallow containers so it cools quickly. The USDA says refrigerated leftovers stay safe for three to four days, and any portion that gets reheated should reach 165°F.

The two-hour limit that governs the serving table also sets the deadline for storage once dinner ends. A bird that sat out through the meal has already used part of that time. Leftovers that reach the fridge late spend longer in the 40°F to 140°F danger zone.

Container shape affects how fast leftovers chill. A deep pot of carved meat or a whole carcass holds heat at its center long after the outside feels cool. That warm core can stay in the danger zone even inside a cold refrigerator. Shallow containers spread the meat into a thin layer. That lets the chill reach every part of it faster.

Slow cooling gives an opening to Clostridium perfringens. That bacterium is a common cause of illness from cooked food held too long at warm temperatures. A large mass of turkey cooling slowly in the fridge fits that pattern. Dividing the meat among several shallow containers shortens the time it spends warm.

The three-to-four-day window sets a firm end date. For a meal served on Thanksgiving Thursday, refrigerated turkey reaches that limit by Sunday or Monday. Leftovers still in the fridge after that point should not be eaten.

Freezing is the option for keeping turkey longer. Moving portions to the freezer before the refrigerator window closes keeps them available after that date.

Reheating is the last safety step. Leftovers should reach 165°F, the same minimum internal temperature the USDA sets for the turkey itself. A food thermometer is the reliable way to confirm it. A dense pile of sliced meat can warm at the edges while the middle stays cool. For that reason, the reading belongs in the center.

With Election Day tomorrow, a Seattle-area tech entrepreneur has a quiz to help voters sort through candidates and ballot measures, while University of Washington researchers have a bingo card for spotting familiar election-fraud rumors. Both offer some last-minute perspective — and a little levity.

Mike Dussault, a former SpaceX and Valve engineer and serial startup founder, built Voter Lifeboat, a free quiz designed to help Washington voters identify candidates and ballot-measure positions that align with their values.

“I’m not making money from it,” Dussault said via email. “I built it to help people vote.”

The app asks 17 questions about taxes, climate, housing, data centers and other issues, then generates a report card showing how closely candidates and initiatives align with a user’s answers. The site includes a detailed methodology and links to sources, and users answer the questions anonymously.

The quiz takes just a few minutes, offering another resource alongside traditional voter guides and endorsements from news outlets and other organizations.

Dussault put AI through its paces to build the tool.

“It was fun to task Claude with so much research and reasoning (to vet all the candidates and initiatives) that it maxed out a Claude Ultra subscription,” he said on LinkedIn.

The University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public (CIP) has served as a watchdog of election-related misinformation for seven years, tracking where it originates and how it spreads online and in the media.

Its Election Rumor Research team this fall created “Rigged Election” Bingo to help people spot recurring conspiracy theories and misleading claims about election fraud.

“Allegedly hacked machines, dead voters, and statistical anomalies are some of the familiar tropes that supposedly ‘prove’ our election system is broken,” the team wrote in a recent post. “These aren’t new ideas.”

Some claims start with real issues, the researchers noted, but exaggerate their scope or omit the safeguards and remedies already in place. The bingo card is designed to help people recognize those patterns and distinguish isolated problems from misleading narratives about the election system.

In Washington, U.S. Attorney Charles Neil Floyd, the top federal prosecutor in Seattle, recently raised allegations of voter fraud. Floyd claimed last month that more than 400 noncitizens had been voting in the state and asked state officials to sequester their ballots.

Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said in a news release that his office was reviewing the allegations and that voter fraud in Washington is “incredibly rare.” He added that the timing of the announcement, a week before the election, “is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results.”
