#5506. Tech Moves: Microsoft loses a CVP to AWS and gains one from Alteryx; Lila Bio and BECU name execs

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 3, 2026 at 10:28 amNovember 3, 2026 at 2:30 pm

— After more than 33 years at Microsoft, Mazhar Mohammed has left to become vice president of AWS Streaming and Messaging at Amazon.

Mohammed joined Microsoft as a software design engineer on Windows NT straight out of a master’s degree program. Over the decades, he also worked on messaging, mobile services and partner experience for cloud services. He most recently served as corporate VP for the commerce and fraud protection platform.

His LinkedIn post was short and to the point. Mohammed said he was “happy to share” the news, and the post featured a photo of an Amazon box with the message “Alexa, play ‘New Beginnings.’”

— Microsoft has named Chad Thompson as CVP of Agent Cloud, a group within the company developing technology that allows businesses to deploy AI agents and put them to work across their organizations.

“My view: enterprise is where AI pays off. Not in demos, but in measurable results. Lower costs, faster cycle times, better decisions, and work that gets done without someone pushing it along,” Thompson wrote in a LinkedIn post.

Thompson joins from Alteryx. He previously spent six years at Amazon, departing as general manager of Amazon Glow. Other past employers include Smartsheet, Exasol and Adobe.

— Gail Carpenter has been named as VP and chief financial officer of Global Entertainment and Advertising at Amazon. She was most recently CFO of Worldwide Stores Finance and has been with the company for 11 years.

— Seattle biotech startup Lila Bio has appointed Kimberly Ma as chief development officer. The company spun out of Nobel laureate David Baker’s lab at the University of Washington and is using AI to design new proteins that can treat cancer with targeted radiation therapy. Last year it announced a collaboration with pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly to develop therapies for solid tumors.

Ma has 20 years of experience in oncology drug development, most recently as a leader at Abdera Therapeutics. She also worked at RayzeBio, where she led the clinical operations team and supported the company’s IPO and its $4.1 billion acquisition by Bristol Myers Squibb in 2024.

— The not-for-profit credit union BECU has named Geoffrey Fonga as VP of AI transformation. The member-owned organization is based in Tukwila, Wash.

“For years, I helped organizations adopt and scale AI as an advisor and a vendor,” Fonga said. “Now I get to do the harder, more rewarding part: leading that transformation from the inside.”

Fonga joins from DataRobot. He previously held leadership roles at McKinsey & Company and Wells Fargo.

— Andre Woodson Jr. has taken a new role at Amazon as manager of U.S. state and local policy communications and external affairs. Woodson was previously a regional field communications manager and has been with the company for more than 12 years.

— Hanna Grene has left Microsoft, where she served as global go-to-market and innovation leader for energy, to join Xcel Energy. She will lead the company’s newly established Enterprise Growth and Commercialization group, effective Nov. 16.

— Seattle-based RevealDx,which is developing AI technology for detecting potentially cancerous lung nodules, has made two leadership appointments:

— Enterprise software company LogicGate has named two new leaders to the business, which is headquartered in Chicago and has multiple C-suite executives based at its Bellevue, Wash., office. Steve Smith has joined as managing director of Europe, the Middle East and Africa, and Amanda Meglemre as general counsel.

— Former Cisco and Microsoft security executive Edna Conway was appointed to the advisory council for Known, a Bellevue, Wash.-based tech company building accountability infrastructure for AI agents. Conway was with Cisco for 20 years before joining Microsoft in 2020 as VP and chief security and risk officer for Azure infrastructure.

— Avalanche Energy, a Seattle-based startup building fusion devices, has named Chris Riegel as head of talent acquisition. He joins from HiringKit, an HR company that Riegel co-founded. Former employers include Amazon and Unity Technologies.

In addition to chasing fusion, Avalanche is leading a team tackling DARPA’s nuclear battery challenge and launching FusionWERX, a commercial-scale testing facility for fusion technologies in Eastern Washington.

— Julie Averill, former chief information officer at lululemon and REI, has joined the UW Foundation Board, which helps raise philanthropic support for the university.

— Technology Alliance has appointed Jen Oleson, a senior director at Seattle-based consulting firm Slalom, to its board. Oleson will serve on the organization’s Research Capacity Committee.

— Ben Helsel has left Premera Blue Cross to join Kaiser Permanente, where he’ll serve as VP and general manager of commercial markets in Washington.

Hiring elite engineers or proven revenue leaders in 2026?

#5505. Raw eggs in eggnog can carry salmonella — here is how to lower the risk

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A guide to whether homemade eggnog is safe, how raw eggs can carry salmonella and how cooking, pasteurized eggs and cold storage lower the risk

Eggnog's thick, custardy body comes from eggs, and many traditional recipes never put those eggs near a stove. Yolks are beaten with sugar, whisked into milk and cream and poured straight into punch cups. That method gives the drink its texture. It also makes a holiday staple a raw-egg drink.

So is homemade eggnog safe? It can be, and the answer depends almost entirely on how the eggs are handled. Raw and undercooked eggs can carry salmonella, a type of bacteria that causes foodborne illness. The chance that any single egg is contaminated is lower than many people assume. It is not zero, though. A punch bowl also spreads one batch across a whole room of guests.

The stakes are not the same for everyone. The CDC and FDA identify certain groups who are more likely to become seriously ill from salmonella. Those groups often share the same table at holiday gatherings. A drink that poses little concern for one guest may be a poor choice for another.

The practical fixes are simple and well established. Heating the egg mixture to the right temperature reduces the risk. So does swapping in pasteurized eggs, keeping the finished drink cold or buying a ready-made carton. None of these steps requires giving up the drink. A few common assumptions do not hold up, however. An egg that looks perfect on the outside can still be contaminated inside. Spiking the bowl with bourbon or rum does not settle the question either.

This guide walks through what raw eggs mean for holiday drinks, one question at a time. It explains how salmonella ends up inside an egg and why eggnog deserves particular attention. It covers who should be cautious, what an infection looks like and how soon symptoms tend to appear. It sets out the cooking temperature the USDA recommends for egg-based custards. It also explains why a thermometer matters more than a spoon test. Later sections look at pasteurized eggs, what alcohol does and does not do, how long eggnog can sit out and lower-risk options from the store. Each section stands on its own, so readers can jump to the question they need answered.

Eggnog made with uncooked eggs is a raw-egg food. It carries the same salmonella risk as any dish built on raw eggs. That risk is low, but it is not zero.

The risk comes from how the drink is traditionally made. Classic recipes add a spirit such as rum, bourbon or brandy to the egg and dairy mixture. Some versions also beat the egg whites separately and fold them in for a lighter, frothier texture. At no point in those recipes does the mixture go on the stove. It goes from the mixing bowl to the refrigerator or straight to the table.

That puts uncooked eggnog in a different category from most egg-rich desserts. Crème anglaise, baked custard, flan and crème brûlée all start with a similar mix of eggs, sugar and dairy. Each of them is heated before it is served. Raw-egg eggnog skips that step entirely. Whatever was inside the eggs ends up in the glass.

That scale matters. A holiday batch combines several eggs in a single bowl or pitcher, and party-size recipes use more. Once the eggs are mixed together, the whole batch depends on every egg that went into it. If one egg is contaminated, the bacteria can spread through the entire mixture. They do not stay confined to one serving.

The batch is then poured out over an evening, often refilled cup by cup as guests come and go. Every person who drinks from it shares the same exposure. One contaminated egg can reach every guest who takes a serving, not only the person whose cup it happened to land in.

The flavor and texture people expect from eggnog do not require leaving the eggs raw. Recipes that heat the egg base or use pasteurized eggs lower the risk. Versions made without eggs remove the raw-egg question altogether.

An egg with a clean, uncracked shell can still carry salmonella inside it. The bacteria can infect a hen's ovaries or reproductive tract and reach the egg before its shell forms.

This route bypasses everything a cook can see. Most people judge an egg by its outside. They look for cracks, stains or traces of droppings, and they throw out anything that looks dirty. Those checks catch some problems. They cannot reveal bacteria already sealed inside the white or yolk.

The strain most closely tied to this kind of internal contamination is Salmonella Enteritidis. A hen infected with it can look and behave normally. She can keep laying eggs that appear ordinary, with no outward sign that anything is wrong.

An egg contaminated this way gives no warning in the kitchen either. It does not smell off, look discolored or taste different. Cracking it into a bowl shows a normal yolk and white. Nothing about its appearance separates it from the other eggs in the carton.

Shells can also pick up bacteria from the outside, through contact with droppings or a dirty nesting area. Washing addresses that surface problem. Most eggs sold commercially in the U.S. are washed before they reach stores. Washing cleans only the shell, though. It does nothing for contamination that began inside the hen.

The same reasoning applies to eggs from a backyard flock, a farmers market or a small farm. Fresh, local eggs are not automatically free of internal salmonella. Any laying hen can become infected, whatever the size of the operation or the way the birds are kept.

Refrigeration slows salmonella growth but does not solve the problem. Cold keeps a small number of bacteria from multiplying quickly. It does not kill the bacteria already present. An egg that went into the refrigerator contaminated comes out contaminated.

That is why the remedy for raw-egg recipes is heat rather than inspection. Cooking eggs to a safe temperature, or using pasteurized eggs, deals with bacteria wherever they sit — on the shell or inside the egg.

Young children, pregnant people, adults 65 and older, and people with weakened immune systems should skip eggnog made with raw eggs. The CDC and FDA identify these four groups as more likely to develop severe illness from salmonella.

The difference shows up in outcomes. A healthy adult who swallows contaminated eggnog may recover without treatment. Someone in a higher-risk group has a greater chance of an infection serious enough to need medical care.

Each group is vulnerable for its own reason. Young children have immune systems that are still developing. Older adults experience a gradual decline in immune function as they age. Pregnancy changes how the body's immune system responds to infection.

The fourth category is the broadest. It includes people receiving chemotherapy for cancer and people taking anti-rejection drugs after an organ transplant. It also includes people living with HIV. Anyone on long-term medication that suppresses the immune system, such as corticosteroids used for some autoimmune conditions, belongs in this group as well.

A single family gathering may include a toddler, a grandparent, a guest in early pregnancy and a relative in cancer treatment. Not every guest tells the host about a pregnancy or a diagnosis. A host pouring from one bowl often cannot know who in the room falls into a higher-risk group.

Making the entire batch with a cooked custard base or with pasteurized eggs removes that guesswork. Either approach means no guest has to be screened, questioned or steered away from the drink.

If a raw-egg version is served at all, clear labeling lets guests choose for themselves. A small card beside each pitcher can state whether the eggs were cooked, pasteurized or raw. Keeping the raw and cooked versions in visibly different containers helps avoid mix-ups. Young children often serve themselves at a punch bowl. A raw-egg batch belongs on a counter or shelf out of their reach.

Salmonella infection usually shows up as diarrhea, fever and stomach cramps, according to the CDC. The agency says those symptoms typically begin between six hours and six days after infection.

That window matters for anyone who drank eggnog made with raw eggs. Illness may start the same evening as a holiday party. It may also start nearly a week later, long after the punch bowl has been washed and put away.

The wide range makes it hard to connect a stomach illness to one glass of eggnog. A person who feels sick on a Tuesday may have eaten dozens of foods since the weekend. Holiday weeks often pack several gatherings, restaurant meals and leftovers into a few days. Any one of them could be the cause.

A simple record helps. Hosts who serve raw-egg eggnog can note which batch was poured on which day and who drank it. If several guests fall ill with the same symptoms, that shared detail is useful to a doctor or a local health department.

The three symptoms can be mistaken for other problems. Rich food and a seasonal stomach virus can both cause cramps or diarrhea. Fever points toward an infection rather than overeating. Symptoms alone still cannot confirm salmonella. A doctor can confirm it with a laboratory test of a stool sample.

Diarrhea drains fluid from the body. Drinking water or an oral rehydration solution helps replace what is lost.

An infected person can also pass salmonella to others. Washing hands with soap and water after using the bathroom and before handling food lowers that risk. The step carries extra weight in a house full of guests sharing one kitchen.

Severe symptoms call for medical care. Warning signs include a high fever, diarrhea that will not let up and blood in the stool. Signs of dehydration, such as passing little urine or feeling dizzy when standing, also need attention. Anyone whose illness is getting worse rather than better should contact a doctor.

Cooking the egg and milk base to 160°F (71°C) turns homemade eggnog from a raw-egg drink into a cooked custard. The USDA gives that target for egg mixtures such as custards. A cooked eggnog base is a stirred custard. The same target applies.

That makes cooked eggnog a close relative of crème anglaise, the pourable French custard sauce. Both start with the same core ingredients: egg yolks, sugar and milk. Both are cooked on the stovetop while being stirred, rather than baked until firm.

The process begins with the dairy. Warm the milk in a saucepan until it steams, without letting it boil. In a separate bowl, whisk the yolks with the sugar until the mixture lightens in color and thickens slightly.

The next step is tempering. Pour a small amount of the hot milk into the yolks while whisking constantly, then add more in stages. This raises the temperature of the eggs gradually. Warmed this way, they are less likely to curdle when they meet the rest of the hot liquid. Then pour the yolk mixture back into the saucepan.

From here, heat control matters most. A heavy-bottomed saucepan spreads heat more evenly than a thin one. That reduces hot spots on the pan floor. A double boiler — a bowl set over simmering water — gives even gentler heat. It takes longer but leaves less room for error.

Keep the burner at low to medium-low and stir without stopping. A silicone spatula or wooden spoon can scrape the bottom and corners of the pan, where egg sets first. If the mixture gets too hot, the yolks can scramble and the texture turns grainy. The base thickens slowly as the egg proteins set.

Once the base reaches 160°F (71°C), take it off the heat. Pour it through a fine-mesh sieve to catch any bits of cooked egg. Stir in vanilla or grated nutmeg at this stage if the recipe calls for them.

Chill the base quickly. Setting the bowl inside a larger bowl of ice water speeds cooling. Pressing plastic wrap directly onto the surface keeps a skin from forming. Cold cream and any spirits are stirred in after the base has fully chilled.

One step in some recipes skips the heat entirely. Some traditional recipes fold in beaten egg whites at the end. Those whites never go through the cooking stage. They stay raw unless pasteurized whites are used.

Only a food thermometer can confirm that an eggnog base has reached 160°F (71°C), the USDA's target for egg mixtures such as custards. Thickening and a coating on the back of a spoon are not reliable substitutes.

The coat-the-spoon test comes from classic custard cooking. A cook dips a spoon into the pot, draws a finger across the back and watches whether the line holds. That check describes texture. It was never designed to measure food safety.

Texture and temperature do not track each other neatly in eggnog. Egg proteins thicken a liquid as they set, but sugar and milk dilute them. A sweeter or thinner base can thicken at a different point than a richer one. Two batches can look the same on a spoon and still sit at different temperatures.

Heat is also uneven inside a pot. Liquid near the bottom and sides runs hotter than liquid at the center or the surface. A spoon pulled from one spot shows what is happening there, not across the whole batch. Stirring for a few seconds before taking a reading evens out those zones.

Where the probe goes matters too. The tip should sit in the middle of the liquid, away from the bottom and walls of the pan. Touching hot metal gives a falsely high number. Digital instant-read models sense temperature near the tip. Dial models read along a longer stretch of the stem, so more of it needs to be submerged.

Give the display a moment to settle before trusting it. A reading taken while the number is still climbing understates the heat. If the base is short of 160°F, return it to the heat and check again.

A thermometer is only as useful as it is accurate. The ice-water method is a simple check. Fill a glass with crushed ice and cold water, stir and insert the probe without touching the glass. It should read 32°F (0°C). Many models can be adjusted if they drift, either with a reset button or a calibration nut under the dial.

Wash the probe in hot, soapy water after each use. That keeps it from carrying bacteria from one food to the next.

Pasteurized eggs let you keep a classic uncooked eggnog recipe while lowering the salmonella risk. Pasteurized shell eggs and pasteurized liquid egg products have been heat treated to reduce Salmonella. They are the standard substitute whenever a recipe calls for raw egg.

The process holds eggs at a controlled temperature long enough to reduce bacteria without cooking the egg. The yolk and white stay liquid. That matters for eggnog, where the drink depends on raw yolks blending smoothly into milk and cream. A pasteurized egg fills the same role in the recipe as an ordinary one.

The two main forms suit different cooks. Pasteurized shell eggs look and crack like regular eggs. They work well in recipes that separate yolks from whites, such as versions that fold whipped whites into the base for a lighter, foamier drink. Pasteurized liquid egg products come in cartons and pour straight into a bowl. They save time when a large batch calls for a dozen or more eggs.

Read the label before buying either one. Most shell eggs on U.S. supermarket shelves are not pasteurized, and the cartons can look nearly identical. Look for the word "pasteurized" printed on the package. If it is not there, treat the eggs as raw.

Liquid products need a closer look too. Some cartons contain whole eggs, while others hold only egg whites or a blend with added ingredients. An egg-white product will not give eggnog the richness or color that yolks provide. Check the ingredient list to confirm what is inside.

Expect a small difference in the kitchen. Pasteurized egg whites can take longer to whip into stiff peaks than untreated whites. A pinch of cream of tartar or a few extra minutes of beating usually helps.

Pasteurization lowers the risk, but it does not protect an egg from contamination once it is cracked or poured. Store pasteurized eggs in the refrigerator, use clean bowls and utensils, and treat the finished eggnog as a perishable drink.

The USDA says alcohol should not be relied on to make raw eggs safe in a drink. Bourbon, rum or brandy changes the flavor and strength of raw-egg eggnog. It does not reliably protect anyone from salmonella.

Liquor is often assumed to sterilize eggnog, and the idea has some basis. Alcohol can damage bacteria at high enough concentrations. Eggnog, however, is not a high-concentration drink. Spirits get poured into a much larger volume of milk, cream, sugar and eggs. Once everything is mixed, the alcohol in the finished drink is far more dilute than the alcohol in the bottle.

Recipes also vary widely. Some call for a heavy measure of liquor in every batch. Others use a splash for flavor, or leave the choice to each guest. Two bowls of eggnog at two different parties can carry very different amounts of alcohol. A home cook has no practical way to measure the strength of a finished batch.

Timing matters as well. Some recipes have the host mix the egg base first and add spirits just before serving. In that case, the raw eggs spend most of their time in the bowl with no alcohol at all. Uneven stirring can also leave some portions stronger than others.

Aged, spiked eggnog — batches mixed with liquor and left to sit in the refrigerator before serving — has drawn attention from food safety researchers. Even so, no proof level or aging period is an established guarantee that raw eggs in the mix are safe to drink.

There is also a practical gap at mixed gatherings. A host who spikes one bowl may make a second, alcohol-free bowl for children and drivers. If both start from the same raw-egg base, the plain version has no claimed protection at all. Children are among the groups the CDC and FDA consider at higher risk of severe salmonella illness.

The more reliable approach is to deal with the eggs themselves. A base cooked to 160°F (71°C) or made with pasteurized eggs lowers the raw-egg risk before any liquor enters the bowl. After that, bourbon, rum or brandy can go in purely for taste. The spirits become a flavor choice rather than a safety measure. The same base then works for both the spiked and the plain versions.

Eggnog is a perishable drink, and the USDA says it should not sit out for more than two hours. That limit drops to one hour when the air is above 90°F. The USDA also says refrigerators should hold 40°F (4°C) or below.

The two-hour clock starts when the eggnog leaves the refrigerator, not when the first guest pours a glass. Time on the counter during setup counts. So does time spent on a buffet table or carried from room to room.

The rule is tied to what the USDA calls the danger zone, the range between 40°F and 140°F. Bacteria grow most rapidly in that range. The USDA says their numbers can double in as little as 20 minutes. A punch bowl left at room temperature sits inside that zone.

Eggnog combines milk, cream, sugar and often eggs. That mix gives bacteria the moisture and nutrients they need. Even a cooked or pasteurized batch can pick up bacteria from ladles, cups and hands once it is served. Keeping it cold limits how fast those bacteria can multiply.

A serving bowl nested inside a larger bowl of ice keeps eggnog cooler on a table. The ice needs topping up as it melts. Another approach is to set out a small pitcher and keep the rest of the batch in the refrigerator. The pitcher can be refilled as needed instead of leaving the whole batch out.

Once the time limit passes, the USDA advice is to discard what is left. Pouring it back into the main container mixes warmed eggnog with the cold supply. The shorter one-hour limit matters at warm-weather events, such as outdoor Christmas gatherings in the Southern Hemisphere.

A refrigerator's dial setting does not show its actual temperature. The USDA recommends an appliance thermometer to confirm the refrigerator stays at 40°F or below. A holiday refrigerator that is packed with food and opened often can run warmer than its setting suggests.

Leftover eggnog belongs in covered containers that go into the refrigerator promptly. Shallow containers chill faster than one deep pitcher, a point the USDA makes about leftovers in general. A lid also keeps out drips and odors from other foods.

Commercial eggnog sold in U.S. grocery stores is made with pasteurized ingredients. That avoids the raw-egg risk of an uncooked homemade batch. Egg-free eggnog goes a step further and leaves eggs out of the recipe entirely.

Pasteurization is a heat treatment applied to the dairy and egg ingredients at a processing plant before the drink is sealed. It takes place under controlled conditions. That control is the main difference between a factory carton and a bowl mixed at home with fresh, uncooked eggs.

Store-bought eggnog sits in the refrigerated dairy case, usually near the milk and cream during the holiday season. The ingredient list typically names milk, cream, sugar and egg yolks, along with spices such as nutmeg. Light or reduced-fat versions replace some of the cream with lower-fat milk. The word pasteurized normally appears on the carton, and buyers can check for it before purchase.

A carton keeps its advantage only as long as no raw eggs go into it. Whisking fresh yolks or beaten raw egg whites into store-bought eggnog for a frothier texture changes that. The added eggs turn the drink back into a raw-egg food.

Egg-free versions come in two main forms. One is a dairy drink made with milk or cream and thickened without eggs. Cornstarch cooked into the milk is a common way to give it a custard-like body. The other is a plant-based nog made from almond, oat, soy or coconut milk. Both typically rely on nutmeg, cinnamon, vanilla and sugar to carry the familiar holiday flavor.

Egg-free nog also works for guests with an egg allergy. Pasteurization does not help that group. The heat treatment reduces bacteria, but the egg proteins that trigger allergic reactions remain in the drink. Anyone avoiding eggs for that reason should read the ingredient list and allergen statement on each package.

None of these options can sit out indefinitely once opened. Commercial dairy eggnog is perishable and belongs in the refrigerator after the seal is broken. Some plant-based cartons are sold unrefrigerated on the shelf. Even those usually need different handling after opening. The storage directions printed on each package spell out what that product requires.

#5504. Florida voters nearly tripled the homeowner tax break — blowing an $11.8 billion hole in county budgets

Many Florida homeowners cheered on Nov. 3, 2026, when more than 60% of voters approved a constitutional amendment to significantly reduce property taxes.

Under the measure, Amendment 3, a homeowner’s tax break known as a homestead exemption would go from the current US$51,400 to $150,000 in 2027 and increase again to $250,000 in 2028. By shielding more of a home’s assessed value from taxation, this exemption effectively lowers homeowners’ tax bills. New Florida residents who buy a home would also reportedly be eligible for a property tax break, but on a more phased-in basis.

But the measure comes with a hefty price tag. The Florida Legislature’s research arm estimated the measure would reduce annual revenue from property taxes by $11.8 billion. This translates to a 30% reduction in revenue for Florida counties and a 13% cut for smaller municipal governments.

While homeowners will get some relief, the budget crunch due to the lower tax revenue will affect other Floridians in more adverse ways. As economists who have been following the debates over Amendment 3, we argue that local governments will struggle to fund basic services with less money. And we expect more sweeping economic consequences as well – including less affordable residential housing and a broader shift of the tax burden away from relatively wealthier homeowners to those who are less well off.

Much of the political momentum for Amendment 3 came from a rise in the cost of living and frustration over rising property taxes. These now average just over $3,000 annually but can run much higher for Floridians with more expensive homes.

In addition to raising the homestead tax exemption, Amendment 3 lowers the cap on annual assessments on rental and commercial properties from a 10% increase to a 5% increase. Since property taxes are based on an asset’s assessed value, this language effectively limits but doesn’t rule out tax hikes for businesses.

So landlords, for example, could still see meaningful annual tax increases as their properties go up in value – costs that would likely be passed on to renters.

Amendment 3 makes clear that school-related property taxes are exempt from these tax cuts. It also lists some theoretical limits on how local governments should use tax dollars, as a way to ensure continued funding for essential services such as public safety, infrastructure or obligations for employee retirement benefits.

But it also states that funds may be used for “expenditures approved” by local and county governments – ambiguous wording that suggests these stipulations can be breached.

Florida property taxes are levied and collected by some 640 local government entities. There’s no state income tax, so any reductions in property tax revenue directly affect local and county governments.

With tax revenue slashed, businesses, landlords and owners of other non-homestead properties like second homes would almost certainly see their taxes go up. This is a typical pattern: When governments cut property taxes for some groups, taxes shift to other groups.

This dynamic is likely to play out with local governments as they try to keep revenue stable: Amendment 3 would force them to hike taxes in other areas to make up for the shortfall. This could include increases in state and local sales taxes, an expansion of the list of goods subject to sales taxes, or a hike in “documentary stamp taxes,” which are required on documents such as deeds, bonds and mortgages.

State and local governments could also impose higher fees for specific services, such as solid waste treatment and stormwater utilities. Another option is to hike permits and inspection fees, fuel taxes or other service charges such as vehicle registration fees.

Finally, local governments could raise tourism-related taxes, such as on food, beverages and hotels. But this recourse wouldn’t help counties with limited tourism, and such revenues fluctuate in any event.

In the end, though, essential services would still almost certainly be affected. Funding for police, fire and emergency medical services is primarily the responsibility of local governments, and, for most counties, they make up the largest line item in their annual expenditures. Reducing property taxes would amount to a direct hit, especially in smaller, less-populated counties.

And if local governments do raise sales tax rates to the extent they can, lower-income Floridians will bear a disproportionate burden as they spend much more of their income on consumption. They’re also far more likely to rent than own a home, so any increased rents would take a bigger toll.

Less noticed in the debate over Amendment 3 was how it would affect the state’s affordable housing shortage. We argue that the structure of the property tax cut will likely create more incentives for counties and developers to build commercial structures instead of more residential housing.

When developers build residential homes, they require a basic level of public services to support residents and the local infrastructure. In fact, property taxes in much of Florida effectively subsidize residential home development: For every dollar that a homeowner pays in property taxes, it costs county governments around $1.20 to provide those services. This gap will only grow when property tax revenues fall.

From the standpoint of local and county governments, then, it may make more sense to focus on commercial or industrial construction as a way to keep tax revenues stable. But with fewer homes built at the expense of business construction – from manufacturing to data centers – the supply squeeze will only drive up prices and rents for the workers who are needed for those jobs.

Now that Amendment 3 is on the books, Florida’s county and local governments will confront major trade-offs. We believe that state officials will come to realize how much of a change has been made – and how quickly their priorities may have to shift.

This article has been corrected to note that the current homestead exemption is $51,400 and that new Florida residents who buy a home are eligible for a property tax break on a phased-in basis.

Portions of this article appeared in a prior article published on July 30, 2026.

Abigail Hall, Professor of Economics, University of Tampa and Aaron D. Wood, Associate Professor of Economics, University of Tampa

#5503. 10 holiday party foods that shouldn't sit out longer than 2 hours

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Holiday party food safety comes down to timing, and these 10 buffet favorites, from shrimp cocktail to eggnog, shouldn't sit out at room temperature longer than two hours

At a holiday party, the clock matters as much as the recipe. A platter set out at 7 p.m. and picked at until midnight has spent five hours at room temperature. Guests keep coming back to it, and it may look no different than when it first arrived.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) sets a clear limit for that situation. Perishable food should not sit at room temperature for more than two hours. When the air is warmer than 90°F, the limit falls to one hour. That shorter window matters for hot kitchens, outdoor gatherings and holidays celebrated during summer in the Southern Hemisphere.

The reason is a temperature band the USDA calls the danger zone. It runs from 40°F to 140°F, and bacteria multiply fastest within it. The USDA says bacteria in that range can double in as little as 20 minutes. Cold food needs to stay at 40°F or below. Hot food needs to stay at 140°F or above. Room temperature falls in between.

Appearance offers no protection. The USDA notes that food can carry illness-causing bacteria without any change in look, smell or taste. A shrimp ring or a bowl of dip can seem fine at the end of the night and still have passed its safe window. The two-hour rule is a safety limit, not a prediction that anyone will get sick. Inspection alone cannot show whether a dish is still within it.

Leftovers follow the same timeline. The USDA advises getting them into the refrigerator within two hours of serving. When they come back out, they should be reheated to 165°F.

Holiday party food safety rests on a few habits. Hosts can serve smaller portions and swap in fresh dishes from the fridge or oven. Bowls can sit on ice, and warm dishes can go into slow cookers or chafing dishes. Each food on a holiday spread has its own weak point, though. Some cool too quickly on the platter. Some are dense and lose heat slowly. Others carry risk in their raw ingredients.

The 10 foods below are a selection of common party dishes that fall under the USDA's two-hour rule. Each slide covers how that specific food is usually served and how to keep it out of the danger zone. The list runs from carved turkey and shrimp cocktail to eggnog, gravy and pumpkin pie.

Carved turkey and sliced ham lose heat faster than a whole roast. Keep them at 140°F or above in a warmed dish, or set them out in small batches.

The difference comes down to surface area. A whole bird or bone-in ham holds heat in its center for some time after it leaves the oven. Carving ends that. Once the roast is cut into thin slices, every piece is exposed to room air.

Those slices fall below 140°F much sooner than an uncut roast would. On a buffet table, sliced meat can spend most of the evening in the USDA danger zone.

Safe cooking is only the first step. The USDA sets 165°F as the safe minimum internal temperature for turkey. It advises checking with a food thermometer in the thickest part of the breast and the innermost parts of the thigh and wing. Reaching 165°F makes the bird safe when it leaves the oven. It does nothing to protect the slices during hours of grazing afterward.

The USDA also recommends letting a whole turkey stand for 20 minutes before carving. That resting time on the cutting board counts as time at room temperature, too.

Ham has its own temperature targets. The USDA says fresh, uncooked ham should reach 145°F, followed by a three-minute rest. Fully cooked hams packaged in USDA-inspected plants can be reheated to 140°F. Cooked ham repackaged anywhere else should be reheated to 165°F.

Warming equipment helps only if it actually holds 140°F. A food thermometer pushed into the middle of a stack of slices shows whether a chafing dish or warming tray is doing its job. If the meat reads lower, it is on the same two-hour clock as every other perishable dish.

Hosts without warming equipment can put out a modest platter instead. The rest of the carved meat stays hot in the oven or cold in the refrigerator. A fresh plate goes out when the first one empties.

Avoid topping up a half-empty platter with fresh slices. The meat already on the plate has been using up its time. Mixing in new pieces makes it impossible to tell how long any single slice has been out. Replace the whole platter instead.

Leftover cooked turkey keeps three to four days in the refrigerator, according to the USDA.

Shrimp cocktail holds up best on a buffet when its serving bowl sits inside a larger bowl of ice, with the ice replaced as it melts. Cooked shrimp is perishable, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) treats it like any other food that must be kept cold.

The ice works best when it reaches up the sides of the inner bowl, not just the bottom. Crushed ice packed around the rim keeps more of the shrimp near a cold surface. Meltwater should be poured off before it pools, with fresh ice added in its place.

Shrimp cocktail is usually served with peeled shrimp hooked over the rim of a glass or fanned around a bowl of sauce. That presentation leaves every piece exposed to room air. A platter that comes out of the fridge cold warms steadily as guests graze. The clock starts when the platter leaves the refrigerator, not when the first guest arrives.

Placement on the table matters as well. A spot next to the stove, in direct sun or on an outdoor patio can run warmer than the rest of the house. Shrimp set out there can fall under the USDA's shorter hot-weather limit. Seafood is a Christmas tradition in Australia, where the holiday comes in summer. Cold prawns are a common centerpiece at outdoor gatherings there.

Many store-bought shrimp rings are sold frozen. The USDA advises thawing frozen food in the refrigerator, in cold water or in the microwave, not on the counter. Counter thawing lets the outer layer warm to unsafe temperatures while the center stays frozen.

Cocktail sauce works best in a small dish served on the side. Pouring sauce over the shrimp, or setting out one large bowl of it, invites repeated dipping across the whole party. A small portion can be cleared away and replaced with a fresh one from the fridge.

The shrimp itself can go out in rounds. A second batch kept refrigerated can replace the first as a complete new platter, rather than being piled onto leftovers. That keeps each serving on its own clock.

Other cooked seafood calls for the same care. Cooked crab claws, lobster meat and seafood salads made with cooked fish or shellfish are all perishable. The Italian American Feast of the Seven Fishes on Christmas Eve can put several of these dishes on one table. Each one needs ice underneath or a return trip to the refrigerator before its time runs out.

Dips made with sour cream, cream cheese or yogurt are cold perishable foods, and the USDA says cold food belongs at 40°F or below. Serve them in small bowls. When a bowl has been out too long, swap in a fresh chilled one instead of refilling it.

This group covers a large share of the holiday snack table. French onion dip is usually built on sour cream. Cheese balls and cracker spreads rely on cream cheese. Ranch dip often sits beside a raw vegetable tray, and tzatziki made with yogurt is a common partner for pita. Each comes out of the fridge cold and starts warming once it reaches the table.

Bowl swapping works because it keeps each portion on a short, trackable clock. Split each batch into a small serving bowl and a backup bowl. Keep the backup covered in the fridge. When the serving bowl reaches two hours at room temperature or runs low, take it away and bring out the chilled one.

Do not scrape leftover dip from the old bowl into the new one. The older portion has already used up time at room temperature. Mixing it in puts that warmed dip back into circulation with the fresh batch.

A bed of ice under the serving bowl slows warming, but it does not stop the clock. The two-hour limit still applies to a dip sitting on ice, and melted ice needs replacing.

Shared bowls also invite double-dipping. A bitten chip or carrot stick can go straight back into the communal supply. Setting a spoon in the bowl lets guests move a portion onto their own plates. Smaller bowls also mean less dip is exposed to each round of grazing.

Some cream cheese dips are served hot, such as spinach-artichoke dip or buffalo chicken dip. Those follow the USDA's hot-food standard instead: 140°F or above. A slow cooker on its warm setting can help hold them there. Once a hot dip falls below 140°F on the counter, the two-hour limit applies.

Dip that has sat out past the limit should be thrown away rather than refrigerated for later. The USDA's own shorthand for uncertain cases is "when in doubt, throw it out."

The cooked potatoes, pasta, eggs and meat in potato salad, pasta salad and egg salad pose more risk on a buffet than the commercial mayonnaise that binds them. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) treats these cold salads as perishable food.

Mayonnaise often takes the blame when a salad is suspected of causing illness. Store-bought mayonnaise is made with vinegar or lemon juice, which makes it acidic. In the U.S., commercial mayonnaise is also made with pasteurized eggs. Neither fact protects the cooked ingredients once the bowl warms up. Diced potatoes, cooked macaroni and chopped hard-boiled eggs are the parts that need temperature control.

Homemade mayonnaise is a different case. Recipes that whisk raw egg yolks into oil carry a risk of salmonella. The USDA advises using pasteurized eggs for any dish that calls for raw eggs. A host making dressing from scratch can buy pasteurized eggs in the shell or in cartons.

Coleslaw has no cooked starch, but it still belongs in the same category. Shredded cabbage is cut produce. The USDA counts cut fruits and vegetables as perishable. A bowl of slaw needs the same cold handling as potato salad.

On a buffet, the USDA's two-hour limit applies to all of these salads. Above 90°F, it drops to one hour.

Mayonnaise-based salads are also common make-ahead and potluck dishes. That adds time before the party starts. Minutes in a warm car count as time out of the refrigerator. The USDA recommends carrying perishable food in an insulated cooler with ice or frozen gel packs.

On the table, set the serving bowl into a larger container of ice. Keep most of the batch in the refrigerator and bring out smaller amounts. Chilling the cooked potatoes or pasta before mixing in the dressing helps the salad start out cold.

Once the limit passes, USDA guidance is to discard what remains rather than refrigerate it. Salad that goes back into the refrigerator within the time limit can be kept as leftovers. The USDA says refrigerated leftovers keep three to four days.

Cut cantaloupe and other sliced melon should be held at or below 40°F, the cold-holding standard the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) sets for perishable food. Slicing through the rind can carry bacteria from the outside of the fruit onto the edible flesh.

Fruit trays can look like the lightest and lowest-risk dish on a holiday table. Hosts often set them out early and leave them in place for the whole party. Whole fruit with an intact rind is a different product from fruit that has been cut.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration's Food Code, a model code state health departments adopt for restaurant inspections, classifies cut melon as a food that needs time and temperature control. That puts sliced melon in the same handling category as cold cuts and dairy dips.

The risk starts on the rind. A cantaloupe has a rough, netted surface that can carry bacteria such as salmonella and listeria, picked up in the field or during handling. A knife drawn through an unwashed rind can drag those bacteria into the fruit.

Washing the whole melon under cool running water before cutting limits what the blade carries inside. A clean produce brush reaches into the netting better than hands alone. Soap and detergent are not recommended for produce. Drying the melon with a clean cloth or paper towel can further reduce surface bacteria. Use a knife and cutting board that have not touched raw meat. The same steps apply to honeydew and watermelon, even though their skins are smoother.

Presentation can help keep the fruit cold. A platter can sit on a tray or shallow pan filled with crushed ice, with the ice replaced as it melts. Keep the rest of the cut fruit covered in the fridge and bring it out in smaller amounts. A fresh platter is a better choice than new pieces piled onto fruit that has already been out.

Ice slows warming, but it does not reset the clock. The USDA's two-hour limit for perishable food at room temperature applies to cut melon. Cut fruit that has passed that limit should be thrown out, not returned to the fridge. Fruit salads, skewers and mixed platters that include melon follow the same rules as plain melon slices.

Quiche, frittata and baked egg casseroles are perishable cooked dishes. They need to stay hot at 140°F or above or go into the refrigerator. A dish resting on the counter between brunch courses is still sitting out, even if the room feels cool.

These dishes turn up at holiday breakfasts, Christmas morning gatherings and New Year's Day brunches. Hosts often bake them early and let them stand while guests arrive. That waiting time counts toward the U.S. Department of Agriculture's two-hour limit for perishable food at room temperature.

The safety work starts in the oven. The USDA lists 160°F as the safe internal temperature for egg dishes. A golden top or a set edge does not confirm that the center has reached it. A food thermometer pushed into the middle of the quiche or casserole gives a direct reading.

Eggs, milk, cream and cheese make up the custard base of a quiche. A frittata adds vegetables, meat or cheese to beaten eggs. Breakfast casseroles and stratas layer bread, sausage or ham with an egg mixture. The eggs, dairy and meat in these dishes are perishable on their own. Baking them together in one pan does not change that.

Make-ahead casseroles raise a separate timing question. Many recipes have the cook assemble a strata the night before and bake it the next morning. Until it goes in the oven, that unbaked dish holds raw eggs and dairy. It belongs in the refrigerator overnight, not on the counter.

After baking, a dish can be kept hot in an oven on a low setting, on a warming tray or in a chafing dish. A thermometer check partway through the meal shows whether the setup is holding temperature.

Another approach is to bake two smaller dishes instead of one large one. The second can wait in the low oven until the first is finished.

Whatever remains after brunch should go into the refrigerator promptly. Cutting a large quiche into portions before chilling lets it cool faster.

Eggnog made with raw eggs carries a risk of salmonella. The USDA advises heating the egg-and-milk base to 160°F, or using pasteurized eggs or a pasteurized store-bought eggnog instead.

Classic eggnog combines eggs, milk, cream and sugar, often finished with a dusting of nutmeg. Many older family recipes whisk the eggs in raw. That raw-egg step is what the USDA guidance targets. Mixing raw eggs into cold dairy does not kill the bacteria.

Cooking the base turns the drink into something closer to a thin custard. The eggs, milk and sugar are heated together over low heat and stirred constantly. Gentle heat keeps the eggs from scrambling before the mixture thickens. A food thermometer confirms when it reaches 160°F. The base then goes into the fridge to chill before guests arrive.

Some recipes fold in whipped egg whites at the end for a lighter texture. Heating the base does not cover whites added afterward. Those versions need pasteurized eggs to follow the USDA's advice. Pasteurized eggs in the shell and cartons of pasteurized liquid egg whites are sold in many U.S. grocery stores.

Cartons of eggnog sold in U.S. grocery stores are pasteurized. That settles the raw-egg question, but the drink is still mostly milk and cream. Homemade and store-bought versions alike are perishable and need to stay cold until they are poured.

The serving bowl is the weak point. A punch bowl of nog on a sideboard drifts toward room temperature as the evening goes on. Guests often ladle from it for hours. The USDA's two-hour limit for perishable food applies to it from the moment it is set out.

Two setups help keep the drink cold. One is a punch bowl set down into a larger bowl or tray of crushed ice, with fresh ice added as the old ice melts. The other is a refrigerated pitcher, poured in small amounts and returned to the fridge between rounds. When the bowl runs low, it should be swapped for a fresh chilled batch, not topped up with new nog.

Spiking the bowl with rum, bourbon or brandy is a common holiday habit. Spiked nog follows the same cold-holding and time rules as any other dairy drink. Whatever remains in the bowl after two hours should be discarded, not poured back into the carton or saved for the next day.

Cooked rice should be cooled and refrigerated promptly. Uncooked rice can carry spores of Bacillus cereus that survive cooking. If the cooked rice sits at room temperature, those bacteria can grow and produce a toxin that reheating does not destroy.

Spores are a dormant, heat-resistant form of the bacterium. Boiling or steaming rice kills active cells but can leave spores intact. As a pot of cooked rice cools on the counter, those spores can germinate and the bacteria begin to multiply.

Bacillus cereus can cause two kinds of food poisoning. One mainly causes diarrhea. The other mainly causes vomiting and is the type most often linked to rice. The toxin behind the vomiting illness is heat-stable. A trip through the microwave or a hot wok does not make rice that sat out safe again. The time rice spends on the counter is what counts.

Fried rice is the best-known example. Many recipes call for rice cooked a day ahead. That works when the rice went into the fridge soon after cooking. Rice left out overnight and fried the next morning carries the risk described above.

Rice turns up on holiday tables in many forms. A pot of steamed white rice, a tray of fried rice and a rice pilaf all start from grains that may carry the spores. Rice-based stuffings and casseroles belong in the same group.

Pasta needs the same attention. Bacillus cereus can also grow in other cooked starches. Pasta dishes with sauce, meat or cheese are perishable. Baked macaroni and cheese, lasagna and baked ziti all fit that description. These dishes are often made in large pans and left on a buffet for second helpings.

The USDA's room-temperature time limit for perishable food applies to all of these dishes. On the table, a warming tray keeps rice and pasta hot. Without a heat source, a pan cools into the USDA danger zone on its own. Bringing out half a pan at a time and keeping the rest in a low oven limits how long any one batch sits exposed.

Cooling speed matters at the end of the night. A deep pot of rice or a full lasagna pan holds heat in its center for a long time. Spreading rice in a thin layer in shallow containers lets it chill quickly. Cutting a lasagna into portions before refrigerating it does the same.

Reheating leftovers properly still matters for both rice and pasta. For rice, though, no amount of reheating makes up for time the grains already spent at room temperature.

Gravy and stuffing need steady heat on the table and fast chilling afterward. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) advises bringing leftover gravy to a rolling boil when reheating it, rather than just warming it through.

Both dishes are moist and dense. A deep bowl of stuffing or a full pot of gravy loses heat slowly from the center. That means it can spend a long stretch inside the USDA's danger zone as it cools toward room temperature.

That slow cooling matters because of one bacterium in particular. The USDA links Clostridium perfringens to cooked meats, poultry and gravies held at unsafe warm temperatures. Gravy is usually built from turkey pan drippings and stock, thickened with flour or cornstarch. Stuffing often includes broth, eggs, sausage or giblets. Ingredients like these make both dishes perishable.

On the buffet, gravy needs to stay hot. A slow cooker set to warm holds it there and frees up stovetop space. A gravy boat rinsed with hot water before filling holds heat longer than a cold one. It still cools between pours. Small refills from a pot kept on a low burner limit how much gravy sits out at once.

Stuffing works best with the same approach. A covered casserole dish on a warming tray keeps it hot. So does a pan returned to a low oven between servings. Bringing out a smaller dish and replenishing it from the kitchen avoids leaving the whole batch exposed.

Stuffing cooked inside the turkey carries its own rules. The USDA advises that the center of the stuffing reach 165°F, even if the meat is already done. It recommends cooking stuffing in a separate dish for optimal safety. It also advises against stuffing a turkey ahead of time and refrigerating it to cook later.

After the meal, the way food is stored decides how fast it chills. The USDA advises removing any stuffing from the turkey cavity and storing it separately. Spreading gravy and stuffing into shallow containers lets them cool quickly in the refrigerator. A deep pot holds warmth in its middle far longer.

Pumpkin pie, cheesecake and cream pies belong in the refrigerator once they have cooled, not on the dessert table for the rest of the evening. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) treats pies and desserts made with eggs, milk or cream as perishable. It advises refrigerating pumpkin pie and custard pies after they cool.

Pumpkin pie is often baked a day ahead and left on the counter under foil, much like a loaf of bread. Its filling, though, is a custard. Pumpkin purée is mixed with eggs and milk or cream, then baked until set. That egg-and-dairy base is what puts it in the perishable category.

Cheesecake follows the same logic. Its filling is built on cream cheese and eggs. Cream pies such as banana cream, coconut cream and chocolate cream use a cooked custard or pastry cream. Many are also topped with whipped cream. All of these are served cold, and a slice warms steadily once it sits out on a plate.

The USDA's two-hour limit for perishable food applies to these desserts from the moment they leave the fridge. Time on the counter while the pie is sliced and passed around counts toward that limit.

Dessert timing makes this easy to overlook. Pies usually come out after a long meal, when guests are lingering and the kitchen is busy with dishes. A cheesecake placed on a sideboard during coffee can stay there until the last guest leaves. By then, nobody is tracking how long it has been out.

A practical approach is to cut slices from a chilled dessert and bring them out in stages. Keep the whole pie or cheesecake in the refrigerator and plate a few slices at a time. Return the remainder to the fridge well before it reaches two hours out. Toppings such as whipped cream can stay chilled until the moment of serving.

Fruit pies are a separate case. Apple $AAPL, cherry and other fruit pies without a dairy or egg filling do not fall under this group. A pie that pairs fruit with a custard or cream layer, however, contains eggs or dairy and returns to the perishable category.

#5501. Gas was pricier on this Election Day than any before it — up almost 40% to $4.15 a gallon since the Iran war began

As Democrats and Republicans look at the overwhelming results of the 2026 midterm election, it’s worth remembering what has become a political axiom in America: “It’s the economy, stupid.” Democratic strategist James Carville famously said that to presidential candidate Bill Clinton in 1992, but he might have said “it’s energy prices” instead. The cost of energy underlies much of the economy, making energy and politics inseparable, especially when gasoline prices rise.

Midterm elections have historically been difficult for incumbent presidents and often shift the balance of power in Washington, D.C.

Many factors affecting gasoline prices are beyond a president’s or Congress’s control. Prices for crude oil and petroleum products such as gasoline are set on global markets as the results of economic forces of supply and demand. Even the companies that produce oil don’t have as much influence as people might think, because of how that oil gets to refineries: Over 60% of the world’s crude oil is transported by ocean tankers, with 20% of global supplies traveling through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been closed, or nearly so, for much of 2026 as the conflict with Iran drags on.

When energy prices rise, other prices, such as food, follow. Sudden spikes in gasoline prices can contribute to higher inflation, both regionally and nationally.

Voters pay attention to those changes, and incumbents are less likely to win reelection. For the 2026 midterm election, gasoline prices were the highest of any previous election. That put Republicans in the precarious position of defending their record.

Four American presidents – Gerald Ford, Jimmy Carter, Ronald Reagan and Joe Biden – confronted the consequences of severe inflation and high fuel prices during midterm elections.

Richard Nixon was the first modern president to truly face an energy crisis that became political. In retaliation for U.S. support for Israel during the October 1973 Yom Kippur War, Arab members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries cut oil production and imposed an oil embargo on the United States. OPEC oil production fell by 5% a month, and crude oil prices rocketed 184% from prewar levels of $4.31 to $10.31 per barrel in March 1974. Nixon’s federal price controls on petroleum didn’t prevent U.S. gasoline prices from increasing 32%.

When Nixon resigned over the Watergate scandal in August 1974, Gerald Ford took office. Inflation was 12.3%, and gas prices were still high.

Right before that year’s midterm election, Ford launched the “Whip Inflation Now,” or WIN, campaign. But Republicans lost 48 House seats and five Senate seats.

“WIN” didn’t work, and by the 1976 presidential election, gas prices were over 60 cents a gallon – adjusted for inflation to late 2026, that’s $3.49. Ford lost his reelection bid to Jimmy Carter.

In Carter’s first two years in office, starting in 1977, the monthly average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. stayed high and even climbed slightly. Inflation hit 9% in 1978.

In the 1978 midterm election, Democrats lost 15 House and three Senate seats. Inflation continued to climb, and by the 1980 presidential election, gas prices were twice what they had been in 1976. Plagued by those figures and the Iranian hostage crisis, Carter lost the 1980 election to Ronald Reagan.

Reagan implemented “Reaganomics” by cutting taxes and regulations, reducing government spending, tightening monetary policy and removing the remaining price controls on petroleum. By the mid-1980s, increased oil production from U.S. and non-OPEC nations led to an oil glut, lowering the average price of crude oil and U.S. gasoline price from previous highs.

In the 1982 midterms, Republicans lost 26 seats in the House and gained one in the Senate.

Reagan won reelection to the presidency in a landslide in 1984, but the challenges for incumbents remained in the 1986 midterms. Though crude oil prices were $15 a barrel and gas had dropped to 82 cents a gallon, Republicans lost five seats in the House and eight in the Senate.

In the lead-up to the midterms during Donald Trump’s first term as president, crude prices had risen about 24% from when he took office in January 2017 to October 2018. And gas prices were up 22%. In the 2018 midterms, Republicans lost 41 House seats but gained two in the Senate.

Over the course of 2020, COVID-19 restrictions slowed the U.S. economy. U.S. crude oil production fell as gasoline demand plummeted by 40%. Prices rose because of pandemic-related supply chain backups.

And from Election Day in November 2020 to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. rose by 66%, from $2.11 to $3.52 per gallon.

Also, as pandemic restrictions lifted and the economy began recovering, demand for gasoline rebounded, straining supplies.

Upon taking office in 2021, Biden took steps to curb rising energy costs, including releasing oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in March 2022, which the Treasury Department suggested helped prevent gasoline price increases of $0.17 to $0.42 per gallon.

But other Biden policy moves made it harder to increase energy supplies. He canceled the Keystone XL pipeline project that would have brought more petroleum into the U.S. and suspended new oil and gas leases in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and the Gulf of Mexico. He also recommitted the U.S. to the Paris climate accord, under which countries have promised to cut their greenhouse gas emissions, generally meaning moving away from fossil fuels as an energy source.

In June 2022, inflation reached 9.1%, a 40-year high. And U.S. gasoline prices reached an all-time high of $4.929 per gallon; adjusted for inflation, that’s $5.60 a gallon today.

The 2022 midterm election wasn’t as bad for Democrats as they might have feared, though it wasn’t a success: The party lost nine House seats and one Senate seat. That’s a reminder that energy prices aren’t the only factor in voters’ minds when they are casting ballots.

During the first 12 months of Trump’s second term, crude oil prices fell 4.5%, U.S. oil production rose 3.3%, from 13.3 million to 13.7 million barrels per day, and the AAA national average price of regular unleaded gasoline fell 4.5%, from $3.12 to $2.98 per gallon.

On Feb. 28, 2026, U.S. military action against Iran disrupted Middle Eastern oil production and oil tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. Initially, shipment volume plummeted, though by the end of September it had recovered to 82% to 92% of prewar levels.

Overall, Middle Eastern crude oil exports are averaging around 24 million barrels a day, exceeding prewar levels in part because of increased use of pipelines out of Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Because of the war with Iran, AAA’s national average price of unleaded regular gasoline has increased by almost 40%, from February’s $2.98 price to $4.15 a gallon as of Nov. 3, 2026.

As the preelection polling had suggested, voters held Trump accountable for high gasoline and grocery prices, as well as an unpopular war.

It was a reminder of a basic economic and political principle: When the economy is doing well, voters are more likely to support incumbents and their parties. And when voters are pessimistic about the economy’s future, they are inclined to vote against incumbents and their parties.

Michael A. Mische, Associate Professor of the Practice of Management and Organization, Marshall School of Business, University of Southern California

#5500. Amazon rewrites its software engineering playbook for an era when AI writes the code

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 12:26 pmNovember 3, 2026 at 12:36 pm

Last month, a small team inside Amazon Web Services called Velocity Labs went from concept to the public release of a new open-source AI model in less than a week.

The group, whose existence hasn’t been previously reported, was formed in April. Velocity Labs has about 35 people, most of them in Seattle. The idea is to think beyond Amazon’s normal product-oriented approach, building quick prototypes in areas of AI that the company sees as underexplored and increasingly important to customers.

“We have noticed how the open-source community, and some of our competitors, experiment with new ideas, and deliver initial products fast,” the company says in job listings. “With Velocity Labs we are building an organization that can move faster, explore more, and make sure AWS is at the cutting edge of innovation in agentic AI.”

Inside the group, scientists and engineers work together, and they’re encouraged to cross over: engineers engage in research, and scientists do engineering work.

Velocity Labs is an example of the ways Amazon is trying “to create organizations that we think are going to be better suited to working with this new set of tools,” said Marc Brooker, an AWS vice president and distinguished engineer who leads the team.

For the vast majority of Amazon’s developers, he said, AI agents now write almost all the code that would have previously been written by hand.

Redefining the role: The team is part of Amazon’s larger rethinking of software development for the AI era, laid out in revised guidelines that the company’s engineering leaders sent to its developers earlier this year.

A letter that accompanied the guidelines, published last week under the byline of Michael “Terk” Terkowitz, a VP and distinguished engineer in Amazon’s stores business, advises engineers to learn AI now and to stay close to their customers and products.

The letter acknowledges that as Amazon has grown, some engineers and managers have become “less connected to their customers and business.”

Amazon has never published its underlying role guidelines for software engineers, and it declined to provide a copy of the revised version for this article. Brooker, one of the authors of the accompanying letter, said in an interview that the update emphasizes measuring engineers and teams by outcomes rather than inputs.

“We had seen these anti-patterns in the industry of folks really focusing on how many tokens are you spending, how many lines of code are you committing,” Brooker said, explaining that those kinds of measures don’t equate to customer value.

Asked whether AI use is part of performance reviews or promotions, Brooker said, “Not directly in a metrics sense.” It could factor in, he said, to the extent that it makes someone a stronger performer.

The letter doesn’t dismiss usage metrics entirely. Amazon has found that they “correlate well with the outputs that matter” and expects that to continue “for some time,” it says.

But what’s important, the letter says, is to use them “with care and judgement.”

Amazon engineers have described pressure to use AI tools. Three developers told The New York Times last year that managers were pushing them to use AI, raising output goals and becoming less forgiving about deadlines, with some coders saying their jobs had begun to resemble warehouse work. Amazon has set a goal for more than 80% of its developers to use AI each week, the Financial Times reported.

In May, Amazon shut down an internal leaderboard called KiroRank — which ranked employees by how much they used Kiro, the company’s AI coding tool — after finding that some were using the tool excessively just to climb the rankings, the FT reported.

Asked whether that episode was part of the impetus for the revised guidelines, Brooker said he didn’t recall the leaderboard or the details surrounding it.

“If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing. Document why, share it with your community of peers, bring it to your manager, and work to find solutions.”

Letter accompanying the revised SDE role guidelines

How the work has changed: Two years ago, most Amazon developers were still writing their code by hand, Brooker said. Today, “for the vast majority of our developer population, almost all of their implementation code is agent generated rather than human written,” he said.

“That is a massive change in the way of working for software engineers,” he said.

Brooker said he used to spend much of his time in a traditional code editor or the command line, and now spends a lot more of it working with agent tools such as Kiro, Kiro Crew and Anthropic’s Claude Code, calling it “a complete change of tools.”

For the company, the transition hasn’t been seamless. In March, Amazon acknowledged that an engineer who followed inaccurate advice from an AI agent contributed to one of several outages on its retail site, though the company disputed a Financial Times report that junior and mid-level engineers would need senior engineers to sign off on AI-assisted changes.

Amazon also pushed back on an earlier FT report that a 13-hour disruption to an AWS service in December happened after engineers let its Kiro AI coding tool make changes, and the tool decided to “delete and recreate the environment.” Amazon blamed user error — a misconfigured role — and said it has since added safeguards, including mandatory peer review for production access.

Still, the letter acknowledges that today’s AI tools won’t help in every situation, and it says that’s OK as long as engineers can explain why.

“If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing,” the letter says. “An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for.”

Inside Velocity Labs: The group is part of the agentic AI division led by Swami Sivasubramanian, which has organized much of its work around small teams of six to eight people, as GeekWire reported in June. Velocity Labs also includes the developers behind Strands, AWS’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents.

The model that Velocity Labs released last month, Strands Decider 2B, is designed to make quick, narrow decisions inside AI agents, such as which tool to use or where to route a request. It’s based on Qwen, an open model from Alibaba, and was released Oct. 1 along with the recipe used to train it.

Brooker built the original version on his own GPU at home after the startup TypeSafe AI unveiled Jev, a similar decision model, on Sept. 15, he wrote on his blog. “Every line of code was written by an agent,” he wrote, though he tried to make sure “the core ideas and insights were mine, or at least I understood them.”

Brooker described the team’s turnaround as less than a week from concept to public release. OpenAI announced a similar hosted service, its Decisions API, the same week, TechCrunch reported.

Brooker credited the team’s speed to its small size and a high level of trust: each person takes ownership of a piece of a project and asks for help when needed. He expects Amazon to create more teams like it, though not across the whole company.

Impact on jobs: Amazon has cut roughly 30,000 corporate jobs since late 2025. CEO Andy Jassy has said he expects AI to shrink the company’s corporate workforce over time.

At the same time, AWS CEO Matt Garman said in April that Amazon is “hiring just as many software developers as we ever had,” Business Insider reported. An Amazon spokesperson told the publication that more than 11,000 interns and early-career software engineers would join the company globally this year.

Asked whether AI will mean fewer engineers at Amazon, Brooker said, “I don’t think it changes the number of engineers.” The company wants engineers who take ownership, are curious and can learn quickly outside their areas of expertise, he said.

AI isn’t the right answer for every problem, Brooker said.

If the right tool is “an AI agent powered by a cutting-edge model, fantastic,” he said. However, he added, if it’s “three lines of Python code, that’s great too.”

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.
