#5499. Which vaccines do you need to travel abroad? 7 shots and their timing

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Vaccines to get before holiday travel include MMR, hepatitis A and yellow fever, and this guide explains seven shots, their dose schedules and how early to book

Travel vaccines work on a schedule, and that schedule starts long before the flight. Many shots need a series of doses spread over days, weeks or months. Others need time after the injection before the body builds protection. A traveler who visits a clinic a few days before a December flight may find some vaccines cannot take full effect in time.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) generally advises travelers to see a health care provider four to six weeks before departure. That window gives multidose schedules time to begin and protection time to develop. Some shots also have limited availability. In the U.S., the yellow fever vaccine is given only at authorized yellow fever vaccination centers.

This guide covers seven vaccines to get before holiday travel. It is a selection, not a complete checklist. Some entries are routine shots that many adults need to update, such as the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. Others depend on destination. Yellow fever occurs in parts of sub-Saharan Africa and tropical South America, while typhoid risk is highest in South Asia. One is tied to a specific journey. Saudi Arabia requires meningococcal ACWY vaccination for Hajj and Umrah pilgrims. Holiday travel often means crowded airports and aircraft, which is why the seasonal flu shot is on the list.

Each entry explains what the vaccine protects against, how many doses it takes and how far ahead it needs to be given. Those details answer two common questions: which vaccines do I need to travel abroad, and how early should I get them?

Recommendations also differ from one traveler to the next. Age, vaccination history, health conditions and itinerary all shape what a provider suggests. Close contact with animals or long stretches far from medical care, for example, can make rabies pre-exposure vaccination worth discussing.

Vaccine schedules and entry rules can change over time. Before a clinic visit, check the CDC and World Health Organization (WHO) destination pages for the countries on the itinerary. Confirm entry requirements with each destination's official sources as well. A provider can then match that guidance to a specific trip and health history.

Measles is a risk on international trips, and the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine protects against it. Two doses of MMR give full protection.

CDC guidance for adult travelers is specific. An adult who travels abroad without evidence of immunity should get two doses. Those doses should be given at least 28 days apart.

That interval sets the planning timeline. A traveler who starts the series less than 28 days before departure cannot finish both doses before leaving. Booking the first appointment well ahead of the trip leaves room to complete the series before the flight. A single dose before departure falls short of the two doses CDC advises for adults without evidence of immunity.

MMR is a routine vaccine, not one tied to a particular destination. That makes the same check relevant before any trip abroad, from a short hop across a border to a long-haul holiday journey. The deciding factor is whether the traveler already has evidence of immunity.

Infants follow a separate rule. A baby aged six to 11 months who is traveling internationally can receive one early dose of MMR before departure. It is meant to cover the child during the trip itself.

That early dose does not count toward the child's routine series. The child still needs two more doses, starting at 12 months of age, to finish the standard schedule.

An infant vaccinated early for a trip ends up with three doses in all: one for travel and two for the routine schedule. A written record of the travel dose lets the child's later appointments account for it.

Parents can raise the early dose with a pediatrician before a holiday trip abroad. Adults unsure of their own status can review vaccination records with a provider before booking travel. Finding a gap early leaves time to complete both doses before departure.

The hepatitis A vaccine is given as two doses, six months apart, and the first dose on its own provides strong protection. A traveler short on time can get that first dose shortly before departure and finish the series later.

Hepatitis A spreads through contaminated food and water. The disease is common in many parts of the world where sanitation is limited.

That route of transmission shapes the risk for travelers. Exposure does not require unusual activities. It can come through ordinary meals and drinks in places where food and water handling fall short. Ice made from contaminated water or produce rinsed in it travels the same route.

The two doses do different jobs. The first shot delivers strong protection on its own. The second turns that early protection into long-lasting protection. That matters for anyone who expects to travel again.

The six-month gap has a practical consequence for holiday planning. A traveler who gets the first shot just before a December trip would be due for the second around June. That appointment falls months after the trip ends. It needs to go on the calendar separately.

Skipping the second dose leaves the series incomplete. The long-lasting protection depends on finishing it. Keeping a record of the first dose makes the follow-up visit simpler, especially if it happens at a different clinic.

This flexibility sets hepatitis A apart from vaccines that must be given by a firm deadline before departure. A late clinic visit still leaves time for the first dose to help. For a traveler booking a last-minute holiday trip, hepatitis A is one shot that does not have to be ruled out for lack of time.

Whether hepatitis A vaccination is recommended depends on the destination. Current destination guidance from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the World Health Organization (WHO) shows where vaccination is advised. A health care provider can confirm the dose timing for each traveler and each trip.

Typhoid vaccine comes in two forms: a injectable Vi polysaccharide shot given at least two weeks before travel, or four oral Ty21a capsules finished at least one week before departure.

Typhoid spreads through contaminated food and water. Risk is highest in South Asia.

The Vi polysaccharide vaccine needs only one injection. That means one clinic visit covers it, as long as the visit falls early enough.

Protection from the Vi shot does not last indefinitely. Travelers $TRV who face continued risk need a booster every two years. Someone who had the injection before an earlier trip should check the date of that dose. If it was given more than two years ago, a booster is due before another trip to an area with typhoid risk.

The Ty21a vaccine is taken by mouth. One capsule is taken every other day rather than daily, for a total of four capsules.

That schedule sets a start date well ahead of departure. Four capsules taken every other day stretch across six days from the first to the last. Adding the one-week buffer means the first capsule should be taken no later than 13 days before the trip begins. A late start can push the final capsule past that window.

The two options need similar lead time. The injection must be given at least two weeks before travel, and the oral course must begin no later than 13 days before. The difference lies in format: one dose at a clinic versus four capsules spread across six days.

Neither vaccine is fully protective. A traveler who has had the shot or finished the capsules can still be infected. Food and water precautions still apply. They target the same route the disease uses to spread. Vaccination and careful choices about what to eat and drink work as two separate layers of protection.

The yellow fever vaccine is a single shot, and the WHO says one dose gives lifetime protection. The shot must be given at least 10 days before arrival for the international certificate of vaccination to be valid.

Yellow fever is a virus spread by mosquitoes. It occurs in parts of sub-Saharan Africa and tropical South America. A holiday itinerary that includes either region is the usual reason to ask a provider about this vaccine.

The vaccine does two separate jobs. It protects the traveler against a mosquito-borne virus, and it produces a document some governments check. A trip can call for one without the other. A traveler visiting an area where yellow fever occurs may want the protection even if no border agent asks for proof.

Some countries require the certificate for entry. The document serves as proof of vaccination at the border. Entry rules differ from country to country. The destination's official requirements are the place to confirm whether a certificate is needed.

The 10-day rule shapes the travel calendar. A shot given fewer than 10 days before arrival leaves the certificate invalid when the traveler lands. The count runs to the arrival date in the country that requires proof, not to the day the trip begins. Travelers $TRV heading to such a country need to book the appointment with that window in mind.

Since July 2016, the international certificate of vaccination has been valid for life. The change matches the WHO's position that one dose protects for life. A traveler who already holds a certificate from an earlier vaccination can present that same document on later trips. For that traveler, the 10-day wait no longer applies, because the original shot already meets it.

In the U.S., the vaccine is not offered at every clinic. Only authorized yellow fever vaccination centers can give the shot. A provider who handles other travel vaccines may not be one of those centers. Finding an authorized center ahead of time keeps the 10-day deadline within reach.

Saudi Arabia requires pilgrims performing Hajj or Umrah to show proof of quadrivalent meningococcal ACWY vaccination. The same vaccine is also relevant for trips to the meningitis belt of sub-Saharan Africa, which is an area of higher risk for the disease.

Meningococcal disease is a serious bacterial infection. It can cause meningitis. It can also cause an infection of the bloodstream. The ACWY vaccine is intended to protect against this infection.

The vaccine's name describes its coverage. "Quadrivalent" means the shot targets four groups of meningococcal bacteria. Those groups are labeled A, C, W and Y.

For pilgrims, the shot is an entry matter as well as a health one. Saudi Arabia requires proof of vaccination, not only the vaccination itself. A traveler should keep the record from the clinic visit and pack it with passports and other travel papers.

Saudi authorities set the timing rules for that proof. The window in which a dose is accepted for entry should be confirmed against the official requirements before travel. Pilgrims vaccinated for an earlier trip should check whether that dose still meets the current rule.

Travel to the meningitis belt raises a different question. The case for the vaccine there rests on the higher risk of disease in the region. A traveler heading to sub-Saharan Africa can raise the ACWY vaccine with a provider at a pre-travel appointment.

Official sources settle the details for each itinerary. Current CDC and WHO destination guidance, along with each country's own entry requirements, shows what applies to a specific trip.

Rabies pre-exposure vaccination is meant for travelers who may have close contact with animals or who will be far from medical care. In 2022, the U.S. Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) recommended a two-dose schedule, with the second dose given seven days after the first.

That schedule fits the whole pre-exposure series inside a single week. A traveler who sees a provider in the weeks before departure can finish both doses before leaving. The short gap also leaves room for holiday plans that come together late, as long as both appointments fall before the flight.

The two groups face different versions of the same problem. Close contact with animals raises the chance of a bite. Distance from medical care makes it harder to reach treatment quickly after one.

The vaccine does not remove the need for medical care after an animal bite. A vaccinated traveler who is bitten still needs to be seen by a medical provider. The earlier shots change the treatment that follows, not whether treatment is needed.

That treatment changes in two ways. Prior vaccination reduces the number of post-exposure doses a bitten traveler has to receive. It also removes the need for rabies immune globulin. A traveler who skipped pre-exposure vaccination may need both rabies immune globulin and a longer series of post-exposure shots.

For a traveler far from medical care, that difference carries practical weight. A shorter post-exposure course means fewer return visits to a provider after a bite. Skipping rabies immune globulin removes one product from the list of what a clinic must supply.

The decision rests on the itinerary. A provider can weigh planned activities and the distance to medical care against the time needed for the two-dose schedule. Recommendations can change. Before booking, current CDC and WHO destination guidance shows what applies to a given trip.

Holiday travelers need a current-season flu shot at least two weeks before departure. Protection takes about two weeks to develop after vaccination.

That two-week lag sets the deadline. A shot given a few days before a flight will not have finished building protection by the time the traveler boards. Someone leaving in late December needs the vaccine by mid-December at the latest.

Flu seasons do not line up around the world. The Northern Hemisphere season generally runs from October to May. That window takes in the year-end holidays across the U.S., Canada, Europe and Japan.

The Southern Hemisphere season generally runs from April to September. A December trip to Australia, Argentina or South Africa falls outside that usual window. A mid-year trip from the U.S. to the same places reverses the picture. Home is between seasons, while the destination is in the middle of one.

The tropics follow a different pattern. Flu can circulate there year-round. Destinations near the equator therefore have no dependable off-season. A trip to Southeast Asia, Central America or the Caribbean can overlap with flu activity in any month.

Holiday travel puts large numbers of people in the same spaces. Trips at this time of year often run through crowded airports and onto full aircraft. A shot timed to take effect before departure means protection is in place for the journey itself, not only for the destination.

The flu vaccine formulation changes every year. A shot from a previous season does not carry over to the new one. A traveler vaccinated last year, or earlier, still needs a new dose before this year's trip. Checking the date of the most recent shot is a quick way to confirm whether it belongs to the current season.

Vaccine recommendations can change. Travelers $TRV should check current guidance from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the World Health Organization before booking. A provider can advise on timing, particularly for trips that cross hemispheres.

#5498. Gen Z voters broke for Democrats 66% to 31% in the midterms — and the Iran war cracked their top three issues

The economy was the top issue for voters in the November 2026 midterm elections, which saw Democrats win decisive majorities in both houses of Congress.

And for young voters, whether in college or not, the economy and jobs, as well as healthcare, were their top concerns, our research at CIRCLE, a nonpartisan, research organization focused on youth civic engagement at Tufts University, shows.

Overall, 27% of young people – meaning people ages 18 to 29 – went to the polls during the midterms, our Nov. 5 analysis shows. This marks the second-highest midterm youth voter turnout in the past 30 years, behind only the 2018 election cycle.

As a scholar at CIRCLE who studies young people and their voting behavior, I think it’s helpful to understand some of the factors that motivated so many young people to vote – and to cast their lot with the Democrats.

Among youth, being enrolled as a college student or not did not make a big difference in who they voted for during these midterms.

But there are some voting trend differences based on young people’s educational attainment, especially in the gap between young people with an education level of high school or less, and those with at least some college experience and more. Those with only a high school degree or less voted Democratic by a 24-point margin, compared with a 42-point margin among those with at least some college education.

College students who are young men also voted Democrat by a 24-point margin. Female college students, meanwhile, voted Democrat at a 45-point margin. A similar gender gap appears among young voters who aren’t in college.

Overall, this gender gap has persisted at least since 2024, as young women then were also voting more Democratic than men were.

About 66% of young people ages 18-29 voted for a Democratic candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives, compared with 31% for a Republican candidate, our data shows. This marks the highest percentage of support for Democratic candidates among all age groups.

Within this group, 70% of young women voted for a Democratic U.S. House candidate in the midterms, as opposed to 59% of young men.

Partisan trends among young voters have fluctuated over the past few decades – in 2000, for example, 49% of young people voted Democratic, while 48% voted Republican.

In 2026, Asian American and Pacific Islander, Black and Latino young people gave Democrat candidates the strongest support, at 81%, 79% and 71%, respectively. By comparison, 61% of white young people voted for Democratic House candidates, with 36% voting Republican.

Across race, education, income and geographic location, young people overwhelmingly indicated that the economy and jobs was their top issue in this election.

Healthcare and the Iran war also showed up as areas of importance for young voters. All three of these issues are connected to young people’s concerns about the cost of living.

We found that voting preferences did vary according to how young people viewed their own financial circumstances, a pattern that held among college students.

Low-income students were more likely than their affluent peers to vote for Democrats.

The issues that matter most to young people have shifted considerably over the past several years.

In 2020, we were seeing different groups of young people prioritize social issues like racism, climate change and gun control.

In 2022, we began to see young people prioritize the economy – their concern about inflation was the second-most important issue to them after abortion.

Now, after the economy, healthcare was ranked second for young voters. The third-most important issue was the war in Iran. This is striking, because in the past, we’ve polled young voters about foreign policy issues like the war between Israel and Palestinians and the war between Russia and Ukraine. Young people have never really ranked these other foreign policy issues as a top area of concern.

Youth voter turnout generally tends to be much weaker in midterm elections than in presidential elections. In 2018, there was 28% turnout for young people – a midterm turnout that was considerably higher than 2014, when only 13% of young people turned out to vote.

Campaigns seem to recognize that young voters tend to be less politically engaged. For example, our research shows that during the 2024 presidential election cycle, more than 1 in 3 young people were never contacted about the election. Among those without college experience, 48% were never contacted.

Our research still shows that college students face logistical barriers to voting.

Young people are frequent movers, which means they might need to reregister whenever they change addresses. The fact that college students may be living on campus while they’re registered to vote from their parents’ address can also create complications.

College students still have more voting information than young people who are not in college. But compared with other age groups, young people receive less voting information – making their turnout in the 2026 midterms all the more remarkable.

Sara Suzuki, Senior Researcher and Research Assistant Professor at CIRCLE, Tufts University

This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

#5497. Exposed to measles? 7 steps to take, from the 72-hour vaccine window to isolation

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Learn what to do if you were exposed to measles, from checking your MMR record and the 72-hour vaccine window to symptoms, testing and isolation

Measles exposure starts a clock. Some of the most useful protective steps are available for only a few days after contact. Decisions made in that short span can shape how the next three weeks unfold. Knowing what to do if you were exposed to measles means knowing which deadlines matter and who to call first.

Measles is highly contagious. Up to 90% of people without immunity who are close to an infected person become infected, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). A single exposure at a clinic, school, airport or workplace therefore carries real risk for anyone who is not protected.

The first question is whether you are already immune. Vaccination and past infection are the usual routes to immunity. Confirming that status can settle the matter quickly. People who cannot document immunity face a different set of choices. Some of those choices depend on age, pregnancy or the state of the immune system.

This guide walks through seven steps in the order most people will need them. It starts with checking vaccination records and other evidence of immunity. It then covers the monitoring period after exposure and the early signs of illness. Those first signs can resemble a cold before any rash appears. The guide also explains why a phone call should come before any visit to a doctor's office or emergency room.

Two time-limited options get their own slides. A dose of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine may offer some protection when given within 72 hours of first exposure. Immune globulin is a separate option that certain high-risk people can receive up to six days after exposure.

The final slide covers isolation. It explains when a sick person is contagious and when exposed people may be asked to stay home from school or work.

None of this replaces individual medical advice. A doctor can assess personal risk. Local and state health departments handle testing and contact tracing. They also set exclusion rules in their area. Anyone who learns of a possible exposure should contact one of them promptly, before the post-exposure windows close.

The first step after a measles exposure is to find out whether you already have presumptive evidence of immunity. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) considers people with that evidence presumed immune. For them, many of the usual post-exposure steps may not be needed.

The CDC accepts four kinds of evidence. The first is written documentation of measles vaccination. The second is a laboratory test showing immunity. The third is laboratory confirmation that you had measles in the past. The fourth is birth before 1957.

Written documentation means an actual record, not a memory of getting shots as a child. Common places to look include a childhood vaccination card, files kept by a pediatrician or family doctor and school or college health records. Many U.S. states also run immunization registries, and a doctor or health department can often search them.

How many documented doses count as enough depends on who you are. For preschool-age children and for adults who are not at high risk, one dose of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is considered adequate. School-age children, college students, health care workers and international travelers need two documented doses.

The gap between one and two doses shows up in protection. The CDC puts the effectiveness of two MMR doses against measles at about 97%. A single dose is about 93% effective. Neither figure reaches 100%. A small share of vaccinated people can still catch measles after an exposure.

The routine U.S. schedule gives the first MMR dose at 12 to 15 months of age and the second at four to six years. A child who followed that schedule and has the paperwork to show it meets the two-dose standard. A baby younger than 12 months has not yet reached the age for a routine first dose.

When records are missing or incomplete, a blood test can answer the question. A doctor can order a test for measles antibodies, and a result showing immunity counts as laboratory evidence. A past case of measles also counts, but only if a laboratory confirmed it. A remembered childhood illness without lab confirmation does not meet that standard.

The 1957 cutoff reflects how widely measles circulated before vaccination. People born before that year are presumed to have been infected as children.

Anyone unsure of their status should share whatever records they have with a doctor or the local health department. Either can judge whether the evidence is sufficient or whether further steps are needed.

Anyone without measles immunity who has been exposed should watch for symptoms through day 21 after their last contact with the virus. That 21-day period reflects the measles incubation period, the stretch between catching the virus and feeling sick.

For most people, symptoms begin seven to 14 days after exposure. The full range runs from seven to 21 days. A person who still feels fine at the end of the second week has not yet cleared the window. Watching through day 21 covers the late end of that range, so slower-developing cases are not missed.

The count starts from the last exposure, not the first. Someone who shared a home, classroom or office with an infected person over several days should date the watch period from the final day of contact. Day 21 then falls three weeks after that last contact. Writing that date down makes it easier to tell a doctor or health department exactly when the window closes.

In a household, each day spent near a sick person counts as a new exposure. The window keeps moving later until that contact ends.

Exposure does not require face-to-face contact. Measles spreads through the air when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes. The virus can remain in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after that person has left a room. Someone who walked into a waiting room, store or airport gate after an infected person had gone may still have been exposed.

That airborne persistence is part of why measles spreads so efficiently among people who are not protected. For someone with no evidence of immunity, a confirmed exposure carries a high chance of infection.

People already protected by vaccination or past infection face a much lower risk. Anyone unsure of their status during the watch period should ask a doctor or the local health department how to proceed. That includes whether to limit contact with others before day 21 passes.

Measles typically begins with a high fever, a cough, a runny nose and red, watery eyes. The rash most people picture comes later, usually three to five days after those first symptoms appear.

That gap matters for anyone tracking their health after an exposure. A person waiting for spots on the skin may already be several days into the illness before the rash shows up.

The fever is often the most pronounced early sign. It can climb above 104°F. A fever that high, along with a cough and irritated, watery eyes, fits the typical early pattern of measles. For someone who shared space with a measles patient, that combination is a reason to watch closely for the next signs.

Koplik spots are a second clue, and they are easy to miss without looking for them. They are tiny white spots that form on the inside of the mouth. They can appear two to three days after the first symptoms begin. Because the skin rash usually comes later, Koplik spots can offer an earlier visible sign that the illness may be measles.

The rash follows a recognizable path. It starts on the face. From there, it spreads downward over the rest of the body.

Measles can also lead to serious complications. They include ear infections, diarrhea and pneumonia. In rare cases, the virus causes encephalitis, an inflammation of the brain.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reports that about one in five unvaccinated people in the U.S. who get measles is hospitalized. The agency also reports that one to three of every 1,000 children who get measles die.

Knowing the order of symptoms helps an exposed person describe what is happening when they seek care. The sequence runs from fever, cough, runny nose and watery eyes, to white spots inside the mouth, to a rash that begins on the face. Anyone who notices these signs after a measles exposure should contact a doctor or the local health department for guidance on next steps.

Anyone who may have measles should phone the clinic, hospital or local health department before showing up for care. A call ahead gives staff time to prepare. That preparation helps keep the virus from reaching other patients in a waiting area.

Measles spreads through the air when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes. One unannounced visit to a crowded lobby can expose many other people. Clinics and emergency rooms often hold people who are already vulnerable, including babies, older adults and patients with weakened immune systems.

Calling first allows the facility to follow a U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) infection-control practice for suspected measles. Staff can place a mask on the patient as soon as they arrive. They can then move the patient into a separate room instead of the general waiting area.

The preferred space is an airborne infection isolation room. This type of room is built to keep air from flowing out into the rest of the building. Some facilities may also tell callers which entrance to use.

The phone call is also the time to share key details. A caller can describe where and when the possible exposure happened and which symptoms have appeared. It also helps to say when those symptoms started and whether there is a record of MMR vaccination. That information helps clinicians decide how quickly the person needs to be seen and where.

Local or state health departments direct measles testing and contact tracing. Measles is a reportable disease in the U.S. Clinicians who suspect a case are expected to notify public health officials. The health department can then identify other people who shared the same space and may need follow-up.

Testing usually involves two samples. One is a throat or nasal swab checked with PCR, a lab method that detects the genetic material of the measles virus. The other is a blood sample tested for antibodies to measles. Those antibodies show how the immune system is responding to the virus.

Results guide what happens next for both the patient and the people around them. A confirmed case can lead the health department to contact others who were at the same clinic, school, workplace or event. A negative result can help clinicians look for another cause of the symptoms.

Anyone unsure whom to call can start with a regular doctor's office or the local health department. Either one can explain where to go and how to arrive without putting others at risk.

People without measles immunity who get an MMR vaccine within 72 hours of their first exposure may gain some protection or have a milder illness. That is the guidance from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

MMR is the combined vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella. It is the same shot children receive on the routine schedule. Given after contact with the virus, it serves as a form of post-exposure prophylaxis.

The CDC describes two possible benefits. A dose given inside the window can provide some protection against infection. For people who still get sick after the shot, it can make the illness milder. Neither outcome is described as a guarantee.

The 72-hour limit is counted from the first exposure, not the most recent one. Someone who shared a household or classroom with an infected person over several days should count from the earliest contact.

Late notice also eats into the window. A person who learns of an exposure two days after it happened has about 24 hours left to get the dose.

The vaccine does no harm if the person was already infected at the time of the shot, according to the CDC. The dose can still be given when it is unclear whether the virus has already taken hold.

Infants can be part of this response. Babies aged six to 11 months can receive MMR as post-exposure prophylaxis, within the same 72-hour window that applies to older children and adults.

That early dose comes with a caveat for parents. A dose given before a child's first birthday does not count toward the routine two-dose MMR series. The child will still need both standard doses later, on the regular schedule.

A doctor or the local health department can arrange the dose. Calling as soon as an exposure becomes known leaves the most time inside the window. Health departments can also confirm whether an exposed person qualifies.

Some people face a high risk of severe measles but cannot safely receive the MMR vaccine or are too young for it. They may qualify for immune globulin, which can be given up to six days after exposure.

Immune globulin is a blood product made from the pooled plasma of many donors. It contains ready-made antibodies, including antibodies against measles. Those antibodies give the recipient temporary, passive protection. The body does not have to build its own immune response first. That lets the treatment help even after contact with the virus has already happened.

The CDC lists three groups to consider for immune globulin after an exposure. The first is infants younger than 12 months. The second is pregnant women without evidence of measles immunity. The third is people with severe immune suppression, such as some patients being treated for leukemia or recovering from a stem cell transplant.

None of the three groups can rely on the MMR vaccine in the usual way. Infants younger than 12 months have not yet reached the routine age for a first dose. MMR is a live-virus vaccine made with weakened forms of the measles, mumps and rubella viruses. It is not given during pregnancy. It is also withheld from people with severe immune suppression. In a body that cannot control it, even a weakened vaccine virus can cause serious illness.

Measles during pregnancy also carries its own risks, including miscarriage, preterm birth and low birth weight.

The type of immune globulin depends on the patient. Infants receive an intramuscular injection. Pregnant women and severely immunocompromised people receive the intravenous form, delivered through an IV line.

Immune globulin does not replace vaccination. Its protection fades as the donated antibodies break down, and it does not create lasting immunity. Those same antibodies can also blunt the response to a live vaccine given too soon afterward. A doctor decides when someone who received immune globulin can later get MMR, once they are eligible.

Anyone in these groups who learns of an exposure should contact a doctor or the local health department right away. Health officials can confirm eligibility, arrange the correct form and keep track of the days left in the six-day window.

A person with measles can spread the virus from four days before the rash appears until four days after it. Anyone who develops measles should stay home through the fourth day after the rash first shows up.

That contagious window opens before the illness is recognizable as measles. During those first days, an infected person can pass the virus to others before anyone suspects the cause. Health departments use the day the rash first appears as the reference point for timing isolation. Writing down that date makes it easier to work out when isolation ends.

For a person whose rash appears on a Monday, the contagious period after the rash runs through Friday. Staying home through that Friday covers the full four days after rash onset.

Staying home means skipping work, school, child care and other shared settings for the whole period. Inside the household, it means keeping apart from anyone who lacks evidence of immunity.

Anyone with measles should avoid contact with infants, pregnant people and people with weakened immune systems throughout the contagious period. Those three groups face a higher risk of severe illness from measles.

Exposed people who never get sick can still be asked to stay home. When the health department directs it, exposed people without immunity are generally kept out of school, child care and work from day five through day 21 after exposure. The exclusion covers people who feel well. An infection can still be developing during that stretch before any symptoms show.

A timely MMR dose can change that outcome. Exposed people who got the vaccine within the recommended window may be allowed to return to school or work. The health department makes that decision. The answer can differ from one jurisdiction to the next.

Questions about when isolation or exclusion ends belong with a doctor or the local health department. The health department sets the end dates and decides when a person can return to work, school or child care.

#5496. Cosmos Hub Approves Gaia v29 With 99.41% Support Ahead of October 28th Upgrade

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Proposal #1059 passed with 49.59% turnout as the chain counts down now to block 33,618,500 on October 28th, where validators are told to run the security-patched v29.0.1 binary, not the version named in the proposal.

The Cosmos Hub's latest upgrade drew almost no opposition. About 168.5 million ATOM voted on Proposal #1059, and only 2,335 ATOM voted No. Under that one-sided result is an unusual change: the Hub's stakers voted to remove the governance route that earlier generations of Cosmos proposals used to change the chain's own settings.

Proposal #1059 schedules the upgrade of the Cosmos Hub to Gaia v29.0.0. It finished voting on October 27 at 12:00 UTC with a PASSED result. The vote approves the upgrade, but the software has not run yet. The chain still has to reach the upgrade height, halt, and restart on the new binary. Until that happens, Gaia v29 is approved but not yet live.

On-chain records show 49.59% of staked ATOM voted, against a 40% quorum requirement. Yes took 99.41% of the vote, or 167,514,965 ATOM. No With Veto took 0.58% (982,855 ATOM), Abstain took 0.01% (14,360 ATOM), and No rounds to 0.00% (2,335 ATOM).

The veto share is the main number to watch in a Cosmos governance vote, because a large enough veto rejects a proposal even if Yes wins. At 0.58%, the veto bloc was far too small to matter. That fits the proposal's nature. It is a maintenance release that removes deprecated code and updates dependencies, and it has no economic or political stakes.

The forum discussion covered one governance point: a delegator's own vote overrides their validator's vote. A few large validators did not decide the result on their own. Delegators could have overridden them, and very few chose to vote differently.

The proposal names v29.0.0, but operators are not supposed to run that build at the upgrade height. On October 23, three days into voting, the Gaia team tagged v29.0.1 and updated the official forum post to recommend it.

The patch changes only one thing: it rebuilds Gaia with Go 1.26.10 instead of Go 1.26.7. That picks up the Go security fix tracked as CVE-2026-111943 (GO-2026-6809). The project's upgrade notes call v29.0.1 a non-state-breaking patch release, so it computes the same chain state as v29.0.0. Nodes that already installed v29.0.0 can switch at any time by replacing the binary and restarting.

Operators using Cosmovisor need to know one detail. The on-chain upgrade name stays v29.0.0, so the v29.0.1 binary still goes into the upgrades/v29.0.0/bin/ directory. If a validator names the folder after the patch version, Cosmovisor will not find the binary when the chain halts. The project's sample service configuration has automatic binary download turned off, which means each operator has to put the correct binary in place before the halt.

Gaia v29 removes the x/params module from the Cosmos Hub. That module is the original, centralized store for parameters, and it backed the legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route. The release changelog lists the change under API-breaking changes: "The legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route and cosmos.params.v1beta1.Query service are no longer available."

In practice, governance has already moved on. Each module now owns its parameters, and changes go through that module's own governance message. The legacy route remained as a fallback, and v29 removes it. The rate-limiting module was the last part of the Hub still wired to the old params subspace. In v29 it no longer depends on it.

The forum Q&A states who is affected. RPC providers, wallets, explorers, and governance dashboards should check whether they still call the params v1beta1 query service or create legacy parameter-change proposals. After the upgrade, those calls will fail on the Hub. For most users nothing changes. The proposal requires no token migration, and balances, delegations, and IBC assets are unaffected.

The second API-breaking item affects multisig accounts specifically. Gaia v29 moves the Hub from Cosmos SDK v0.53.4 to v0.53.8, and the changelog warns: "As of cosmos-sdk v0.53.8, --gas auto gas simulation is broken for multisig senders. Multisig transactions must specify a fixed --gas value until this is fixed upstream."

This matters in practice. The Hub's weekly update of October 22 said the problem applies to the Community Pool migration multisig. That multisig is handling a USDC.n migration spend that was moving toward an on-chain proposal during the same week. Treasury signers, custody desks, and DAO operators who build transactions with --gas auto will need to set gas by hand until the upstream SDK is fixed.

The same release also brings CometBFT from 0.38.23 to 0.38.25, the IBC rate-limiting middleware from 10.1.0 to 10.7.0, and runc from 1.2.8 to 1.3.6. It also moves the build toolchain from Go 1.25 to Go 1.26.

The upgrade handler, the code that runs once at the upgrade height, does more cleanup than the proposal summary describes. It first deletes everything in the deprecated provider store, the state left over from the Hub's time as an Interchain Security provider. Next it wipes the legacy x/params store. Last, it removes a receipt left behind by the earlier v28.3.1 balance migration.

The code also shows how cautious the Gaia team is about the upgrade. The stores stay mounted, and their contents are cleared as ordinary state changes. Unmounting them entirely could cause version-mismatch errors when nodes load the chain from disk. Gaia v29 has also run on the Hub's provider testnet since October 13, about two weeks before mainnet.

At 15:32 UTC on October 27, Mintscan showed block 33,618,500 as "not yet created". The chain was at block 33,604,199, with 14,301 blocks to go. At the recent average block time of 5.722 seconds, the Mintscan countdown for block 33,618,500 estimated the height for about 14:16 UTC on October 28. The forum's original estimate was 13:50 UTC. The real time depends on how fast blocks are produced over the next day.

When the chain reaches that height, block production stops. It restarts only after validators holding more than two-thirds of voting power are back online on the new binary. That makes the vote result only half the story. The other half is whether validators show up on v29.0.1 promptly, so that the halt lasts minutes rather than hours.

#5495. Filing: Amazon’s previously announced layoffs include 95 jobs in Washington state

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 6:11 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 7:26 am

A notice made public Tuesday evening, disclosing about 95 Amazon job cuts in Washington state, is part of the company’s previously reported layoffs in its retail business, not a new round of reductions, a spokesperson confirmed.

The filing lists software engineers, product managers and program managers among the affected employees. Most are based in Amazon’s Seattle offices, but others work in Bellevue and Redmond, at warehouses in Sumner and Pasco, or remotely.

Reuters reported in early October that Amazon was laying off fewer than 1,000 corporate employees, mainly in its Stores unit, which runs the company’s e-commerce business. Amazon confirmed to GeekWire at the time that “hundreds” of Stores employees were affected. The notice covers only employees based in Washington state.

“We’ve adjusted parts of our Stores business because we believe this structure will better enable us to deliver on our priorities,” Amazon said in a statement at the time.

Most affected employees were notified in October, including 43 on or about Oct. 7, when the Stores cuts were first reported. Others received notice in September or as early as July 3, according to the filing.

The federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act requires large employers to give workers and the government advance notice of mass layoffs. Washington’s version of the WARN Act generally requires 60 days’ notice when a covered employer eliminates 50 or more jobs within 30 days across its Washington operations, excluding part-time employees.

Amazon has made a series of smaller filings under the state law in the past year, including notices covering 121 jobs in August, 57 tech jobs earlier in the summer and 84 jobs last December.

The latest notice covers employees at 17 Amazon offices and warehouses in Seattle, Bellevue, Redmond, Sumner and Pasco, plus 15 remote workers in the state.

The list also includes risk managers, several directors and other senior employees. Employees who land other jobs inside Amazon before their separation dates won’t be laid off, the notice says.

The Stores cuts were much smaller than Amazon’s major corporate cutbacks since last fall. The company eliminated about 14,000 corporate roles globally in October 2025, including 2,303 in Washington, followed by another round in January that included 2,198 Washington employees.

#5493. ‘Everyone knows why we lost,’ JD Vance points to the Iran war — which has already cost at least $38 billion and 19 American lives

While votes were still being counted in the U.S. midterm elections, administration figures in Washington were already inviting speculation over how the results might be connected to the conflict with Iran.

On the morning after the election, Vice President JD Vance wrote on X that the major reason for the dramatic loss for Republicans was the American public’s opposition to the war. “Everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there,” he wrote, in reference to the ongoing conflict that began with U.S.-Israeli airstrikes against Iran in late February 2026.

While it is rare for a vice president to make such a critical proclamation about their own administration’s policy, President Donald Trump later stated that he did not disagree with Vance’s appraisal of the role that frustration with the Iran war played in voters’ minds.

But whether this changes Trump’s view on next steps in the ongoing conflict remains unclear. Reporting over the past few weeks has indicated that the U.S. military has been actively preparing options and increasing capabilities in the Persian Gulf region in the event the president directs a resumption of hostilities.

As an expert on Middle East affairs and a former senior official at the National Security Council during the first Trump administration, I’m aware that months of conflict have failed to bring Iran to its knees, force regime change or militarily defeat a perceived threat to U.S. assets and allies. Escalating now is unlikely to change those realities – and it carries the additional risk of further damaging Republicans in the eyes of Americans voters as they turn toward the 2028 presidential race.

Even if Trump were to ratchet up the conflict, moreover, it’s unclear how much wiggle room he’ll have come January facing a Democratic Congress almost uniformly opposed to the war.

Part of the issue facing Iran war hawks in Washington now is that the conflict has caused serious setbacks for the regime in Tehran without satisfying the officially stated strategic reasons for going to war.

They argue that pulling back now – as welcome as that might be for Americans struggling with the associated rising cost of fuel – may allow Iran to rebuild before the conflict is “won.” Moreover, it would render the military and reputational costs already sunk by Washington as wasted.

Among the achievements of this war touted by the Trump administration has been the death of former Supreme Leader Ali Khameini, along with the killing of scores of senior leaders within the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps – including individuals like the former head of Iran’s National Security Council Ali Larijani. Significant elements of Iran’s air defense and radar network, ballistic missile and drone production, and storage and launch sites have also been destroyed. And Iran’s already outdated navy and air force has been further degraded.

Meanwhile, the U.S.-imposed naval blockade against Iranian-linked shipping in the Persian Gulf cut off a crucial lifeline for Iran’s economy. And additional sanctions and economic penalties imposed by Washington have served to further devalue Iran’s currency and deprive Iran of additional financial links to the international banking system.

Yet for all the U.S. successes in degrading the Iranian military by limitless aerial bombardment and the significant financial pressure against the Iranian economy, an obvious endgame remains elusive.

Despite weakening the Iranian government – now led by Ali Khameinei’s son, Mojtaba, and a new echelon of senior IRGC commanders – the Islamic Republic remains intact. Moreover, it still possesses enough ballistic missiles and drones to hold the region at risk, while continuing to impose significant control over its population.

Meanwhile, U.S. military spending continues to rise. In September, the U.S. Congressional Budget Office assessed that the military costs of the Iran War had already totaled US$38 billion. Since then, that number has only increased. And that is to say nothing of the associated global economic costs that have resulted from Iran’s de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz – a key shipping route for oil and gas.

Should Trump decide to change course on Iran, he – and others – may think that the money, effort and lives of 19 American servicemen killed in the conflict would have been spent with no obvious objective achieved. Yet continued military expenditure with no strategic endgame could only magnify those same costs.

To Iran, the midterm results have not changed its public position. Mojtaba Khameini has issued statements directing the IRGC to widen the conflict in the region and perhaps beyond should the U.S. and Israel attack again. At the same time, a statement attributed to him indicates that hostilities between the United States and Iran will persist regardless of the balance of party political power in Washington.

This raises questions about the prospects for diplomacy. During the summer, the U.S. and Iran agreed to an initial 14-point memorandum of understanding that, if finalized, could have brought a permanent end to the hostilities. But since the 60-day clock on that agreement lapsed, no parallel diplomatic agreement has emerged.

Even with the major shift in the U.S. political landscape, it remains unclear whether Trump will resume operations against Iran before the new Congress is sworn in. The messy election result in Israel – which has left the pro-war, and potentially outgoing, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyanu with potentially more reason to double-down in Iran – only complicates matters.

The U.S. military certainly appears to be ready to engage in a new round of attacks against Iran if so directed, and Iran is ready to retaliate. But given the shortcomings in the U.S. inventory – with munitions and missile and air defense capabilities depleted by eight months of war – escalation is something Trump and his inner circle will have to consider with caution.

Iran might force the issue by engaging in asymmetric attacks in the region or beyond that they have not attempted already. Or it could launch a coordinated offensive with its partners in the region – notably the Houthis in Yemen, who have become more active in their own conflict with Saudi Arabia in recent months.

But save an event that the Trump administration perceives is giving it cover to act, there are no clear indications emerging from Washington as to which way it will move.

Vance diagnosed a widely perceived political problem for Republicans: Voters don’t want more war. But what he noticeably didn’t mention was a practical solution. The Middle East conflict – and the United States’ role in it – are, as such, locked in a stalemate.

America and Iran have both borne significant political, military and economic costs. A decision not to pursue an endgame would leave those sunk; doing so may only increase them.

Javed Ali, Associate Professor of Practice of Public Policy, University of Michigan

#5492. Newborn holiday safety: 10 steps from hand washing to car seats

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Protecting a newborn at holiday gatherings starts with clean hands, healthy guests and safe sleep — here are 10 practical steps for parents hosting or visiting family

A newborn's first holiday season puts two forces in the same room. Relatives want to hold the baby, pass the baby around and plant kisses on a tiny face. The baby has an immune system that is still developing, with little time to build defenses of its own.

The timing adds pressure. In the U.S. and much of the Northern Hemisphere, the winter holidays fall during cold and flu season. Gatherings move indoors, and guests arrive from different households, schools and airports. An infection that causes a mild cold in an adult can make a young infant seriously ill.

Travel and unfamiliar houses bring their own complications. A baby who sleeps in a bassinet at home may end up near a couch, a guest bed or a pile of coats. Feeding and nap routines bend around dinner times. Candles, hot drinks and decorations sit close to busy hands.

None of this means families have to skip the season. Protecting a newborn at holiday gatherings comes down to a set of practical habits. Many of them cost nothing. Clean hands, healthy guests and up-to-date vaccines among the adults lower the chance of an infection reaching the baby. Safe sleep and car seat rules still apply away from home. A clear plan for a fever saves time if one appears.

Parents set the rules for their own child. Telling relatives ahead of time, by text, email or phone call, avoids correcting someone at the door with the baby already in their arms. A short message about hand washing, staying home when sick and holding off on kisses gives guests a chance to prepare. It also presents the requests as a household policy rather than a judgment of any one person.

The 10 tips below are a practical selection, not a complete checklist. They cover germs, vaccines, handling, sleep, fever, household hazards and travel. Each one stands on its own. Parents can use the ones that fit their gathering. A pediatrician can advise on a specific baby's situation, including when larger crowds make sense for that family.

Every guest who wants to hold the baby should wash their hands with soap and water first. Soap and water is the standard step for anyone handling a newborn. It clears away germs picked up on the way in before they reach the baby.

Hands carry whatever they touch. At a holiday gathering, that includes door handles, coats, serving spoons, shared remote controls and the hands of other guests. Washing before contact closes off one of the most direct routes from a crowded house to the infant.

Hand sanitizer is a fallback, not a replacement. It suits hands that look clean. It is the wrong tool when hands are visibly dirty. After peeling potatoes, carving a roast or clearing greasy plates, guests need soap and water. A bottle of sanitizer near the nursery or the sofa can serve guests who already washed and have touched only clean surfaces since.

A wash on arrival covers germs from the car, the train or the airport. One wash does not last all afternoon, though. Guests should wash again after eating. Food and shared dishes leave residue on fingers. Phones pass from pocket to table to countertop and rarely get cleaned. Anyone who has been scrolling should wash before taking the baby. The same goes for anyone who has petted the family dog or cat.

A little setup makes the request easy to follow. Set out soap at the sink closest to where the baby will be. Paper towels spare guests from sharing one damp cloth across many hands. A small sign by the sink or a quiet reminder from the parent holding the baby works for guests who missed any earlier message.

The rule applies to every guest, grandparents included, with no exceptions for close family. Parents can set the pattern by washing in plain view before picking up the baby themselves. Older siblings and young cousins can follow the same routine, with an adult nearby to help small children reach the sink.

Anyone with a fever, cough, runny nose, vomiting or diarrhea should skip a gathering where a newborn will be present. Mild symptoms still count. A slight sniffle can still signal a contagious infection.

A written request gives every guest the same standard to check against. Relatives can reread it on the morning of the gathering. They can then decide for themselves, without a phone call to the parents.

The wording can stay simple and direct. A line such as "If you're feeling sick, please sit this one out and we'll catch up by video" makes the point without a long explanation. Naming the specific symptoms helps. Some people do not think of a runny nose or an upset stomach as being sick. Spelling them out removes the guesswork.

The rule needs to apply to everyone, including grandparents and close relatives who expected to hold the baby first. A guideline that bends for one person is harder to hold for the next. Parents can ask a partner or another trusted relative to repeat the message. That way the request does not rest on one person.

Symptoms sometimes appear on the day itself. A guest who wakes up with a cough or a stomach bug may feel pressure to show up anyway, especially once travel plans are set. Telling relatives that a last-minute cancellation is welcome makes that choice easier for them.

Older siblings and cousins fall under the same request. Children often arrive at holiday gatherings carrying colds from school or day care. A child with a fever, cough or runny nose meets the same standard as an adult. Their parents need the same notice. The decision to keep a child home rests with them.

Video calls give sick relatives a way to take part. A call during the meal or the gift opening lets a grandparent or aunt see the baby and join the conversation from home. An in-person visit can then be rescheduled for a quieter day, after the relative has recovered.

Before a holiday gathering, ask the adults and older children who will be near your newborn whether their Tdap, flu and COVID-19 vaccines are current. Vaccinated relatives are less likely to carry these infections to a baby who is too young for full protection.

Whooping cough, also called pertussis, is the main reason this question matters. It is a bacterial infection of the airways. It spreads when an infected person coughs or sneezes. In a newborn, it can become serious quickly.

The Tdap vaccine protects against pertussis, along with tetanus and diphtheria. Protection for the baby can begin before birth. The CDC recommends Tdap during pregnancy, usually in the third trimester. The mother makes antibodies that pass to the baby. Those antibodies give the baby some protection in the first months of life.

Maternal antibodies are a starting point, not a complete shield. The people who hold, feed and sit beside the baby still matter. A grandparent or aunt with an unrecognized cough can expose an infant during a single afternoon visit.

Flu is the second part of the conversation. Babies cannot receive a flu shot until they are six months old, according to the CDC. A newborn at a winter gathering has no flu vaccine of its own. Vaccinated adults and siblings around the baby become a practical layer of protection.

COVID-19 vaccination for adults belongs in the same discussion. Holiday events tend to pack people into warm indoor rooms during the months when respiratory viruses circulate widely.

Older children belong in the same conversation as adults. Cousins and siblings often want to touch the baby. They may also be less consistent about covering a cough. Ask their parents about the children's vaccine status, not only their own.

Raise the vaccine question days or weeks before the event. Asking early gives relatives time to talk with their own doctor or pharmacist. It also gives parents time to decide who will hold the baby.

A short message noting that the baby is too young for some vaccines frames the request around the infant rather than the relative. If someone is not vaccinated, parents can ask that person to greet the baby from a distance. The baby's pediatrician can help parents decide which shots to ask about for their family.

Keep kisses off a newborn's face and hands at holiday gatherings. Anyone with a cold sore should not kiss the baby or get close to them. The herpes simplex virus that causes cold sores can be dangerous to newborns.

On an adult, a cold sore can look like a minor blemish on the lip. For a baby in the first weeks of life, the same virus poses a serious risk. That contrast is why the rule applies to every guest, with no exceptions for close family.

The face and hands are the areas to protect. A kiss on the cheek or forehead puts an adult's mouth close to the baby's eyes, nose and mouth. Hands need the same protection. Newborns often bring their hands to their mouths. A kiss on the fingers can end up at the baby's lips.

A relative with a visible cold sore should keep their distance from the baby for the whole visit. Skipping the kiss is not enough on its own. That person should not hold the baby or lean in for a close look. A parent can ask them to say hello from across the room.

Holiday kissing is often a reflex rather than a decision. Grandparents, aunts, uncles and family friends may lean in and kiss a baby without thinking about it. A parent holding the baby can turn the baby's face toward their own shoulder as someone approaches. The parent can follow with a calm reminder that the baby's face and hands are off-limits.

Affection still has an outlet. Relatives can admire the baby from nearby, talk or sing to them, or hold the baby's feet through socks or a sleeper. A gentle touch through clothing keeps contact well away from the face and hands.

The same request applies to older children at the gathering. Cousins and siblings often want to kiss a new baby. A parent can redirect them to a wave or a gentle foot squeeze instead.

A smaller gathering and a shorter stay limit how many people a newborn meets in a single day. Fewer guests mean fewer exposures to the colds and other infections that circulate indoors during the holidays. Each additional visitor is another set of hands near the baby and another person breathing close to its face.

Hosting at home gives parents the most control over the setting. They decide who receives an invitation, which room the baby stays in and when the event ends. The baby's crib, changing supplies and feeding setup also stay where they belong.

When the gathering happens at a relative's house, a shorter visit can do the same job. Parents can arrive after the first rush of guests or leave before the meal stretches late into the evening. For large extended families, two smaller visits on separate days can replace one long, crowded one.

Hosts can also stagger invitations. Inviting relatives in small groups across an afternoon or a weekend spreads out contact with the baby. Each visitor gets more unhurried time with the newborn than a full living room would allow.

A quiet room helps at a gathering of any size. A bedroom or study away from the main party gives parents a place to feed, change and settle the baby. Newborns feed on demand, and their hunger rarely lines up with the time dinner is served. A separate room lets feeding happen when the baby needs it rather than when the party pauses.

Sharing the schedule in advance keeps the plan clear. A message to the host a few days ahead can cover when the family will arrive and how long it plans to stay. It can also explain that the baby may spend part of the visit away from the crowd. Relatives who know the plan beforehand have time to adjust their own expectations.

Parents can leave early at any point. A fussy, overtired or overstimulated baby is a clear signal to head home. Agreeing on an exit plan before arriving, including who drives and when, makes the departure quick.

Wearing a newborn in a soft carrier or wrap keeps the baby close and out of a long line of eager arms. Another option is to name one designated holder, such as a parent or one trusted relative, who keeps the baby for the whole visit.

At a holiday gathering, each handoff brings another set of hands, another sweater and another face close to the baby. A carrier changes the default. Relatives can still see the baby, talk to the baby and stand nearby. The baby stays on one adult's body instead of moving around the room.

A carrier also gives parents an easy answer when a guest asks to hold the baby. Saying the baby is settled in the wrap can land more gently than a flat refusal. It shifts the focus from the guest to the baby's routine.

A designated holder serves the same purpose for families who do not own a carrier or whose baby is not comfortable in one. Pick that person before the event and let relatives know in advance. Guests then know whom to ask. The baby is not handed from cousin to cousin during dessert.

Babywearing has its own safety rules, and they apply in a busy room just as they do at home. The baby's face must stay visible at all times. The airway must stay clear. Fabric, a scarf or a coat should never cover the baby's nose and mouth. The adult wearing the baby should be able to see the baby's face just by glancing down.

Crowded holiday rooms make that check easy to forget. Conversation, music and cooking all pull attention away. Glancing down often keeps the rule in place.

Hot drinks are the other hazard to plan around while wearing a baby. Coffee, tea, cider and cocoa are common at holiday tables. An adult wearing a baby should skip them or set them well out of reach. A spill from that height would land directly on the baby.

A newborn at a holiday gathering should sleep exactly as at home: alone, on the back, on a firm, flat surface with no loose blankets, pillows or bumpers. The American Academy of Pediatrics sets out these rules, and they apply in a relative's house just as they do in the nursery.

Most holiday homes are not set up for an infant. Guest rooms tend to have soft mattresses, stacks of pillows and heavy quilts. Living rooms have sofas and armchairs. None of these is a safe sleep surface for a baby, even for a short nap during dinner.

One fix is to bring the sleep space along. A portable crib or bassinet that meets current safety standards gives the baby a firm, flat surface wherever the family ends up. Setting it up soon after arrival, before the house fills, means there is a ready place to lay the baby down once drowsiness sets in.

Keep the inside of that crib or bassinet empty except for the baby. Relatives sometimes add a folded blanket for warmth, a soft toy as a gift or a pillow to make the space look cozy. Each of those items should come out before the baby goes in. Crib bumpers fall under the same rule.

Back sleeping applies to every sleep, naps included. A baby who dozes off in a grandparent's arms should be moved onto the back in the portable crib. Leaving the baby asleep face down on a lap or shoulder does not meet the rule.

Sleeping alone also rules out sharing an adult bed or a sofa with the baby. Late in the evening, a tired parent or relative may drift off with the baby on their chest. Placing the baby in the separate sleep space before the adults start to nod off avoids that situation.

A quieter room for the crib can help the baby settle away from music and the main crowd. Telling the hosts ahead of time that a portable crib is coming lets them clear a spot for it.

A rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher in a baby younger than three months needs prompt medical attention. The American Academy of Pediatrics treats that reading as a reason to contact a doctor right away, not something to watch overnight.

The number is the same on a holiday as on any other day. Parents at a family dinner may feel pressure to wait until the party ends. Parents on a long trip may want to wait until the drive is over. The threshold does not bend around a schedule. If the thermometer shows 100.4°F or above, the next step is a call to the pediatrician or a visit to medical care.

The rule refers to a rectal reading. A hand on the forehead cannot confirm the number. Neither can a relative's sense that the baby feels warm. Packing a thermometer in the diaper bag for a holiday visit removes the guesswork. Parents who have never taken a rectal temperature can ask the pediatrician to walk them through it at a routine appointment before the season starts.

The pediatrician's phone number belongs in the plan too. Save the after-hours line in your phone before leaving home. For an overnight stay in another town, look up the nearest hospital or urgent care location ahead of time. Finding that information at 2 a.m. in an unfamiliar house is harder than finding it in advance.

Write down each reading and the time it was taken. A note on your phone is enough. Having both details ready makes a call to a nurse or doctor faster and clearer.

Temperature is only one signal. A baby who is feeding poorly, seems unusually sleepy or is acting unlike their usual self is also worth a call to the doctor, with or without a fever. A parent who notices a change can call even if no one else at the gathering sees a problem.

Hosts can help by offering a private spot where a parent can check the baby's temperature without an audience. Relatives can help by supporting a parent who decides to step away and phone the doctor.

A newborn's spot at a holiday gathering should be free of tobacco smoke, vape aerosol, open flames and small decorative objects. Secondhand smoke and vaping aerosol are both hazards to infants. Candles, fireplaces, hot drinks and ornaments add risks that a nursery at home does not have.

Start with the air in the room. Ask any relative who smokes or vapes to do it outdoors, away from doors and windows. Ask them never to smoke or vape while holding the baby. Smoke can drift inside when a door opens. Place the baby's spot far from the patio or porch exit. Keep the infant out of cars and closed porches where someone has been smoking.

Open flames come next. Holiday tables often carry lit candles, and living rooms may have a fire going in the hearth. Keep the baby clear of both, along with anyone carrying the baby. A guest leaning over a centerpiece with an infant in their arms can bring a blanket or sleeve near a flame in seconds. Ask hosts to move candles off low tables and away from walkways.

Hot drinks pose a quieter danger. Mulled cider, coffee and tea get passed across crowded tables and counters. Ask guests to put their cup down before taking the baby. Keep the baby away from the stove and the serving area.

Crowded rooms multiply these hazards. A packed kitchen or living room means more elbows, more bumps and more spills near the baby. Set the baby's spot outside the main path between the kitchen and the dining table.

Decorations deserve a sweep before the baby settles in. Tinsel, small ornaments and button batteries are choking and ingestion hazards. Button batteries turn up in light-up decorations, musical greeting cards and remote controls. A newborn cannot reach for much, but these items end up on floors, couches and in older children's hands.

Older siblings and cousins may try to share a new toy by dropping it into the bassinet. Keep the baby's sleep and play space clear of small objects. Store gifts with small parts or battery compartments away from that space. Check the bassinet or play mat each time before setting the baby down.

A newborn should ride in a correctly installed rear-facing car seat on every holiday trip, however short. Bulky coats stay out from under the harness, and the seat is for the ride only, not for naps once the family arrives.

Rear-facing is the correct position for a newborn. The seat supports the head, neck and back together. That support matters for a baby who cannot yet hold up their own head. A short drive across town to a relative's house calls for the same setup as a long highway trip.

A correct installation matters as much as the direction the seat faces. The seat's instruction manual and the vehicle owner's manual both explain how to secure it. The two should be read together. A trip in a different car, such as a grandparent's or a rental, means installing the seat again from scratch. It should not be assumed to fit the same way it does at home.

Winter clothing creates its own risk. A puffy coat or snowsuit under the harness can compress in a crash. That can leave the straps too loose to hold the baby in place. Thin layers under the harness keep the fit snug. A blanket or coat can go over the baby once the straps are buckled.

Car seats are built for riding, not for sleep at the destination. A baby who dozes off on the drive should be moved to a flat, separate sleep space once the car stops. Leaving a sleeping baby in the car seat in a corner of a busy room is the habit to avoid.

Holiday traffic can stretch drive times. Planning stops before leaving keeps feeding and diaper changes on schedule. Feeding works best with the car parked and the baby lifted out of the seat. A bag within reach should hold diapers, wipes, a change of clothes, feeding supplies and a spare blanket.

An adult riding in the back seat beside the baby can keep an eye on the baby's position between stops. Leaving early, or splitting a long drive across two days, leaves room for unplanned breaks.

#5491. Starfish Space loses contact with its Otter spacecraft, ending satellite inspection mission

by Alan Boyle on Nov 3, 2026 at 10:50 pmNovember 3, 2026 at 11:10 pm

Starfish Space says it can no longer receive data from its first full-scale Otter space vehicle, bringing a $15 million NASA mission to inspect inoperable satellites to a premature end.

In a LinkedIn post, the Tukwila, Wash.-based startup said its Otter 24C spacecraft was not able to complete all the objectives for the mission, known as Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability (SSPICY). “Starfish and NASA are exploring opportunities to fulfill mission objectives through other Starfish missions,” the company said.

The Otter spacecraft was sent into low Earth orbit aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket on Oct. 1. “Following a successful launch and deployment, Starfish established two-way contact with the spacecraft and successfully commanded Otter 24C, downlinking significant telemetry during early operations,” Starfish said.

However, the mission team lost contact with the oven-sized spacecraft during the commissioning process. “An investigation into the loss of communications has determined that fault protection on the satellite bus provided by Astro Digital had an error that turned off the radio and prevented re-establishing communications,” the company said.

Starfish, NASA and Astro Digital determined that the spacecraft was unrecoverable.

In today’s update, Starfish said it is working closely with Astro Digital to fix the fault protection system and update testing procedures for future Otters.

“Developing new capabilities in space requires taking on difficult challenges, learning quickly and applying those lessons to what comes next,” Starfish said. “The work completed through Otter 24C will directly contribute to the success of future Otter missions as Starfish continues developing the technologies and operations required to make satellite servicing a routine capability in orbit.”

Greg Stover, director of the Advanced Research and Technology Division at NASA Headquarters, said in a news release that “commercial capabilities like Starfish’s are critical for a competitive U.S. space economy and strong American leadership in low Earth orbit.”

“Technology demonstrations allow us to quickly test new systems, learn from their performance, and iterate so that we are pushing the boundaries of what’s possible with every mission,” Stover said. “NASA will continue taking on bold challenges in close collaboration with our industry partners.”

Several other Otter missions remain on tap — including a satellite disposal job for the Pentagon’s Space Development Agency, two commercial satellite servicing missions in geostationary Earth orbit, and two servicing missions for the U.S. Space Force.

Starfish Space is also continuing to test an Otter Pup prototype that was launched into orbit last year. Last week, it posted a video to LinkedIn showing a close approach to a target satellite known as ElaraSat. The company says it is preparing for a docking attempt “and a chance to make history.”
