#5490. Democrats just won control of Georgia Power’s regulator for the first time in 30 years — and its OpenAI data center contract was entirely redacted

“This story was originally published by Grist. Sign up for Grist’s weekly newsletter here.”

Beginning in January, three of the five officials on the Georgia Public Service Commission will be Democrats. It will be the first time the party has controlled the powerful energy regulation board in 30 years. The commission, which regulates utilities including the state’s largest electric provider, Georgia Power, has come under more scrutiny in recent years due to rising power bills and the high energy demands of data centers.

Now, Democrats plan to focus on affordability, clean energy, and closer scrutiny of Georgia Power.

“There’s a long laundry list of things that need to be looked into,” said Democratic commissioner Peter Hubbard, who won his reelection bid this week. “And so we’ll have to triage, in fact, and decide how best to move forward.”

One of his first priorities will be launching an affordability docket, he said — a series of hearings that would delve into the reasons for high power bills and ways to save customers money. Hubbard said he and his fellow Democrats also plan to bring close scrutiny to upcoming Georgia Power requests around making more energy and adjusting customer rates. Shelia Edwards and Alicia Johnson are the other two Democrats on the PSC.

But any changes, especially to power bills, will likely take time.

“We may not be able to expect immediate effects on our wallets,” said Emory University associate professor Kristin Phillips, who studies energy burden and the PSC. “But I think we can expect immediate change in the types of decisions that are made.”

Affordability and high energy bills were driving issues in the campaigns both this year and last year, the two elections that together resulted in the new Democratic majority on the commission.

“We knew that we had to connect the dots between energy and affordability,” said Brionté McCorkle of Georgia Conservation Voters, a group that campaigned for the Democratic candidates and worked to draw attention to the PSC elections. “It’s not just this obscure regulatory body like it used to be treated. Its decisions directly affect household budgets, communities, health, and our energy future.”

Chris Womack, the CEO of Southern Company, Georgia Power’s parent company, also acknowledged the central importance of affordability during the company’s third-quarter earnings call on Thursday. But Womack said he’s confident the utility can address those concerns with the new commissioners.

“If you look at what we have been doing with rate freezes, with benefits, with how we are providing benefits from growth to customers — existing customers — as well as to the communities, we think that’s a strong platform to stand on,” he said.

Since the data center boom in Georgia began, Georgia Power has maintained that the increased revenue would more than pay for the new infrastructure to serve them, which the utility argues would keep rates lower for residential and small business customers. The utility calls this “downward pressure.” It doesn’t mean rates will go down, but rather that any increases would be offset by the influx of revenue from data centers.

The utility recently doubled down on that promise as part of its deal to serve a massive new OpenAI data center. The deal, Georgia Power said, would bring $15 of not savings but downward pressure per month for what Georgia Power calls the “typical” residential customer.

Separately, Georgia Power also credited the increased revenue from data centers for the temporary rate freeze approved last year. But the rate freeze received criticism from some advocacy groups. Instead of first holding a PSC hearing to give advocates a chance to verify the utility’s financial claims, Georgia Power announced the temporary rate freeze. Advocates feel that the backward process left them unable to confirm whether the company was delivering on its promises and fully shielding ordinary customers from data center costs.

It’s part of a broader criticism often leveled at the PSC and Georgia Power: lack of transparency. The OpenAI contract was entirely redacted, and only a summary provided to the public after it was approved. Specific details involved in service contracts, deals to buy energy, and construction costs are often redacted from the utility’s public filings under the auspices of trade secrecy.

“I absolutely think transparency is potentially one of the biggest impacts here,” said Phillips of the election results. “It has been often on advocates to push on the way that the PSC communicates about the decisions that it’s making, and I’m hoping that there will be more clarity and transparency.”

The Democrats on the commission have promised to bring increased scrutiny to the next rate-setting process, due in 2028, along with Georgia Power’s long-term plans to make and deliver energy, its forecasts about rising demand, and other issues. Hubbard has also proposed conducting a rate case for the state’s natural gas utilities, which he said hasn’t been done in over a decade. And he said they’ll push for other changes going forward.

“We’ll continue with an agenda next year and the year after that to take advantage of this four-year period when we have the majority and can push for long-lasting reforms and shifting the direction of the state in terms of energy,” Hubbard said.

This article originally appeared in Grist at https://grist.org/georgia-psc/democrats-take-control-of-georgias-powerful-utility-regulator/.

Grist is a nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to reporting on climate change.

#5489. Elon Musk once said the Cybertruck would be Tesla’s ‘best product ever.’ Now he’s winding down production

Elon Musk said Friday Tesla would be phasing out the production of the Cybertruck, the boxy-looking electric pickup he once pitched as the future of his EV maker.

In a post on X, Musk said: “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”

The changes to Cybertruck production come seven years after Musk introduced the vehicle at a splashy Sci-Fi-themed event at Tesla’s design studio in Hawthorne, Calif., complete with pyrotechnics and a live demonstration of the car’s “armor glass” in which Tesla’s lead designer shattered two Cybertruck windows with a steel ball. Just a month before the launch event, Musk had touted the vehicle as Tesla’s “best product ever” during Tesla’s third quarter earnings call in 2019.

“This could be totally wrong. I could be totally out to lunch here, but I think the Tesla Cyber Truck is our best product ever. That’s my opinion,” he said at the time.

Yet, the Cybertruck, which starts at a whopping $92,490, has been popular, but it has struggled to find the mass appeal of other Tesla vehicles like the Model Y and Model 3.

After production delays pushed the vehicle’s launch date to 2023 from a previously promised 2021 launch, production still fell short of the between 250,000 and 500,000 Cybertrucks Musk predicted Tesla would eventually produce annually.

Tesla sold 38,965 Cybertrucks in the U.S. in 2024 and then just 20,237 in 2025, a decline of 48%, according to estimates by Kelley Blue Book. In the first half of the year, Kelley Blue Book’s parent company Cox Automotive also estimated Tesla sold a total of 7,263 Cybertrucks, which would put them on track for yet another year-over-year sales decline this year. Tesla does not break out its Cybertruck sales in its public filings.

Musk has now pivoted the company’s future prospects to the autonomous Cybercab, which he announced to fanfare at an event in 2024. The first Cybercabs hit roads in Austin, Texas, in September. Tesla also has Robotaxi operations, using the Model Y, in Houston, Dallas, and Fort Worth in Texas as well as Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida, with plans for more U.S. cities to be included later.

Tesla did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

The shift away from Cybertruck production comes as Tesla seeks to convince investors autonomous technology can drive growth in the future by surpassing traditional EV sales, which have fallen since President Donald Trump ended the EV tax credit last year. Tesla sells the most EVs of any company in the U.S.

The EV maker has positioned its Cybercab, a two-seater without a steering wheel or pedals, as key to its expansion into autonomous transportation and robotics.

But the new vehicle also faces hurdles. Federal auto safety regulators in September opened an investigation into whether Tesla properly certified that the Cybercab complies with federal vehicle safety standards. At the end of October, Tesla submitted its answers to questions from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), but requested its responses remain sealed because they are “confidential business information.” The NHTSA has not yet ruled on Tesla’s confidentiality request, according to Electrek.

In the autonomous robotaxi market, Tesla is entering late. Alphabet’s Waymo already operates in 15 U.S. cities and reportedly provides 500,000 rides per week, it said in an X post earlier this year.

For its part, the Cybertruck has been hit with 11 recalls since customer deliveries began in November 2023, according to Reuters. Price changes that made it significantly more expensive than Musk’s original vision have also stood in the way of mass adoption. Tesla advertised a starting price of $39,900 when it introduced the truck in 2019—but by the time deliveries began in 2023, Tesla was advertising a version of the vehicle expected to cost $60,990.

Tesla raised the price of several models of the Cybertruck this month and discontinued orders for the cheapest model, the Dual Motor AWD. That means the cheapest Cybertruck model still available starts at $92,490, up from the $84,990 price the same model reached in August after previous price hikes, according to Electrek.

Tesla has previously tried introducing less expensive versions of the Cybertruck to attract buyers. The company launched a rear-wheel-drive Cybertruck in 2025 but pulled it from the lineup months later.

Musk’s Friday post also leaves existing Cybertruck owners in limbo. Tesla has not said how long it will continue selling remaining inventory or supplying replacement parts, though winding down the vehicle’s production does not mean it will end support for existing vehicles.

Musk, for his part, still appeared enthusiastic about the truck Friday.

In response to a user highlighting Musk’s Cybertruck announcement as the end of an era, the CEO replied: “True, but the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time.”

Role: Reporter Marco Quiroz-Gutierrez is a reporter for Fortune covering general business news.

#5488. Norovirus season and holiday gatherings: how the winter vomiting bug spreads

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Norovirus season overlaps with holiday gatherings, and these 10 facts explain how the winter vomiting bug spreads, how long it stays contagious and how to prevent it

Norovirus is at its most active during the busiest stretch of the social calendar. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) lists November through April as the peak period for norovirus outbreaks in the country. That window covers Thanksgiving, Christmas, Hanukkah, New Year's Eve and the travel around them. Norovirus season and holiday gatherings share the same ingredients: crowded kitchens, shared serving spoons, long buffet tables and relatives arriving from different households.

Norovirus causes acute gastroenteritis, an illness of the stomach and intestines that brings on vomiting and diarrhea. In the U.K. and elsewhere it goes by a blunter name: the winter vomiting bug. The CDC also counts it among the leading causes of foodborne illness in the U.S. That puts food at the center of the holiday risk.

The winter vomiting bug's reputation for tearing through households comes from its biology. A very small number of viral particles is enough to make someone sick, while an infected person can shed billions of them in vomit and stool. That imbalance means a small lapse in hygiene can pass along enough virus to infect someone else.

The virus does not need a fever or a diagnosis to move between people. It travels on hands, food, drinks and surfaces. Some infected people never develop symptoms but can still spread it. Others keep shedding it after they feel better. Those traits turn the usual holiday rhythm — cook together, eat together, hug goodbye — into an efficient route for transmission.

Holiday hosts face a specific version of the problem. A home kitchen has no health inspector. The person preparing the stuffing may be the same person who was sick the night before. Everyday habits can also leave the virus behind, from relying on hand sanitizer instead of soap and water to wiping up a mess without disinfecting the spot afterward.

The 10 slides that follow offer a selection of practical points about how norovirus spreads and how to prevent it. They explain why the illness is not a form of the flu, why cases climb in colder months and how long a person stays contagious. They also cover the handwashing and cleanup steps the CDC recommends. Each slide stands on its own, so readers can go straight to norovirus symptoms, cleanup or kitchen safety.

Norovirus is a group of related viruses that cause acute gastroenteritis, an inflammation of the stomach and intestines. It is unrelated to influenza, which infects the respiratory system.

The mix-up starts with everyday language. Many people describe a sudden bout of vomiting and diarrhea as "the stomach flu." That label is a misnomer. Influenza is caused by influenza viruses and affects the nose, throat and lungs. Norovirus affects the digestive tract.

Both illnesses tend to circulate in winter, and both are often described with the word "flu." Shared timing and a shared nickname do not make them related. They come from different virus families and attack different parts of the body.

The distinction has practical weight. Treating norovirus as a kind of flu can steer attention toward coughs and sneezes. Its route runs through the digestive system instead. The precautions that matter most center on hands, food and bathrooms.

In the U.K. and other countries, a plainer nickname is common: the winter vomiting bug. The phrase names a digestive symptom instead of a respiratory one. It also ties the illness to the colder months, when outbreaks are most frequent.

In the U.S., the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) calls norovirus the leading cause of vomiting and diarrhea from acute gastroenteritis. Sudden stomach illness can have other causes, including bacteria and other viruses. Of all of them, norovirus is the one the CDC places first.

The agency also lists norovirus among the leading causes of foodborne illness in the country. That second role connects the virus to kitchens, restaurants and any meal someone else prepares.

The word "acute" in acute gastroenteritis signals an illness that starts suddenly rather than developing over weeks. The term itself is built from Greek roots for stomach and intestine, with "-itis" marking inflammation. Neither part of the name refers to the lungs.

In the U.S., norovirus outbreaks are most common from November to April, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The virus does not disappear the rest of the year. Cases and outbreaks still occur in spring and summer, just less often.

That six-month window covers about half the year. It begins in late autumn, as temperatures fall across much of the country, and lasts well into spring.

It also overlaps with a heavy stretch of travel and hosting. Families cross the country by car and plane to spend several days under one roof. Guests from different households share meals, towels and sleeping space, often for a long weekend or more.

Researchers have not settled why the virus favors the colder months. Two explanations are commonly proposed, and neither has been proven.

The first centers on behavior. Cold weather pushes people indoors, where they spend more time in close contact in kitchens, living rooms, classrooms and offices. Norovirus spreads through direct contact with infected people, contaminated food and drink, and contaminated surfaces. Crowded indoor spaces give it more chances to move from one person to the next.

Schools and child care centers, which are well-known outbreak settings, are in session through most of the peak months. A holiday visit concentrates that contact further, with many guests using one kitchen and one bathroom for several days.

The second centers on the virus itself. Norovirus may survive better in cold conditions. That could help it last longer outside the body during winter. This remains a hypothesis rather than an established finding.

The year-round pattern matters for gatherings outside the peak months. A spring wedding, a summer barbecue or a graduation party can still lead to an outbreak if someone attending is infected. The calendar changes how often outbreaks happen. It does not remove the risk.

A very small number of norovirus particles is enough to make a person sick, according to the CDC. A sick person, by contrast, can shed billions of particles in vomit and stool.

Set side by side, those two amounts show the scale of the problem. One infected person releases far more virus than it takes to infect another person. A single patient's vomit or stool can hold enough to reach many people.

Contamination does not have to be visible. A smear too small to notice on a fingertip, a serving spoon or a bread roll can carry enough virus to infect someone. The particles need only reach a person's mouth. The danger lies less in how much contamination is present than in whether any of it gets there.

The virus has several ways to make that trip. It can arrive in food or a drink that picked up contamination. It can pass from a surface to a hand and then to the mouth. It can also spread through direct contact, such as caring for someone who is ill or sharing their utensils.

A single lapse can start a chain of cases. One unwashed hand after a bathroom visit can pass enough virus to infect several people who share a meal. Each person who falls ill then becomes a new source, shedding billions of particles of their own.

The low dose also changes what counts as clean. Reducing the virus on a hand or a counter is not the same as removing it. When a very small number of particles can cause illness, whatever survives a quick wipe or rinse can still make someone sick.

The same logic applies to portion size. A single bite or sip from a contaminated dish can be enough to cause illness. Eating less of a suspect food offers little protection when so little virus is needed.

Shared platters and buffets spread norovirus because the virus travels by the fecal-oral route, and a communal dish gives many hands access to the same food. One guest with traces of the virus on their fingers can contaminate a dish that many others then eat from.

The fecal-oral route sounds clinical, but it describes ordinary behavior. Traces of stool or vomit from an infected person end up on hands, food or objects, and another person swallows them. Norovirus moves this way through contaminated food and drink. It also spreads through direct contact with someone who is sick and through objects that pass from hand to hand.

A holiday spread brings all three paths together at one table. Guests reach into bowls of nuts and chips with bare fingers. They pick up the same serving spoon or pair of tongs that the previous person held. A cheese board or a tray of cut vegetables may sit out for hours while people return for second and third helpings.

Communal dips add another layer. A guest who dips a cracker, takes a bite and dips again returns that cracker to a bowl others share. Anything on the guest's fingers goes into the dip along with it.

The type of food also matters. Ready-to-eat items — salads, sliced fruit, sandwiches, cut vegetables and baked goods handled after baking — get no further cooking before they are eaten. Any virus that lands on them goes straight to the next person who takes a portion. Leafy greens and fresh fruit are among the foods commonly linked to norovirus outbreaks.

Raw oysters carry a separate risk that starts before the food reaches the table. Oysters and other shellfish feed by filtering large volumes of water. When that water is contaminated, the shellfish can take in norovirus and hold it. Serving them raw on a seafood platter leaves no step to remove it.

Hosts can cut down on shared contact in practical ways. Plating individual portions limits how many hands touch the same food. Giving each dish its own serving utensil and keeping a dedicated spoon in every dip does the same. Setting out small bowls so guests can take a portion of dip, rather than dipping into a shared one, keeps one person's crackers out of everyone else's food.

The CDC reports that most foodborne norovirus outbreaks begin with an infected food worker who touches ready-to-eat food with bare hands. A cook who is sick, or who has only just recovered, can pass the virus to everyone who eats the meal.

Ready-to-eat food is anything served without further cooking after it is handled. That includes salads, sandwiches, sliced fruit, bread rolls and garnishes. No cooking step stands between the preparer's fingers and the diner's mouth.

Norovirus travels by the fecal-oral route. Invisible traces of stool or vomit on someone's hands can transfer to whatever that person touches next. For a cook, the next thing touched is often food meant for a crowd.

The CDC's guidance for food workers is specific. They should stay home while they are sick and for at least 48 hours after their symptoms stop. The end of vomiting and diarrhea does not mark the end of the risk to others.

The same rule carries over to a family kitchen during the holidays. A relative who offers to toss the salad, carve the roast or arrange a cheese board is acting as a food handler for that meal. If that person's symptoms ended less than 48 hours earlier, the CDC's benchmark for food workers points to handing the job to someone else.

Hosts can plan for this ahead of time. Asking guests to stay out of food preparation if they have recently been ill applies the standard restaurant workers are expected to follow. A store-bought dish can stand in for a homemade one. So can a contribution saved for a later gathering.

Holiday cooking also tends to involve more hands than an everyday dinner. Several people may chop, plate and taste the same dishes in a shared kitchen. Each extra handler is another chance for one infected person to reach the food.

Food workers are not the only route. Food can also be contaminated at its source, before it reaches any kitchen. A healthy cook cannot remove that risk. A sick cook, by contrast, is a risk a host can avoid.

Norovirus can survive on hard surfaces such as doorknobs and countertops for a long time, according to the CDC. The agency also notes that the virus resists some common disinfectants.

Those two traits let the virus outlast the person who left it behind. A guest can pick it up from a surface long after the infected person has left the room. Some household disinfectants do not reliably kill it.

The path from a surface to an infection is short. Norovirus spreads by the fecal-oral route, and contaminated surfaces are one link in that chain. A person touches a contaminated faucet handle and then touches their mouth. That is enough to let the virus in. The same hands can also carry it onto food or onto the next object they handle.

Bathrooms and kitchens need particular attention. Infected people shed the virus in stool and vomit. Toilet seats, flush handles, sink taps and the floor around a toilet can all pick it up as a result. Kitchen countertops, cutting boards and refrigerator handles sit beside food that guests may eat without further cooking.

Other frequently handled objects belong on the same list. Doorknobs, light switches, television remote controls, phones and stair railings pass through many hands in a single afternoon. During a holiday visit, one bathroom and one kitchen may serve far more people than on an ordinary day.

Shared spaces outside the home show the same pattern on a larger scale. Cruise ships, nursing homes, schools and child care centers are well-known settings for norovirus outbreaks. Each one puts many people in repeated contact with the same rails, tables, toys or fixtures. In child care centers, diaper changes and shared toys add to the number of surfaces the virus can reach. In nursing homes, many of the people exposed are older adults, a group at higher risk of dehydration from norovirus.

A crowded family gathering shares those features. Relatives eat together, use the same bathroom and handle the same serving spoons, glasses and chair backs throughout the day. The virus is microscopic. A surface does not need to look dirty to carry it.

Norovirus usually announces itself with vomiting, watery diarrhea, nausea and stomach pain. These symptoms typically begin 12 to 48 hours after exposure, according to the CDC, and most people recover within one to three days.

Some people also develop a fever, a headache or body aches. Those complaints appear alongside the vomiting and diarrhea, not in place of them.

The delay between exposure and illness matters during a busy holiday week. A guest who picks up norovirus at an evening meal can feel fine the next morning. That guest may not get sick until later that day or the day after. In the meantime, the guest can travel home, visit other relatives or sit down at another table.

The same 12-to-48-hour window means the most recent meal is not always the cause. An illness that starts on a Sunday night could trace back to a meal eaten one or two days earlier. Anyone trying to identify a source should consider every meal, party and shared dish from the previous two days.

Dehydration is the main risk of norovirus. Repeated vomiting and diarrhea strip fluid from the body. A person who is too nauseated to drink can struggle to replace it. When fluid losses outpace what a person can drink, dehydration sets in.

That risk is most serious for young children, older adults and people with other health conditions. Warning signs of dehydration include urinating less than usual, a dry mouth and throat, and dizziness. Anyone caring for a sick child or an older relative during a gathering should watch for those signs.

No antiviral drug specifically treats norovirus. Care focuses on replacing the fluids the body has lost. Oral rehydration solutions are a common way to do that.

Antibiotics are not part of the treatment. They act on bacteria, not viruses. Taking them for norovirus offers no benefit.

People with norovirus are most contagious while they are sick and during the first few days after they recover. The virus can keep turning up in their stool for two weeks or more after they feel well again, according to the CDC.

Feeling better and being free of the virus are two different milestones. The vomiting and diarrhea usually pass within one to three days. The shedding does not stop at the same time. A guest who recovered before a holiday dinner may still carry the virus into the host's kitchen and bathroom.

While a person is sick, vomit and diarrhea both release virus into the surroundings. A single episode of vomiting can leave virus on nearby surfaces, floors and fabrics. Once symptoms stop, stool becomes the main route left. Hands that are not washed properly after using the toilet can carry the virus onto shared food, serving spoons and door handles.

Timing matters for holiday plans. A relative who was sick on a Wednesday and felt better by Friday is still in the most contagious stretch at a Saturday gathering. The CDC advises infected food workers to stay home for at least 48 hours after symptoms stop. By that standard, the same relative would still be inside the window for handling food on Saturday.

The shedding that continues for two weeks or more keeps handwashing important long after a person returns to normal routines. For a toddler who has just recovered, every diaper change during that period is a possible point of transmission. The same holds for a recovering adult who shares a bathroom with guests or helps plate food.

Not everyone who carries norovirus shows it. Some infected people never develop symptoms, yet they can still pass the virus to others. That makes symptom checks an incomplete safeguard at a crowded gathering. A host cannot tell by looking which guests are shedding virus.

Washing hands with soap and running water for at least 20 seconds is the main hand-hygiene step the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends against norovirus. Alcohol-based hand sanitizer is less reliable against this virus and works as an extra layer, not a substitute.

That distinction matters during the holidays. Pump bottles of sanitizer often sit by the front door, the buffet table or the bar cart. Guests may use a quick squirt and assume their hands are clean before reaching for food. Against norovirus, the CDC notes that alcohol-based products do not work as well as they do against many other germs.

Sanitizer still has a role. The CDC allows it as an addition to handwashing. The problem comes when a squirt from a bottle takes the place of a trip to the sink.

The CDC singles out several moments when handwashing matters most. The first is after using the toilet. The second is after changing diapers. The others are before eating and before preparing food. Each of those moments falls along the fecal-oral route that norovirus uses to move from one person to the next.

Holiday gatherings stack those moments close together. A parent may change a diaper in a guest bedroom and then return to the kitchen to stir a pot. A guest may leave the bathroom and head straight for a cheese board. A host may plate dessert minutes after clearing dirty dishes. Each of those transitions is a point where soap and water can interrupt the virus's path to someone's mouth.

The 20-second minimum applies every time. Hands should be wet under running water, lathered with soap and then rinsed. A quick rinse without soap, or a wash cut short, falls below that standard.

Hosts can make the sink the easy option. Keeping soap stocked at every sink and leaving clean towels or paper towels within reach gives guests what they need. A sanitizer bottle can stay out too, as long as it sits beside the sink rather than standing in for it.

Clean up vomit and stool from a person with norovirus right away, using disposable gloves and paper towels. The CDC then advises disinfecting the area with a chlorine bleach solution or an EPA-registered disinfectant approved for use against norovirus.

Speed matters because those fluids carry the virus in large amounts. Norovirus spreads through contaminated surfaces and direct contact as well as through food. A spill left on a bathroom floor or a guest-room rug during a holiday visit can expose anyone who walks through or touches the area.

The CDC also suggests wearing a mask during cleanup if one is available. Gloves keep the virus off the cleaner's hands. Hands are a common route for the virus to travel from a contaminated surface to the mouth.

Paper towels soak up the bulk of the mess first. They go straight into the trash once used. Reusable cloths and sponges can carry the virus to the next surface they touch. Disposable materials avoid that problem.

Disinfection comes after the visible mess is gone. Norovirus resists some common household disinfectants. The CDC's guidance points to chlorine bleach or to a product the EPA has registered as effective against norovirus for that reason. A cleaner that works on other germs may not be enough. Checking labels for a norovirus claim before a holiday gathering means the right product is already on hand if someone falls ill.

Soiled bedding, towels and clothing need their own treatment. The CDC advises washing them on the hottest water setting available. They should then be machine dried on high heat.

Once the gloves come off, hands still need a wash with soap and running water. Gloves reduce exposure, but they do not replace that final step.

Kitchen habits add another layer of prevention. Fruits and vegetables should be washed before they are eaten or served. Oysters and other shellfish should be cooked thoroughly. Shellfish harvested from contaminated water can carry norovirus.

#5487. Rover hires Textio co-founder Jensen Harris and former Amazon exec Vik Rajagopal

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 7:07 am

Seattle-based pet care marketplace Rover is adding two executives to its leadership team: former Motus CFO Vik Rajagopal as chief financial officer and Textio co-founder Jensen Harris as president of marketplace, product and technology.

Rajagopal succeeds Charlie Wickers, who served as Rover’s CFO from 2022 to 2025. Harris succeeds Brent Turner, who was Rover’s president and chief operating officer before he was named CEO last year.

Rajagopal spent nearly a decade at Amazon, starting in 2011 as a finance lead for Amazon Global Selling, the program that helps sellers reach customers in other countries. He later became a general manager in Amazon’s retail business, running the U.S. shoes and luggage stores and the home store, as well as Amazon’s U.S. Vendor Success Program.

He left Amazon in late 2020 to become CFO of Logos, a maker of Bible study software backed by private equity firm Cove Hill Partners. He was promoted to CEO about a year later, replacing the company’s founder, and led Logos until April 2024. He was most recently CFO at Motus, which makes software that companies use to manage and reimburse employees who drive for work.

Earlier in his career, Rajagopal was an investment banker at Wells Fargo Securities and worked in corporate development at Symantec. He holds a bachelor’s degree from Yale and an MBA from Northwestern’s Kellogg School of Management.

“Rover is a Seattle company that was built the right way from day one — solving a real customer pain point with a strong product, solid economics, and a culture that is poised for long-term success,” Rajagopal said in a news release on Wednesday.

Harris co-founded Seattle-based Textio in 2014 with Kieran Snyder, his wife, after both worked on productivity software at Microsoft. The startup used AI to analyze workplace writing such as job posts and performance reviews. Harris was Textio’s CTO for nearly eight years, then chief experience officer, before taking over as CEO from Snyder in January 2024. He handed the CEO role to Colleen Gallagher in January 2026 and remains with Textio as founder emeritus.

Textio has raised $42.5 million from investors and went through rounds of layoffs in 2024 and 2025 under Harris. As CEO, he led the launch of Lavalier, an AI-based interview intelligence platform.

Before Textio, Harris spent more than 15 years at Microsoft, where he led the redesign of the Office user interface that produced the Ribbon, and later led user experience for Windows and the touch interface for the original Surface.

After leaving the CEO role at Textio, Harris founded Expedition 60, a firm that helps companies rework how they build software with AI.

“Our pets give us unconditional love, and they deserve the very best in return,” Harris said in a statement, adding that he shares a home with “three very opinionated cats.”

Rover was born at a 2011 Seattle Startup Weekend event, where venture capitalist Greg Gottesman pitched the idea. Aaron Easterly led the company as CEO for 14 years, taking it through the pandemic, a public offering and a $2.3 billion take-private deal with Blackstone in 2024. He stepped down last year and became executive chair, handing the CEO role to Turner.

Rover now operates in 18 countries across North America, Europe and Australia, and says sitters and walkers on its platform have provided 50 million bookings to date. Its brands include cat-sitting marketplaces Meowtel and Cat in a Flat, and Australia-based Mad Paws. Beyond sitting and walking, Rover now offers training in the U.S. and is testing other services.

#5486. The midterms didn’t stop the AI buildout. They simply repriced it—and OpenAI is already promising to pay up

Two days after what appears to be voters rejecting data centers in town after town, OpenAI went shopping for something it can’t build: permission.

On Thursday, the company published a National Community Compact, in which the company pledged to pay for the electricity and grid infrastructure of the data center campuses it owns and operates. It also pledged to post financial guarantees before major spending begins, so other utility customers aren’t stuck with the bill if a project is delayed or canceled. The company told Fortune this has been months in the making and is something they’ve been pledging in their data center campuses already—the compact is simply the first time OpenAI put in writing a number of pledges it has already undertaken.

Mining and energy companies have a name for what OpenAI is after: a social license. (If you’re interested, you can read my grad school capstone about social license in Peru, which has since been enacted into law). These are a type of Community Partnership Agreements (CPAs) that entails getting a community’s ongoing consent to operate: No zoning board grants it, and no tax abatement buys it. Instead, companies earn it by showing the people next door that a project leaves them better off—or at least no worse off. Lose it, and permits stall, lawsuits pile up, and local officials find reasons to say no.

So following the Democratic wave on Tuesday, the AI industry found out how little of that license it had left. And distinctly, the midterm turnout wasn’t a cry from voters to stop the buildout, but simply to put a new price tag on it, and OpenAI is the first major AI company to agree to pay it since the votes were counted.

Data centers were on the ballot in roughly 40 localities across the country. By Wednesday morning, about 28 measures had passed in 25 localities, all of them opposing data centers. Chief among them were the 18 municipalities in Ohio, which already has 125 data center moratoriums.

Sunbury, Ohio, banned data centers over 25 megawatts, 79% to 21%, after Amazon proposed a $2 billion campus there. In Trenton, Ohio, where Amazon Web Services is already building a 250-megawatt data center, a ban passed 80% to 20%. In Hubbard, Ohio, a ban won 76% to 24%, and the mayor has since said a proposed 300-megawatt project is dead.

But voters weren’t saying no to data centers: The ballot measures were to place limits on data centers, rather than full-out bans.

In Perry, Ohio, 87% of voters required hyperscale developers seeking tax breaks to post financial guarantees and meet noise limits, the same safeguard OpenAI offered two days later. Grove City, Ohio, banned nothing. By 55% to 45%, it required a public vote on any project over 50 acres, 20 megawatts or 500,000 gallons of water a day. Most of the bans set a size threshold, meaning a modest server farm can still come to town, but a gigawatt campus can’t.

This wasn’t limited just to the Democratic party: Former Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy pledged a moratorium on construction until the legislature acted, and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott had already paused new grid connections for data centers in August. The common complaint was the electric bill: More than 70% of Americans polled said they’d oppose a data center planned near them, with rising power prices the top reason.

Corporations largely have benefitted from local/municipal/state/federal praxis: Get a tax credit for coming here to my jurisdiction. The examples are endless: Think of the $33 billion taxpayers have spent on getting a sports stadium built, of which they rarely see the full amount brought back into the community. Perhaps the most famous example of tax incentives proving futile is none other than Amazon’s HQ2 debacle, in which Newark, NJ, offered $7 billion in tax incentives to Amazon to locate their second headquarters there, and New York City offered “only” $3 billion. Amazon was always going to pick Queens, but the company was smart enough to play more than two dozen jurisdictions across the country against each other to gain the biggest tax reward.

So the AI buildout is no different. For most of the boom, the industry’s offer to communities was simple: We bring tax revenue and construction jobs, you bring the tax breaks. But Tuesday showed that offer was no longer on the table.

Now, hyperscalers are making a new offer, which looks a lot like a social license agreement. In January, Microsoft launched a “Community-First AI Infrastructure” plan, pledging to pay its own way on electricity, pay full local property taxes without asking for tax breaks, replenish more water than it uses, and offer free AI training in local schools and community colleges. A week later, OpenAI said every Stargate campus would get its own community plan. By this fall, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Oracle, xAI, OpenAI, and Amazon had signed a non-binding White House pledge to build or buy the power their facilities need.

That’s repricing in action. Instead of asking towns for discounts, the industry now offers to cover the grid upgrades, the water, the training and, in OpenAI’s case, a guarantee against walking away. Previously, every one of those costs used to fall on the community.

Bans don’t make demand for computing power disappear. They move it. Harwood, the lone town that voted the industry’s way, sits near a data center that Applied Digital is already building. The projects pushed out of Sunbury and Hubbard will look for counties that still say yes, at whatever price those counties set.

While it is absurd to think of some newly-elected members of the Democratic wave advocating to put “a pause on advanced AI development, regulation of this out of control industry, and a ban on artificial superintelligence,” as Congresswoman Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.) posted on Election Day, it isn’t all that obscene to think that voters came out to rethink how the AI buildout is working in their communities and for them.

Catherina covers markets, the economy, energy, tech, and AI.

#5485. 10 facts on why raw cookie dough is risky during holiday baking

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Flour is closer to a farm product than a finished food. Wheat grows outdoors, exposed to rain, irrigation water and soil. Birds, deer and rodents move through the same fields. If droppings from those animals reach the crop, bacteria such as E. coli can settle on the grain before harvest.

The milling process is built to separate the kernel, not to sanitize it. Grain is cleaned and often tempered with water, then ground and sifted to split the starchy endosperm from the bran and germ. Whole wheat flour keeps the bran and germ, but it goes through no added safety step. Ordinary flour sold for home baking typically has no heat treatment or other kill step.

The label on the bag does not change this. Bleached or unbleached, all-purpose or whole wheat, bread flour or cake flour — each one is still a raw ingredient meant to be cooked before eating.

Dry storage does not make flour safe. Bacteria cannot multiply in a low-moisture food, but some can survive in it for long periods. A bag bought for last year's holiday baking can still carry whatever it left the mill with.

The strains of concern are Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, often shortened to STEC. They differ from the many harmless strains of E. coli that live in the human gut. Several U.S. outbreaks of STEC illness have been traced to flour rather than to eggs.

Contamination can happen in two ways. Salmonella can sit on the outside of the shell, picked up from the hen's environment. It can also be inside the egg. The strain Salmonella Enteritidis can infect a hen's ovaries and reach the egg before the shell forms. That means an egg can look clean, smell normal and still carry the germ.

Cracking an egg into a bowl gives no visual warning. A contaminated yolk looks the same as a safe one. Freshness and a clean shell offer no guarantee against bacteria inside the egg.

Commercial eggs sold in the U.S. are washed before they reach stores. Washing removes the thin natural coating on the shell. That is why eggs sold in the U.S. need to stay refrigerated. The FDA advises keeping eggs in a refrigerator set at 40 degrees Fahrenheit or below. Cold storage slows bacterial growth but does not kill Salmonella already present.

The FDA and USDA also advise throwing out eggs with cracked or dirty shells. A crack gives bacteria on the surface a path into the egg.

Pasteurized eggs are the main fix for recipes eaten raw. Pasteurized in-shell eggs are heated in their shells to a temperature that kills bacteria without cooking the egg. They are sold in many U.S. grocery stores and are marked as pasteurized on the carton. Liquid egg products sold in cartons are pasteurized as well. Either option can stand in for regular eggs in a dough recipe.

Switching eggs does not make raw dough fully safe. Flour carries its own separate risk, which pasteurized eggs do not address.

Flour made by General Mills $GIS was linked to a 2016 outbreak of Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O121 and O26, according to the CDC. The agency reported that 63 people in 24 states became sick, and 17 of them were hospitalized.

The investigation showed that flour alone could carry a dangerous strain of E. coli. No egg was needed for raw dough to make someone sick.

The case started with patients, not with a product. Public health laboratories compare the genetic fingerprints of bacteria taken from sick people. When samples from people in different states match, investigators treat them as one outbreak and look for a shared source.

Interviews came next. Health officials asked patients what they had eaten and handled in the days before they fell ill. Several reported eating or handling raw homemade dough or batter. That pattern pointed toward an ingredient found in many home kitchens rather than a single restaurant meal.

The trail led to flour produced at a General Mills facility in Kansas City, Missouri. Laboratory testing of flour samples found the outbreak bacteria. That result gave investigators physical evidence to go with the interview data.

General Mills recalled flour sold under its Gold Medal and Gold Medal Wondra brands, along with Signature Kitchens flour. The recall widened in July as more test results and illnesses came in.

Flour recalls depend on shoppers checking the bag itself. A recall notice identifies affected products by details printed on the package, such as the product name, size and dates. A household that bought flour before the notice went out has to compare its own bag against that list. Holiday baking often draws on flour bought earlier in the year, when a recall may have been missed.

The outbreak also showed that a sealed bag from a major brand is no guarantee against contamination. The bacteria in this case did not come from a dirty kitchen or careless storage at home. The flour was contaminated before it reached store shelves.

Investigators then had to work out which ingredient carried the bacteria. E. coli O157:H7 is more commonly associated with undercooked ground beef and fresh produce than with sweets. The eggs in the dough were pasteurized. That made eggs an unlikely source. Investigators considered flour the likely source, although they did not confirm it as the definitive cause.

The investigation widened the conversation about raw dough. Warnings about tasting dough had long focused on eggs. After 2009, public-health officials also pointed to flour as a raw ingredient with its own risk.

An outbreak of E. coli O26 traced to flour sickened 21 people in nine states in 2019, according to the CDC. The outbreak added to a record of illnesses linked to raw flour.

E. coli O26 belongs to a group called Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, often shortened to STEC. Most E. coli strains live harmlessly in the intestines of people and animals. STEC strains are different. They release a toxin that can damage the lining of the gut.

O157 is the best-known STEC serogroup in the U.S. O26 is one of several other serogroups that public health laboratories also track. The 2019 outbreak was not the first flour investigation to involve a serogroup other than O157.

Linking illnesses to flour takes detective work. The CDC coordinates PulseNet, a national network of public health laboratories. The network compares the DNA fingerprints of bacteria taken from sick patients. When samples from different states match closely, investigators treat the cases as a possible outbreak with a shared source.

Next come interviews. Health officials ask patients what they ate in the days before they got sick. They then look for foods that come up more often than expected among healthy people.

The process takes time. Several weeks can pass between the day someone falls ill and the day that case is formally tied to an outbreak.

Recalled flour can stay in home kitchens long after an announcement. Flour recall notices typically list the affected lot codes or best-by dates. Checking a bag against those details shows whether it is part of the recall. The CDC advises people to throw away recalled flour rather than use it. It also advises washing any container where that flour was stored.

That advice matters during the holidays, when bakers reach for bags opened earlier in the year. A recall notice from the spring can still apply to flour used in December.

Severe stomach cramps, diarrhea that is often bloody and vomiting are the main signs of a Shiga toxin-producing E. coli infection, according to the CDC. These symptoms typically begin three to four days after a person swallows the bacteria.

The E. coli strains tied to raw flour and dough outbreaks in the U.S., including O157:H7, O121 and O26, all belong to this Shiga toxin-producing group. The toxin damages cells that line the intestine. That damage is the reason blood can appear in the stool.

Fever is possible, but the CDC notes it is usually not very high. Most people recover within five to seven days. Some infections are mild. Others become severe or life-threatening.

The most serious complication is hemolytic uremic syndrome, known as HUS. The condition destroys red blood cells and can lead to kidney failure. The CDC reports that HUS usually develops about a week after symptoms first appear. It often starts as the diarrhea is improving, which can make a patient seem to be getting better.

Warning signs of HUS include urinating less often, feeling very tired and losing pink color in the cheeks and inside the lower eyelids. People who develop HUS are usually treated in a hospital. Most recover within a few weeks, but some are left with permanent damage.

The CDC advises contacting a health care provider for diarrhea that lasts more than three days. The same advice applies to diarrhea with a fever above 102 degrees Fahrenheit, to bloody diarrhea and to vomiting so frequent that liquids will not stay down. Signs of dehydration call for a doctor too. Those include passing very little urine, a dry mouth and throat, and dizziness when standing up.

Antibiotics are not recommended for suspected Shiga toxin-producing E. coli infections, according to the CDC. Diagnosis depends on laboratory testing of a stool sample. Mentioning raw dough or raw flour gives a clinician useful information about a possible exposure.

Fever is one of the clearest differences between salmonellosis and Shiga toxin-producing E. coli infection. With that type of E. coli, the CDC notes, any fever is usually not very high. Some people with Salmonella also have nausea, vomiting or a headache. Most people recover without specific treatment, the CDC reports. Antibiotics are generally reserved for people who are severely ill or at risk of complications.

Recovery is not always quick. The CDC reports that some people's bowel habits do not return to normal for a few months. A smaller group develops reactive arthritis, which causes joint pain that can last months or years. In rare cases, the infection spreads from the intestines into the bloodstream and other parts of the body.

Diarrhea and fever together can drain the body's fluids fast. The CDC advises contacting a doctor for diarrhea with a fever above 102°F or diarrhea lasting more than three days without improvement. Bloody stool, vomiting that prevents keeping liquids down and signs of dehydration also warrant a call. Those signs include very little urination, a dry mouth and dizziness when standing up.

A doctor cannot confirm Salmonella from symptoms alone. Diagnosis requires a laboratory test, usually of a stool sample. Confirmed cases are reported to public health officials. Those reports are how clusters of illness linked to a single food come to light.

Children under five, adults 65 and older, pregnant people and people with weakened immune systems face the highest risk from raw dough. The CDC and FDA name these four groups as most likely to become seriously ill from foodborne germs. For them, the bacteria in raw flour and raw eggs can do more harm than they would to a healthy adult.

Young children face that risk for more than one reason. Their immune systems are still developing. Their small bodies also lose fluid quickly through diarrhea and vomiting. Dehydration can set in faster than it does in an older child or adult.

The CDC reports that hemolytic uremic syndrome, the kidney complication linked to Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, is most common in children under five. That is the same family of bacteria behind several U.S. outbreaks traced to flour and raw dough. In many households, children are also the ones handed the mixing spoon or the beaters.

Adults 65 and older face a different set of problems. The FDA explains that the immune system and organs become less able to recognize and fight off harmful bacteria with age. The FDA also notes that stomach acid declines in older adults. Stomach acid is one of the body's first defenses against germs in food. Many people in this age group also manage chronic conditions such as diabetes or kidney disease. Those conditions can make recovery harder.

Pregnancy changes the immune system as well. The FDA's food safety guidance for pregnant people treats both the pregnant person and the developing baby as at higher risk from foodborne illness.

People with weakened immune systems make up a broad group. The CDC includes people living with cancer, diabetes, liver or kidney disease, HIV or an organ transplant. It also includes people taking medicines that suppress the immune system, such as chemotherapy drugs or anti-rejection drugs after a transplant.

Many people in these groups look healthy, and a host may not know a guest's medical history. Holiday kitchens often hold grandparents, toddlers, expecting parents and friends undergoing treatment at the same time. A bowl of dough set out for tasting reaches all of them at once.

No-bake recipes raise the same issue. Truffles, bars and fillings that fold in raw flour never reach the oven. Without commercially heat-treated flour, those treats never get a kill step.

Holiday baking adds small moments when raw dough gets eaten without much thought. A finger run through cake batter counts. So does a pinch of pie crust scrap or a bite of gingerbread dough left over after cutting out shapes. Each of those bites skips the one step that makes the dough safe.

The edible label is what separates these products from the refrigerated dough sold in logs, tubs or pre-cut squares. A package that lists oven directions is meant to be baked. Its contents should be handled as raw dough. That holds even when the flavor and branding match an edible version on the next shelf.

Homemade no-bake recipes are a separate question. Some call for heating flour in an oven or microwave before mixing it with butter and sugar. Home heat-treating is not a proven way to make flour safe to eat raw. A kitchen version should not be treated as equal to a commercial product sold as edible.

Cleanup is the other half of safer holiday baking. Raw flour and raw egg can contaminate anything they touch. Flour dust also spreads easily and can settle on counters beyond the mixing bowl. Wash hands with soap and water after handling dough, flour or eggshells. Bowls, spoons, beaters, measuring cups and countertops that touched raw dough need washing too.

Children need the same rule in two forms. They should not eat raw dough, and they should not play with it. That includes homemade play dough and salt dough ornaments made with uncooked flour. Hands that have shaped raw dough should be washed before a child touches food or puts fingers in their mouth.

#5484. Finpilot raises $10M for AI agents that handle the grunt work for institutional investors

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 7:04 am

Seattle startup Finpilot, which uses AI agents to take the paperwork off the plates of people who invest money for hospitals, pension funds and foundations, has raised $10 million in a Series A round.

The round was led by Bay Area venture firm Lobby Capital, with participation from Madrona, which led Finpilot’s $4 million seed round in 2024. Finpilot, which has raised about $14.5 million since its 2023 founding, plans to use the new funding to expand its product and hire across the company.

Its customers include in-house investment teams at institutions and firms that manage money on their behalf. In the industry, they’re known as allocators, because they spread capital across outside fund managers. Much of their information arrives from fund managers as PDFs and spreadsheets, and someone has to read the reports, pull out the numbers and enter them into the right systems.

Finpilot pulls that information into one place and has its agents handle much of the work. The idea is to let investment teams spend their time on judgment and decisions, not on reading data from documents and typing it into a database, said Lakshay Chauhan, Finpilot’s co-founder and CEO, in an interview.

“Nobody wakes up like, ‘All right, I’m excited to do that,'” he said.

It’s a change of course for the company. When GeekWire covered its seed round, Finpilot was building a ChatGPT-style tool for analysts researching public companies. It shifted to allocators in mid-2024, Chauhan said, after concluding that AI added only marginal value in public markets, where Bloomberg and S&P Capital IQ had already organized most of the data.

“There’s no Bloomberg for what they do,” he said of allocators.

Customers include Seattle Children’s, Children’s Health in Dallas, Hackensack Meridian Health in New Jersey, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Wyoming, the Wyoming Retirement System, outsourced investment firm TIFF, and Seattle wealth management firm Laird Norton Wetherby. Some of those institutions hadn’t changed their core systems in 15 years, Chauhan said.

Finpilot has about 28 institutional customers in all, and revenue has grown tenfold since the start of the year, he said. It hasn’t lost a customer yet, he noted.

How it works: Finpilot pulls an institution’s data from its portfolio management system, document storage and other sources into a single record, matching each fund, holding and client to one identifier. Users ask questions in a chat window and set up agents to handle recurring work.

In an example Chauhan described, an agent could review updates from 35 private equity managers at the end of a quarter, figure out what changed and point an analyst to the three things that need attention. Agents also prepare briefings before meetings with fund managers, and they ask a person for approval when a step needs one.

Some customers run Finpilot alongside their existing software. Others have used it to replace older customer relationship management and research management systems, where investment teams log their dealings with fund managers.

Chauhan said Finpilot most often gets compared with general-purpose AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, including finance-focused versions like Claude for Financial Services, and with legacy CRM vendors.

Chauhan said the difference is accuracy. A 10-page report from a chatbot has to be checked number by number before it goes to a chief investment officer. In Finpilot, every number links back to the document it came from, so it can be checked.

In finance, he said, “you cannot be wrong.”

Finpilot runs its own in-house model for the high-volume job of reading financial documents, and uses models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google for other tasks. It doesn’t train AI models on customer data and keeps each customer’s data separate, Chauhan said.

Founders: Chauhan grew up in India and came to the U.S. for a master’s degree in aerospace engineering. He interned at Boeing in Seattle, but when he graduated, he said, many full-time aerospace jobs required U.S. citizenship or permanent residency, and he was in the country on a visa.

He went to work for an engineering optimization software company and studied quantitative investing on the side. That led him to a paper by John Alberg, co-founder of Seattle investment firm Euclidean Technologies, which uses machine learning to pick stocks. Chauhan called Alberg repeatedly to propose working together, and Alberg eventually hired him. Chauhan later led AI at Euclidean.

Alberg is Finpilot’s co-founder and executive chairman but isn’t involved in day-to-day operations. His late father, Tom Alberg, co-founded Madrona.

Finpilot has about 14 employees, up from four in 2024. All are based in Seattle except one in Boise, Idaho. The company recently moved into the AGC Building on Lake Union after outgrowing its old office.

What’s next: Finpilot plans to fill six or seven jobs in the next few months, in product, marketing, client success, sales and business development, and about as many early next year.

Part of the money will go to implementation teams, Chauhan said. Their job is to sit down with each customer, learn how its investment team works and show it how to redo that work with AI agents.

#5483. Nearly Half of the Stolen Binance Basket Had a Freeze Button

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Tether, Circle and Ripple could freeze their tokens within hours of the Binance theft, and they did.

There is no one to call for the stolen bitcoin, ether and TRX, which makes up most of the money Binance is unlikely to get back.

In most hacks, the stolen total is the headline. In the Binance breach, the more useful number is how much of the stolen money could be stopped.

On-chain trackers estimate the stolen basket at more than $5.6 billion. Binance itself has put the estimated impact at $6.3 billion and says nearly $3 billion is frozen. That freeze was possible only because of how the stolen money was made up.

Almost half of it was in tokens whose issuers can freeze them. The rest was in assets that no company, foundation or council can stop on their main blockchains.

That second half explains why recovery stalled at about $3 billion despite a fast industry response. It is also the part Binance will most likely have to pay for itself.

The per-asset breakdown from on-chain trackers is:

Sorting by whether the issuer can freeze the token gives a near-even split:

That one division shaped everything that happened after the theft.

The response on the freezable side was unusually fast:

The pattern is the same in every case. A company that issues a token on a public blockchain usually keeps a way to block specific addresses from moving it. Critics see that power as a central point of control, but in this theft it worked. Within hours, the largest dollar-value block of the stolen money could not be moved.

There was one notable intervention outside the token issuers. On Arbitrum, the Arbitrum Security Council took emergency action and moved 74,559,805 ARB and 8,425 ETH, about $30.5 million, out of an address connected to the exploit.

It shows that some layer-2 networks keep emergency powers their base layers lack. The amount was small next to the size of the theft.

The other half is a different story. Bitcoin has no issuer. Ether on Ethereum's main network has no admin key. TRX is Tron's native coin, and no token issuer sits between the holder and the blockchain. Once these assets reached the attacker's wallets, stopping them depended on exchanges refusing deposits and investigators tracking the funds, not on any freeze function.

Together, the $1.45 billion in BTC, $875 million in ETH and $234 million in TRX make about $2.56 billion. That is close to Binance's own numbers: about $3 billion frozen out of a $6.3 billion estimated impact leaves roughly $3.3 billion still in play, and most of it is in assets nobody can freeze.

The bitcoin figure is the most contested part of the basket. Some BTC moving out of Binance-linked wallets during the incident may have been Binance moving its own reserves to safety rather than attacker withdrawals. So the true unfreezable total could be lower than $2.56 billion, but the split between the two groups is unlikely to change much.

The attacker appeared to understand this difference and acted on it right away.

On-chain records show the main sweep on Ethereum used an EIP-7702 delegation. This feature lets a regular wallet hand control to a smart contract. Within minutes, the drained hot wallet's contents, including more than 1.6 billion USDT, had moved to attacker-controlled addresses.

The clearest example of the next step is on Aave. According to Aave's governance forum update from risk manager LlamaRisk, one wallet in the exploiter's cluster acted between 20:58 and 21:01 UTC:

That trade left freezable USDT locked inside Aave as collateral and gave the attacker wrapped ether, which no issuer can freeze. The position stays over-collateralized, and LlamaRisk said it "does not put Aave suppliers at risk." The ETH, however, was already gone.

Aave responded on a large scale. Between 21:42 and 23:04 UTC, its guardian multisigs froze:

The freezes blocked new deposits and borrowing. Reports also describe stablecoins being swapped for ETH on Uniswap.

The race was easy to see in the timeline. Each hour before an issuer froze its token was another hour to swap that token for ether. Tether and Circle reacted within the first hour, so most of the stablecoin stash was frozen before it could be converted.

A freeze stops the attacker, but it does not put money back in Binance's accounts. Frozen tokens stay locked at the attacker's addresses until the issuer decides what to do with them. In past cases, issuers have destroyed frozen tokens and reissued the same amount to the rightful owner, usually after legal or law-enforcement checks. That process takes time, and each issuer has its own procedure.

Binance has said that its initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. According to the company, that laptop let the attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked, and that it has revoked the affected address authorization and is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms.

Deposits and withdrawals were suspended while security checks continue. Binance has not yet given a date for reopening them.

Binance has said it will cover all losses using its SAFU fund and its own money. Grouping the stolen basket by freezability gives a rough picture of what that bill could be.

The roughly $3 billion that is frozen should eventually be recovered, depending on how and when each issuer releases or reissues the tokens. The bitcoin, ether and TRX are another matter. Unless exchanges block deposits and investigators recover funds as they are laundered, that part is effectively gone. It accounts for most of the money Binance will have to cover from its own reserves.

The theft also raises a question for the whole industry. The assets that limited the damage were the issuer-controlled tokens that crypto purists often criticize. The assets that caused the real loss were the ones built so that no one can stop them. Exchanges have long decided hot-wallet sizes by liquidity needs. After this theft, they may also consider which assets in those wallets can still be stopped once they leave.

#5482. Amazon plans its first large-scale data centers in Washington state as residents raise concerns

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:46 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:36 am

Amazon is moving toward building its first large-scale data centers in Washington state, with a proposed campus in Walla Walla County and a second in the Tri-Cities that the company confirmed this week.

The expansion into Amazon’s home state comes amid nationwide pushback against the rapid deployment of new AI data centers. Tuesday’s election underscored the scrutiny facing data center developers, with voters in communities across several states backing limits on new projects. In Eastern Washington, the Amazon proposals have drawn calls for greater environmental oversight and a temporary halt to data center development.

Amazon already has a substantial footprint in neighboring Oregon, where industry tracker Baxtel lists 64 AWS data center sites. Expansion there has divided communities, with residents pushing for restrictions over power and water concerns while some Eastern Oregon officials warn that slowing development would jeopardize jobs and tax revenue.

Both proposed Washington campuses would initially include three data center buildings. The Walla Walla County site covers roughly 134 acres in Wallula Gap, while the Tri-Cities campus is on a 1,000 acre property in the city of West Richland and could eventually grow to 21 buildings. The company is already operating smaller data centers in the state, including Seattle.

The Tri-City Herald first reported Monday that Amazon was behind the West Richland project. The company plans to hold a community open house Nov. 19 to discuss the proposal.

A full build-out of the West Richland campus could create more than 1,000 full-time data center jobs, Amazon said. Dallas real estate firm Trammell Crow initially purchased the property from the estate of agricultural businessman Frank Tiegs, who died in 2024, before selling it to Amazon.

Nearby residents have raised concerns about the planned campus, in part because of its proximity to about 200 homes. Residents asked the local city council to approve a temporary moratorium, but at a meeting Tuesday evening, council members adopted rules that removed a data center noise exemption, banned them in light industrial zones, and prohibited cryptocurrency mining. The council failed to pass a moratorium, NonStop Local reported.

Amazon says the upcoming open house will give residents an opportunity to ask questions about the planned development. A spokesperson described a “science fair” format, with booths hosted by experts discussing water and energy usage, job creation, noise and environmental impacts.

“We’re committed to growing responsibly and we want the community to leave the Open House with a better understanding of this project and what it could mean for the area,” the spokesperson said via email.

At Wallula Gap, a recent public-comment period offers an indication of the scrutiny Amazon faces.

Of the 706 submissions received during a 30-day comment period that closed Oct. 12, only 23 — about 3% — supported the project, according to an analysis by the Walla Walla Union-Bulletin. Most of the supportive comments came from the area, and many predicated their support on more stringent oversight of the proposed facility near the Columbia River.

More than 500 submissions came from outside Walla Walla County, according to the Union-Bulletin. Many included template language calling for an Environmental Impact Statement — a higher level of environmental assessment than currently required for the campus.

The proposed facility is located at the Wallula Gap Business Park, on property formerly owned by the Port of Walla Walla. The three proposed single-story data center buildings would create approximately 120 to 150 full-time jobs, Amazon said.

The land is zoned for “industrial agriculture – mixed” applications, which the company said includes data centers. Amazon’s involvement in the project was first reported by the Tri-City Herald in February.

Amazon’s FAQs for the two sites address several issues raised by residents, including electricity costs and water use.

Rising electric bills nationwide and the climate impacts of new gas power plants and backup diesel generators have made energy use a top concern. Amazon said it will work with local utilities and other officials “to ensure that our data centers do not raise electricity bills for people in our communities.”

The company reports that it matched all electricity consumed across its global operations with renewable energy sources in 2023 and 2024. That annual, company-wide accounting measure does not mean each facility runs on renewable electricity around the clock.

Amazon also points to its investment of “billions of dollars in nuclear energy projects,” including a proposed small modular reactor plant near the Tri-Cities that could come online in the 2030s.

“This project will provide net-new carbon-free energy for communities in the Pacific Northwest, including Eastern Washington,” Amazon said in its FAQ.

Amid concerns about water shortages, Amazon touts water-use rates that it says beat other tech companies and are much lower than irrigated farming. Those rates, however, do not include water used in electricity generation. Many power plants use water to produce steam that drives electricity-generating turbines and for cooling, with some water lost through evaporation.

At both locations, Amazon says it will pay 100% of its property taxes rather than seek tax breaks for building in the communities. The company says its taxes are higher than most industrial uses and directly support schools, roads, fire and police, and other services.

Beyond addressing concerns about its data centers, Amazon is making a broader case for why communities should welcome them. Last month, the company launched its Built Together initiative, committing more than $1 billion in additional investments over five years to U.S. communities where it operates data centers. The funding supports efforts including free community college, energy upgrades for homes and buildings, and workforce training.

In announcing the program, Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman framed data center development as part of a global race for AI dominance. He warned that local and state moratoriums could harm the U.S. economy and national security.

“If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations,” Garman said. “As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.”

In West Richland, residents will have an opportunity to question Amazon’s plans — and the assurances accompanying them — at the company’s upcoming open house.

Editor’s note: Story updated 11/5 to note that Amazon is operating smaller-scale data centers in Washington, but not campuses of the scope being proposed in Eastern Washington.
